case_summary.text: IT : Once income derived from property held under by assessee-trust was applied in accordance with charitable objects in view of specific exemption granted by a special order issued by CBDT, there would be no violation of section 13(1)(d) so as to deny exemption

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust entered into an agreement with a private limited company for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to it, since object of transfer agreement was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally and purpose of charity was not violated, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 could not be denied
AO can't deny exemption if trust entered into agreement to ensure that hospital was managed professionally: ITAT
IT: Where genuineness of trust and objects of trust being charitable had not been disputed even if trustees had mismanaged or misutilised funds, exemption under section10(22) could not be denied

IT : Director (Exemption) having allowed accumulation of income of assessee-trust in terms of section 11(2) after being satisfied with objects of trust, exemption under section 11 could not be denied to assessee on ground of non-application of income for charitable purpose

INCOME TAX: Where assessee-trust earned rental income from leasing property but trust deed only enabled trustees to hold and manage property for charitable objects without treating leasing as an independent object, and receipts including rental income were applied solely to charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 could not be denied since leasing was only incidental to charitable purpose

IT: Exclusion of amounts received by virtue of section 10(22A) is not subject-matter of section 13(1) or any of its further conditions where assessee society duly registered under Indian Societies Act was entitled in law to claim exemption of its income under section 10(22A), fact that managing trustee/founder director in trust was participating in profits of income of trust would not disentitle institution to claim aforesaid exemption
No denial of sec. 11 exemption if trust earning rental income to fund its charitable objects: ITAT

IT : Where assessee-turst invested funds in a company in which its trustee was managing director and his wife was a director, it was a case of violation of section 13(1)(c) and exemption under section 11 would not be available to assessee
Trust entitled to exemption even if it charged fee for commercial activity, being incidental to its charitable cause

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where Venture Capital Funds (VCFs) established as trust were managing funds of contributors and thereby rendering service to contributors, in view of fact that they had violated principles of mutuality by concerning themselves in commercial activities and had discretion over distribution of dividend/profit to entities other than subscribers, they could no longer be treated as trusts for purposes of taxation statutes and thus, said services rendered by trust squarely fell under Asset Management as applicable under Banking and Other Financial Services leviable to service tax

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing its funds and same was registered in name of managing trustee, however, assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased
Charitable trust entitled to sec. 11 exemption as funds were used for charitable purposes without misappropriation:HC

IT : Where assessee-trust had been formed on basis of transferring of assets of sole proprietorship concern of one 'M' and 'M' was also managing trustee of trust, this fact in no way interfered with granting of registration under section 12A to assessee

IT : Where all members of assessee-trust were engaged in whole time management activities of Trust and as regular time teachers and were being paid salaries from earning of these schools and were not being paid any extra salary for management work, there was no violation of provisions of section 13(2)(c) and assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11

INCOME TAX: Where assessee-trust registered under section 12A derived income from letting out property, royalty, and allied activities and applied such income for charitable purposes, with no finding of non-genuineness or misapplication of income, such receipts could not be treated as commercial activity merely by their nature and exemption under section 11 was allowable.

IT : SLP granted against High Court's ruling that merely because assessee-trust incurred expenditure in excess of income in relevant previous year for charitable purposes out of accumulated charity fund, it could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(a)
SC granted SLP against ruling that a charitable trust was entitled to sec. 10(23C)(vi) exemption

INCOME TAX : Assessee-trust formed for limited purpose of managing statutory obligations in form of gratuity payable to employees of parent trust would fall within ambit of advancement of general public utility and, hence, its activities was to be considered as a charitable as defined under section 2(15) and, accordingly, assessee was to be granted registration under section 12AA
No exemption if trust failed to establish that purchase of ‘Jaguar’ was for charitable activities: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where funds of assessee-charitable trust were managed by member of trustees headed by District Collector and audit report was submitted before competent authorities before completion of assessment proceedings, since there was sufficient compliance to claim exemption under section 10(23C)(v), claim could not be denied merely on ground that assessee generated surplus income
CIT(E) has no power to examine whether trust is eligible exemption; ITAT rightly directed CIT to grant registration
AO can’t deny sec. 11 exemption without considering actual charitable activities of trust: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-association of third party administrators (ATPA) was engaged in primary aim and objective to organise and arrange all licensed third party administrators (TPAs) to be members of trust for mutual betterment of TPA business, merely because certain benefits accrued to TPA members and certain objects of trust were for advancement of business of TPA, it would not ipso facto render trust to be non-charitable
IT: Where status of assessee trust was of charitable society, claim of assessee for exemption under section 11(1) was to be allowed
Exemption to a trust couldn't be denied in absence of findings on non-utilization of funds for stated objects

IT: Fee charged by trust for processing subsidy applications could not be deemed as commercial receipts if it was incidental to its charitable objectives. Thus, assessee-trust was entitled to exemption under Section 10(23C)(iv).

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust, registered under section 12A, and engaged in providing medical help, education help and relief to poor had let out its halls and buildings for earning rental income so as to fund its charitable objects, proviso to section 2(15) would not be attracted and assessee could not be denied exemption under section 11
Excess of income over exp. can’t be a reason to hold that trust isn’t engaged in charitable activities: HC
Exemption to trust couldn't be denied under sec. 11 as long as its primary object remains charitable
Section 167B not applicable to charitable trust if it was carrying out charitable activity as per trust deed: ITAT
SC dismissed review petition against ruling that collection of fee won’t affect charitable nature of trust

IT : SLP granted against High Court's ruling that where assessee, a charitable trust, incurred expenditure in excess of income in previous year relevant to assessment year for charitable purposes, out of accumulated charity fund, it could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(a)

IT : Where assessee-trust claimed exemption under section 11 in respect of income earned from a business carried on by it and primary objects of trust were charitable in nature, it was eligible for exemption
No denial of exemption if surplus earned on incidental activities was ploughed back for use towards trust’s object: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust, set up to address national issues relating to real estate sector, earned revenue from activities of holding conventions, exhibitions etc., since activities that were carried out by assessee were with sole intent of attaining object for which trust was established, activities of assessee would not be hit by exclusion carved out in definition of 'charitable purpose' in section 2(15) and as such, assessee was eligible for exemption under section

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where Venture Capital Funds (VCFs) established as trust were managing funds of contributors and thereby rendering service to contributors in view of fact that they had violated principles of mutuality by concerning themselves in commercial activities and had discretion over distribution of dividend/profit to entities other than subscribers, they could no longer be treated as trusts for purposes of taxation statutes and thus,
CIT can invoke sec. 263 if issue related to trust’s charitable nature wasn’t adjudicated by AO: ITAT

IT: Where assessee-trust formed to carry out educational activities, filed an application for issuance of exemption certificate under section 10(23C)(vi) which was rejected on ground that it was empowered to collect funds and accept funds and it could also manage other institutions, since assessee had not taken up any other object mentioned in trust deed, and exclusively carried out activities of education, impugned order denying exemption was to be set aside

IT: Where exemption under section 10(23C)(vi) was denied on ground that society purchased a property in name of its director with funds of society, but it was found that property belonged to said society, exemption could not be denied

IT : Where donation received by assessee-trust is kept in deposit account and income earned therefrom is utilized for charitable purposes, assessee is entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(d) in respect of said income

INCOME TAX : Where assessee educational trust was denied exemption under section 11 on ground that remunerations paid to two trustees as a professor and an administrative officer respectively were not in proportion to pay scale of professors and administrative officers and it was done to divert funds by assessee-trust, thus, section 13(1)(c) was breached, revenue cannot sit in armchair of assessee and decide pattern of working of trust and cannot manage or control managerial affairs of trust, accordingly, impugned denial of exemption by making reference to section 13(1)(c) was unjustified
Exemption to trust couldn't be denied alleging non-application of income if DIT approved of accumulation of income
Exemption couldn't be denied to a trust created for benefit of Christians but also serving public at large
INCOME TAX : ITAT denies tax exemption to a trust whose only 'charity' was to let out Kalyana Mandapams on commercial basis at exorbitant rents
Mere charging of fee from members or non-member couldn't disentitle trust from section 11 exemption, SLP dismissed

INCOME TAX : Interest income earned by assessee-charitable trust on its funds which were deposited in bank, would be income directly arising from property of trust and would be exempt under section 11(1)(a)
IT: Where aims and objects of assessee-trust were charitable and profit earned from said activities was incidental in nature, assessee was not hit by proviso to section 2(15)

IT : As long as objects of trust were charitable in character and purpose or purposes mentioned in Form No. 10 were for achieving objects of trust, merely because details were not furnished, assessee could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(2)
SC dismissed SLP against ruling allowing sec. 11 exemption to trust ploughing back profits made from charitable activity

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1946-47 to 1948-49 - Assessee executed a deed of trust whereby they settled certain amount on various charities and appointed themselves as trustees - Later, in accordance with terms of trust deed, trustees assessees were appointed as managing agents of a company - Before Income-tax authorities, trustee claimed that income derived from managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Revenue authorities, however, held that income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Whether word "property" in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend "business," and if question fell to be decided solely on terms of that sub-section, managing agency formed by assessees/trustees must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether fact that trustees had option at any time to throw up managing agency was no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

FACT: 'P; 'L' and 'LS' executed a deed of trust whereby they settled a sum on various charities specified therein and appointed themselves and two others as trustees. The trust deed provided inter alia that the trustees mights with the help of the trust fund, for and on behalf of and for the benefit of the trust, carry on such business including the taking up and conducting the managing agency or selling agency of any company in such name or names as they in their absolute discretion might think fit and proper. Later the trustees were appointed as managing agents of a company. The agency was to be for a period of 20 years; but it was open to the trustees to throw it up on giving three months' notice. The managing agents were to get a remuneration of 10 per cent of the net annual profits. Before the Income-tax authorities, the assessee/trustees claimed that the income derived from the managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The Income-tax authorities held that the income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court held that no part of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which was the only property settled on trust was actually invested in the managing agency business, which could not, therefore, be regarded as trust property, and that the income received from that business was not within the exemption enacted in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: The 'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation.

'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation. It is true that a public charity is perpetual in character, and that means that it is capable of enforcement, so long as there is any property left which can be appropriated for its objects. And even if some or all of the objects become incapable of fulfilment, the trust properties will be devoted to the performance of similar or allied charitable purposes on the doctrine of cy-pres. But so far as the trust properties themselves are concerned, they will be held only on the incidents to which they are subject under the law. Thus, if the property is a leasehold interest, it must cease on the termination of the lease. Likewise, if trust property is alienated under circumstances binding on the trust, it will go out of the trust. But that does not operate as an extinction of the trust, unless there is no property at all left, with which the trust could be carried out. That is the principle enacted in section 77(c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which in terms, however, applies only to private trusts. Therefore, the fact that the trustees have the option at any time to throw up the managing agency is no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust.

In the result, it could be held that the word 'property' in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend 'business', and if the question fell to be decided solely on the terms of that sub-section, the managing agency must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

With aforesaid observation, the case was remanded to High Court for a fresh disposal on merits.

[Matter remanded to High Court]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether section 4(3)(i) relates to income from business held under trust and section 4(3)(ia) relates to income from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution where that business itself is not held on trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where business of managing agency was held in trust, it could be concluded that business carried on by trustees fell under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: Under a trust deed dated the 15-6-1945, according to the decision of the Privy Council the business of a managing agency was held in trust. Therefore, the income derived from managing agency was held by the Supreme Court as falling with section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act since the word "property" in that sub-section includes business as well. But it was contended before the Supreme Court that although the income might appear to fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act has been narrowed down by the provision in section 4(3)(ia) which deals with income from business and, therefore, the Sub-section that really applies to the determination of the question as to whether the income sought to be taxed in the hands of the trustees was exempt from tax in section 4(3)(ia) and not section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. It was common ground that if section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act was the section under which the exemption claimed was to be determined, the conditions laid down in that sub-section for the purpose of granting an exemption were not satisfied and, therefore, the assessees would not be entitled to an exemption. The question was, therefore, of vital importance to the assessees as to whether their case fell within section 4(3)(i) of section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether where assessee-trust had incurred expenses from charity fund and they were in excess 
of income earned, it was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a) - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-trust was constituted by one ‘J’ who was the manager of certain religious and charitable funds. By the deed of indenture, it was declared that the respective assets of the religious and charitable funds would be in favour of the trustees who would hold the management and operate the respective assets of those funds for the purposes stated in the trust deed. Thus, the assessee claimed exemption on that ground. The Assessing Officer held that since the expenses incurred were in excess than the income derived from various funds, the trustee was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a). The AAC, however, allowed the appeal. On further appeal, the Tribunal restored the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: The assessee had incurred expenses from the charity fund and had incurred excess expenses than the income earned. Thus, the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a). [Para 8]

The reference so made stood disposed of accordingly. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Denial of exemption) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee-trust was conducting its activities in carrying out charitable activities, i.e., education, relief to poor, etc. - During year, assessee purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing funds of assessee-trust and same was registered in name of managing trustee - Assessing Officer denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to extent of value of that vehicle on ground that objects of assessee trust were carrying out of charitable activities and fund collected for this charitable purposes was utilized for enjoyment of trustees by means of purchase of said vehicle in name of managing trustee which was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c) - Assessee submitted that car was purchased in name of managing trustee for simple reason that it gave relief by way of lower road/life tax and insurance charges - However, assessee could not prove as to what use this asset was put to by trust in work of trust and for purposes for which trust had been set up - Whether since assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased by assessee-trust with its funds and registered in name of managing trustee - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing its funds and same was registered in name of managing trustee, however, assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased

Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Denial of exemption) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee-trust was conducting its activities in carrying out charitable activities, i.e., education, relief to poor, etc. - During year, assessee purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing funds of assessee-trust and same was registered in name of managing trustee - Assessing Officer denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to extent of value of that vehicle on ground that objects of assessee trust were carrying out of charitable activities and fund collected for this charitable purposes was utilized for enjoyment of trustees by means of purchase of said vehicle in name of managing trustee which was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c) - Assessee submitted that car was purchased in name of managing trustee for simple reason that it gave relief by way of lower road/life tax and insurance charges - However, assessee could not prove as to what use this asset was put to by trust in work of trust and for purposes for which trust had been set up - Whether since assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased by assessee-trust with its funds and registered in name of managing trustee - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: ■

The assessee-trust was carrying out charitable activities like education, relief to poor, etc.

■

The Assessing Officer found that a vehicle purchased by the trust was registered in the name of the managing trustee and thus, the case of the Assessing Officer was that the assessee purchased the above said vehicle and registered in the name of the trustee was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c). Further, the case of the Assessing Officer was that the income or property of the assessee was diverted in favour of the managing trustee of the assessee and it was a clear violation as per clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 13 read with section 13(1)(c). The assessee explained that the car was purchased in the name of the managing trustee with the sole objective of saving considerable amount of road tax and insurance. However, the Assessing Officer rejected the explanation and denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to the extent of value of that car.

■

HELD: The Tribunal had entertained certain misconceptions as to the true nature and character of the building in question. Neither under the partition deed nor under the settlement deed the building had been taken as a partible property. It was only the devolution of the lands which had been set apart for the maintenance of the said building that had been provided for both under the partition deed and the latter settlement deed. Both the documents clearly dealt with the right to manage the building. The stone slab and the notice board in front of the building showed when it was founded and for what purpose the building was to be used.

It is well established that no express words of gift either directly or indirectly in the shape of a trust are required to create a dedication. All that is necessary is that the religious purpose or object of the donor shall be clearly specified and that the property intended for the endowment should be set apart and dedicated of those purpose.

It is also well established that the existence of a trust can be established even by the conduct of parties. Though normally a Hindu while dedicating property to a deity or any other religious or charitable object ordinarily goes through the ceremonies of sankalpa and samarpan, it could not be said that those ceremonies are essential to creation of a an endowment. The performance of these ceremonies is only relevant to show the intention of the grantor, and if there is clear and unequivocal manifestation of intention to create a trust and there is formal divestiture of the ownership in the property on part of the donor with the intention to devote it to religious and charitable purpose the dedication must be deemed to be complete. The deduction of property is not a sacrament but a secular act; but the mere renunciation of ownership by the donor with a particular object is sufficient to create an endowment. The Tribunal had not kept in mind these general and accepted principles while considering the question as to whether the building was trust property or not. There was a subsequent litigation between the daughter-in-law of the deceased, R, the adopted son of the deceased, and ‘D’ the adopted son of daughter-in-law, wherein daughter-in-law questioned, inter alia, the validity of the partition deed dated 1-3-1950, and in the course of the entire litigation the parties proceeded on the basis that the building was a trust property and the dispute between them was as to the right of management of the trust.

The conduct of the parties right from 1942, when the building was constructed, clearly showed that the building was constructed, clearly showed that the building had been specifically set apart and used for religious and charitable objects. Therefore, the view taken by the Tribunal that the building was not a trust property and as such its value had to be added on to the estate of the deceased could not be accepted.

On the question as to whether the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm could pass on his death, the observation of the Tribunal that a managing agency business could not have any goodwill could not be accepted. The Supreme Court in J. K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that the managing agency business had got goodwill.

In the instant case, the material found during the course of survey operation clearly established the collection of money over and above the fee prescribed by the Government for admission of a student. Therefore, it was a clear case of sale of education by the assessee-society. Thus, the assessee could not be considered as a charitable institution under section 2(15 ). [Para 9] Any income derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose, should not be included in the total income. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee was not holding any property under trust for charitable purpose. It was also not the case of the assessee that any income was derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose. Moreover, it was also not the case of the assessee that any income in the form of voluntary contributions was received with a specific direction to form part of the corpus of the society. The assessee-society was running educational institution and deriving income from such institution. The assessee had also collected money over and above the fees prescribed for admitting students under management quota. In other words, the educational institution was used as a tool/apparatus for collecting money over and above the fees prescribed. The assessee-society had no other source of income/receipt. The society owned the educational institution. The Legislature has visualized two situations. One is religious and another is charitable. Section 11 provides for exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust for charitable and religious purpose. ‘Education’ falls within the definition of charitable purpose. Therefore, any income derived from property held under trust for charitable purpose and applied for education, is eligible for exemption under section 11. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee had not derived any income from any property held under trust. The only source of receipt was the education itself, i.e., from educational institution. [Para 11]

The next question that fell for consideration was whether the educational institution owned by the assessee-society would be regarded as a property held under trust by the society. Section 11 speaks of the property held under trust. The Legislature visualized two situations. One is income derived from the property held under trust and another is application of that income derived from the property held under trust for a charitable purpose. Therefore, there is a clear distinction between the property held under trust and the charitable activity. In the instant case, the assessee-society was carrying on charitable activity by establishing educational institution. Therefore, the charitable activity of the assessee was education. The income, if any, derived from the property held under the Trust and applied for the educational activity, would be construed as application of income for the purpose of charitable purpose. Therefore, the expenditure incurred in establishing the educational institution, namely, acquisition of land, construction of building, etc., are all application of income for charitable activity. If any income was generated in the course of educational activity, the said income would be construed as if it was generated in the course of carrying on the charitable activity. Therefore, such receipt/income received in the course of carrying on charitable activity was also eligible for exemption, provided the same was applied or set apart for educational purposes. However, such receipt/income cannot be construed as derived from property/business held under trust. Since such receipt/income is inevitable or consequential while carrying on the activity of education, such income also becomes eligible for exemption. The educational institution is an apparatus for carrying out the charitable activity. Therefore, the educational institution or charitable activity itself cannot be construed as the property held under trust. The establishment of an educational institution is an activity of charity. Therefore, by any stretch of imagination, the charitable activity, cannot be held as the property held under trust, even though the income/receipt incidental to such activity is eligible for exemption. However, the money collected over and above the prescribed fee for admitting students cannot be construed as income derived from/incidental to the activity of carrying on charitable activity. [Para 12]

It is a well-settled principle of law that a business held under a trust is also a property. Section 11(4) also makes it very clear that the property held under the trust includes a business undertaking. If the assessee-society runs a business incidental to the attainment of the object of the society and separate books of account are maintained by the assessee, the income derived from such business, shall be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust. The Apex Court in Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/ 115 Taxman 126 considered the provisions of section 11(4A) and held that if the business income is derived from business held under the trust and the same is utilized by the institution for achieving object of the institution, then it could be said that such income is applied for charitable purpose. The assessee-society in question had no property or business whatsoever under trust. Moreover, it was not the claim of the assessee that any income was derived from the property or business held under trust. [Para 13]

to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision. The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

On reference : HELD: By the Insurance Act, 1938, a "principal agent" is defined as meaning "a person, who, not being a salaried employee of an insurer, in consideration of any commission, (i) performs any administrative and organizing functions for the insurer and (ii) procures general insurance business whether wholly or in part by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents of behalf of the insurer". Evidently a principal agent by the definition does not merely render personal service but is concerned with performing certain administrative and organizing functions and the procuring of general insurance business by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents. Such an agent by the very definition will be regarded as carrying on the business of a principal agent. He is not merely an employee engaged for rendering services of a personal nature: he is invested with the right as an agent to perform the administrative organizing functions for the insurer and to procure general insurance business by employing, directly or indirectly, insurance agents. By section 42A of the Insurance Act principal agents are required to obtain a certificate from the Controller of Insurance or an officer authorized by him entitling them to conduct the business of principal agency, and the certificate remains in operation for a period of twelve months only from the date of issue but is liable to be renewed. It is also true that under Part A of the Sixth Schedule to the Insurance Act certain terms are deemed to be included in every contract between an insurer carrying on general insurance business and a principal agent. Under clause 2 of Part A of the Sixth Schedule the principal agent has to procure or cause to be procured through insurance agents such an amount of general insurance business as will yield a gross premium income of not less than Rs. 20,000 in each calendar year. Under clause 4, in the event of the principal agent failing to comply with the requirements of clause 2 in any two successive calendar years, the contract shall, without prejudice to the provisions of clause 3, terminate on the 31st day of March immediately following the second calendar year. Under clause 3 the agency is also liable to be forfeited in the events set out in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) thereof. By clause 5 certain restriction are placed upon the principal agent but an account of these provisions, which impose certain restrictive conditions upon the principal agent it could not be said that the appointment of a principal agent gave rise to a bare service agreement and that the remuneration paid was not for the conduct of a business but for performance of personal service. The circumstance that the appointment was liable to be terminated at short notice and the agency was not permanent and was liable to be forfeited in the events set out hereinbefore would not, affect the character of the agency as business. Following the observation made by the Supreme Court in J.K. Trust's case [1957] 32 ITR 535 the principal agency conducted by the assessee was a business and, therefore, "property" within the meaning of section 4(3)(i). Being property which was capable of being settled upon trust by the deed of trust, dated 17-2-1951, it was lawfully settled upon trust for charitable purposes. The taxing authorities are primarily concerned with the question whether the income sought to be taxed in income from property, which is held on trust for religious or charitable purpose. If the business of the principal agency was transferred to the trustees under a deed of settlement, and from that business income was received, the income will fall within section 4(3)(i) and be exempt from tax in the hands of the trustees. Therefore, under the terms of appointment made with the company firm became the principal agents conducting a business and that business was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i ) and that the alteration, sometime after their appointment as principal agents, in the constitution of the from did not alter the character of the income earned in the course of the business. The income which is liable to be included in the total income of the assessee, was income derived from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution, unless that income fulfils the conditions prescribed by clause (b). The expression "such income" in the proviso refers to the income derived from property (which expression includes a business) held for religious or charitable purposes. But that did not justify the submission that the business which was referred to in clause (b) of the proviso must be business which is held for charitable or religious purposes. The business referred to in clause (b) of the proviso need not be business which is held for religious or charitable purposes, provided it is business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution.

connotes ownership as well as possession. The word 'held' cannot be interpreted only to mean in the sense of possession but would also mean an owner who is not in actual possession. In some cases, it has been held that word "held" connotes the existence of a right or a title in the holder. In the instant case, the land acquired by SMC was under legal ownership of the trust and was possessed by the trustees on behalf of the trust in their fiduciary capacity. The term 'held' has also been explained as to mean factual management. Thus, when an asset forms part of the property, it is held by the trustees for the benefit of the beneficiaries and it is not material as to whether it is held by the trustees in their names or in the name of another. Thus, the lands in question were held under the trust and there was no dispute that objects of the trust were religious and charitable.

Meaning of words 'held under trust'

The trust is a non-corporial body. It is run by persons called trustees for the benefit of persons or for the purposes or objects stated in trust deed. Therefore, a property owned by a non-corporial body like trust is held by trustees for the trust. Therefore, the phrase 'held under trust' would only mean property in possession of the trustees but legally owned by the trust. Since the term 'the property' has been interpreted in widest possible terms even the business or the organization itself would have been treated as property held under trust.

Meaning of 'property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes'

The term 'held wholly for charitable and religious purposes' would mean that property in question is not assigned to any other purpose or used directly or indirectly either in the objects clause of the trust or by the trustees in practice. Assigning of corpus, i.e., capital asset wholly for the purpose of charitable work and not assigning for any non-charitable purpose would be sufficient compliance of provisions of section 11(1A). The Circular No. 72 of the Board further supports this proposition. If the assigner partly assigns the property for charitable work and partly for non-charitable work or the property after assigning or acquisition is partly assigned to charitable work and partly to non-charitable work then on transfer of such asset, proportionate exemption to the extent asset is assigned for charitable work would be available and no exemption to capital gain in respect of that portion thereof which arises from that part of the property which is assigned for or held for non-charitable purposes, would be available. It is not the case that passive holding of the land or non-use of the land would mean that it is assigned or held for non-charitable purposes. Non-use of the land or passiveness of the land is not equivalent to its holding for non-charitable purposes which alone can forfeit the exemption as per sub-section (1A) of section 11 and Circular No. 72, dated 6-1-1972. [Para 14]

Thus, the argument of the department that land should be put to use for getting exemption from capital gains was not correct. As seen above, the word 'wholly' relates to and qualifies the word 'purpose'. If the trust is established for charitable or religious purpose and there is no other object for which property of the trust is utilized then property of the trust so held and thereafter so transferred can only give rise to income/capital gains which has to be considered within the provisions of section 11(1) and 11(1A) only. The income or capital gains from the property held under the trust can be denied exemption only to the extent the property is assigned or used or held for any non-charitable purpose or other than the objects of the trust. The assignment or use for non-charitable work would be required to be proved from the positive facts and mere non-use or keeping the property idle or passive cannot be interpreted to mean that it was used or assigned to non-charitable work. Since in the instant case, the department had only alleged non-use for charitable purpose and there was no material on record that the land was used for non-charitable work, it was to be held that the assessee could not be denied exemption from the capital gains in accordance with provisions of section 11(1A), read with section 11(5). Accordingly, the assessee was entitled to exemption from the capital gains as it had complied with the provisions of section 11(5). The appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Investment in specified securities) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee society was running a cancer hospital - Assessing Officer noticing that assessee made an investment in chit fund company, denied benefit of exemption under section 11(5) by holding that chit fund subscription would not amount to investment or deposit as specified under section 11(5) - Therefore, Assessing Officer rejected claim of exemption under section 11 - However, it was found that assessee's contribution to chit funds was made only as an arrangement for better management of funds of assessee - Whether there was no violation of section 11(5) and assessee was eligible to claim exemption under section 11 - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where contribution to chit funds was done only as an arrangement for better management of society's funds, exemption under section 11 could not be denied

FACT: The assessee was society running a cancer hospital. It filed NIL return of income after availing exemption under section 11.

The Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee made an investment in chit fund company, thereby it denied the benefit of exemption under section 11(5) by holding that the chit fund subscription would not amount to investment or deposit as specified under section 11(5). Therefore, the Assessing Officer rejected the claim of exemption under section 11.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was eligible for exemption under section 11, even though it had not obtained notification under section 10(23C). It was also observed that as there was violation of section 11(5), exemption could not be allowed.

On second appeal:

HELD: The assessee has spent the entire income earned in the year for the objects of the trust. As it has incurred excess amount, there is no surplus amount which needs to be invested under section 11(5). Section 11(5) comes in to operation only when trust has accumulated or set apart the amount under section 11(2). In the case of the assessee, there is a no surplus fund and hence, the question of investment or deposit as specified under section 11(5) does not arise. Contribution to chit fund in this case is not an investments or deposit as specified under section 11(5). It is, as submitted, only an arrangement for better management of funds of the assessee. The assessee has been complied with the provisions of section 11(1)(a) by applying entire amount for the objects of the trust. Therefore, there is no violation of section 11(5) and the assessee is eligible to claim exemption under section 11. Hence, the grounds of the assessee are allowed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income, from property held under - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessing Officer disallowed exemption claimed by assessee-
 trust under section 11 on two grounds, namely, (a) that even though assessee’s buildings were being used by other societies of same group for charitable activities, such use could not be treated as use by assessee for carrying out its own charitable activities; and (b) that major expenditure was on account of agricultural and dairy activities carried on by it which was not in nature of application of its income for charitable purpose - Commissioner (Appeals), however, upheld assessee’s claim - Whether where buildings of assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature, such use could very well be treated as use by assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for purpose of exemption under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether since agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by assessee-society as separate business activities, same constituted ‘property held under trust’ as provided in section 11(4) and in any case income of said activities was to be determined after deducting expenditure incurred in connection with said business - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, gross income being more than sufficient to cover expenses incurred in connection with said activities, allowance of same by Commissioner  (Appeals) as application of its income hardly made any difference in ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to revenue - Held, yes
Circulars and Instructions - CBDT’s Circular No. 1132, dated 5-1-1978

FACT: The Assessing Officer was of the opinion that the buildings of the assessee-society, which were constructed by applying its income, were being used by other societies of the same group, though for their charitable activities, and, thus, it did not mean that income of the assessee was being applied for charitable purpose, because such use could not be treated as use by the assessee for carrying out its own charitable activities. He also found that the major expenditure was on account of agricultural and dairy activities carried on by it, which was not in the nature of application of its income for charitable purpose. He, therefore, disallowed the exemption claimed under section 11.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) however upheld the assessee’s claim.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: In the Circular No. 1132 issued by the CBDT, it has been clarified that the payment of a sum by one charitable trust to other for utilisation of the donee-trust towards its charitable objects is proper application of income for charitable purpose in the hands of donor-trust and donor-trust will not lose exemption under section 11 merely because the donee trustee did not spend the donation during the year of receipt itself. In the instant case, the buildings of the assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature and that being so, such use could very well be treated as use by the assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for the purpose of exemption under section 11. Moreover, exemption under section 11 was allowed to the assessee-society for the assessment years 1992-93 and 1993-94 by the department in the similar facts and circumstances. As such, the Commissioner (Appeals) was fully justified in treating the use of assessee’s property by other societies for charitable purposes as charitable activity carried on by the assessee and accordingly in allowing exemption under section 11 as claimed. The impugned order was, therefore, upheld. [Para 7]

Agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by the assessee’s society as separate business activities and the same, therefore, constituted ‘property held under trust’ of the assessee-society as provided in sub-section (4) of section 11 and income of the said activities, in any case, was to be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act, i.e., after deducting the expenditure incurred in connection with the said business. The assessee-society had derived income from the said activities and the amount being more than sufficient to cover the expenses incurred in connection with the said activities, the allowance of the same by the Commissioner (Appeals) as application of its income as claimed by the assessee hardly made any difference in the ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to the revenue. [Para 8]

Hence, the revenue’s appeal was to be dismissed.

in respect of such business. [Para 7]

Thus, if a property is held under trust, and such property is a business, the case would fall under section 11(4) and not under section 11(4A). Section 11(4A) would apply only to a case where the business is not held under trust. Thus, there is difference between property or business held under trust and business carried on by or on behalf of the trust. [Para 8] In the present case, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is that running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not held under trust, but it was business commenced/carried on by the Society, subsequent to the formation of trust. Though the business was commenced by the Society and it was carried on by the Society after its formation, it cannot be said to constitute property held under trust under section 11(4), it is only the business which is held under the trust that would enjoy exemption in respect of its income under section 11(1) and there is a distinction between the objects of a trust and the powers given to the trustees to effectuate the purpose of the trust. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the Memorandum of Association of the assessee. The running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not even in the contemplation of the Memorandum of Association on the basis of which the Society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust. Section 11(1) confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose.

Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1), was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust. In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

There is no connection between the activities relating to running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall and the attainment of the objects of the trust. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall are used for charitable purposes would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The application of income generated by the business is not relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. [Para 10]

The contention of the assessee that the surplus funds generated from the running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were spent towards charitable activities and therefore, the assessee is entitled for exemption under section 11(4) is not acceptable. Initially, the assessee carried on the business itself which is not at all property held under trust. This activity is a business activity and the provisions of section 11(4A) is applicable. [Para 11]

Further, there is no nexus between the activities carried on and the objects of the assessee that can constitute an activity incidental to the attainment of the objects, namely, to promote cause of charity, mission activities, welfare, employment, diffusion of useful knowledge, upliftment and education and to create an awareness of self-reliance among the members of the public etc. Being so, it is to be held that the assessee is not entitled for any exemption under section 11. [Para 14]

FACT: ■

The assessee, a statutory body, was engaged in development of housing scheme across the State and had been granted registration under section 12AA. It had claimed exemption under section 11.

■

The Assessing Officer denied the assessee’s claim for exemption under section 11, holding that its activities were commercial in nature and were hit by the proviso to section 2(15). ■

On cross appeal:

HELD: Exemption under section 11

■

The issues raised by the Assessing Officer that the activities of the assessee-Parishad carried on as per its objects laid down in section 15 of U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965 were not charitable activities do not hold any water after the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Asstt. CIT (Exemptions) v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 143 taxmann.com 278/291 Taxman 11/449 ITR 1 (SC), which categorically states that statutory bodies engaged in housing development, town planning etc., are involved in objects of, “general public utility” (GPU) and therefore are entitled to be considered as a charities in the GPU category. It is also observed that even earlier, the Allahabad High Court, in its orders in the case of Lucknow Development authority and others, dated 16-9-2013, in which the assessee was one of the parties, had held that the objects of the assessee society were admittedly charitable and that it was entitled to the benefit of registration under section 12AA. Therefore, once the objects and functions of the assessee-Parishad have been held to be charitable by the High Court and not challenged or overturned by way of appeal to the Supreme Court, it is held that it is not open for the Assessing Officer to contend that such objects are not charitable on the grounds that certain activities of the assessee-Parishad yielded surplus. Furthermore, it is found that the Commissioner (Appeals) had held in his order that once the registration had been granted under section 12AA, the income of the assessee had to be computed as per section 11 and not under any other head of income. There is no infirmity in this line of reasoning. For this reason, it is held that the Commissioner (Appeals) was perfectly justified in directing the Assessing Officer to compute the income of the assessee-Parishad in the manner provided under section 11, with reference to the information contained in Form 10B. [Para 19]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01 - Assessee-society was formed, inter alia, with main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard - It was duly registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860 - It was also registered under section 12A - Assessee claimed exemption under section 11 - Assessing Officer denied exemption holding that, assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return, and, thus, it was earning profit and not doing any charity - However, it was found from records that assessee was duly recognised by HNB Garhwal University and strictly following university regulations with regard to admission charging of fees and course curriculum and had on its governing body nominee of State Government, HNB University and AICTE functioning under Human Resources Ministry and, thus, in fact Government managed and moreover, any surplus arising to society was utilized into activities of society and did not find its way to pocket of persons who were running society/institution - Whether, in view of said facts, it could be said that assessee was not a profit making institution and it was rendering services of education to general public and was eligible for exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-society was formed, inter alia, with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. It was duly registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. It was also registered under section 12A. For the relevant assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01, the assessee claimed exemption under section 11. The Assessing Officer denied the exemption holding that the assessee was not deriving any income out of the property held under trust, and that the income of the assessee was from fee charged from the students on account of tuition fee and other charges and whatever property had been acquired subsequently was as a result of application of this income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: The assessee was a registered society duly incorporated and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1862. The society was formed with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. The income which the assessee received in the form of tuition fee and other receipts could not have been received but for the organization and, therefore, the tuition fee and other receipts derived from other organizations was income derived from property held under trust. Such tuition fee and other receipts, received by the assessee were directly and substantially arising from the organization, which was the property held under the trust. The Assessing Officer's assertion that whatever property in the shape of office building, furniture, computer was simply an application of income was not sustainable. It is well-settled that property acquired by an organization from its own income is also a property held under trust. Thus, fixed assets and current assets held by the assessee as on 31-3-1999 and 31-3-2000 were properties held under trust. Further, the Delhi Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case vide order dated 15-12-2003 had held that department cannot guide a charitable institution as to how it should carry on its charity. It is sufficient compliance with the relevant provisions of law in case surplus of the institution is utilized into activities of the institution and does not find its way to the pocket of the persons who were running the society/institution. There was no allegation by the department that the funds had been siphoned off. Therefore, the Commissioner should not have withdrawn the registration granted to the assessee under section 12AA.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income form property held under - Assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60 - Assessee was an association of persons - Constitution of assessee revealed that neither standing committee nor managing committee nor even members of assessee could use property of assessee for any purpose except that covered by object clause of assessee - Neither before ITO nor before AAC any contention was raised by revenue that object for which assessee was constituted was not charitable one - Whether property of assessee was held under trust or under legal obligation and, therefore, assessee was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was an association of persons. The Constitution of the assessee provided for an elected standing committee, the constitution, functions and duties of the said standing committee. The Constitution also provided for a smaller body which was entitled managing committee and its constitution and other functions. The Constitution further provided that to carry out the objects of the parishad, the standing committee could raise funds and accept donations, presents charities, etc., and would have power to administer them. The issue that arose for decision was as to whether having regard to the terms of the constitution of the assessee-association, the properties of the assessee-association were held under trust or other legal obligation so as to qualify for exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

On reference:

HELD: It is now well-settled that a formal deed of trust is not absolutely essential in order to come to a conclusion that any particular property is held under trust or other legal obligation. The provisions contained in the Constitution of the assessee bound not only the standing committee and the managing committee but they equally bound every member of the assessee. In view of the provisions of the Constitution, it was impossible to urge that it would be open either to the standing committee or the managing committee or even the members of the assessee to use the property of the assessee for any purpose except that covered by the object clause of the assessee.

In that view of the matter, no other view was possible save and except to hold that the property of the assessee was held under trust or a legal obligation. As it was not open for the revenue to urge that the object was not for a charitable purpose in view of the fact that such a contention was not raised either before the ITO or at the stage of appeal before the AAC on behalf of the revenue, the provisions of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 were directly applicable.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

■

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

■ The record further reveals that the revenue has not brought any material to establish that the rental income earned by the trust was diverted for any non-charitable purpose or that the dominant character of the trust had ceased to be charitable. On the contrary, the Income and Expenditure Account demonstrates that the receipts of the trust, whether derived from grants, donations, interest or rental income, were applied only towards the charitable objects of the trust. Thus, the source from which the income was generated has not altered the fundamental charitable character of the institution. [Para 8.5]

■

It is a settled proposition of law that the decisive test is the dominant object of the institution and not the source of its income. Income derived from property held under trust, including rental income, does not lose the benefit of exemption under Section 11 and Section 12 merely because such income arises from leasing of trust property, so long as it is applied towards the charitable purposes for which the trust has been established. The leasing of trust property, in the facts of the present case, is only an incidental mode of augmenting resources to fulfil the charitable objects and cannot be construed as an independent commercial object of the trust. [Para 8.6]

■

Accordingly, while the Tribunal disagrees with the reasoning assigned by the Commissioner (Appeals) in holding that earning rental income was itself one of the objects of the trust, the Tribunal nevertheless upholds the ultimate conclusion that the assessee cannot be denied exemption on this ground. The reasoning adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) is incorrect; however, the conclusion reached by him is sustainable on the basis that the rental income was merely incidental to the charitable activities and was admittedly applied towards the charitable objects of the trust. Consequently, the ground raised by the Revenue on this issue is devoid of merit and is dismissed. [Para 8.7]

■

Accordingly, the Tribunal concurs with the findings recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue. The ground raised by the Revenue challenging the allowability of exemption merely because the assessee earned rental income is devoid of merit and is, therefore, dismissed. [Para 8.8]

HEADNOTE: I. Section  11,  read with section  12,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  341,  read with section  335  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Charitable or religious trust  -  Exemption of income from property held under (Rental income)  - Assessment year  2013-14  - Assessee, a charitable trust claimed exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Assessing Officer denied exemption by treating assessee as an AOP on ground that assessee had earned substantial rental income by leasing its immovable properties which amounted to a commercial activity inconsistent with its charitable character - It was noted that trust deed contained a separate enabling provision conferring powers upon Board of Trustees - It was also noted that trustees were merely authorised to acquire, hold, manage or otherwise deal with land, buildings and other immovable properties with funds of trust for effectuating charitable objects of trust - Furthermore, Income and Expenditure Account demonstrated that receipts of trust, whether derived from grants, donations, interest or rental income, were applied only towards charitable objects of trust - Whether thus, income derived from property held under trust, including rental income, did not lose benefit of exemption under section 11 and section 12 merely because such income arises from leasing of trust property, so long as it is applied towards charitable purposes for which trust has been established - Held, yes - Whether since leasing of trust property was only an incidental mode of augmenting resources to fulfil charitable objects, same could not be construed as an independent commercial object of trust and assessee could not be denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Held, yes [Para 8.6] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, a charitable trust claimed exemption under sections 11 and 12.

■

The Assessing Officer denied exemption by treating the assessee as an Association of Persons (AOP) on ground that assessee had earned substantial rental income by leasing its immovable properties which amounted to a commercial activity inconsistent with its charitable character.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim on ground that the Assessing Officer had not brought cogent material to show that the assessee’s activities ceased to be charitable.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: (i) Rental income and leasing of properties

■

The principal basis adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) for allowing the assessee's claim is the observation that one of the objects of the trust was to lease out properties and earn rental income. However, on a careful examination of the original trust deed as well as the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the Tribunal finds that the observation is factually incorrect and contrary to the material available on record. The original trust deed, enumerates the charitable objects of the trust, namely: (i) genetic research and agricultural education; (ii) conservation of land, water and genetic resources; (iii) sustainable agriculture and environmental protection; (iv) family planning and population control; and (v) improvement of the status and literacy of women. Subsequently, by way of the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the additional charitable objects of Relief to the Poor and Education were incorporated. Significantly, neither the original trust deed nor the addendum includes, as an object of the trust, carrying on the activity of leasing or renting of immovable properties for earning rental income. [Para 8.2]

■

What is, however, contained in the trust deed is a separate enabling provision conferring powers upon the Board of Trustees. Clause VIII merely authorises the trustees to acquire, hold, manage or otherwise deal with land, buildings and other immovable properties with the funds of the trust for effectuating the charitable objects of the trust. Such an enabling clause cannot be elevated to the status of an independent charitable object. The power to acquire and manage trust properties is only incidental to the effective administration of the trust and to facilitate the attainment of its charitable purposes. Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that leasing of properties itself constituted one of the objects of the trust is clearly erroneous and is not borne out from the trust deed. [Para 8.3]

■

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

FACT: The assessee, a registered society, was established, inter alia, (a) to promote, organise and encourage scientific research in the hosiery manufacturers, inventions, investments and design, (b ) to find out way and means of progress, development and improvement of hosiery industry and to safeguard and to protect its investments, (c) to procure, encourage and formulate means for collective buying of industrial raw materials and machinery on a no-profit-no-loss basis, (d) to encourage and formulate ways and means for collective selling of hosiery products, (e) to make arrangements for setting up of woollen hosiery yarn spinning plant on co-operative basis in order to provide the industry its basic raw materials on fair prices, and (f) to procure, allocate, distribute to hosiery manufacturers woollen hosiery yarn, their basic raw material, on a no-profit-no-loss basis. To meet its office and administrative expenses, the assessee charged annual subscription, special subscription and allocation charges (i.e., charges for allocation of raw yarn) from its members. For the assessment years 1969-70 and 1970-71, the ITO treated the allocation charges as the assessee's income under section 28(iii) and taxed the same. He also repelled the assessee's contention that it was entitled to exemption under section 11 (1)(a). On appeal, the AAC sustained the ITO's order. On second appeal, the Tribunal sustained the AAC's order, holding that although the activity of the assessee was covered by the definition "charitable purposes" as contemplated in section 2(75), yet the assessee's income which was covered by section 28(iii), was not income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a), so that it was not entitled to exemption from tax.

On reference:

HELD: By virtue of section 11(4) "property held under trust" includes a business undertaking so held. Therefore, it could not be accepted that the income derived by the assessee was not income from property as envisaged under section 11(1)(a). That apart, a perusal of the aims and objects of the assessee-society led to the conclusion that the income derived by it was income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a). Accordingly, the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the amount received by the assessee on account of allocation charges was not income from property held under trust.
