The provisions of section 4(3)(i ) confer an exemption of income from property only where the property itself is held under a trust or other legal obligation. It does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created in respect of any property, but only the income derived from any particular property or source is itself held in trust as where it is set apart or charged for a charitable purpose. That is clear upon the terms of the section itself and upon the authorities. In the instant case, all the income which the assessee derived or received was in the shape of grants and subscriptions from members which could not possibly have been received by it except from its business. Therefore, the entire income of the assessee must be held to be income derived from its business which was its property. If this contention was correct, then it was further submitted that there could be also no doubt upon the terms of its memorandum of association and its purposes and objects that the assessee was holding the business in trust for charitable purposes.

Supreme Court in J.K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that "Business" would undoubtedly be property in the connotation in which it is used in section 4(3)(i). In the light of this pronouncement of the Supreme Court it is clear that "business" itself can be property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) and upon that principle the business of the assessee in the instant case would be "property" held by the assessee.

Under the circumstances, the view taken by the Tribunal was the correct view and the income of the assessee would be exempt under the provisions of section 4(3)(i).

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity. The educational institution being run by the assessee was for the general benefit of the public and not for the benefit of any class or section of the public, as (a ) the institution was duly recognized by HNB Garhwal University and strictly followed all procedures with regard to admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum as laid down by the university, and (b) the nominees of State Government, HNB University and AICTE (functioning under the Human Resources Ministry) were on the governing body of the society and, therefore, the assessee had no choice in matters of admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum. The institute, was, in fact, State Government managed.

It was also found that the working system of the assessee was as per the guidelines laid down by the University. In respect of fixing and charging fees from students, the society management had no powers. Fee was being charged from students strictly as specified and laid down by the University. The governing body of the society had no powers to workout the cost and thereafter to add on the element of overheads and profits. Therefore, there was no question of building huge margins of profits in the fees structure as conceived by the Assessing Officer.

From a plain reading of the main objects given in the Memorandum, it could very well be discerned that the society had been formed with the sole objective of imparting and spreading computer education. Further, the assessee-society was virtually Government managed. Therefore, the question of functioning like a commercial profit making institution was totally unfounded. Thus, the fees charged by the assessee was simply receipt in the hands of the society and not profit.

Further, the assessee was rendering services of education to the general public. Therefore, its activities clearly fell within the ambit of charitable purpose as defined under section 2(15). Charging of fees does not in anyway dilute the aspect of charitable purpose. It is the end use and spirit and objective which matters.

In the assessment order, the Assessing Officer had not been able to appreciate the difference in the words 'charitable purposes' as are used in the Act and the word 'charity' as had been used by the Assessing Officer in his order. The word 'charity' as used in English language and recognized in English law, implies as an act motivated by pity and may require benevolence to manifest it. However, exemption under section 11 has been prescribed with reference to 'charitable purposes' and not 'charity'. The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act.

Therefore, the property from which income was derived by the assessee was held under trust and such property was held for charitable purpose and the income derived from trust was property which was being applied for charitable purpose. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, was carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust.

Section 11(1) of the Act confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose. Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1) of the Act, was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust.

In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the charitable trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

It is thus necessary to consider the question whether the said activities carried on by the assessee were incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. One fails to see any connection between the activities relating to running of "Community Hall" with attainment of the objects of the trust. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from running of "Community Hall" is used for charitable purposes would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The application of income generated by the business is not relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. [Para 10]

It was contended by the assessee that the surplus funds generated from the running of "Community Hall" was spent towards charitable activities and therefore, the assessee is entitled for exemption under section 11(4) this contention cannot be accepted. Initially, the assessee carried on the business itself which is not at all property held under trust. This activity is a business activity and the provisions of section 11(4A) of the Act is applicable. [Para 11]

It was contended that if the profits of the business carried on by the trust are utilized by the trust for the purposes of achieving the objectives of the trust, then the business should be considered to be incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust as observed by the Supreme Court in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/115 Taxman 126. [Para 12]

Prima facie the said observation would appear to support the assessee's case in the sense that even if running of "Community Hall" is held not to constitute a business held under trust, but only as a business carried on by or on behalf of the trust, so long as the profits generated by it are applied for the charitable objects of the trust, the condition imposed under section 11(4A) of the Act should be held to be satisfied, entitling the trust to the tax exemption. On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: Assessee has not disputed the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) that rentals received from its Kalyanamandapams had to be considered under the head income from business. In fact the High Court while remitting the question back to the Commissioner (Appeals) for assessment years 1997-98, 1998-99 etc., had indicated that income of the assessee from the Kalyanamandapams was more in the nature of business income. Obviously, assessee cannot now raise a plea against the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that income of the assessee from renting out Kalyanamandapams were business income, and it has wisely done so. However, it is peeved on the view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) that such business income could not be considered as income earned from a property held under the Trust, thereby disentitling the assessee from taking advantage of section 11(4). The Commissioner (Appeals) was of the opinion that Kalyanamandapams having being built by the assessee subsequent to its formation in the year 1959, could not be considered as property under trust. The assessee during the course of his arguments has stated that the land on which Kalyanamandapams were built was part of the original settlement and the building were built therein by the assessee from its income. Be that as it may, there is no dispute that the land and building was owned by the assessee society, whether it was part of original settlement or not. It is opined that, once income of a trust is used by it to acquire a property, the property so acquired will be property held under trust. Income from such property will be income from property under the trust. Thus, rental income received by the assessee from Kalyanamandapams though it was in the nature of income from business, such income was nothing but income from property held under trust.[Para 9]

Whether assessee could be denied exemption claimed by it under section 11(1) by virtue of sub-section (4A) thereof?

To answer the question, whether assessee can be denied the exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)(4A) it is to be seen whether renting out the Kalyanamandapams could be considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects of the assessee as they appear in its Memorandum of Association. By virtue of clause (d) of the objects clause, assessee can purchase, build and let out properties for its other purposes. The purpose mentioned in clause (a) clearly indicate promotion of any object which was wholly and solely charitable in nature. No doubt Commissioner (Appeals) had mentioned this to be a very wide expressions, disentitling it from claiming exemption under section 11. It is true that clause (a) is of a wide amplitude. However what needed to be remembered is that the assessee was having registration under section 12A since 11-4-1975, and such registration still continued. If the main object of the assessee was too wide, as mentioned by the Commissioner (Appeals), it would not have been given such registration. Having given such registration, which was alive since 1975, revenue cannot now turn back and say that the main object was very wide and assessee could not be given benefit of section 11(1). Activity of renting out Kalyanamandapams could be construed as only incidental to the attainment of its main object. Assessee therefore could take advantage of section 11(4). There is no dispute that assessee had maintained separate books for its Kalyanamandapams. The audited accounts filed along with its return clearly show separate income and expenditure for each of the activities, including Kalyanamandapams. Sub-section 4A would not apply to the assessee once its business is considered as incidental to the attainment of its main objects.[Para 10]

On appeal to the High Court: HELD: The crux of the matter, is as to whether the 'investment' can also amount to 'application' or not. There is nothing in the provisions of section 11(1) to curtail or narrow down the meaning of the word 'application', which by definition is of wider import. The scheme of section 11 is to advance the cause of charity by allowing the religious or charitable trusts to employ their funds in such a manner, for the purpose of charity or for advancing the cause of charity. There is nothing contrary placed from the side of revenue to even indicate that purchase of immovable property in question even on lease basis was not going to serve the cause of charity as per the objects of the charitable trust in question in any manner. The investment in immovable property, if it serves the cause of charity immediately or even in near future, the rental income or otherwise cannot be said to be not serving the objects of the trust at all. On the contrary, investment in immovable property which is intended to be used for serving the cause and objects of the trust is more committed and firm 'application' of income of the trust. The burden, therefore, was on the revenue to establish that the 'investment' was for the purpose, other than, for subserving the objects stipulated in the trust deed. The revenue has utterly failed to bring on record any evidence to the contrary to the claim of exemption by assessee on the ground that the immovable property in question was being taken on lease to create a theatre or auditorium, which would be used for the purpose of the group of artists or their families or even serve the cause of general public in times of floods or to provide education to the children, etc. Unless there was evidence on record to show that the said investment of the immovable property was being used for the purpose altogether different from the objects of the trust deed, the denial of exemption on an assumed distinction between the 'application' and 'investment' was not only too far-fetched, but beyond the scheme of section 11 itself and the said view of the Tribunal, therefore, cannot be countenanced. [Para 15]

Therefore, the assessee in the instant case while making the advance in question for purchase of immovable property in question even on lease basis, cannot be said to have not applied its income during the year in question for the charitable purposes within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) and, therefore, the assessee was clearly entitled to exemption under the said provision in respect of the said investment in immovable property. [Para 16]

It cannot be said that such advance did not crystalise in any 'application of income' and was in suspended animation as already indicated above that nothing contrary was brought on record by revenue that this advance did not crystalise in any 'application of income' in favour of the assessee during the year or even subsequently. On the contrary, it was contended at the bar by the assessee that the leasehold rights were secured by the assessee with the said investment and building on the said leasehold land is under construction as of now. However, no findings could be given on facts in this regard, but per se also there is no hesitation in holding that the advance or investment in the said leasehold proprty by the assessee's charitable trust in the year in question could be held to be 'application of income' within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) and therefore, the assessee was entitled to the exemption. HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether for running a charitable activity, establishment has to be maintained, which requires payment of salaries and other establishment expenses and application of income for said purpose cannot be alien to charitable objects which are to be advanced - Held, yes - Whether nature of regulatory mechanism operated by market committees involves incurring of expenditure on establishment and mere fact that such an expenditure has been incurred, cannot be a ground to hold that application of income was not for charitable purpose - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a statutory entity under the provisions of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961. Its activities were covered by section 2(15) and it had been registered under section 12AA. During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer held that the assessee was not eligible for exemption under sections 11 and 12 as major portion of its income was spent on running of administration, i.e., for paying salaries and other allowances to the employees and office expenses and, thus, major part of its income was not being spent for charitable purposes which was statutorily required for exemption. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that income was being used for charitable purposes and, therefore, the assessee was eligible for exemption under sections 11 and 12. The Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On the revenue's appeal to the High Court :

HELD: It cannot be disputed that for running a charitable activity, the establishment has to be maintained, which requires payment of salaries and other establishment expenses. Application of income for the said purpose cannot be alien to the charitable objects which are to be advanced. Without establishment, the charitable objects cannot be achieved at all. There is no provision that income cannot be spent for the said purpose. That being the position, the view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal could not be held to be debatable. It was not the case of the revenue that expenditure in running the administration was either excessive or unreasonable. The nature of regulatory mechanism operated by the market committees involves incurring of expenditure on establishment. Thus, mere fact that such an expenditure was incurred, could not be ground to hold that the application was not for charitable purpose. [Para 9]

Therefore, the appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 12]

On 23-11-1972, under section 17 of the Act in respect of the assessment years in question, the notices were issued on the ground that the trustees had been not only using and utilising the properties of the said trust for their own personal purposes, but had also been using and applying income therefrom directly or indirectly for their own personal benefit and/or had been acting contrary to the express provisions of the said trust.

On writ : HELD: Under section 11(1)(a), in order to be entitled to exemption income must not only be derived from the property held under trust only for charitable or religious purposes but the income entitled to exemption must be to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes, i.e., charitable or religious purpose in India or where such income is accumulated for application to such purpose in India, i.e., religious or charitable purpose to the extent the income so accumulated is not in excess of 25 per cent of income from the property or Rs. 10,000, whichever is higher. Therefore, two separate independent conditions are required to be fulfilled, that is to say, the income must be derived from the property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, and, secondly, the application or accumulation of such income in the manner indicated in clause (a ) of sub-section (1) of section 11 of the Act. 'Charitable purpose' or 'purpose of charitable or religious nature' have not been defined in the Wealth-tax Act, 1957. Therefore, it must bear the same meaning as in the Income-tax Act but under the provisions of the Income-tax Act not only should the income be derived from a trust or legal obligation of public purpose of a charitable or religious nature but the income so derived must to a certain extent be so applied. The position under the Wealth-tax Act seems to be a little different. Wealth-tax Act assessed the owning or having or possessing of the property and section 5(1)(i) of the Act stipulated that the condition for exemption was that the property must be held by the assessee under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a religious or charitable nature in India. Therefore, the holding of a property by the assessee either under a trust or other legal obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature is the statutory requirement entitling the assessee to exemption under the Act. In the ground for reopening as noted before it was not disputed that the assessees upon whom the impugned notices had been issued were not holding the property under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a charitable or religious nature. What was being suggested was that holding the property as trustees or under obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature the assessees were committing breaches of trust in acting contrary to the trust and misusing the funds of the trust for their personal benefit. The application of the money held under a trust or under legal obligation is not a relevant consideration for exemption under section 5(1)(i) of the Act. Therefore, the revenue had no material to believe that the income of the assessee had escaped assessment. This position manifests a lacuna in the present provision of law. The position, therefore, is that if the trustees hold the property for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature and if they misapply or commit breach of trust, they will continue to enjoy exemption under the Wealth-tax Act. This position should receive consideration by the legislature in order to bring it at par with the provisions of the Income-tax Act. But until that is done, the petitioners were entitled to succeed on the point that there were no grounds for believing that the wealth of the assessee had escaped assessment or had been under-assessed.

In the aforesaid view of the matter, the notices are hereby quashed and the respondents were restrained from giving effect to the same.

Note: The case was decided in favour of assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 28(i), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable and religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Application of income) - Assessment years 1997-98 to 2000-01 - Whether where Memorandum of Association of assessee-society confers power on assessee to improve, manage, cultivate, develop, exchange and grant on lease its property, construction of residential complex would fall within scope of objects of society and, thus, assessee is entitled to exemption under section 11 - Held, yes - Assessee, a charitable trust, was permitted under its Memorandum of Association to construct a commercial-cum-residential complex on a part of its land - Assessee sold flats to various persons - Difference in figure of Rs. 1,61,23,950 was found in sale deed and agreement to sell which was alleged to be misappropriated by manager of assessee - Thereafter assessee had filed revised returns, wherein it had offered additional income of Rs. 1,61,23,950 for all respective years and had claimed exemption under section 11(2) to extent of 25 per cent of assessed income - Assessing Officer added said additional income as assessee's business income - However, Tribunal held that amount of Rs. 1,61,23,950 never reached assessee, as it had been misappropriated by said manager, and, hence, it had to be treated as an application of income under section 11 - Whether since assessee itself had offered its additional income and there was no material on record to show that this amount and misappropriated amount was one and same, order of Tribunal was to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 4] [Partly in favour of revenue]IT: Where assessee, a charitable trust, had itself offered misappropriated fund as its additional business income, said additional income could not be held as application of income under section 11

FACT: The assessee, a charitable trust, was permitted under its Memorandum of Association to construct a commercial-cum-residential complex on a part of its land.

The assessee sold the apartments/commercial premises to various persons by agreements to sell and then sale deeds. The Tribunal disitmissed appeals filed by revenue holding that amount of Rs. 1,61,23,950 never reached assessee, as it had been misappropriated by its manager, and, hence, it had to be treated as an application of income.

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under [Business held in trust] - Assessment year 1977-78 - Whether even if business of insurance was carried out by assessee-society for carrying on primary purpose of charitable activities in accordance with aims and objects of trust, assessee would still be entitled to exemption - Held, yes [Para 9][In favour of assessee]IT : Where income from business was applied for charity as per aims and objects of assessee-society, its income will be exempt

FACT: The assessee, a society engaged in charity was assessed in status of 'Association of Persons'.

The Assessing Officer found that the assessee was also carrying insurance business to earn profit and therefore, held that it could not get exemption under section 11.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) supported the ITO.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held insurance business was held on trust and income from said business was applied to charitable purpose. Therefore, the assessee's income would be exempted under section 11.

On appeal before High Court:

HELD: The dominant purpose of the respondent-society was advancement of general public utility and not for education alone. The aims and objects was to work and establish agencies and depots for the purchase and sale of goods of all descriptions, borrow money and to get insurance agencies of the different companies and to do insurance work for the purpose of applying income there from for objects mentioned above. The respondent-society had obtained the licence from the Government of India, Department of Insurance as an insurance agent under Part II of the Insurance Act, 1938 for general insurance business only. It had worked as insurance agent and had applied the income in charitable activities. The Tribunal has held that the insurance business is wholly held in trust and outside the purview of section 13(1)(bb). The Tribunal has followed decision of this Court in the case of this very assessee as also the earlier orders of the Tribunal in the matter.[Para 6]

In the assessment years 1973-74, 1974-75, 1975-76 and 1976-77, the Tribunal has taken the view that the assessee-society was established for advancement of any other object of general public utility. The view expressed by the Tribunal for the assessment year 1973-74 has been approved by this Court wherein notice under section 148 issued for the assessment year 1960-61 was under challenge. Thus, a different view cannot be taken and it is to be opined that the dominant object of the assessee-society was for the charitable purpose as defined in section 2(15). The question of applicability of section 13(1)(bb) to the facts of the case would not arise for the reason that the Tribunal has found that the business of insurance was carried under trust for carrying on the primary purpose of charitable activities in accordance with the aims and objects of the trust. Thus, section 11 was applied and it cannot be excluded. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 13(1)(c), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessee-trust owned properties which were settled by L and H, who were joint owners thereof - Assessee had leased out aforesaid property to a company on a rent of Rs. 4,000 per month for purpose of residence of P, who was managing director of company and husband of L and father of H-ITO held that premises in question could fetch a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month and, hence, the assessee had allowed the trust property being used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of the authors of the trust and their relatives under section 13(1)(c), read with section 13(2)(b) - Whether in view of fact that property in question was governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act and standard rent of property was below Rs. 4,000 there was no direct or indirect benefit to authors of assessee and their relatives and, therefore, assessee was entitled to exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-trust owned the properties which were settled by L and H, who were joint owners thereof. At the time of the settlement, one company was a tenant in the aforesaid property. The company had taken the premises on lease for the purpose of residence of P and his family, who was the managing director of the company and the husband of L and the father of H. The company was paying Rs. 4,000 per month as rent to the assessee. While completing the assessment for the relevant assessment year, the ITO held that premises in question could fetch a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month and, hence, the assessee had allowed the trust property being used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of the authors of the trust and their relatives under section 13(1)(c), read with section 13(2)(b). He, therefore, disallowed exemption under section 11 to the assessee and made addition of certain amount to the income of the assessee, i.e., an amount of difference between the market rent and the actual rent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal:

HELD: It was no longer in dispute that the property in question was governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act and the standard rent of this property was below Rs. 4,000 per month which was the rent being paid by the company. In view of the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the cases of Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. NDMC [1980] 122 ITR 700, Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 435, and Amolak Ram Khosla v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 589 since in the instant case the rent payable by the company to the assessee was considered to be more than the standard rent assessable under the Delhi Rent Control Act it was not permissible to say that the rent charged by the assessee was inadequate and was intended to confer any benefit on the settlors or their relatives. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to exemption under section 11 and the addition made by the ITO to the rental income was not justified.

In the instant case, the Tribunal had found that the assessee had constructed shops from its own funds and that the income therefrom could be utilised only for carrying out its objects. It could not be distributed amongst its members. The shops, etc., owned by it were, thus, held by it under a legal obligation. The stocks and the organisation will also come within the ambit of property. Hence, it satisfied the first condition, viz., holding property under a trust or legal obligation. The restrictive clause "not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit" qualifies or governs the fourth category of charitable purposes mentioned in the definition given in section 2(15), viz. , "the advancement of any other object of general public utility". It is the object of general public utility and not its advancement or accomplishment which must not involve the carrying on of any activity for profit. The object of the assessee-association was admittedly object of general public utility. The Tribunal had held that this object involved the carrying on of an activity for profit.

3. The law is well settled that if there are several objects of a trust or institution, some charitable and some non-charitable and the trustees or the managers in their discretion can apply the income or property to any of those objects, the trust or institution would not be liable to be regarded as charitable and no part of its income would be exempt from tax. If, however, its primary or the dominant purpose is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but just merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purposes, would not prevent the trust or the institution from being a valid charitable trust.

In the instant case, the assessee's aforementioned objects were both charitable and non-charitable. Its objects, inter alia, of encouraging industry and improving the breeding of cattle, etc., could not be described as charitable purposes. Since all its objects appear to enjoy an equal status and stand on the same footing and since its trustee could apply the income to any of those objects, it could not be regarded as charitable and no part of its income was exempt. The Tribunal had also found that none of the objects was dominant in nature. No definite part of the business or of its income was related to charitable purposes only.

4. Hence, the holding of agricultural and industrial exhibition and cattle fair involved an activity for profit, within the meaning of section 2(15) and that the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a). Further, the assessee could not be said to have held property under trust within the meaning of section 11(1)(b) and, consequently, was not eligible for exemption thereunder in respect of amounts actually spent on charities.

The natural corollary that followed was that the income derived from such transactions could not be called an income from the business. Assuming that it was a business as contemplated under section 2(13), the same was exempted under section 11. Further, the submission that the income would be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust could not also be disbelieved. [Para 12] The licence to run races and betting itself could be treated as property and the said property was obtained with the consent of the Hyderabad Race Club. The term ‘property’ itself has got widest import for income-tax purposes and inclusive of holding a licence. But, it is not every case of business which can be treated as property. If it were to be so treated, section 13(1)(bb) would lose its meaning. It may be that a business itself may be settled in trust of the trustees who may conduct a business on their own under the powers given to them in the trust deed. In the instant case, it was difficult to accept that the assessee-trust was conducting the business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter-venue betting for few occasions in a year. Thus, there could not be any doubt that the income derived by the trust for the relevant assessment years was from the property held under trust and as such it was exempted under section 11.

Assuming even if it was not treated as income from the property held under the trust, it could be treated as voluntary contribution given by the Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee-trust as contemplated under section 12. The conduct of the Hyderabad Race Club in respect of the transaction was only a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contributions could be characterized only as a capital receipt in the assessee’s hands. Thus, it could not be held that there had been business in the normal sense in such arrangement and in the facts and circumstances, it was not such a business which would be hit by section 13(1)(bb). It was only an activity which could constitute the property or an arrangement involved in transfer of funds from Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee’s institution in a form recognized by law and not shown to be colourable exercise or otherwise as contended by the revenue. Since it could not be said to be a business and the income derived could not be said to be a business income, the provisions of section 13(1)(bb) were not attracted. The assessee-trust was an institution, which satisfied the conditions under section 2(15), read with section 11 and as such, conclusion reached by the Tribunal should be upheld. [Para 13]

None of the objects of the trust could be said to be non-charitable in nature. Rather the objects of the trust were purely of a charitable nature. The main objects of the trust were advancement and propagation of education, medical aid and relief to the poor. In fact, promotion of sports and games was also one of the charitable objects. Merely because a discretion was vested in the trustees to utilize the income for any one or more of the objects would not make any difference. Since there was no payment of club’s funds to the trust, there was no scope for the retrieval of the funds of the race club from the assessee-trust. Thus, it satisfied the test that the objects of the trust were not only charitable in nature, but also of general public utility and as such, attracted the provisions of section 11 and, therefore, the income derived by the trust was exempted under section 11. [Para 14]

Thus, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the assessee was an institution which satisfied the conditions of section 2(15), read with section 11 and the derived income was from the property held under the trust and even otherwise, it could only be treated as a voluntary contribution given by the Hyderabad Race Club and it could not be said that the activities carried on by the assessee constituted a business and even if it were to be a business, it was not such a business as would be hit by section 13(1)(bb). [Para 15]
