■ A perusal of section 13 would indicate that if the assessee society has availed the services or purchased any object from any specified person contemplated in sub-clause (3) and paid to such specified person in excess of what may be paid reasonably for such service in open market, then excess would be disallowed. In other words, for example, if assessee society has availed the services of an Engineer who happened to be a specified person under sub-clause (3) and paid him the service charges which he could not command in the open market, then such excess amount will be disallowed to the assessee and benefit of Section 11 would not be available on such an amount. It will be taxable. For example, assessee can purchase an item for Rs.100 but from a specified person, it has purchased at Rs.120, then this excess Rs.20 will be added to the taxable income of the assessee and benefit of section 11 will not be available to the assessee Society. A perusal of the complete assessment order reveals that Assessing Officer has nowhere made analysis of the remuneration/ honorarium paid to the members of the Management Committee vis-à-vis their services utilized for the benefit of the Society. All the persons are qualified persons, they have devoted their time for managing the affairs of the Society and it has paid only honorarium, not regular salary. Similarly, it has provided traveling facility to them which was only for fulfilling the objects of the Society. In other words, in assessment year 2015-16, a little higher amount is being incurred by the assessee because the member of the Management Committee has to travel outside India for inspection of a plane which was to be used in Aviation Wing of the Engineering College. The Assessing Officer has not examined this aspect as to how this type of facilities can be availed from the open market and the price of such services. He has simply narrated that these persons are gainfully implied in their other activities also and therefore, payment of honorarium to these persons is not in accordance with law. This cannot be a logic for denying the benefit to them. The intention of the section is not as such. It is the assessee who has to manage its affairs and to decide what is necessary for its functioning. The Assessing Officer can only examine whether excess is being paid or not, but he has not carried out any Investigation in that area. The Assessing Officer has not assigned any reason as to why he is departing from the principle of consistency where such honorarium has been allowed to these per sons. Similarly Traveling Expenses has been allowed to the assessee in earlier years. The Commissioner (Appeals) failed to record any finding qua this aspect in right perspective and blindly up held the assessment order. Therefore, all these grounds of appeal are allowed.[Para 12.1]

headnotes.text: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1946-47 to 1948-49 - Assessee executed a deed of trust whereby they settled certain amount on various charities and appointed themselves as trustees - Later, in accordance with terms of trust deed, trustees assessees were appointed as managing agents of a company - Before Income-tax authorities, trustee claimed that income derived from managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Revenue authorities, however, held that income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Whether word "property" in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend "business," and if question fell to be decided solely on terms of that sub-section, managing agency formed by assessees/trustees must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether fact that trustees had option at any time to throw up managing agency was no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether section 4(3)(i) relates to income from business held under trust and section 4(3)(ia) relates to income from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution where that business itself is not held on trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where business of managing agency was held in trust, it could be concluded that business carried on by trustees fell under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Denial of exemption) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee-trust was conducting its activities in carrying out charitable activities, i.e., education, relief to poor, etc. - During year, assessee purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing funds of assessee-trust and same was registered in name of managing trustee - Assessing Officer denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to extent of value of that vehicle on ground that objects of assessee trust were carrying out of charitable activities and fund collected for this charitable purposes was utilized for enjoyment of trustees by means of purchase of said vehicle in name of managing trustee which was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c) - Assessee submitted that car was purchased in name of managing trustee for simple reason that it gave relief by way of lower road/life tax and insurance charges - However, assessee could not prove as to what use this asset was put to by trust in work of trust and for purposes for which trust had been set up - Whether since assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased by assessee-trust with its funds and registered in name of managing trustee - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]

Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Denial of exemption) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee-trust was conducting its activities in carrying out charitable activities, i.e., education, relief to poor, etc. - During year, assessee purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing funds of assessee-trust and same was registered in name of managing trustee - Assessing Officer denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to extent of value of that vehicle on ground that objects of assessee trust were carrying out of charitable activities and fund collected for this charitable purposes was utilized for enjoyment of trustees by means of purchase of said vehicle in name of managing trustee which was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c) - Assessee submitted that car was purchased in name of managing trustee for simple reason that it gave relief by way of lower road/life tax and insurance charges - However, assessee could not prove as to what use this asset was put to by trust in work of trust and for purposes for which trust had been set up - Whether since assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased by assessee-trust with its funds and registered in name of managing trustee - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing its funds and same was registered in name of managing trustee, however, assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased

II - Section 11 of Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 2008-09 - Whether where for purpose of set up an educational institution assessee and trust purchased agricultural land as trust cannot purchase agricultural land, funds were routed through one of trustees, no adverse inference could be drawn - Held, yes - Whether where managing trustees were paid much higher in comparison to Principal and other staff whose activities were confined to their rank while these trustees had versatile experience, administrative and managerial skill and by their unstinted efforts and far-sightedness they were managing students, carrying on other administrative work, coordinating with government agencies, higher payment made to them could not be doubted - Held, yes - Whether since these trustees had to commute on day-to-day basis to various Government agencies, and other allied places which were scattered all over vast city of Ahmedabad, this cannot be branded at any stretch of imagination that trustees had been provided with excessive amenities - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, on these grounds exemption could not be denied to assessee-trust - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Property held under trust) - Assessment years 1987-88, 1991-92, 1997-98, 1998-99, 2006-07 and 2008-09 to 2014-2015 - Whether once income of a trust is used by it to acquire a property, property so acquired will be property held under trust and income from such property will be income from property under trust - Held, yes - Assessee society was having income from two Kalyanamandapams - According to Assessing Officer these properties were not settled by settlor as trust property and hence could not be considered as properties held under trust and thus he held that income earned by assessee from its Kalyanamandapams could not be treated as income from house property but only as income from business - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld order of Assessing Officer holding that Kalyanamandapams having being built by assessee subsequent to its formation could not be considered as property under trust - However, assessee submitted that land on which Kalyanamandapams were built was part of original settlement and buildings were built therein by assessee from its income - Whether thus, rental income received by assessee from Kalyanamandapams though it was in nature of income from business, such income was nothing but income from property held under trust - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT: Property (i.e. Kalyanamandapams) built by assessee society from its income, subsequent to its formation, on land, which was part of original settlement, was to be considered as property under trust and income therefrom was income from property under trust  IT: Where predominant activity of assessee society was charity, it would be eligible for exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1951-52 to 1954-55 - A partnership firm was formed by four brothers - Firm was appointed as chief agent of an insurance company - Subsequently, brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming trustees would hold said business of chief agency of said company and all benefits and profits to arise from said business upon trust for public charitable purposes - Whether principal agency conducted by assessee-trust was a business and, therefore, "property" within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which was capable of being settled upon trust - Held, yes - Whether income of assessee-trust not being one which was not governed by proviso to section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as amended by Act 25 of 1953, but was governed by operative part of section 4(3)(i), it was exempt from tax - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income form property held under - Assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60 - Assessee was an association of persons - Constitution of assessee revealed that neither standing committee nor managing committee nor even members of assessee could use property of assessee for any purpose except that covered by object clause of assessee - Neither before ITO nor before AAC any contention was raised by revenue that object for which assessee was constituted was not charitable one - Whether property of assessee was held under trust or under legal obligation and, therefore, assessee was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Business expenditure-Assessee-company was trustee of religious and charitable trust-ITO paid management charges to an association for managing its affairs-ITO and ACC rejected claim for deduction of such charges paid-Tribunal allowed assessee's claim-Whether tribunal right in law-Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religions trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1990-91 and 1991-92 - Where a particular clause of trust deed empowered trust to start educational agencies for earning income to achieve aims and objects of trust and Tribunal had further found that surplus was transferred to trust and utilized in purchase of land and construction of sabha bhavan, merely because assessee started an educational agency to earn income, it could not be said that it was running business so as to attract section 11(4A) [In favour of assessee]

SECTION 11, READ WITH SECTION 2(15), OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CHARITABLE OR RELIGOUS TRUST-EXEMPTION OF INCOME FROM PROPERTY HELD UNDER-ASSESSEE-TRUST WITH OBJECTS AS STATED UNDER HEADING ‘CHARITABLE OR RELIGIOUS PURPOSE’ WAS REGISTERED UNDER THE BOMBAY PUBLIC TRUST ACT-COMMISSIONER CERTIFIED THAT IT WAS AN INSTITUTION/ FUND ESTABLISHED IN TAXABLE TERRITORIES FOR CHARITABLE PURPOSE-BUT FOR A CERTAIN CENTRE OF MANAGEMENT STUDIES WAIVING AMOUNT DUE TO IT FOR PARTICIPATING IN PROGRAM SPONSORED BY ASSESSEE WITH ITS COLLABORATION, THERE WOULD HAVE BEEN PRACTICALLY NO INCOME TO ASSESSEE TAKING ALL RELEVANT ASSESSMENT YEARS INTO CONSIDERATION BECAUSE SURPLUS IN TWO YEARS 1976-77 AND 1977-78 WOULD HAVE BEEN OFFSET BY DEFICITS OF IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING AND SUCCEEDING YEARS-WHETHER PREDOMINANT OBJECT OF ASSESSEE WAS TO CARRY OUT OBJECT OF GENERAL PUBLIC UTILITY WITH A VIEW TO SUBSERVE CHARITABLE PURPOSE RATHER THAN TO EARN PROFIT AND, THEREFORE, ASSESSEE WAS ENTITLED TO EXEMPTION UNDER SECTION 11-HELD, YES.

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether where assessee-trust had incurred expenses from charity fund and they were in excess 
of income earned, it was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a) - Held, yes

Section 13, read with sections 11 and 12, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Related party transaction) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-trust operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital - In order to address financial difficulties faced by assessee, it entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) involved in healthcare sector, for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to SCPL - In return, assessee would receive either a fixed amount of Rs. 1 crore or 40 per cent of SCPL's profit, whichever was higher, as management fees - Assessing Officer was of view that said agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for benefit of related parties - Consequently, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied - It was noted that object of transfer agreement with SCPL was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally, and in doing so, purpose of charity was not violated as a reputed hospital of such huge size required professional handling - Further, agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable property to SCPL but to counter huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals - Whether, on facts, there was no infirmity in order of Commissioner (Appeals) in allowing exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 13, read with section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption - Whether manager of a trust can be treated as manager of institution referred to in clause (cc) of sub-section (3) of section 13 - Held, no - Whether 'trust' and 'institution' referred to in section 13 are different entities - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in holding that there was no violation of section 13 by assessee-trust in advancing money to its manager to warrant denial of benefit of section 11 - Held, yes

Section 11, read with section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income, from property held under - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessing Officer disallowed exemption claimed by assessee-
 trust under section 11 on two grounds, namely, (a) that even though assessee’s buildings were being used by other societies of same group for charitable activities, such use could not be treated as use by assessee for carrying out its own charitable activities; and (b) that major expenditure was on account of agricultural and dairy activities carried on by it which was not in nature of application of its income for charitable purpose - Commissioner (Appeals), however, upheld assessee’s claim - Whether where buildings of assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature, such use could very well be treated as use by assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for purpose of exemption under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether since agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by assessee-society as separate business activities, same constituted ‘property held under trust’ as provided in section 11(4) and in any case income of said activities was to be determined after deducting expenditure incurred in connection with said business - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, gross income being more than sufficient to cover expenses incurred in connection with said activities, allowance of same by Commissioner  (Appeals) as application of its income hardly made any difference in ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to revenue - Held, yes
Circulars and Instructions - CBDT’s Circular No. 1132, dated 5-1-1978

Section 5(i), read with section 21A, of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957 - Exemption - Property held by charitable trust - Whether assessee-trust was entitled to exemption under section 5(1)(i) and not liable to tax under section 21A - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether for running a charitable activity, establishment has to be maintained, which requires payment of salaries and other establishment expenses and application of income for said purpose cannot be alien to charitable objects which are to be advanced - Held, yes - Whether nature of regulatory mechanism operated by market committees involves incurring of expenditure on establishment and mere fact that such an expenditure has been incurred, cannot be a ground to hold that application of income was not for charitable purpose - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Religious or charitable trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies created a trust and purported to endow it with share held by him in certain transport companies - Contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately but companies in which N was interested were to have benefit of assets set apart by him - N was managing trustee and empowered to borrow to any extent on properties conveyed to trust not only for trust but for his own use trustees were empowered, so long as N held office of managing trustee, to sell immovable properties belonging to trust for purpose of floating other companies - Foundation of institution was apparently to be left over until companies had made sufficient money for purpose - N also reserved right to revoke trust at any time - Whether on facts properties in question were not held under trust for charitable purpose within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 13, read with  section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Sub-section (1)(c))- Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee-trust invested funds in a company where its trustee was managing director and his wife was a director - Whether it was a clear case of violation under section 13(1)(c) and assessee would not be entitled to exemption under section 11 - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee-turst invested funds in a company in which its trustee was managing director and his wife was a director, it was a case of violation of section 13(1)(c) and exemption under section 11 would not be available to assessee  IT : Where capital gain earned by assessee-trust became non-exempt under section 11 due to contravention of section 13(1)(c), such capital gain would be taxed at maximum marginal rate in terms of section 164(2) and benefit of section 112 could not be given to it

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable of religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 2006-07 - Where certain immovable properties of assessee-trust were held by another organization 'IFA' registered under section 12A, for benefit of assessee and during relevant assessment year when said properties were sold, sale consideration along with interest was returned by IFA to assessee, it could not be said that assessee had effected revocable transfer and, therefore, was not entitled to exemption under section 11 [In favour of assessee]

Section 11, read with section 13(1)(c)(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1978-79, 1979-80 and 1980-81 - Two cinemas, being property of assessee-trust, were given on hire to a company - Company further gave management and control of cinemas to a firm which consisted of two partners being wife and son of trustee of assessee-trust - Whether income of trust property was diverted to prohibited persons and, thus, exemption of income of trust derived from these cinemas was hit by provisions contained in section 13(1)(c)(ii) - Held, no.

Section 11, read with sections 2(15), 10(20) and 12A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961  - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessee was a Statutory Authority established under provisions of Gujarat Maritime Board Act, 1981 for predominant purpose of development of minor ports within State of Gujarat - Management and control of assessee was essentially with State Government having no profit motive - Whether assessee was not precluded from claiming exemption under section 11(1) in light of definition of words 'charitable purposes' as defined under section 2(15), even if it had ceased to be a local authority under section 10(20) - Held, yes

Section 5(1)(i) of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957 - Exemptions - Charitable trust - According to trust deed, if settlor left no wife or children, trust properties were to be applied for such charitable purpose as might be decided upon by trustees - Whether having regard to specific provision in trust deed, discretion given to trustee was not to choose any purpose, but only purposes which were charitable for which trust properties and income therefrom could be utilised - Held, yes - Whether mandate in trust deed was clear that properties of trust should be applied solely for charitable purposes and assessee-trust was entitled to exemption notwithstanding discretion given to trustees to choose from various charitable purposes - Held, yes

II. Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Computation of exemption) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Whether where assessee-trust incurred administrative and establishment expenses, same were to be treated as part of application of income for charitable activities and, thus, accumulation under section 11(1)(a) was to be worked out by taking gross receipts in place of net receipts - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Trust deed of a trust provided that income of trust fund should be applied for benefit of any of past, present and future officers, members of staff and other employees of company ‘A’, or of any company within the management of company A, and their dependents of whatever race or class who in uncontrolled discretion of Administrators shall be deserving of consideration or help, more especially on account of indigence, ill-health or other necessitous circumstances on their retirement - By a supplementary deed, administrators were directed to pay more regard to indigence or ill-health or other specially necessitous circumstances of person or persons whose cases were being considered rather than to length of service - Whether use of fund to relieve a person from ‘some other special necessitous circumstances’ could not be said to be for relief of poverty - Held, yes - Whether further, since fund was for benefit of employees of only company ‘A’ and their subsidiary concerns, fund was not property held in trust wholly for charitable purposes - Held, yes

Section 13, read with sections 11 and 12 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Benefit to specified persons) - Assessment years 2003-04 to 2008-09 - Assessee a registered charitable organization carried on work of education through four members, who worked in dual capacity i.e. as whole time administrators, as also regular time teachers, and were being paid salaries from earning of these schools - Members were not being paid separately for managerial work done by them - Members were also furnishing their income tax returns regularly as individuals and were duly showing their income received as salaries from assessee and their said returns had also been continuously accepted by revenue - Assessee was availing benefit of exemption of its income under sections 11 and 12 - Tribunal partially affirmed salaries paid to two of trustee members and rejected claim of assessee with regard to two others - Assessee claimed that once it was registered as a charitable organization and its accounts were being accepted since very beginning, it was entitled to benefits of exemption - It further claimed that all four members had not only huge teaching experience to their credit but were also whole time employees of assessee and thus were closely associated with management as also in running of schools of assessee - It also claimed that completion of assessment against assessee as a normal business entity was also wrong and misfounded - Whether since assessee trust/society was pursuing an object of general public utility, conclusion drawn by Assessing Officer that petitioner-society was not a charitable society was misfounded - Held, yes - Whether all four members were engaged in whole time management activities of Trust and were also rendering administrative functions qua running of schools for which they were not being paid any extra salary - Held, yes - Whether thus, there was no violation of provisions of section 13(2)(c) and assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11 - Held, yes [Paras 32, 39  40] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where all members of assessee-trust were engaged in whole time management activities of Trust and as regular time teachers and were being paid salaries from earning of these schools and were not being paid any extra salary for management work, there was no violation of provisions of section 13(2)(c) and assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11

Section 11, read with sections 12AA and 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1990-91 to 1993-94 and 1999-2000 - Assessee society was formed for benefit of local people, upliftment of poor, education and other social and charitable activities - A land was given by District Collector to assessee, to construct a kalyana mandapam on specific condition that it should function for benefit of local people, mainly weavers and agriculturists - Accordingly, assessee constructed a kalyana mandapam and collected minimum nominal charges from users to meet maintenance, repairs and renovation expenses - Exemption claimed by it under section 11 was denied by Assessing Officer on ground that assessee had not undertaken any charitable activity since its inception except constructing and running a marriage hall, which was purely a commercial activity and did not have any charity involved in it - Whether by constructing kalyana mandapam and letting out same after collecting nominal rent to meet maintenance, repairs and renovation expenses sufficiently satisfied object, viz., benefit of local people, mainly weavers and agriculturists, which was condition under grant given by Collector - Held, yes - Whether failure or non-diversion of accumulated funds for any other charitable purpose by itself would not divest right conferred on assessee to claim exemption under section 11 - Held, yes
Circulars and Notification : CBDT Circular No. 762, dated 18-2-1998

SECTION 11 OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CHARITABLE OR RELIGIOUS TRUST
-EXEMPTION OF INCOME FROM PROPERTY HELD UNDER TRUST-TRUST 
CREATED BY SETTLING A RUNNING BUSINESS WITH OBJECT OF APPLYING ENTIRE INCOME FOR BENEFIT OF TWO OTHER PUBLIC CHARITABLE TRUSTS-WHETHER EXEMPTION COULD BE DENIED SINCE TRUST WAS CARRYING ON BUSINESS-HELD, 
ON FACTS, NO-WHETHER ITO WAS RIGHT IN CONSTRUING THAT ONLY CASH PAYMENTS COULD BE TREATED AS APPLICATION OF INCOME-HELD, ON FACTS, 
NO

Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under [Business held in trust] - Assessment year 1977-78 - Whether even if business of insurance was carried out by assessee-society for carrying on primary purpose of charitable activities in accordance with aims and objects of trust, assessee would still be entitled to exemption - Held, yes [Para 9][In favour of assessee]IT : Where income from business was applied for charity as per aims and objects of assessee-society, its income will be exempt

SECTION 11 OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CHARITABLE OR RELIGIOUS TRUST-EXEMPTION OF INCOME FROM PROPERTY HELD UNDER-MEMBERS OF ASSESSEE-SOCIETY WERE EMPLOYEES OF A PRIVATE ORGANISATION- THE OBJECTS OF THE SOCIETY INCLUDED SPORTS, RECREATION, CULTURAL ACTIVITIES AND REPRESENTATION OF BONA FIDE GRIEVANCES TO THE MANAGEMENT BESIDES OTHER OBJECTIVES LIKE FINANCIAL AID TO MEMBERS- WHETHER MEMBERS OF SOCIETY DID NOT CONSTITUTE A SECTION OF PUBLIC AND COULD NOT BE TREATED AS A CHARITABLE TRUST-HELD, YES

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Three different amounts for three different purposes and an immovable property was settled on assessee-trust - It was provided in trust deed that income, profits and interest from one of aforesaid amounts and premises were to be utilised for maintenance, up-keep and improvement of aforesaid premises - It was also mentioned in trust deed that trustees had power to amalgamate such contributions or donations either with corpus or income, profits and interest income of trust premises or trust - Income received from aforesaid premises, which became surplus after meeting maintenance expenses, etc., was to be spent for charitable purposes described under trust deed - Whether such expenditure on charitable purposes out of income from trust premises was exempt under section 11 - Held, yes.

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with section 19 of Bombay Trust Act, 1950 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1964-65 to 1969-70, 1972-73 and 1973-74 - Lands of some villages were said to have been granted by one Mughal Emperor for upkeep of Roza in year 1670 under a Sanad and grants were confirmed by sanads issued during British regime - A suo motu enquiry was started under section 19 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 - As a result of that inquiry, Dy. Charity Commissioner made an order directing that assessee- Roza Trust be registered as a Public Trust - On appeal Charity Commissioner confirmed order of Dy. Charity Commissioner - He held that assessee-trust was a public trust and lands of villages were properties of said trust - Question for consideration was as to whether income from lands in question was income of assessee-Roza Trust assessable in hands of said trust and exempt under section 11 or whether it was assessable in hands of Sajjadanashin of Trust i.e., ‘SM’, as income from his private property - Tribunal on material before it, which included orders made by Dy. Charity Commissioner and Charity Commissioner, documents such as Sanad issued by Mughal Emperor and Sanads of Government, Survey Settlement register and historical account given in text-books, came to finding that these lands of four villages belonged to assessee-trust - Whether while it is true that tax authority, during assessment proceedings, can always inquire into question of ownership of property and decide issue in context of relevant provisions of said Act, in order to ascertain income of the assessee for bringing it to tax, it will not be open for tax authorities to ignore relevant evidence of statutory registration of a public trust and fact of the properties having been registered as properties of such public trust under provisions of Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 - Held, yes - Whether finding of Charity Commissioner in an inquiry 
under section 19 of Bombay Public Trust operates as findings in rem and cannot be ignored by authorities under Income-tax Act - Held, yes - Whether Sajjadanashin of Roza Trust was spiritual leader and integral part of Roza Trust and, therefore, provision for Sajjadanashin was not a provision for man but for institution and therefore, expenses incurred on 
 Sajjadanashin by assessee-trust could not be held to be expenses for private property - Held, yes - Whether Tribunal was justified in holding that income from lands in question was assessable in hands of assessee-trust and not in hands of Sajjadanashin and further that trust was entitled to exemption in respect of income spent as ‘Madad-E-Maash’ on maintenance of Sajjadanashin, his family and descendants - Held, yes - Whether amount received by Sajjadanashin was to be taxed as income in his hands - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under trust (Business held in trust) - Assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95, 2001-02 and 2005-06 to 2007-08 - Assessee-trust was created with objects of establishing and maintaining of schools, colleges and study circles, advancing education and research study on modern and ancient Indian thought, etc. - After formation of trust, a business was commenced in name of trust for manufacture of katha - Assessee claimed exemption under section 11 in respect of its income and filed a return of income on that basis - Assessing Officer denied exemption - High Court by impugned order held that since katha business was commenced by trustees with aid and assistance of borrowings from sister concerns it could not be case of 'property being held under trust' within meaning of section 11(4) but would only be a case of business being carried on by and on behalf of trust and mere fact that whole or some part of income from katha business was earmarked for application of charitable objects would not render business itself being considered as incidental to attainment of objects of trust - Whether Special Leave Petition filed against impugned order was to be granted - Held, yes [Paras 19 to 22] [In favour of assessee]IT: SLP granted against High Court's ruling that where business was commenced by trustees with aid and assistance of borrowings from sister concerns, it could not be a case of 'property being held under trust'

III. Section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Sub-section (3)) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Whether provisions of section 13(3)(cc) would not extend to manager (or her spouse) of trust - Held, yes [Para 11.1] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) – Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under – Assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56 – Claim of assessee trust for exemption of its income under section 4(3)(i) was rejected by ITO on ground that business of trust carried on by managing trustee on behalf of trust fell within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and hence its business income was not exempt from taxation – Whether where trust carries on business and business itself is held in trust and income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for purpose of religious or charitable character, conditions prescribed under section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and income is exempt from taxation - Held, yes – Whether claim of exemption cannot be denied even if business were to be conducted by someone else acting on behalf of trust, and proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to such businesses as are not held under trust and, therefore, field of its operation is distinct and separate from that covered by main provision of section 4(3)(i) – Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid legal position, assessee being a religious and charitable trust, was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act for assessment years in question – Held, yes

Section 11 [corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922], read with  section 2(14), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religions trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1968-69 - Whether where business of Kuris (unit fund) was itself held by assessee under a trust for religious or charitable purpose, it could not be said that business was conducted 'on behalf of' religious or charitable institution to advance any object of general public utility and therefore, income derived by assessee from Kuris was exempt from taxation was exempt from taxation under section 11(1)(a) - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Application of income) - Assessment year 2008-09 - High Court by impugned order held that where assessee-trust incurred expenditure in excess of income in previous year relevant to assessment year for charitable purposes, out of accumulated charity fund, it could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(a) in respect of income of previous year relevant to assessment year, which had been admittedly applied for charitable purposes - Whether Special Leave Petition filed against impugned order was to be granted - Held, yes [Para 2] [In favour of revenue]IT : SLP granted against High Court's ruling that merely because assessee-trust incurred expenditure in excess of income in relevant previous year for charitable purposes out of accumulated charity fund, it could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(a)

SECTION 11 OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CHARITABLE OR RELIGIOUS 
TRUST-EXEMPTION OF INCOME FROM PROPERTY HELD UNDER TRUST-
WHETHER HANDING OVER OF ACCUMULATED INCOME TO ANOTHER CHARIT-
ABLE TRUST WOULD AMOUNT TO APPLICATION OF INCOME FOR CHARITABLE PURPOSES-HELD, YES

Section 13,  read with section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption [Sub-section (1)(b)] - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-society was formed with object to promote, sustain and carry out programmes and activities of Church, which were, among others, educational, charitable, religious, social and cultural etc. - It was registered under section 12A - Assessee filed return claiming exemption of income under section 11 - Revenue authorities opined that even if society's activities were for both charitable and religious purposes, since it was for benefit of one religious community alone section 13(1)(b) would be attracted and it could not be granted exemption under section 11 - Tribunal, on basis of documents submitted by assessee, found that priests were not managing affairs of society - It was also noted that activities of assessee-society, though both religious and charitable, were not exclusively meant for one particular religious community - Tribunal thus allowed assessee's claim for exemption of income - Whether findings recorded by Tribunal being findings of fact, no substantial question of law arose therefrom - Held, yes [Paras 15 and 16][In favour of assessee]IT: Assessee-society formed with object to promote, sustain and carry out programmes and activities of Church, was eligible to claim exemption under section 11

Section 11, read with section 13(1)(c), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessee-trust owned properties which were settled by L and H, who were joint owners thereof - Assessee had leased out aforesaid property to a company on a rent of Rs. 4,000 per month for purpose of residence of P, who was managing director of company and husband of L and father of H-ITO held that premises in question could fetch a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month and, hence, the assessee had allowed the trust property being used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of the authors of the trust and their relatives under section 13(1)(c), read with section 13(2)(b) - Whether in view of fact that property in question was governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act and standard rent of property was below Rs. 4,000 there was no direct or indirect benefit to authors of assessee and their relatives and, therefore, assessee was entitled to exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1961-62 to 1963-64 - An association of persons, chiefly engaged in horse racing, declared and made a trust - As per said trust deed, surplus funds were to be disposed of, (i) by making improvements to racing facilities, and/or (ii) by making donations at discretion of trustees to any recognised institution for social, cultural and physical benefits of people - Whether surplus funds really emanated from a property which was not a subject-matter of trust and as such in absence of any legal obligation fastened thereto, no exemption could be allowed under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether further, since trustees had indefeasible alternative right to apply funds to other purposes, without making any donation to charitable purposes no part of its income was exempt from tax - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from properties held under - Assessment year 1956-57 - By an indenture of trust, ‘D’ and his wife both doctors, settled upon trust an immovable property and two maternity hospitals which were run by them - Primary object of trust was to carry on and promote educational, health, cultural, social and economic interest of people particularly of backward and lower classes - Substance of indenture of trust itself was that all trust properties were transferred by both settlers to trustees and trustees made declaration that they would hold properties for objects of trust from date of deed - One of recitals clearly indicated that it was business of conducting two maternity homes that had been settled upon trust, because net annual income which was to accrue to trust from said hospitals to be arrived at after deducting all expenses for maintaining and running hospitals and after making payment to ‘D,’ s wife as provided in trust deed for managing said hospitals for and on behalf of trust during her lifetime - Whether as trust deed was duly registered it was sufficient in law to effect a valid transfer - Held, yes - Whether since business of running and conducting maternity homes itself was settled upon trust, conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act were fulfilled and, hence income from maternity homes was exempt from taxation - Held, yes - Whether for conducting maternity hospitals presence of a doctor was essential and therefore, amount paid to wife of ‘D’ was a part of normal expenditure of conducting and managing said hospitals which was allowable as admissible deduction in computation of income of trust in hands of trustees as association of persons - Held, yes

Section 11 of the income-tax act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether on facts under head ‘charitable purpose - meaning of’, assessee could be allowed exemption under section 11 - Held, no

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 2006-07 - Whether benefit of accumulation upto 15 per cent of income should be calculated with reference to total receipts of charitable institution and not with reference to net income worked out for assessment being balance amount worked out after allowing deduction for administrative and other expenses - Held, yes

Section 11(1)(a), read with sections 11(4) and 28(iii), of the Income-tax act, 1961-charitable or religious trust-exemption of income from property held under trust-objects of assessee, a registered society, included promotion and development of hosiery industry and it used to procure, allocate and distribute to its members woollen hosiery yarn on no-profit-no-loss basis-assessee used to charge subscription, and allocation charges from its members-before tribunal, assessee claimed allocation charges received by it to be exempt from tax-whether tribunal correct in holding that although assessee's activity fell within the definition of "charitable purposes", yet its income was covered by section 28(iii) and was not income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) and was hence not entitled to exemption-held, on facts, no

Section 13(2)(h), read with section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Withdrawal of exemption - Assessee had constituted a trust and corpus of trust was invested in a partnership firm in which he had substantial interest - Whether in view of section 13(2)(h) interest derived from trust property was not exempt - Held, yes
Words and phrases - Expression 'fund' occurring in section 13(2)(h) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under Assessment year 1984-85 - Whether donation made by a charitable trust to another charitable trust would tantamount to application of income for charitable purposes and, hence, was eligible for exemption - Held, yes - Whether assessee, a charitable trust, was exempt, from tax, under section 11(1A), on capital gains arising from sale of certain immovable property held by it - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Application of income) - Assessment year 2008-09 - High Court by impugned held that where assessee, a charitable trust, incurred expenditure in excess of income in previous year relevant to assessment year for charitable purposes, out of accumulated charity fund, it could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(a) - Whether Special Leave Petition filed against impugned order was to be granted - Held, yes [Para 2] [In favour of revenue]IT : SLP granted against High Court's ruling that where assessee, a charitable trust, incurred expenditure in excess of income in previous year relevant to assessment year for charitable purposes, out of accumulated charity fund, it could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(a)

Section 11, read with section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Tribunal held that provisions of section 13(2)(h) were not applicable to assessee's case and thus exempted assessee from tax under section 11, in respect of income arising to it from interest on FD's and property donated by 'S' – Whether in view of decision in CIT v. Sir Sobha Singh Public Charitable Trust, [2001] 250 ITR 475 (Delhi), Tribunal was justified in so holding – Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1984-85 and 1985-86 - Whether expression ‘the business is mainly carried on by the beneficiaries of the institution’ in section 11(4A)(B), as it stood prior to 1-4-1992, would only mean that the activities of the business are mainly managed and controlled by the beneficiaries of the institution; it is not necessary that each and every beneficiary should personally condudct the business of assessee institution ; expression only means that the work in connection with the business of the trust or institution should not be carried on by outsiders or agents or managers or by strangers, who are not the trustees or the beneficiaries - Held, yes

facts.text:
'P; 'L' and 'LS' executed a deed of trust whereby they settled a sum on various charities specified therein and appointed themselves and two others as trustees. The trust deed provided inter alia that the trustees mights with the help of the trust fund, for and on behalf of and for the benefit of the trust, carry on such business including the taking up and conducting the managing agency or selling agency of any company in such name or names as they in their absolute discretion might think fit and proper. Later the trustees were appointed as managing agents of a company. The agency was to be for a period of 20 years; but it was open to the trustees to throw it up on giving three months' notice. The managing agents were to get a remuneration of 10 per cent of the net annual profits. Before the Income-tax authorities, the assessee/trustees claimed that the income derived from the managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The Income-tax authorities held that the income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court held that no part of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which was the only property settled on trust was actually invested in the managing agency business, which could not, therefore, be regarded as trust property, and that the income received from that business was not within the exemption enacted in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

Under a trust deed dated the 15-6-1945, according to the decision of the Privy Council the business of a managing agency was held in trust. Therefore, the income derived from managing agency was held by the Supreme Court as falling with section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act since the word "property" in that sub-section includes business as well. But it was contended before the Supreme Court that although the income might appear to fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act has been narrowed down by the provision in section 4(3)(ia) which deals with income from business and, therefore, the Sub-section that really applies to the determination of the question as to whether the income sought to be taxed in the hands of the trustees was exempt from tax in section 4(3)(ia) and not section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. It was common ground that if section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act was the section under which the exemption claimed was to be determined, the conditions laid down in that sub-section for the purpose of granting an exemption were not satisfied and, therefore, the assessees would not be entitled to an exemption. The question was, therefore, of vital importance to the assessees as to whether their case fell within section 4(3)(i) of section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act.

On reference:

■

The assessee-trust was carrying out charitable activities like education, relief to poor, etc.

■

The Assessing Officer found that a vehicle purchased by the trust was registered in the name of the managing trustee and thus, the case of the Assessing Officer was that the assessee purchased the above said vehicle and registered in the name of the trustee was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c). Further, the case of the Assessing Officer was that the income or property of the assessee was diverted in favour of the managing trustee of the assessee and it was a clear violation as per clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 13 read with section 13(1)(c). The assessee explained that the car was purchased in the name of the managing trustee with the sole objective of saving considerable amount of road tax and insurance. However, the Assessing Officer rejected the explanation and denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to the extent of value of that car.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the view of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

‘N’ was the karta of a joint Hindu family. The joint family properties included a building which had been set apart for use of pilgrims visiting the town. Subsequently the family properties were partitioned under a partition deed between ‘N’ and his adopted son, ‘R’ as also minor, ‘D’ the adopted some of his pre-deceased son. Under that partition the building in question was directed to be maintained by ‘N’ with the income from certain lands over which he had been given a life-interest. Later on N died. At the time of his death he was a partner in the firm having a 3/16th share in the profits and losses of the said firm. The accountable persons filed an estate duty return admitting a net dutiable estate including the share capital and the share of profit and interest of the deceased in the managing agency firm, but did not include the value of the share of the deceased in the goodwill of the said managing agency firm. It also did not include the value of the building. The Assistant Controller of Estate Duty, however, proposed to value of building at Rs. 62,000 and 3/16th share in the goodwill of the firm and to include the same in the estate of the deceased. The accountable persons objected to this proposal and contended that the value of the building could not be included in the estate of the deceased because it had been set apart only for charitable purposes, with regard to the goodwill, it was contended that in the case of managing agency business, there was no goodwill at all, and that in fact the accountable persons had not obtained any amount from the firm towards the value of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the firm. The Assistant Controller, however, overruled these objections and held that the building was not a trust property and that it was owned by the deceased at the time of his death, and, therefore, its value was includible in the estate of the deceased. On the question of goodwill, the Assistant Controller held that the managing agency firm did possess goodwill and on the death of the deceased the accountable persons were entitled to 3/16th share in the goodwill of the business of the firm and as such a sum being the value of the 3/16th share had to be included in the estate of the deceased.

On appeal, the Appellate controller upheld the order of the assistant controller and reduced the value of the building.

On further appeal the Tribunal upheld the order of the Appellate Controller in respect of inclusion of value of building holding that a mere provision for the maintenance of the building by the deceased and thereafter by others could not amount to creation of a trust with reference to the building and that the exclusive use of the building from 1942 to 1958, for religious and charitable purposes did not amount to a permanent dedication of the building as a trust property. As regards the inclusion representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm, the Tribunal held that goodwill cannot be associated with the business of managing agency firm because the managing agency business is governed by the terms of the agreement between the managing agency firm and the company and the right of managing agency was more personal and could not pass on to a successor. The Tribunal also held that no share in the goodwill of the business passed to the accountable persons on the death of the deceased and that in any event no amount was actually paid to the accountable persons by way of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the business. In that view the Tribunal deleted the sum representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm.

On reference:

The assessee-trust was constituted by one ‘J’ who was the manager of certain religious and charitable funds. By the deed of indenture, it was declared that the respective assets of the religious and charitable funds would be in favour of the trustees who would hold the management and operate the respective assets of those funds for the purposes stated in the trust deed. Thus, the assessee claimed exemption on that ground. The Assessing Officer held that since the expenses incurred were in excess than the income derived from various funds, the trustee was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a). The AAC, however, allowed the appeal. On further appeal, the Tribunal restored the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

By an indenture of trust dated 23-8-1954, one ‘D’ and his wife settled upon trust two maternity hospitals which were run by them and an immovable property for the purposes and objects contained in the said deed of trust. The assessee were the trustees under the said trust. The primary object of the trust was to carry on and promote the educational, health, cultural, literary, social and economic interests of the people, particularly of the backward and poorer classes. The important recitals in the trust deed were to the effect that the net annual income from the said hospitals, after deducting all the expenses for maintaining and running the hospitals including a sum of Rs. 750 per month which should be paid regularly to ‘D’s wife for managing the said hospitals for and on behalf of the trust during her lifetime, should accrue to the trust from year to year and that Dr. Divekar and Dr. Nalini Divekar did transfer the above said property and both the hospitals to the Trustees. And that the monies and properties of the trust were to be applied, firstly in payment of the expenses of carrying out of the trust and then in carrying out the other objects. The assessee claimed exemption under section 43(1)(i) of the 1922 Act. Even though the ITO accepted that the business in maternity homes was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act, he however took the view that its income was not exempt under the said section because it did not fulfil the requirements of proviso (b) thereto. This view was arrived at by him because he took the view that the primary purpose in conducting or running the two maternity homes or hospitals was not to give free medical facilities but charge the patients and then to apply the income for certain objects. Even the amount paid to D’s wife claimed as a deduction was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that the same was paid by the association of persons to one of its own members.

On appeal, the AAC held that the income from the trust was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and that the salary paid was an allowable deduction in computation of the assessees’ income.

On revenue’s further appeal, the Tribunal took the view that there was no actual transfer of immovable properties to the trustees if regard be had to the language employed in the document. On the assumption that the properties were considered to have been managed on behalf of a charitable institution the Tribunal took the view that the conditions laid down in proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) were not satisfied in the case and the income was, therefore, not exempt from tax.

It, however, affirmed the finding of the AAC that salary to ‘D’s wife was an allowable deduction.

On reference:

The assessee was an association of persons. The Constitution of the assessee provided for an elected standing committee, the constitution, functions and duties of the said standing committee. The Constitution also provided for a smaller body which was entitled managing committee and its constitution and other functions. The Constitution further provided that to carry out the objects of the parishad, the standing committee could raise funds and accept donations, presents charities, etc., and would have power to administer them. The issue that arose for decision was as to whether having regard to the terms of the constitution of the assessee-association, the properties of the assessee-association were held under trust or other legal obligation so as to qualify for exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

On reference:

Assessee was managing trustee of charitable trust whose one eighth income from certain trust properties was denied exemption under section 4(3)(i) on ground that the same was to be set apart for such members of descendants of settlers who might be suffering from financial stress.

On reference :

One ‘R’ had settled a business on trust with the assessee foundation for charitable purposes. The trust deed specifically provided that the income should be used for charitable purposes but not for running a business for profit. The Tribunal held the assessee was a charitable trust and its income was entitled to exemption.

On application under section 256(2):

The assessee-trust was constituted with object to sponsor and provide educational facilities for catering courses, etc. 'K' executed a deed in favour of the assessee transferring movable and immovable property of a hotel 'V'. The said transfer was treated as a gift in the hands of 'K' and brought to tax under the provisions of the Gift tax Act, but on appeal, levy of gift tax was set aside by the Tribunal holding that there was no gift and it was only a permission granted for a college to manage the same free of rent. The assessee entered into an agreement with 'T' for the purpose of administration and operating of 'V' and claimed that it was providing training facilities from 'V'. The Assessing Officer rejected its claim holding that running of 'V' through 'T' was only a device to avoid tax and there was no charitable activity carried on its part. In the wealth-tax assessment, the Assessing Officer considered property of 'V' as the assessee's wealth and computed wealth tax liability payable by it. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), relying on the finding recorded in the gift tax proceedings where it was held that there was no gift at all, held that there was no taxable wealth in hands of the assessee and cancelled assessment order. On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was eligible for exemption under section 5(1)(i).

On revenue's appeal to the High Court:

■

The assessee-trust was registered under section 12A(a) and operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital and a medical college. Due to financial difficulties, the assessee entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) for the transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of the hospital to SCPL. In return, the assessee would receive either a fixed amount or a percentage of SCPL''s profit as management fees. The assessee had incurred heavy debts and faced a negative net worth. The agreement was seen as a means to ensure the assessee''s survival and continued charitable activities, as SCPL took over the hospital''s operations and liabilities.

■

The Assessing Officer scrutinized the agreement and found that it violated the basic principles of charity for which the trust had been granted registration under section 12AA. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for the benefit of related parties. Consequently, the trust''s claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied. The Assessing Officer also reclassified the Trust''s income as that of an Association of Persons (AOP), which would only be allowed to deduct its expenditures.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal by revenue to the Tribunal:

The assessee was a public charitable trust created by a deed dated 30-7-1960, recognised as such by the Charity Commissioner and other authorities including the Income-tax Department which granted exemption under section 11 from year to year. A cinema theatre was donated by the settlor himself to the trust in 1966. The assessee gave the theatre on licence during the assessment year 1977-78. However, in order to protect the trust property the assessee had maintained the control and management over cinema theatre and had engaged its own staff and supervisors. The ITO denied exemption under section 11 to the assessee by invoking section 13(1)(bb) [omitted with effect from 1-4-1984], as in his opinion the addition of theatre to the trust property had brought to trust within the mischief of the above provision. The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the ITO’s order.

On second appeal, the assessee contended, inter alia, that the lease was a purely part-time hiring out of certain assets held by it as an investment and not as a business proposition and that the theatre could not be called a commercial asset. On the other hand, the department contended, inter alia, that the theatre was a commercial asset with which the assessee was carrying on of a specific business, and the assessee had licence from the, various authorities for all these activities.

The settlor N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies, created a trust and purported to endow it with the shares held by him in six transport companies. He constituted himself the managing trustee of the trust and gave himself full power to deal with its assets. The managing trustees claimed refund of tax paid in respect of dividends declared on the shares held in these transport companies. The income-tax authorities refused to allow a refund. Their reason was that the shares were not held under trust wholly for charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i).

On reference:

A partnership firm was formed by four brothers. No deed of partnership was said to have been executed in respect of this firm. The firm was appointed the chief agent an insurance company as from 1-9-1950. On 17-2-1951, the aforesaid brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming the trustees would hold the said business of the chief agency of the said company and all the benefits and profits to arise from the said business upon trust for public charitable purposes. The said declaration of trust was registered with the Registrar of Assurances.

The assessee claimed that as from 17-2-1951, the income from agency business should be assessed in the hands of the trustees and should be allowed exemption under section 4(3)(i). The ITO, however, made the assessment in the status of an unregistered firm. The ITO held that there was no charitable trust created by the deed dated 17-2-1951. On appeal, the AAC reversed the findings of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no proper and valid contract between the insurance company and the trustees as such; that the letter of appointment was only a service agreement; that there had been no transfer of property to the trustees wholly for charitable purposes; that the alleged transfer of the agency agreement did not amount to the transfer of property. The Tribunal also held that before the income of a trust for charitable purposes was exempt from tax, it must satisfy the conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i), i.e., and in the instant case the business not being carried on the course of carrying out the primary purpose of the trust, the income was not exempt form liability to pay tax.

On reference :

The assessee-company was the trustee of a religious and charitable trust within the meaning of section 11. Its affairs were managed by another trust association to whom it paid Rs. 10,000 as management charges and claimed the same as an admissible deduction. The ITO rejected the claim on the grounds (i ) that the exact amount actually incurred for such management was not ascertainable; and (ii ) that there was no necessity for any other expenditure (apart from salary allowances, legal charges, postage and other incidental charges) for its management, especially, when its sources were only income from rent and interest. On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's order. On further appeal, the Tribunal upheld the assessee's claim, holding (i) that the assessee was governed by the Charitable and Religious Trust Act, 1922 (and not by the Indian Trust Act, 1882) and the Act did not place any restriction on payment of remuneration to the trustees for managing the trust affairs; and (ii) that the impugned payment was for the purpose of the trust and was for the services rendered.

On reference:

The assessee was a charitable trust. During the course of assessment, the ITO found that certain sum had been paid to the manager of the trust as loan. The Assessing Officer treated the manager as a person referred to the section 13(3) and, hence, act of advancing loan to manager was hit by provisions of section 13(1)(c) and 13(2)(a). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the appellant-trust could not be said to have used any part of its income directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person referred to in section 13(3). Therefore, the provision of section 13(1)(c) was not applicable. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the Commissioner (Appeals)'s order that the assessee was a trust and not an institution.

On reference :

The assessee-Chamber of Commerce received amounts in the accounting period relevant to the assessment year in question for the issuance of certificates for survey and weighment. It was proposed to treat the said receipts as income for the purpose of assessment. The assessee contended that the income in question was derived from the property held under trust wholly for charitable purposes and, therefore, was exempted under section 11(1)(a). The Tribunal accepted the assessee's contention, allowed the assessee's claim.

On reference :

The appellant-assessee was a trust whose object was to organize, encourage, spread, impart and promote all kinds of educational as well as charitable institutions. The trust deed obligated the trustees to utilize the entire income and corpus of the trust only for the development of the activities and properties of the trust and to carry on only such trade, commerce and industry as can be carried on either in the course of actually carrying out of any or part of any of purposes of its Ashram and its International Centre of Education. It had been treated as a public charitable trust within the meaning of section 11 of the 1961 Act. The assessee claimed exemption under section 5(1) for the properties held by it. The Tribunal disallowed the exemption on ground that the properties held by the trust were not held for charitable purposes.

On appeal :

On 18-1-1956, the assessee settled certain agricultural lands in a trust. As provided in the deed of settlement, the income from the settled properties were to be utilised for the upkeep and maintenance of the public temples; for the expenses of the repair and replacement of any ornaments and utensils and other articles required for the said temples and performance of pujas, festivals, etc. In respect of a portion of a settled property where the settlors wife was residing, it was directed that she would reside therefor her lifetime and the building would be maintained properly. The GTO held that the gifts were for religious purpose and not for charitable purpose, and, hence, the assessee was not entitled to exemption. On appeal the AAC, though provided some relief, affirmed the order of the GTO in main. On further appeal, however, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the expression "charitable purpose" in section 5(1)(vi) includes "religious purposes". The Tribunal further held that the building in a portion of which the settlor’s wife was residing was a trust property and the direction given was only for the purpose of maintenance of the trust property. The object was, therefore, a charitable one. The Tribunal therefore, granted exemption to the assessee.

On reference :

The Assessing Officer denied granting of exemption under section 11 to assessee trust running schools apparently based on the transaction relating to the agreement to sale for purpose of agricultural lands and huge salary, free use of motor cars provided to the Managing Trustee etc. The case of the Assessing Officer was that the ultimate beneficiary from the student fees and contributions were the family of the Managing Trustee and the assessee was collecting huge fees and contributions from poor and needy students, but, it was enriching itself and its trustees. However, the Assessing Officer to grant said exemption.

On second appeal:

The assessee-trust had been formed by the settlor for the benefit and maintenance of his daughter S in her lifetime. Any excess income left after her maintenance was to be used for charitable purposes. After her death, the entire income was to be used for charitable purposes according to the terms of the trust deed. The managing trustee had absolute discretion to sell, mortgage or dispose of the trust property and to use it for chari- table purposes. S died on 22-7-1973. For the assessment year 1974-75, the assessee-trust claimed exemption from tax under section 11 which was allowed in the original assessment. Subsequently, however, the ITO reopened the assessment and withdrawn the exemption allowed. He also held that the income received by the trust could not be stated to be received specifically on behalf of or for the benefit of any one person in terms of section 164(1). On appeal, the Commissioner confirmed the order of the ITO.

On writ:

The respondent-trust was established for managing and running the activities popularly known as ‘Dharam Kanta’, a service of weighing precious metals provided for the benefit of public in general. It was clear from the trust deed that the beneficiaries of the trust were the general public. The trust deed also provided for a mechanism to run the activities of the trust and also made a provision for carrying on the business activities of the trust. A specific provision was to be found in the trust deed to the effect that the Committee of Management appointed by the board of directors consisting of the trustees was to carry on the business through the employees engaged for the purpose. The assessee-trust claimed exemption under section 11(4A). The assessee’s claim was disallowed.

The Tribunal, while allowing the appeals, held that the business activities of the trust having being conducted by the charitable trust for charitable object, without any object of earning profits and gains out of the charges collected by it from the weighment facility provided to the public, the assessee-trust was entitled to claim exemption under section 11(4A).

On appeal, the revenue, relying on the text of clause (b) of sub-section (4A), contended that though the business was being carried out by the charitable institution for charitable purpose, but the same was not being carried out by the beneficiaries of the institution and as such the trust was not entitled to claim the exemption under section 11(4A).

The property in question was purchased by the partners of the assessee-firm in their names as trustees of the trust known as 'Ganapatrai Sagarmull Charitable Trust'. The Court in the case of Ganpatrai Sagarmal ( Trustee) for Charity Fund v. CIT [1963] 47 ITR 625 (Cal.), examined the trust deed and came to the conclusion that the properties described as trust properties had remained as properties of the settlors and, therefore, the entire income was chargeable to tax in the hands of the settlors. However, for the assessment years 1973-74 and 1974-75 the Tribunal found that the property in question was transferred to and vested in the trustees of the charitable trust only. The infirmities that were pointed out by the Court earlier had been removed by the parties, who created a separate trust and registered it vesting the trust property in the trustees. The Tribunal also found that the municipal tax receipt showed that the property in question was registered in the name of the trust. The certificate of registration under section 12A issued by the Commissioner clearly showed that the revenue had examined the trust deed and satisfied itself before granting the aforesaid registration. The assessment order for the assessment year 1973-74 made on the trust, though said to be a protective measure, showed that the property in question belonged to the trust and that did not belong to the assessee. On facts, the Tribunal held that the property in question did not belong to the assessee, but belonged to the trust and that the income from the aforesaid property could not be included in the hands of the assessee.
