On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) supported the ITO.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held insurance business was held on trust and income from said business was applied to charitable purpose. Therefore, the assessee's income would be exempted under section 11.

On appeal before High Court:

The assessee-trust had received a donation during the year 1977-78 of a sum of Rs. 3,50,000 from another charitable trust ‘H’. This H was donated a sum of Rs. 85,000 by the assessee during the year under consideration relevant to the assessment year 1980-81. The Assessing Officer held that by making the donation of Rs. 85,000, the assessee applied its income and property for the benefit of H, thus attracting the provisions of section 13(1)(c)( ii) and consequently lost an exemption under section 11. On appeal, the AAC also confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal, the assessee, inter alia, contended that it would not be correct to say that H was a ‘person’ and that if a donation had been made by one charitable trust to an other and if it could be proved to the satisfaction of the concerned authorities that it was not for the benefit of the donee-trust or its beneficiaries, there was no infraction of the provisions of section 13 and consequently the donor-trust could not be visited with any adverse consequences.

The settlor by a trust deed dated 5-3-1968 created the assessee trust and settled upon trust shares of certain companies. The net income of the trust fund after providing for expenses of collection and other outgoings for the period up to 31-3-1983 was to be made over by way of gift or donation to another trust so that the later trust should utilize the net income in its hands for all or any one or more of the charitable purposes mentioned in the deed of the said trust. The Tribunal found that the property of the assessee-trust could be said to be held wholly for charitable purposes and the exemption under section 11 would be available to the assessee-trust. In so far as the nature of assessment was concerned, the Tribunal took the view that the trustees of the assessee-trust were representative assessees in terms of section 160(1)(iv), as the income was received by the trustees on behalf of or for the benefit of the donee trust and the provisions of section 161(1) would come into play. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the tax, if any, would be leviable upon the assessee in the like manner and to the same extent as it would be leviable upon the donee trust, the income of which would be exempt from tax to the extent contemplated in section 11 of the Act.

On reference:

The assessee was asked to substantiate its claim of treating indigent/poor patients on concessional basis, in reply to which, the assessee contended that this being a first year of operation, it could not provide free medical relief to a large number of indigent/poor patients. The Assessing Officer held that going by the amount received from treatment of indigent poor patients, it was amply clear that the earning of profit was the pre-dominant activity of the trust and carrying out charitable activity was only incidental. Ltd. to the trust hospital, exercising vital powers which he had reserved for himself. The shifting, as per the Assessing Officer, was done to the scope of profit/gain by setting up of the trust. Considering the amounts of consultancy receipts paid to the managing trustee and the corresponding IPD/OPD receipts in the hands of the trust, the Assessing Officer held that Dr. K, the managing trustee himself alone had diverted the income by using the trust infrastructure for his profit/gains, in clear violation of provisions of section 13(1)(c), read with section 13(2)(b) and 13(2)(g). The Assessing Officer held that the business was carried on not by the assessee-trust but by the Board of Directors of the company who were managing the business. He, therefore, held that the provisions of section 11(4) were not applicable and the provisions of section 11(4A) were applicable. He further, held that the profits and gains of the business were not incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. On reference:

On reference :

The assessee-trust was set up by a Race Club HRC for certain specified charitable purposes including promotion and encouragement of public activities in sports and games. The initial corpus of the trust was only a very small amount but an explanatory statement attached to the resolution of the club whereby the trust was created, clarified that further accretions to the corpus could be made through donations and conduct of races under the auspices of the trust. The assessee-trust was allowed the benefit of profits on races and inter-venue betting conducted under the auspices of the trust on a few days in a year. The assessee’s claim for exemption of such income under section 11 was rejected by the ITO on the grounds (i) that the assessee was not a charitable institution inasmuch one of its object was promotion of sports or athletic activities which could not be considered to be charitable, and (ii) that the assessee’s income from races and inter- venue betting as aforementioned was not income from property but income from business and was hit by the prohibition contained in section 13(1)(bb), disentitling the assessee from exemption under section 11. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was a charitable trust and qualified for exemption under section 11 but that only income from the initial corpus was income from property held in trust and was eligible for exemption. In this view, he upheld the ITO’s disallowance of exemption in respect of income from races and inter-venue betting on ground (ii) supra.

On second appeal, the assessee argued that its aforementioned income from races and inter-venue betting under arrangement with the settlor- club was income from property held in trust and not business income, while the revenue contended that the assessee was not a charitable institution.

The lands of some villages were said to have been granted by one Mughal emperor for the upkeep of the Roza in the year 1670 under a Sanad and grants were confirmed by the Sanads issued during the British regime. A suo motu enquiry was started under section 19 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. As a result of that inquiry, the Dy. Charity Commissioner made an order directing that the assessee-Roza Trust be registered as a Public Trust. On appeal the Charity Commissioner confirmed the order of the Dy. Charity Commissioner. He held that the assessee-trust was a public trust and the lands of villages were the properties of the said trust. However, the ITO assessed the income of village lands as income in the hands of ‘SM’, the Sajjadanashin of the trust. Protective assessment was, however, made in respect of that income in the name of the assessee-trust. The AAC, on appeal, upheld the finding of the ITO but cancelled the protective assessment which was made in the name of the assessee-trust and assessed the income in the hands of the Sajjadanashin. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the AAC had committed an error in setting aside the protective assessment.

The Tribunal concluded that the lands in question were Wakf properties belonging to the assessee-trust, and that the exemption under section 11 was available to the assessee-Roza Trust, provided the condition mentioned therein were fulfilled. It was held that the actual expenditure on the Sajjadanashin and his family not exceeding Rs. 30,000 would not be included in the income of the Roza Trust, but such amount spent by the Sajjadanashin on his maintenance as Madad-E-Maash was taxable in his hands as income. The Tribunal restored the matter to the ITO to assess the income of the lands as the income of the assessee-trust and grant the benefit under section 11 subject to fulfilment of the conditions mentioned therein, bearing in mind that the income actually spent by Sajjadanashin on his maintenance not exceeding Rs. 30,000 was not to be included in the income of the Roza Trust.

The issue for consideration for the High Court was as to whether the income from the lands in question was the income of the assessee-trust assessable in the hands of the said Trust and exempt under section 11 or it was assessable in the hands of ‘SM’, the Sajjadanashin of the trust, as income from his private property.

Statutory Provisions, Sixth Council Directive 77/388/EEC of 17 May, 1977

Article 13B(d)(6) : Member States are to exempt the following from VAT under conditions which they are to lay down for the purpose of ensuring the correct and straightforward application of the exemptions and of preventing any possible evasion, avoidance or abuse: 'management of special investment funds as defined by Member States.'

Issue Involved

Were the services received by assessee eligible for exemption ?

The assessee, a charitable trust, had been created by the settlers by transfer of shares of certain companies, in which the settlors or the persons referred to in section 13(3) of the 1961 Act had substantial interest. On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee trust, registration under section 12AA, filed its return and claimed exemption under section 11(1)(a). During the year, the assessee had temporarily given loans and advances to one, MGA to earn interest income on the surplus fund for a short period of time. An interest income was received by the assessee in the next year which was utilized for charitable purposes of this Trust.

The Assessing Officer held that the said amount being accumulated amount had not been applied by the assessee for charitable purposes and, accordingly, made an addition of the said amount.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order passed by the Assessing Officer.

In instant appeal the assessee contended that when the assessee had applied 85 percent of its income for charitable purposes as per the provisions of section 11(1)(a), then the amount in question though might not be an investment as per the modes prescribed under section 11(5), the same could not be held as application of income for non-charitable purposes. Thus, the assessee had submitted that as per the provisions of section 13(1)(d) only the income on such investment could not be taxed and the principal amount could not be added or charged to tax. Hence, the assessee had submitted that at the most the interest income earned on such advances/loans could be charged to tax and not the principal amount when the assessee has already complied with the conditions as prescribed under section 11(1)(a) to the extent of application of 85 percent of income for charitable purposes.

The assessee society was getting subscription from persons belonging to 'K' community scattered all over India. In addition the assessee also had income from a house property. It was stated in the memorandum of association that income arising out of the said house property was to be spent amongst other activities of running dispensary, schools, etc. in the village from which place all the 'K's' came. The claim of the assessee that it was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act was negatived by the ITO. On appeal, the AAC, held that a part of the income from this house property was devoted to charitable objects only and such, a portion of the income was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. On further appeal to the Tribunal, this claim to partial exemption was overruled. According to the Tribunal whether the objects of the society were charitable or not, had to be gathered from the memorandum of association and if the association or its executive committee was entitled to spend amounts under any of the clauses of the objects clause, some of which were charitable in nature and others not, the only conclusion to come to was that the institution was not solely for the purposes of charity.

On reference:

The assessee was a public religious and charitable trust registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. A scheme for this trust was originally framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad way back in 1960 after finding in a suit that the suit properties were part of a public religious , trust and that the defendants were in possession as trustees for and on behalf of the general worshippers of the temple. The Court gave directions setting down the duties and obligations of the pujaries who, as trustees and managers of the temple, were allowed two-thirds of the income of the trust properties for purposes of their maintenance and temple expenses. Subsequently, in Second Appeal No. 565 of 1942, by a judgment-creditor of the then pujari-trustees, the Bombay High Court had occasion to observe that the original scheme framed by the District Court lent strong support to the view that the remuneration payable to the trustees or managers was for the services rendered by them and was their personal property. The present scheme of the trust was framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad in 1960. Under clauses 12, 13 and 14 of this scheme, after meeting outgoings on account of rates, taxes, assessment and expenses incidental to the administration of the trust and worship of the deity of the temple and also current repair and upkeep charges, the trustees were under obligation to distribute the surplus income by setting apart 50 per cent thereof for reserve fund and dividing the remaining 50 per cent equally between the two hereditary trustees, which was to be treated as their absolute property. The amount standing to the credit of the reserve fund was to be invested according to the provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, but out of the annual contribution to the fund, 20 per cent was to be utilised for religious, educational and/or medical purposes with the sanction of the District Court. In the assessment for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64, the previous years being Samvat Years 2017 and 2018, respectively, the trust claimed that the entire income from its property should be exempt from tax under section 11(1)(a). The ITO disallowed the claim holding that the properties of the trust were not held wholly for religious and charitable purposes, since the payment of 50 per cent of the surplus income to the two hereditary trustees was not for charitable purposes, inasmuch as it was not by way of remuneration or salary for the services rendered by them as employees and what they received was out of the income of the trust. According to the ITO, the only income which was entitled to be exempt under section 11(1)(b) would be the amount actually spent for religious purposes and 20 per cent of the amount of contribution set apart as reserve fund. On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's view that the case would fall under section 11(1)(b) as the income was only partly applied for religious purposes. He also rejected the alternative claim of the trust that the said payments must be treated as allowable expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal also rejected the claim and confirmed the view of the ITO and the AAC, holding that the true effect of the payments to the hereditary pujaris was the application of the income and it had no direct or indirect relation to the services, if any, rendered by them.

The 'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation.

It is true that a public charity is perpetual in character, and that means that it is capable of enforcement, so long as there is any property left which can be appropriated for its objects. And even if some or all of the objects become incapable of fulfilment, the trust properties will be devoted to the performance of similar or allied charitable purposes on the doctrine of cy-pres. But so far as the trust properties themselves are concerned, they will be held only on the incidents to which they are subject under the law. Thus, if the property is a leasehold interest, it must cease on the termination of the lease. Likewise, if trust property is alienated under circumstances binding on the trust, it will go out of the trust. But that does not operate as an extinction of the trust, unless there is no property at all left, with which the trust could be carried out. That is the principle enacted in section 77(c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which in terms, however, applies only to private trusts. Therefore, the fact that the trustees have the option at any time to throw up the managing agency is no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust.

In the result, it could be held that the word 'property' in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend 'business', and if the question fell to be decided solely on the terms of that sub-section, the managing agency must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

With aforesaid observation, the case was remanded to High Court for a fresh disposal on merits.

[Matter remanded to High Court]

■

The issue under consideration has been decided by the Tribunal in favour of the assessee in earlier year’s orders and also by the recent order passed by the ITAT Ahmedabad in the assessee’s own case for assessment year 2016-17 in ITA No. 416/Ahd/2020 vide order dated 20-07-2022 wherein the Tribunal held that the agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable to SCPL but to counter the huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals. Therefore, the Commissioner(Appeals) has correctly held that the activity of the trust was carried on in accordance with its objects and in the best interest of charity, therefore, the exemption under section 11(1)(a) has rightly been allowed by the Commissioner(Appeals). Similarly, the Commissioner(Appeals) has clearly held that section 13((1)(c)(ii) could apply only if any part of the charitable income of the trust has been used or applied for the benefits of the said persons during the previous year. But, since no portion of the income of the assessee has been applied for said person, therefore, the case of the assessee fell outside the scope of this section. Further, the trust is in receipt of income by way of management charges from SCPL and also all of its liabilities have been taken over by the same therefore there is a fact that there is no undue benefits of the use of trust property have been taken by any other persons. Similarly, there is no diversion of income of the trust as per Explanation of section13(2)(d) and 13(2)(g) as the trust has been benefitted greatly and its deficit of trust duly reduced to a great extent. Thus, the Commissioner(Appeals) has analyzed the facts correctly and given a judicious finding which does not call for any interference from outside. [Para 6]

■

Accordingly, in view of the above, there is no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner(Appeals) so as to call for any interference.[Para 7]

■

In the result, the appeal of the Department is dismissed.[Para 8]

The Tribunal had entertained certain misconceptions as to the true nature and character of the building in question. Neither under the partition deed nor under the settlement deed the building had been taken as a partible property. It was only the devolution of the lands which had been set apart for the maintenance of the said building that had been provided for both under the partition deed and the latter settlement deed. Both the documents clearly dealt with the right to manage the building. The stone slab and the notice board in front of the building showed when it was founded and for what purpose the building was to be used.

It is well established that no express words of gift either directly or indirectly in the shape of a trust are required to create a dedication. All that is necessary is that the religious purpose or object of the donor shall be clearly specified and that the property intended for the endowment should be set apart and dedicated of those purpose.

It is also well established that the existence of a trust can be established even by the conduct of parties. Though normally a Hindu while dedicating property to a deity or any other religious or charitable object ordinarily goes through the ceremonies of sankalpa and samarpan, it could not be said that those ceremonies are essential to creation of a an endowment. The performance of these ceremonies is only relevant to show the intention of the grantor, and if there is clear and unequivocal manifestation of intention to create a trust and there is formal divestiture of the ownership in the property on part of the donor with the intention to devote it to religious and charitable purpose the dedication must be deemed to be complete. The deduction of property is not a sacrament but a secular act; but the mere renunciation of ownership by the donor with a particular object is sufficient to create an endowment. The Tribunal had not kept in mind these general and accepted principles while considering the question as to whether the building was trust property or not. There was a subsequent litigation between the daughter-in-law of the deceased, R, the adopted son of the deceased, and ‘D’ the adopted son of daughter-in-law, wherein daughter-in-law questioned, inter alia, the validity of the partition deed dated 1-3-1950, and in the course of the entire litigation the parties proceeded on the basis that the building was a trust property and the dispute between them was as to the right of management of the trust.

The conduct of the parties right from 1942, when the building was constructed, clearly showed that the building was constructed, clearly showed that the building had been specifically set apart and used for religious and charitable objects. Therefore, the view taken by the Tribunal that the building was not a trust property and as such its value had to be added on to the estate of the deceased could not be accepted.

On the question as to whether the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm could pass on his death, the observation of the Tribunal that a managing agency business could not have any goodwill could not be accepted. The Supreme Court in J. K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that the managing agency business had got goodwill.

The Tribunal was, therefore, in error in holding that the managing agency had no goodwill at all. The Tribunal had also taken the view that as no share in the goodwill of the business was actually paid to the accountable persons towards the deceased’s share in the goodwill, it was no possible to say that any share in the goodwill passed on the death of the deceased and that section 53 could not be invoked in the instant. That view of the Tribunal could not be accepted. The question was not whether the accountable persons had the benefit of the deceased’s 3/16th share in the goodwill but the question was whether that share legally passed to or vested in the accountable persons on the death of the deceased.

The Supreme Court in Khushal Kumar Shan v. Khorshed Banu [AIR 1970 SC 1147, 1149 held that an agreement between the partners that the name, the place of business and the reputation of the firm are to be utilized by the surviving partners will not necessarily warrant an inference that it was intended that the heirs of the deceased partner will not be entitled to a share in the goodwill.

A cursory perusal of the terms of the deed would show that the managing trustee was the heart and soul of the trust. The terms of the trust deed expressly provided for the trust funds being employed in any trade, industry or business, which meant that the trust could carry on the business just like an individual or a firm or a limited company. It was not the contention of the department that the trust was a mere fiction or that it was illusory. Thus, a valid trust had been constituted and the trust carried on the business during the relevant accounting years.

It is not an invariable canon of construction that the proviso in a statute should be read as a qualification or limitation upon the effect of the main enactment. The function of the proviso is very often to deal with an excepted class of cases, which may be within the principal enactment but for it. It would not however be correct to say that a proviso should always be assumed to be and read as an exception. A substantive provision may also appear in the form of a proviso and if the clear meaning of the proviso establishes that it is not a qualifying clause of the main provision it is bound to be given effect without straining to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision.

The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

’ is a saleable commodity. In the instant case, the material found during the course of survey operation clearly established the collection of money over and above the fee prescribed by the Government for admission of a student. Therefore, it was a clear case of sale of education by the assessee-society. Thus, the assessee could not be considered as a charitable institution under section 2(15 ). Therefore, the assessee was not eligible for exemption under section 11. [Para 9] Any income derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose, should not be included in the total income. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee was not holding any property under trust for charitable purpose. It was also not the case of the assessee that any income was derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose. Moreover, it was also not the case of the assessee that any income in the form of voluntary contributions was received with a specific direction to form part of the corpus of the society. The assessee-society was running educational institution and deriving income from such institution. The assessee had also collected money over and above the fees prescribed for admitting students under management quota. In other words, the educational institution was used as a tool/apparatus for collecting money over and above the fees prescribed. The assessee-society had no other source of income/receipt. The society owned the educational institution. The Legislature has visualized two situations. One is religious and another is charitable. Section 11 provides for exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust for charitable and religious purpose. ‘Education’ falls within the definition of charitable purpose. Therefore, any income derived from property held under trust for charitable purpose and applied for education, is eligible for exemption under section 11. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee had not derived any income from any property held under trust. The only source of receipt was the education itself, i.e., from educational institution. [Para 11]

The next question that fell for consideration was whether the educational institution owned by the assessee-society would be regarded as a property held under trust by the society. Section 11 speaks of the property held under trust. The Legislature visualized two situations. One is income derived from the property held under trust and another is application of that income derived from the property held under trust for a charitable purpose. Therefore, there is a clear distinction between the property held under trust and the charitable activity. In the instant case, the assessee-society was carrying on charitable activity by establishing educational institution. Therefore, the charitable activity of the assessee was education. The income, if any, derived from the property held under the Trust and applied for the educational activity, would be construed as application of income for the purpose of charitable purpose. Therefore, the expenditure incurred in establishing the educational institution, namely, acquisition of land, construction of building, etc., are all application of income for charitable activity. If any income was generated in the course of educational activity, the said income would be construed as if it was generated in the course of carrying on the charitable activity. Therefore, such receipt/income received in the course of carrying on charitable activity was also eligible for exemption, provided the same was applied or set apart for educational purposes. However, such receipt/income cannot be construed as derived from property/business held under trust. Since such receipt/income is inevitable or consequential while carrying on the activity of education, such income also becomes eligible for exemption. The educational institution is an apparatus for carrying out the charitable activity. Therefore, the educational institution or charitable activity itself cannot be construed as the property held under trust. The establishment of an educational institution is an activity of charity. Therefore, by any stretch of imagination, the charitable activity, cannot be held as the property held under trust, even though the income/receipt incidental to such activity is eligible for exemption. However, the money collected over and above the prescribed fee for admitting students cannot be construed as income derived from/incidental to the activity of carrying on charitable activity. [Para 12]

It is a well-settled principle of law that a business held under a trust is also a property. Section 11(4) also makes it very clear that the property held under the trust includes a business undertaking. If the assessee-society runs a business incidental to the attainment of the object of the society and separate books of account are maintained by the assessee, the income derived from such business, shall be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust. The Apex Court in Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/ 115 Taxman 126 considered the provisions of section 11(4A) and held that if the business income is derived from business held under the trust and the same is utilized by the institution for achieving object of the institution, then it could be said that such income is applied for charitable purpose. The assessee-society in question had no property or business whatsoever under trust. Moreover, it was not the claim of the assessee that any income was derived from the property or business held under trust. [Para 13]

The issue is whether, on the facts and circumstances of the case and having regard to the terms of the trust deed, it can be said that the activities carried on by the assessee in the form of running of community hall, was itself held under the trust. [Para 6]

It is to be noted that section 11(1) grants exemption to the income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India. There is no exhaustive definition of the words "property held under trust" in the Act; however, sub-section (4) says that for the purposes of section 11, the words "property held under trust" includes "a business undertaking so held". [Para 7]

If a property is held under trust, and such property is a business, the case would fall under section 11(4) and not under section 11(4A). Section 11(4A) would apply only to a case where the business is not held under trust. Thus, there is difference between property or business held under trust and business carried on by or on behalf of the trust. [Para 8]

This distinction was recognized by the Supreme Court in the case of Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1978] 121 ITR 1/[1979] 2 Taxman 501 wherein it was observed that if a business undertaking is held under trust for a charitable purpose, the income therefrom would be entitled to the exemption under section 11(1) of the Act. In the present case, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is that running of community Hall was incidental to the object of the trust, it was not business commenced/carried on by the assessee. Though the business was commenced by the trust and it was carried on by the trust after its formation, it cannot be said to constitute property held under trust.

Under section 11(4), it is only the business which is held under the trust that would enjoy exemption in respect of its income Under section 11(1) and there is a distinction between the objects of a trust and the powers given to the trustees to effectuate the purpose of the trust. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption Under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the trust deed of the assessee.

The running of " Community Hall" was not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of "Community Hall" was not even in the contemplation of the trust deed on the basis of which the society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, was carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust.

Section 11(1) of the Act confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose. Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1) of the Act, was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust.

In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the charitable trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

In the Circular No. 1132 issued by the CBDT, it has been clarified that the payment of a sum by one charitable trust to other for utilisation of the donee-trust towards its charitable objects is proper application of income for charitable purpose in the hands of donor-trust and donor-trust will not lose exemption under section 11 merely because the donee trustee did not spend the donation during the year of receipt itself. In the instant case, the buildings of the assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature and that being so, such use could very well be treated as use by the assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for the purpose of exemption under section 11. Moreover, exemption under section 11 was allowed to the assessee-society for the assessment years 1992-93 and 1993-94 by the department in the similar facts and circumstances. As such, the Commissioner (Appeals) was fully justified in treating the use of assessee’s property by other societies for charitable purposes as charitable activity carried on by the assessee and accordingly in allowing exemption under section 11 as claimed. The impugned order was, therefore, upheld. [Para 7]

Agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by the assessee’s society as separate business activities and the same, therefore, constituted ‘property held under trust’ of the assessee-society as provided in sub-section (4) of section 11 and income of the said activities, in any case, was to be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act, i.e., after deducting the expenditure incurred in connection with the said business. The assessee-society had derived income from the said activities and the amount being more than sufficient to cover the expenses incurred in connection with the said activities, the allowance of the same by the Commissioner (Appeals) as application of its income as claimed by the assessee hardly made any difference in the ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to the revenue. [Para 8]

Hence, the revenue’s appeal was to be dismissed.

By virtue of section 11(4) "property held under trust" includes a business undertaking so held. Therefore, it could not be accepted that the income derived by the assessee was not income from property as envisaged under section 11(1)(a). That apart, a perusal of the aims and objects of the assessee-society led to the conclusion that the income derived by it was income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a). Accordingly, the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the amount received by the assessee on account of allocation charges was not income from property held under trust.

Under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act, income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes to the extent to which such income is applied to such trust are liable to be exempted. In the instant case, the finding given by the AAC was that the assessee was the manager of the Gurudwara and that all monies received at the Gurudwara were used to be spent towards religious, educational and charitable purposes. The income received from the shops by way of rent was also used to be utilised for the said purpose. In this view of the matter, the inference was irresistible that the entire property was Gurudwara property and the same was being held by the assessee as a manager or shebait under a legal obligation wholly for religious and charitable purposes. As the entire income had to be applied for religious and charitable purposes the same was liable to be exempted under sections. 4(3)(i) and 4(3)(ii) of the 1922, Act.

A charitable trust may be created by words sufficient to show the intention. So long as there was a clear manifestation of intention to create a charitable or religious trust and there was a formal vesting of the ownership of the property the dedication was complete.

Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in holding that the income from Gurudwara and attached shops was entitled to exemption.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Furthermore, regarding the nature of scheme, it is found that the project is towards development of a township comprising of Niji Khatedari Scheme, residential scheme, commercial complex in Narayan Vihar, and not merely a residential complex as alleged by the Commissioner (Exemption). Accordingly, once an asset (movable/immovable) becomes the property of the assessee society, it continues to remain its property the benefit wherefrom does not pass/revoked by the trustee(s) and continues to remain with the society. The trust property is separate from the trustee property and cannot interchangeably stated to be the same. It is seen from the order of the Commissioner (Exemption) that adverse inference is drawn solely on the basis that factum of ownership of the flat at Safdarjung Enclave is not proved. However, the same appears to be baseless insofar as the Deed dated 20-11-2013 is placed on record that shows to the contrary, and no rebuttal is forthcoming regarding the same. [Para 65]

That therefore, without considering the overall activities of the assessee society, the department cannot cherry pick expenses/investments incurred in due course of charitable activities and proceed to cancel the registration of the assessee on said basis under section 10(23C)(vi); it stands established that the assessee has not provided any benefit to the trustee nor the funds of the assessee, been diverted for personal benefit of trustees or any third person and all investments made by the assessee satisfy the modes specified under section 11(5). [Para 69]

In light of the above discussion, the impugned order passed by the Commissioner (Exemptions), Jaipur withdrawing approval granted to the assessee in terms of section 10(23C)(vi) is set aside and restoration of registration with effect from assessment year 2013-14 and onwards is directed. In the result, appeal of the assessee is allowed. [Para 71]
