The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act. Therefore, the property from which income was derived by the assessee was held under trust and such property was held for charitable purpose and the income derived from trust was property which was being applied for charitable purpose. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

1. The Tribunal and the High Court had in earlier years interpreted the aims and objects of the assessee-society as meant for an object of general public utility not involving an activity for profit. These factors not having undergone any change in the later years, the ITO could not record a finding contrary to the ones recorded by the Tribunal and the High Court.

2. Though the assessee-society extended aid to various institutions, the management and control of each of them vested not in the society but in the respective managing committees for each of the institutions. Therefore the aims and objects of the assessee-society could not be treated as one establi-shed for 'education'. The activity of the assessee in providing grant-in-aid of school building, etc., would fall only under the head 'advancement of any other object of general public utility'.

3. The volume, frequency, continuity and regularity of the insurance transac-tions with a profit motive showed nothing but the carrying on of the business by the society as an insurance agent. At the same time, the said business by the assessee was 'property' as held by the Supreme Court in J.K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 and the said property in view of the aims and objects of the assessee-society had been held for charitable purposes within the meaning of section 2(15). Therefore, the entire income of the assessee-society from insurance business was exempt under section 11.

Where a settlor creates a trust, it lies within his power to also make a provision as to the management of the trust property. It is perfectly permissible for a settlor to nominate any person as trustees for first trustees and where there were more than one trustee, a managing trustee. It is also within his power to regulate the appointment of trustees in future as well as the managing trustee. There is no prohibition in law if the settlor himself takes over the function of the managing trustee after the trust has come into being. When the settlor himself becomes a trustee or managing trustee a change undergoes in his capacity from one of an owner of property to that of trustee holding the trust property for the benefit of the beneficiaries or for the purpose of working out the directions in the deed of trust. If for such work, any remuneration is provided for by the terms of the trust deed, that would not, amount to the reservation of any interest for the purposes of section 12(1).

The Department was, therefore, not entitled to rely on clauses 6 and 19 to contend that there was reservation of interest of the trust property and, therefore, the value of Kale Bhawan was liable to be treated as a part of the dutiable estate.

There could hardly be any doubt that clause 23 of the trust deed was a repository of the express power of revocation which could be exercised after the period of 10 years from the date specified therein and if the trust could not function for any reason. It could not be held that merely because in the case of a public trust a power to revoke is reserved by the settlor, such property must be deemed to pass on the death of the settlor for the purposes of section 12(1). When section 12(1) refers to the reservation by the settlor of the right to exercise the power of revocation, it obviously presupposes that such a power of revocation can be validly and legally reserved by the settlor. In other words, even if the document of trust does contain a clause expressly reserving the power of revocation if in law such a power of revocation is impossible to the either reserved or exercised, the Department would not be entitled to rely on the latter part of section 12(1) merely because in the settlement the settlers purported to reserve the power of revocation.

It cannot be disputed that once a trust for a charitable purpose is created in a given case, the trust fund can grow and grow to a size much larger than what was endowed originally by the settlement in the given case. Donations may be given to the trust or immovable property may be gifted to the trust by persons who want their property to be utilized for the same purpose for which the trust is created. Whether the trust is in favour of an idol and is of a religious nature or whether the trust is intended to achieve charitable purposes would in that context be wholly irrelevant. The real question is whether in such a case, it would be permissible for a settlor to revoke the trust so as to undo the trust itself and thus affect not only the trust property settled by him but certain other properties also which may have been endowed in favour of the trust or dedicated to that charity. There is no express provision of law permitting this to be done. On first principles, permitting such a power to be exercised by the settlor would open the floodgates of a device which would enable people to use the creation of the trust as a means for getting back larger property than what was originally settled as trust property.

There is unanimity in the view that in the case of a charitable endowment or trust once the dedication is completed there is no power of revocation left with the settlers. Even though in a given case the settlor has reserved the power to revoke the trust, such a reservation would be wholly invalid and the power cannot be invoked so as to undo the settlement.

Apart from the general principle that in the case of a public trust, where dedication is complete, a power of revocation does not vest in the settlor, in so far as the instant trust was concerned there could not be any ground which could be wholly irrelevant because there were overriding provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act under which a public trust was not being given effect to, the Charity Commissioner could step in and see that the trust funds were applied to a charitable purpose. It was, therefore, clear that the so-called power of revocation was wholly redundant and ineffective. If the power of revocation was redundant and ineffective and indeed wholly invalid the mere reservation of a power by a clause in the trust deed could not attract the applicability of the provisions of section 12(1).

The question as to whether the applicants fell within the coverage of section 65(68) as manpower recruitment agency was debatable, having regard to its wide scope of the definition. However, the applicants had made out a strong prima facie case on the ground that they were not prima facie a commercial concern in the light of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal’s order wherein the bench had before it the details of surplus and deficit income and expenditure of the applicants for the years 1990-94 when coming to its conclusion that the applicants were entitled to exemption under section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The extension of the exemption under section 11 of the Income-tax Act was available because prima facie the Bench of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal had accepted the contents of the applicants that they were charitable trust. In this view of the matter, the requirement of pre-deposit of Service-tax and penalty involved in the instant case was to be waived and recovery thereof was to be stayed. [Para 3]

V. Sridharan for the Appellant. Ajay Saxena for the Respondent.

On a perusal of the entire records, it is apparent that even though the assessee trust is running Kalyana Mandapam, Gnanavapi and Community Hall, the income derived therefrom cannot be construed as business income as the very object of the trust is for charitable purpose and it should be incidental for the trust. [Para 19]

The fact remains that there is no record to show that all the income derived from Kalyana Mandapam, Gnanavapi and community hall is not used for the objects of the trust but whereas the fact remains that they spent all the income earned from letting out from the Kalyana Mandapam, Gnanavapi and Community Hall only for the educational purpose and medical relief to the poor, which are the objects of the trust. The assessee was entitled for exemption and income derived from Kalyana Mandapam, Gnanavapi and Community Hall cannot be treated as business of the trust. The trust has not conducted any business. Whatever income earned from the Kalyana Mandapam, Gnanavapi and Community Hall, is utilised for the educational purpose and the society is running educational Institution, which is the primary object of the trust; on the other hand, running Kalyana Mandapam, Gnanavapi and Community Hall is not a primary object. [Para 20]

The contention of the assessee is that in view of the above objects of the trust to be fulfilled, which is for a charitable purpose, the income therefrom would be entitled to exemption under section11(1). [Para 21]

Whether the income derived from letting out of Kalyana Mandapam, Community Hall and Gnanavapi owned by the assessee is the income from the house property or business income and whether the same is liable to be taxed or exempted is the other question. The contention of the assessee is that since utilization of the surplus income from the running of Kalyana Mandapam, Community Hall and Gnanavapi are for the objects of the trust, it is exempted from tax. [Para 22]

Both the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal have not discussed about the facts in respect of the surplus income having been utilized for the objects of the trust, viz., running educational institution, providing medical relief to the poor, etc. Absolutely there is no discussion of the facts relating to the utilization of earned income from letting out of Kalyana Mandapam and Gnanavapi towards charitable objects such as education and medical relief to the poor as given in the objects of the trust. Further, the Assessing Officer has not looked into the fact as to whether the entire income from Community Hall, Kalyana Mandapam and Gnanavapi are utilised for fulfilling the objects of the trust that is being education, Medical relief and relief to the poor. In such circumstances, the order dated passed by Tribunal, is set aside. The matter is remitted back to the Assessing Officer for de novo consideration as to whether the entire revenue derived from letting out of Kalyana Mandapam, Gnanavapi and Community Hall are utilized for charitable objects of the trust and also to consider as to whether the income received from the properties of the trust namely, Community Hall, Kalyana Mandapam and Gnanavapi to be classified as "income from House Property" or "business income" since the income therefrom is utilized for charitable purpose of the trust. [Para 23]

The assessee was a registered society duly incorporated and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1862. The society was formed with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. The income which the assessee received in the form of tuition fee and other receipts could not have been received but for the organization and, therefore, the tuition fee and other receipts derived from other organizations was income derived from property held under trust. Such tuition fee and other receipts, received by the assessee were directly and substantially arising from the organization, which was the property held under the trust. The Assessing Officer's assertion that whatever property in the shape of office building, furniture, computer was simply an application of income was not sustainable. It is well-settled that property acquired by an organization from its own income is also a property held under trust. Thus, fixed assets and current assets held by the assessee as on 31-3-1999 and 31-3-2000 were properties held under trust. Further, the Delhi Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case vide order dated 15-12-2003 had held that department cannot guide a charitable institution as to how it should carry on its charity. It is sufficient compliance with the relevant provisions of law in case surplus of the institution is utilized into activities of the institution and does not find its way to the pocket of the persons who were running the society/institution. There was no allegation by the department that the funds had been siphoned off. Therefore, the Commissioner should not have withdrawn the registration granted to the assessee under section 12AA.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity.

The educational institution being run by the assessee was for the general benefit of the public and not for the benefit of any class or section of the public, as (a ) the institution was duly recognized by HNB Garhwal University and strictly followed all procedures with regard to admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum as laid down by the university, and (b) the nominees of State Government, HNB University and AICTE (functioning under the Human Resources Ministry) were on the governing body of the society and, therefore, the assessee had no choice in matters of admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum. The institute, was, in fact, State Government managed.

It was also found that the working system of the assessee was as per the guidelines laid down by the University. In respect of fixing and charging fees from students, the society management had no powers. Fee was being charged from students strictly as specified and laid down by the University. The governing body of the society had no powers to workout the cost and thereafter to add on the element of overheads and profits. Therefore, there was no question of building huge margins of profits in the fees structure as conceived by the Assessing Officer.

From a plain reading of the main objects given in the Memorandum, it could very well be discerned that the society had been formed with the sole objective of imparting and spreading computer education. Further, the assessee-society was virtually Government managed. Therefore, the question of functioning like a commercial profit making institution was totally unfounded. Thus, the fees charged by the assessee was simply receipt in the hands of the society and not profit.

Further, the assessee was rendering services of education to the general public. Therefore, its activities clearly fell within the ambit of charitable purpose as defined under section 2(15). Charging of fees does not in anyway dilute the aspect of charitable purpose. It is the end use and spirit and objective which matters.

In the assessment order, the Assessing Officer had not been able to appreciate the difference in the words 'charitable purposes' as are used in the Act and the word 'charity' as had been used by the Assessing Officer in his order. The word 'charity' as used in English language and recognized in English law, implies as an act motivated by pity and may require benevolence to manifest it. However, exemption under section 11 has been prescribed with reference to 'charitable purposes' and not 'charity'. The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act.

The expression ‘charitable purpose’ is a generic term in law and has assumed a definite meaning in India law. The expression is wide enough to included both ‘charitable purpose’ as well as ‘religious purpose’. If the legislature desired to give this well understood term a limited meaning, it would be reasonable to assume that the legislature would have in express terms said so.

Here, in certain sections of the earlier enactment, the words used were either ‘religious charitable purposes’ or ‘public purposes of a charitable or religious nature’. In the instant Act the words ‘religious purpose’ have been omitted but the omission has been of unnecessary words only. As stated earlier, the expression ‘charitable purpose’ is wide enough to include public religious purposes also.

Further there is positive indication in the Act itself that the expression ‘charitable purpose’ has been used in a wider sense covering religious purposes and not in a restricted sense. It would be noticed that exemption in respect of gifts made for charitable purpose falling under clause (v ) is not restricted to any period. The exemption is available all the time. Exemption under sub-clause (a) of clause (vi), i.e., relating to gifts made to charitable purpose not falling under clause (v), is available only when the gift has been made before the 1st day of April, 1958. Both clauses speak of gifts to charitable purpose. When clause (v) is read along with the relevant clause of section 15B of the Indian Income-tax Act, it leaves no doubt that the expression ‘charitable purpose’ includes religious purpose as well.

It would be reasonable to assume that the legislature in omitting the words ‘religious purposes’ must have only intended to omit the unnecessary words which occurred in the earlier Acts and as already pointed out there is an indication in the Act itself, and when clause (v) is read there is no doubt that the expression ‘charitable purpose’ has been used in the Act in a wider sense and not in a restricted sense.

When the property is held under a trust or under a legal obligation for religious and charitable purposes its income does not enter ‘total income’. When a donation is given to an institution or fund established for public religious and charitable purpose, the income is exempt from tax. When a property is held under trust or legal obligation relating to charitable or religious nature it is not liable to be included in the wealth of a person for the purpose of levy of wealth-tax. Similarly, if an expenditure is incurred for any public purpose of religious or charitable nature, it is excluded from the expenditure which attracts tax. There is no reason why a person should not be entitled to exemption from tax in respect of gifts made for public religious and charitable purposes.

Therefore, the Tribunal was not in error in taking the view it had taken as to the interpretation of the expression ‘charitable purpose’.

The entire property had been settled on trust and the portion in which the settlor’s wife was staying was also a trust property. She had been given only a right of residence in that portion of the trust property for her lifetime. The trustees had been given a direction to take possession of that portion of the property on the death of the settlors wife for the purposes of the trust. It being a trust property, it was incumbent on the trustees to maintain this property in good repair in the interest of the trust. Lest the trustees might think that there was no obligation on them to keep in good order that part of the property in which the lady was staying, the direction appeared to have been given in the trust deed. In our opinion, therefore, the Tribunal also was right in not accepting this contention of the revenue.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

It is now well-settled that a formal deed of trust is not absolutely essential in order to come to a conclusion that any particular property is held under trust or other legal obligation. The provisions contained in the Constitution of the assessee bound not only the standing committee and the managing committee but they equally bound every member of the assessee. In view of the provisions of the Constitution, it was impossible to urge that it would be open either to the standing committee or the managing committee or even the members of the assessee to use the property of the assessee for any purpose except that covered by the object clause of the assessee.

In that view of the matter, no other view was possible save and except to hold that the property of the assessee was held under trust or a legal obligation. As it was not open for the revenue to urge that the object was not for a charitable purpose in view of the fact that such a contention was not raised either before the ITO or at the stage of appeal before the AAC on behalf of the revenue, the provisions of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 were directly applicable.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The charging section 3 provides that there shall be charged for every assessment year the wealth-tax in respect of the net wealth on the corresponding valuation date of every individual, HUF and company at the rate or rates specified in Schedule I. The wealth-tax is, therefore, to be levied only on three categories of assessees, individuals, HUFs and companies. Section 21A provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 5(i), where any property is held under trust for any public purpose of a charitable or religious nature in India and any one of the three conditions stipulated in the said section are satisfied, wealth-tax shall be leviable upon, and recoverable from, the trustee in the like manner and to the same extent as if the property is held by an individual who is a citizen of India and resident in India for the purposes of the Act. It is, thus, clear that the trustees of a public charitable trust are liable to pay wealth-tax in the same manner and to the same extent as if the property is held by an individual. [Para 6]

When clause (xxiii) of section 5(1) is read in the aforesaid background, it is clear that only companies are not covered by the exemption and the other two categories of assessees are entitled to claim the exemption. When the trustees are subjected to the levy of wealth-tax as if the trust property is held by trustees as individuals, the revenue cannot deny exemption to the trust or the trustees on the ground that they are not individuals. [Para 7]

A Division Bench of the Rajasthan High Court in CWT v. Bhangur Charitable Trust [1987] 164 ITR 249/ 32 Taxman 160 has elaborately discussed the aforesaid aspect and has held that the exemption laid down under section 5(1)(xxiii) is available to a trust in respect of shares held by the trustees. [Para 8]

Accordingly, Tribunal was right in holding that assessee was entitled to exemption under section 5(1)(xxiii).

Section 11(1) grants exemption to the income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India. There is no exhaustive definition of the words "property held under trust" in the Act; however, section 11(4) says that for the purposes of section 11, the words "property held under trust" "includes a business undertaking so held". Sub-section (4A) provides that exemption shall not be available to any business income of a trust unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objectives of the trust and separate books of account are maintained by such trust in respect of such business. [Para 7]

Thus, if a property is held under trust, and such property is a business, the case would fall under section 11(4) and not under section 11(4A). Section 11(4A) would apply only to a case where the business is not held under trust. Thus, there is difference between property or business held under trust and business carried on by or on behalf of the trust. [Para 8]

In the present case, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is that running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not held under trust, but it was business commenced/carried on by the Society, subsequent to the formation of trust. Though the business was commenced by the Society and it was carried on by the Society after its formation, it cannot be said to constitute property held under trust under section 11(4), it is only the business which is held under the trust that would enjoy exemption in respect of its income under section 11(1) and there is a distinction between the objects of a trust and the powers given to the trustees to effectuate the purpose of the trust. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the Memorandum of Association of the assessee. The running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not even in the contemplation of the Memorandum of Association on the basis of which the Society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust. Section 11(1) confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose.

Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1), was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust. In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

There is no connection between the activities relating to running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall and the attainment of the objects of the trust. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall are used for charitable purposes would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The application of income generated by the business is not relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. [Para 10]

■

If scheme of Section 11 is being perused, then it would reveal that income derived from the property held under the Trust wholly for charitable or religious purpose, if applied to the extent of 85 per cent on its objectives, then such income will not fall in the total income assessable of an assessee. In other words, if Rs.100 is being derived from the property held under the Trust and Rs.85 is being applied towards the charitable objective of the Trust, then nothing will be taxable upon such a ‘Charitable Society’ or Trust. However, section 13 has contemplated certain exceptions. [Para 12]

■

A perusal of section 13 would indicate that if the assessee society has availed the services or purchased any object from any specified person contemplated in sub-clause (3) and paid to such specified person in excess of what may be paid reasonably for such service in open market, then excess would be disallowed. In other words, for example, if assessee society has availed the services of an Engineer who happened to be a specified person under sub-clause (3) and paid him the service charges which he could not command in the open market, then such excess amount will be disallowed to the assessee and benefit of Section 11 would not be available on such an amount. It will be taxable. For example, assessee can purchase an item for Rs.100 but from a specified person, it has purchased at Rs.120, then this excess Rs.20 will be added to the taxable income of the assessee and benefit of section 11 will not be available to the assessee Society. A perusal of the complete assessment order reveals that Assessing Officer has nowhere made analysis of the remuneration/ honorarium paid to the members of the Management Committee vis-à-vis their services utilized for the benefit of the Society. All the persons are qualified persons, they have devoted their time for managing the affairs of the Society and it has paid only honorarium, not regular salary. Similarly, it has provided traveling facility to them which was only for fulfilling the objects of the Society. In other words, in assessment year 2015-16, a little higher amount is being incurred by the assessee because the member of the Management Committee has to travel outside India for inspection of a plane which was to be used in Aviation Wing of the Engineering College. The Assessing Officer has not examined this aspect as to how this type of facilities can be availed from the open market and the price of such services. He has simply narrated that these persons are gainfully implied in their other activities also and therefore, payment of honorarium to these persons is not in accordance with law. This cannot be a logic for denying the benefit to them. The intention of the section is not as such. It is the assessee who has to manage its affairs and to decide what is necessary for its functioning. The Assessing Officer can only examine whether excess is being paid or not, but he has not carried out any Investigation in that area. The Assessing Officer has not assigned any reason as to why he is departing from the principle of consistency where such honorarium has been allowed to these per sons. Similarly Traveling Expenses has been allowed to the assessee in earlier years. The Commissioner (Appeals) failed to record any finding qua this aspect in right perspective and blindly up held the assessment order. Therefore, all these grounds of appeal are allowed.[Para 12.1]

It was not the case of the revenue that the income of the trust had been applied for any purpose which could not be regarded as charitable purpose. According to the trust deed, the discretion given to the trustee was not to choose any purpose, but only purposes which were charitable for which the trust properties and income therefrom could be utilised. The word 'properties' in the trust deed, having regard to the context, must be understood as including the income derived from the properties, as the deed specifically provided that the trust property shall be applied for charitable purposes. The reference to the application would indicate that the author of the trust intended that all that belonged to the trust was to be utilised for the purpose of charity. The mandate was, therefore, clear that the properties of the trust which, having regard to the context, should include the income from the properties, should be applied solely for charitable purposes.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the trust was a valid charitable trust and in directing the WTO to redo the assessment in the light of the provisions of section 21(1) , read with section 21A.

The trust had been entitled to exemption in respect of its accumulated income under section 11(2) in CIT v. S.RM. M.Ct. Tirrupani Trust [1984] 150 ITR 642 (Appendix). This decision involved an inferential finding that the trust was a charitable institution as contemplated under section 11(1 ). Consequently, section 104(2)(iii) would be a bar for the levy of super tax under section 104(1 ) in the instant case.

The High Court held that the trust was not entitled to exemption under section 11 of the Income-tax Act because it did not satisfy the definition of 'charitable purpose' under section 2(15). Since such a definition is not present in the Wealth-tax Act, the claim for exemption has to be considered de hors that definition. The Court's observation about the necessity for scrutinising the objects of the trust is also not relevant, since such a criterion is absent for the purpose of the Wealth-tax Act. Further, as held by the Bombay High Court in the case of Trustees of K.B.H.M. Bhiwandiwalla Trust v. CWT [1977] 106 ITR 709 , not all the objects of a trust need be charitable or religious, since the word 'wholly' is significantly absent in section 5(1)(i ). It would be sufficient if the objects of the trust considered as a whole satisfies the public purpose specified. The High Court had given a clear finding that religious purpose was clear in this case, and this by itself would suffice for granting exemption, since under the Wealth-tax Act, property held in trust for a public purpose of a charitable or religious nature, is exempt. The discretion given to the trustees to apply the income for different purposes does not give any discretion to exclude religious purpose altogether. Considering all these aspects, the trust property would be exempt under section 5(1)(i ).

Section 11(1) provides that in order to support a claim for exemption of income under this section, the principal object for consideration would be whether the property from which the income is derived should be the trust or other legal obligation. Secondly, the property should be so held for charitable or religious purposes which enures to the benefit of the public. Thirdly, the exemption is confined only to such portion of the trust income as is in fact applied to charitable and religious purposes.

The expression "legal obligation" cannot be separated from the "property" itself which in the instant case was a horse-racing concern, inasmuch as law enjoins that such property must be held under a trust or other legal obligation and not the fund derived therefrom.

In the instant case, the association of persons were not the subject-matter of a trust and only a trust had been created in respect of the surplus fund. The surplus fund really emanated from a property which was not a subject-matter of the trust and as such in the absence of any legal obligation fastened thereto, no exemption could be allowed under section 11.

In this connection it has been held by the Privy Council in Mohammed Ibrahim Raza v. CIT AIR 1930 PC 226 that if there are several objects of a trusts of which some are charitable and some are non-charitable, and the trustees in their discretion are to apply income to any of the objects, the whole trust fails and no part of the income is exempted from tax.

In the instant case, clause 3(a ) of the said deed envisaged that the surplus fund may be applied for making improvements to the racing facilities available at Jorhat by way of increased stake money, by increasing the facilities available to the members of the public or in such other manner connected with the races as the trustees shall consider desirable. Such object did not come within the exemption clause 10(23). Therefore, the trustees had the indefeasible alternative right to apply the funds to such purposes, without making any donation to charitable purposes. In such circumstances, the matter was hit by the above decision of the Privy Council.

In the result, the Tribunal was not right in holding that the assessee was a charitable institution within the meaning of section 11(1).

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

It was clear that the object of the trust was mainly charitable. It had been found by the Commissioner and the Tribunal that the properties owned by the assessee were held by it in trust. Section 5(1)(i) is applicable to 'any property held under trust or other legal obligation for any public purpose of a charitable or religious nature in India'. The assets held by the assessee were not assets forming part of any business. There was no finding that any part of the assets of the trust was used for any purpose outside India. The activities of the trust were running schools and managing the Mosque and Darga in Coimbatore. The activities of the assessee-trust were charitable, running of schools being the primary object. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of section 5(1)(i).

Since it was seen that the trust was a charitable trust and the property held under that trust was for any public purpose of charity, grant of exemption under section 5(1)(i ) could not be denied.

From the provisions of section 5(1)(i ), it is clear that the wealth-tax shall not be payable in respect of asset held by the trust for charitable or religious purpose. Section 5(1)(i ) grants exemption in respect of property held by the assessee under the trust or other legal obligation for any public purposes of charitable or religious nature in India up to the assessment year 1992-93. However, exemption under section 5(1)(i) has a proviso which withdraws exemption from wealth-tax in respect of public, charitable or religious trusts/institutions with effect from 1-4-1986, viz., the assessment year 1986-87 by the Finance Act, 1985. On that aspect, the Commissioner (Appeals) had already directed the Assessing Officer to recompute the net wealth of the assessee-trust with reference to market value of the property forming part of the business of the assessee-trust and the assessee-trust clearly conceded and stated that it had not taken any appeal on that issue.

It is clear from a comparison of section 5(1)(i ) with section 13(1)(d) of the Income-tax Act, that the word ‘wholly’ is not to be found under section 5(1)(i ). This omission is deliberate, intentional and the Legislature advisedly avoided or omitted the said words from section 5(1)(i ). Thus, for the purpose of claiming exemption under section 5(1)(i), it is a sine qua non that the property must be held under the trust wholly for purpose of charitable or religious nature in India; it is sufficient if the trust could be said to be primarily or dominantly for a public purpose of charitable nature in India.

The assessee-trust was a charitable trust in view of the objects mentioned in the trust deed. There was no justification to hold that the assessee-trust was not entitled to exemption under section 5(1)(i) in respect of the assets held by the trust. Hence, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that it was a charitable trust and not a private trust was upheld. Further, still the income from the property held by the trust was not exempt under section 11(5) read with section 13(1)(d ) of the Income-tax Act, grant of exemption under section 5(1)(i ) fully applied to the assessee-trust, conditions for grant of exemption from wealth-tax under section 5(1)(i ) being wholly different and distinct from the grant of exemption under section 11(5), read with section 13(1)(d ) of the said Act. In view of that, the assessee-trust was entitled to exemption under section 5(1)(i ).

In the result, the department appeals were to be dismissed.

As per the charging section, i.e., section 3, the wealth-tax is to be levied only from three categories of assessees, namely, individuals, HUF and companies. From a reading of section 21A, it is clear, that the trustees of a public charitable trust are liable to pay wealth-tax in the same manner and to the same extent as if the property is held by an individual. [Para 6]

When section 5(1)(xxiii ) is read in above background, it is clear that only companies are not covered by the exemption but the other two categories of the assessees are entitled to claim the exemption. When the trustees are subjected to the levy of wealth-tax as if the trust property is held by the trustees as individuals, the revenue cannot deny exemption to the trust or the trustees on the ground that they are not individuals. [Para 7]

Under section 11(1)(a), in order to be entitled to exemption income must not only be derived from the property held under trust only for charitable or religious purposes but the income entitled to exemption must be to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes, i.e., charitable or religious purpose in India or where such income is accumulated for application to such purpose in India, i.e., religious or charitable purpose to the extent the income so accumulated is not in excess of 25 per cent of income from the property or Rs. 10,000, whichever is higher. Therefore, two separate independent conditions are required to be fulfilled, that is to say, the income must be derived from the property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, and, secondly, the application or accumulation of such income in the manner indicated in clause (a ) of sub-section (1) of section 11 of the Act. 'Charitable purpose' or 'purpose of charitable or religious nature' have not been defined in the Wealth-tax Act, 1957. Therefore, it must bear the same meaning as in the Income-tax Act but under the provisions of the Income-tax Act not only should the income be derived from a trust or legal obligation of public purpose of a charitable or religious nature but the income so derived must to a certain extent be so applied. The position under the Wealth-tax Act seems to be a little different. Wealth-tax Act assessed the owning or having or possessing of the property and section 5(1)(i) of the Act stipulated that the condition for exemption was that the property must be held by the assessee under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a religious or charitable nature in India. Therefore, the holding of a property by the assessee either under a trust or other legal obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature is the statutory requirement entitling the assessee to exemption under the Act. In the ground for reopening as noted before it was not disputed that the assessees upon whom the impugned notices had been issued were not holding the property under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a charitable or religious nature. What was being suggested was that holding the property as trustees or under obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature the assessees were committing breaches of trust in acting contrary to the trust and misusing the funds of the trust for their personal benefit. The application of the money held under a trust or under legal obligation is not a relevant consideration for exemption under section 5(1)(i) of the Act. Therefore, the revenue had no material to believe that the income of the assessee had escaped assessment. This position manifests a lacuna in the present provision of law. The position, therefore, is that if the trustees hold the property for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature and if they misapply or commit breach of trust, they will continue to enjoy exemption under the Wealth-tax Act. This position should receive consideration by the legislature in order to bring it at par with the provisions of the Income-tax Act. But until that is done, the petitioners were entitled to succeed on the point that there were no grounds for believing that the wealth of the assessee had escaped assessment or had been under-assessed.

In the aforesaid view of the matter, the notices are hereby quashed and the respondents were restrained from giving effect to the same.

Having regard to the terms of the Trust Deed, it can be said that the activities carried on by the assessee in the form of running of community hall, was itself held under the Trust. [Para 6]

It is to be noted that section 11(1) grants exemption to the income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India. There is no exhaustive definition of the words 'property held under trust' in the Act; however, sub-section (4) says that for the purposes of section 11, the words 'Property held under trust' 'includes a business undertaking so held'. [Para 7]

Thus, if a property is held under trust, and such property is a business, the case would fall under section 11(4) and not under section 11(4A). Section 11(4A) would apply only to a case where the business is not held under trust. Thus, there is difference between property or business held under trust and business carried on by or on behalf of the trust. [Para 8]

This distinction was recognized by the Supreme Court in the case of Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1980] 121 ITR 1/[1979] 2 Taxman 501 wherein it was observed that if a business undertaking is held under trust for a charitable purpose, the income therefrom would be entitled to the exemption under section 11(1). In the present case, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is that running of the auditorium hall was not held under trust, but it was business commenced/carried on by the Society, subsequent to the formation of trust. Though the business was commenced by the Society and it was carried on by the trust after its formation, it cannot be said to constitute property held under trust under section 11(4), it is only the business which is held under the trust that would enjoy exemption in respect of its income under section 11(1) and there is a distinction between the objects of a trust and the powers given to the trustees to effectuate the purpose of the trust. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the Memorandum of Association of the assessee. The running of auditorium hall was not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of auditorium hall was not even in the contemplation of the Memorandum of Association on the basis of which the society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, was carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust. Section 11(1) confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose. Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1), was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust. In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

There is no connection between the activities relating to running of the auditorium hall and the attainment of the objects of the trust. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from running of auditorium hall is used for charitable purposes would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The application of income generated by the business is not relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. [Para 10]

The essential conditions which enable an assessee to earn exemption are (i) the property from which the income is derived should be held under trust or other legal obligation; (ii) the property should be held for religious or charitable purposes; (iii) then where the property is held wholly for religious or charitable purposes the exemption will be available if the income, is, in fact, applied or accumulated for application to such purposes; and (iv) where property is held in part only for religious or charitable purposes the exemption is confined to income in fact applied or finally set apart for application for such purposes.

It will be clear from section 4 of Act 1922 that for a purpose to be charitable purpose, it must have a public character. In other words, it must be directed to the benefit of the community or a section of the community and not to the benefit of particular private individuals.

To summarise the effect of the provisions of the present trust deed it was held that (i) a trust had been created; (ii) its objects were as set out in clause 2 thereof; (iii) the trustees had full discretion to spend the trust fund and in doing so they might spend their entire funds on one object to the exclusion of the other and thus within the framework of the trust deed they might be able to spend the entire funds for the aid of the members of the settlor’s family. If they decide to spend for the particular object mentioned in clause 2(vi) of the trust deed then the trustees were under no obligation to spend it over persons other than the family of the settlor.

For all the relevant assessment years the trustee had not spent anything for the purposes of their family members and the entire amount had been expended on charitable objects only, but, in spite of anxious consideration, that could not induce to take any different view from that warranted by the language of the section. It was for an assessee to show that this case was covered by the exemption and in view of the nature of the objects specified in the trust deed the exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the Act, 1922 was not available to the assessee. The amendments made in the trust deed could not be held to be retrospective in operation.

Therefore the finding of the Tribunal that the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) was justified.

'Gift' as defined in section 2(xii ) means the transfer by one person to another of any existing movable or immovable property made voluntarily and without consideration in money or money's worth. 'Property' under section 2(xxii) includes any interest in property, movable or immovable, and under section 2(xxiv) 'transfer of property' means any disposition, conveyance, assignment, settlement, delivery, payment or other alienation of property, and includes amongst other things, the creation of a trust in property. The settling in trust of a fund as a charitable fund would be the creation of a trust in property and would, therefore, amount to transfer of property. There would, therefore, be a gift within the meaning of the Act if there is a creation of trust in property for a charitable purpose. There can, therefore, be no doubt whatsoever that there had been a gift under the respective trust deeds within the meaning of the Act.

If the creation of a trust in property for a charitable purpose is a gift for a charitable purpose and if the gift is so made under the trust deed as to belong to charitable fund, which was created under the trust deed for a charitable purpose, the gift could be said to be made to a fund for charitable purpose within the meaning of section 5(1)( v).

The language of section 5(1)(v ) need not be restricted so as to cover gifts made to an institution or fund subsequent to its being established and not include those that are given at the very inception or commencement of the institution or fund. It may be pointed out that a gift when it is made to a charitable fund adds to it and becomes part of it. The very initial gift by which the fund starts/constitutes the part, to which the further gifts are added. All gifts, together form the fund, which is augmented by them. If the subsequently gift, which are parts of the fund itself, are gifts to the fund, the initial gift, which starts the fund itself, could as well be a gift to the fund. Even if one was to take the view that a gift to be exempted under section 5(1)(v) must be made to a fund after it has come into existence, the trust deeds in the instant case could be regard as consisting the fund in the sense of a receptacle in which the donations go and donating the gifts to them.

Having regard to the definitions of the words "gift", "property" and "transfer of property" under the Act and the provision of section 5(1)(v ), which allows exemption in respect of gifts to charitable institutions or funds, under section 5(1)(v), the initial gifts, which were made for the purpose of starting or constituting a fund for charitable purposes of the kinds specified in section 5(1)(v) would be entitled to exemption under the said provision in the same manner in which the subsequent gifts to the fund would be.

Therefore, the initial gifts made under the respective trust deeds by the assessees in the instant case were rightly held by the AAC and the Tribunal as entitled to exemption.

In this regard, the assessee points out that the alleged violations seen collectively are much less than 15 per cent of the gross receipts allowed to be accumulation in terms of 3rd proviso to section 10(23C)(vi). The assessee submits that the said accumulation is unfettered and not subject to any restrictions under the provisions governing exemption available to a charitable trust/society under section 10 and 11. [Para 50]

■ The underlying principle emanating from the judicial precedents is that an absolute and unconditional exemption has been granted to trusts for accumulation of funds upto 15 per cent of income under section 11(1)(a) vis-a-vis satisfaction of special conditions provided under section 11(2) to claim exemption of trust funds (up to 85 per cent). The conditions applicable towards claiming benefit of exemption of trust funds under section 11(2) cannot be stretched and applied with respect to application of funds automatically/absolutely allowed exemption by virtue of ad-hoc exemption under section 11(1)(a). [Para 53]

■

The Commissioner (Exemption) erred to correctly apply the legal position elucidated above to the facts of the assessee while withdrawing approval under section 10(23C)(vi), where alleged misapplication of trust funds was much lesser that 15 per cent of gross receipts for assessment year 2013-14, application of which was otherwise unconditionally/absolutely allowed to the assessee. [Para 54]

■

Regarding the issue of investments made in real estate transactions, the coordinate bench in first round of proceedings has accepted the same to be within the prescribed modes of investment as per section 11(5). As regards the aforesaid being in furtherance to the charitable objects of the assessee, the assessee submits that above said investments in real estate transactions were made by the assessee as part and parcel of its valid application of income within section 11(1), towards its charitable and educational purposes and hence cannot be doubted to be as a valid mode of investment as per section 11(5)(x). [Para 55]

■

Per contra, the revenue submitted that the Commissioner (Exemption) was justified in observing that Society is purchasing luxurious flat for the benefit of the trustee and giving advances without any reciprocal benefit hence, resulting in violation of clause (b) of 3rd proviso of section 10(23) as the fund are not invested into prescribed modes. [Para 56]

■

Regarding the next issue of advance to construction company, it is found that this bench in the first round of appeal has affirmed the same to be well within the permissible mode of investment prescribed vide section 11(5)(x) which is accepted by both parties. [Para 57]

■

Now regarding the nexus of making such investment to the objects of the assessee society, the following undisputed facts are placed before the Tribunal:- (i) Assessee society is running multiple school, branches spread across states within the country and affiliated to governing authorities such as the CBSE, presupposing frequent work related travel by senior staff personnel; (ii) Operational functions of the assessee society such as managing trustee, trustee/treasurer administrator etc., are undoubtedly carried out by skilled and qualified personnel, who merely happen to be related to one another; (iii) Assessee society is a renowned educational institution reporting a surplus on a year-on-year basis with a consolidated gross receipt of over Rs. 40 crores with surplus of over Rs. 2.5 crores for assessment year 2013-14 itself; (iv) Assessee society as a matter of practice parks the surplus funds generated during course of rendering charitable activities towards acquiring of fixed assets on a prudent basis as per the financial records. [Para 58]

■

On giving a thoughtful consideration to the factual position emerging from the above, it is found that the sole premise of drawing adverse finding qua investment in residential flat being located in a posh society of Delhi, to have been utilized only for the personal purposes of the trustee and his family is short sighted and lacks merit. [Para 59]

■

It is held that the assessee society as a matter of practice invests its surplus towards acquisition of fixed assets which is as per the prescribed modes of investment. Further to carry out the objects of the assessee society in a smooth and efficient manner, the assessee society has also invested in residential properties out of the above. [Para 60]

■

The word 'immovable property' by natural reading, will include any type of land, residential or commercial property or any other form of property, which can be termed as immovable property as defined in the Transfer of Property Act. Thus, the society/management is allowed to invest its surplus in immovable property, including residential property. Thus, there cannot be a bar on management of Society to invest its surplus funds in acquisition of a residential property as the law does not mandate any extra bar. [Para 61]

■

(i) Rental income and leasing of properties

■

The principal basis adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) for allowing the assessee's claim is the observation that one of the objects of the trust was to lease out properties and earn rental income. However, on a careful examination of the original trust deed as well as the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the Tribunal finds that the observation is factually incorrect and contrary to the material available on record. The original trust deed, enumerates the charitable objects of the trust, namely: (i) genetic research and agricultural education; (ii) conservation of land, water and genetic resources; (iii) sustainable agriculture and environmental protection; (iv) family planning and population control; and (v) improvement of the status and literacy of women. Subsequently, by way of the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the additional charitable objects of Relief to the Poor and Education were incorporated. Significantly, neither the original trust deed nor the addendum includes, as an object of the trust, carrying on the activity of leasing or renting of immovable properties for earning rental income. [Para 8.2]

■

What is, however, contained in the trust deed is a separate enabling provision conferring powers upon the Board of Trustees. Clause VIII merely authorises the trustees to acquire, hold, manage or otherwise deal with land, buildings and other immovable properties with the funds of the trust for effectuating the charitable objects of the trust. Such an enabling clause cannot be elevated to the status of an independent charitable object. The power to acquire and manage trust properties is only incidental to the effective administration of the trust and to facilitate the attainment of its charitable purposes. Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that leasing of properties itself constituted one of the objects of the trust is clearly erroneous and is not borne out from the trust deed. [Para 8.3]

■

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

■

The record further reveals that the revenue has not brought any material to establish that the rental income earned by the trust was diverted for any non-charitable purpose or that the dominant character of the trust had ceased to be charitable. On the contrary, the Income and Expenditure Account demonstrates that the receipts of the trust, whether derived from grants, donations, interest or rental income, were applied only towards the charitable objects of the trust. Thus, the source from which the income was generated has not altered the fundamental charitable character of the institution. [Para 8.5]

■

It is a settled proposition of law that the decisive test is the dominant object of the institution and not the source of its income. Income derived from property held under trust, including rental income, does not lose the benefit of exemption under Section 11 and Section 12 merely because such income arises from leasing of trust property, so long as it is applied towards the charitable purposes for which the trust has been established. The leasing of trust property, in the facts of the present case, is only an incidental mode of augmenting resources to fulfil the charitable objects and cannot be construed as an independent commercial object of the trust. [Para 8.6]

■

Accordingly, while the Tribunal disagrees with the reasoning assigned by the Commissioner (Appeals) in holding that earning rental income was itself one of the objects of the trust, the Tribunal nevertheless upholds the ultimate conclusion that the assessee cannot be denied exemption on this ground. The reasoning adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) is incorrect; however, the conclusion reached by him is sustainable on the basis that the rental income was merely incidental to the charitable activities and was admittedly applied towards the charitable objects of the trust. Consequently, the ground raised by the Revenue on this issue is devoid of merit and is dismissed. [Para 8.7]

■

Accordingly, the Tribunal concurs with the findings recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue. The ground raised by the Revenue challenging the allowability of exemption merely because the assessee earned rental income is devoid of merit and is, therefore, dismissed. [Para 8.8]

Such a deeming provision of revenue contribution is held as income derived from the trust which is subject to computation and conditions laid down in sections 11 to 13. Sub-section (3) of section 13, clause (cc ) provides that any trustee of the trust or manager (by whatever name called) of the institution comes within the persons referred to in clause (c) of sub-section (1) and clause (a) of sub-section (2) for the purpose of exemption under section 11. The trust and institution referred to in section 13 are not one and the same thing and they are different entities. Clause (cc) of sub-section (3) of section 13 refers to the manager of the institution and not to the manager of the trust and in the instant case the advance had been given to the manager of the trust and not to the manager of the institution. In view of these admitted facts, no interference was called for in the order of the Tribunal.

The activity of the trust fully accords with the objects set out in the deed of trust. The said activity is claimed to be a non-commercial activity without any motive of profit. The income-tax assessment in the case of the assessee for the assessment year 1986-87 was completed under section 143(1) accepting the return of income filed by the assessee including its claim for exemption. Therefore, the stand taken by the Assessing Officer in the wealth-tax proceedings is different from the view taken in the income-tax proceedings. In the gift-tax proceedings, it has been categorically held that there is no gift as understood in law and what is transferred is only the right to enjoy the property. The exemption granted under section 10(22) continues to apply to the assessee even to this day. If the assessee is not liable to pay any income-tax on the income derived from the activity carried on by it and when it is held not liable to pay gift-tax for the transfer of property in its favour, the levy of wealth-tax on the very same property on the ground the activity conducted by the assessee in respect of the property in dispute does not constitute a charitable or religious purpose is difficult to accept. In fact, section 5(1)(i ) provides that wealth-tax shall not be payable by an assessee in respect of the assets mentioned therein and such assets shall not be included in the net wealth of the assessee. One such asset is any property held by him under trust or other legal obligation for any public purpose of a charitable or religious nature in India. Under the provisions of the Act, the income derived from such property is exempt from income-tax on the ground that the said income is utilized for a public purpose or charitable or religious nature. If the said property is held to be a charitable property, it cannot be said that the trust is liable to pay tax. That is precisely what the Appellate Commissioner as well as the Tribunal have held. In fact, the Appellate Commissioner has taken the trouble of setting out the facts, the contents of each document, the law on the point and the discussions contained in the collateral proceedings and has come to a reasoned conclusion that wealth-tax is not payable by the assessee. There is no infirmity in the said order. It is based on legal evidence. In that view of the matter, there is no merit in all the appeals. Accordingly, these appeals are to be dismissed. [Para 11]

There is nothing on record to show that the managing trustee 'V' was in fact inflating the construction cost for his benefits. If the Assessing Officer was having any doubt, he could have summoned the office bearers of the trust and concerned parties related to construction expenditure incurred. That having not been done, he could not have disputed the genuineness of the expenditure. There was absolutely no material before the Assessing Officer to show that the managing trustee in fact inflating the construction cost for his benefits. The revenue has failed to bring on record any evidence in the form of bill, voucher or other records proving that the amount of purchase which has been accounted for in the construction cost, was used by the managing trustee for his personal benefit.

There is no evidence that the income of the society was used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of managing trustee. It is not the case of the revenue that the managing trustee benefited directly or indirectly as provided in sub-section (2) of section 13. The term 'benefit' excludes from its ambit a two way process. If the person in the prohibited category renders services and in lieu thereof a benefit is provided then the case does not fall in clause (ii) of section 13(1)(c). The expenditure incurred on those interested persons would be a compensation for such services. A benefit would be said to have been given to the persons of prohibited category, if they in return do nothing but only enjoy the fruits of the trust/society and take away the funds/income of the society for their personal benefit or discharging personal obligation. There is no such situation in the case under consideration.

Section 13 carves out an exception to the general exemption granted under sections 11 and 12 to income derived by trusts/charitable institutions. The onus lies on the revenue to bring on record, cogent material/evidence to establish that the trust/charitable institution is hit by provisions of section 13. As noted above, the Assessing Officer made out the case on presumption since there is a difference between the cost of construction shown in the books of account and estimated by the DVO.

The Assessing Officer had neither brought on record any evidence nor able to point out modus operandi how was the managing trustee directly or indirectly benefited out of the construction cost of building of the society. There is no need to mention that the registered society running educational programmes are managed by Trustees. The day-to-day activities of the society are supposed to be administrated and controlled by the managing committee by holding various meetings and passing resolution etc. The building in which impugned investment stated to be made has been stated to be shown by the society in its books of account. Therefore, if any benefit is going that would be going to the society only and in these circumstances there is no violation of section 13. [Para 16]

In the light of above discussion, it is opined that the Assessing Officer has wrongly invoked section 13 and has wrongly withdrawn benefit of section 11 read with section 12. Consequently, the appeal filed by the assessee is allowed. [Para 21]

The trust deed was executed by the settlor with the intention that the income from the properties transferred should be utilised for the maintenance of his daughter S and the balance, if any, for charitable purposes. The properties had been transferred to be held in trust according to the terms mentioned in the trust deed. The Commissioner, after referring to the various clauses of the trust-deed had concluded that the trust could not by any accepted standards be regarded as a charitable trust for the reason that the purposes of the trust included maintenance and meeting the needs of any other relatives of the donor at the absolute discretion of the managing trustee and a trust created primarily for the benefit of the members of the settlor's family was not for charitable purposes. Clause 10 of the trust-deed gave to the managing trustee to have the final voice in all matters concerning the utilisation of the income and disposal of the trust property. It was open to the managing trustee to utilise the entire income for the maintenance and meeting the needs of any of the relatives of the donor at his absolute discretion. Besides, the individual shares of the persons on whose behalf the income was received, were also indeterminate.

Therefore, the assessee-trust was not a charitable trust and the writ was accordingly dismissed.

To decide the instant appeal, it was not necessary to resolve the controversy as to whether or not the benefits of the assessee-trust were open to the wider public. The parent body, Z, had been accepted to be and held by the depart-ment to be entitled to exemption under section 11. It was as a part of the activity of Z that the education fund for specific purposes, i.e., granting scholarships to the children of the employees of the members of Z, was created. If the department held that this particular function of Z, performed through the education fund was not charitable, Z itself could not be said to be a charitable institution holding property in trust for charitable purposes. The very fact that the revenue had not denied exemption under section 11 to Z would ensure that all the activities of that association including the education fund would be entitled to exemption under section 11. Indeed, looking to the origin of the funds and the nature of the assessee-trust, it would appear that even treating it as a separate taxable entity was a mistake, even though the assessee had filed a separate return. The assessee-trust was, accordingly, entitled to exemption under section 11.

This Court has held in CWT v. Adarsh Gram Trust [D.B. Civil WT Reference No. 53 of 1972, dated 3-12-1984] that as the assessee-trust was created wholly for charitable purposes, the income derived from its property held under trust was exempt from payment of income-tax on account of the provisions of section 11(1)(a). For the reasons given in the aforesaid judgment and following the same, the assessee-trust was held to be entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a ).

There seems to be no connection whatsoever between the commission earned by the managing agents and the keeping in deposit of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000. It is difficult to see how it could possibly be stated on the facts of this case that the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which constitutes the trust fund is invested in the managing agency business. Reliance has been placed by Sir Jarnshedji on a decision of the Privy Council in All India Spinners' Association v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay [1944] 12 ITR 482 . In that case two questions arose for the decision of the Privy Council. One was whether there was a trust or other legal obligation under which the property from which the income was derived was held, and the second was whether it was a trust or legal obligation for the relief of the poor or for any other object of general public utility. The High Court of Bombay had taken the view that it was not a charitable trust within the meaning of the Income-tax Act. That finding was not accepted by their Lordships of the Privy Council. On the other question whether the property was held upon trust within the meaning of the Act, their Lordships of the Privy Council pointed out that by clause 3 of the trust deed it was expressly provided that the funds and assets of the association were to vest in the trustees to be held for the purposes of the association, and their Lordships further held that the property of the association consisted of the organization and the undertaking as well as the fluctuating stock of yarn and cloth. Therefore the income for which the All India Spinners' Association was claiming exemption was the income derived from the whole organization and undertaking of the association, which organization and undertaking included the stock of yarn and cloth.

Then reliance has been placed on another Privy Council decision in Commissioner of Income-tax v. Currimbhoy Ebrahim & Sons [1935] 3 ITR 395 and in that case the Privy Council was considering the meaning to be given to the expression "property". They were construing the word "property" as used in Section 42(1) of the Act and the opinion their Lordships gave was that the word " property " as it occurs in sub-section (1) of Section 42 could not be given so special a colour but was used as an ordinary English word to be taken in its usual signification subject to the context provided by the rest of the sub-section, and this expression of opinion of the Privy Council is relied upon ,by Sir Jamshedji for urging that the expression "property" used in Section 4(3)(i) is used in its widest signification. The Privy Council has emphasised the fact that there is no definition given of the expression "property" in the Act, and "property" must be construed in its plain natural meaning subject to the context in which that expression occurs. Sir Jamshedji has advanced a very interesting argument that "property" in the sense used in Section 4(3)(i) is used in the sense in which it includes all proprietary rights, both rights in rem and rights in personam, and according to Sir Jamshedji even if the commission earned by the managing agents was as a result of a contract and the commission constituted a benefit under the contract, the benefit under the contract would be property within the meaning of Section 4(3)(i). In our opinion it is unnecessary to decide this question because, as we have already pointed out, the only property which is held on trust in this case is the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 in respect of which the trust has been constituted. It is unnecessary to launch upon an inquiry as to whether benefits under a contract would or would not constitute property because as far as this case is concerned there ft no benefit under any contract which has been held under trust. It is either the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 with which we are concerned or any business started with the assistance of that sum of Rs. 1,00,000, and as already pointed out in this particular case the managing agency commission is derived neither from the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 nor from any business which has been started with the assistance of that sum of Rs. 1,00,000.
