2.4 Rationalisation of taxation regime for charitable trusts and institutions under sections 11 to 13

The existing provisions of section 11 contain a primary condition that for grant of exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust, such income should be applied for the charitable purposes in India, and where such income cannot be so applied during the previous year, it has to be accumulated in the prescribed modes.

2.4-1 New sub-section (6) - No depreciation if purchase of asset claimed as application of income

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted new sub-section (6) in section 11, with effect from 1-4-2015. The said sub-section (6) provides that where any income is required to be applied or accumulated or set apart for application, then, for such purposes the income shall be determined without any deduction or allowance by way of depreciation or otherwise in respect of any asset, acquisition of which has been claimed as an application of income under this section in any previous year (See also Para 2.3).

2.4-2 New sub-section (7) - No exemption under any clause of sec. 10 except clauses (1) and (23C) if registration u/s 12A or 12AA in force

New sub-section (7), inserted with effect from 1-4-2015, applies to a trust or an institution which has been granted registration (under section 12AA or under section 12A) for purposes of availing exemption under section 11. In terms of new sub-section (7), where such registration is in force for a previous year, then such trust or institution shall not be entitled to any exemption under any provision of section 10 [other than that relating to exemption of agricultural income and income exempt under section 10(23C)].

The amendment overcomes the decision of the Tribunal in Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mum. - Trib.). In Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt. DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mumbai - Trib.) the assessee claimed that dividend income on shares and unit and long term capital gain on sale of shares are exempt u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) respectively. The AO denied the exemption on the ground that section 11 exclusively deals with the income derived from the property held under trust and not u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38). Hence the AO held that there is a violation u/s 13 and as a result of the same exemption u/s 11 is denied. The assessee cannot claim the alternative claim for exemption u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) because these sections do not deal with income derived from the property held under the trust. On appeal, the CIT(A) concurred with AO’s view. On further appeal, however, ITAT ruled in favour of the assessee-trust and held that "the income which is exempt u/s 10 cannot be brought to tax by virtue of sections 11 and 13 of the Act because no such pre-condition is provided either u/s 10 or 11 to 13. Therefore, sections 11 to 13 would not operate as overriding effect to the section 10 of the Act. The language of these provisions does not suggest that either section 10 is subjected to the provisions of sections 11 to 13 or sections 11 to 13 has any overriding effect over section 10. Therefore, the benefit of section 10 cannot be denied by invoking the provisions of sections 11 to 13 of the Act. Once the conditions of section 10 are satisfied then no other condition can be fastened for denying the claim under section 10 of the Act".

Amendment to section 11 now overcomes the above judicial ruling.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted new sub-section (6) in section 11, with effect from 1-4-2015. The said sub-section (6) provides that where any income is required to be applied or accumulated or set apart for application, then, for such purposes the income shall be determined without any deduction or allowance by way of depreciation or otherwise in respect of any asset, acquisition of which has been claimed as an application of income under this section in any previous year (See also Para 2.3).

2.4-2 New sub-section (7) - No exemption under any clause of sec. 10 except clauses (1) and (23C) if registration u/s 12A or 12AA in force

New sub-section (7), inserted with effect from 1-4-2015, applies to a trust or an institution which has been granted registration (under section 12AA or under section 12A) for purposes of availing exemption under section 11. In terms of new sub-section (7), where such registration is in force for a previous year, then such trust or institution shall not be entitled to any exemption under any provision of section 10 [other than that relating to exemption of agricultural income and income exempt under section 10(23C)].

The amendment overcomes the decision of the Tribunal in Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mum. - Trib.). In Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt. DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mumbai - Trib.) the assessee claimed that dividend income on shares and unit and long term capital gain on sale of shares are exempt u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) respectively. The AO denied the exemption on the ground that section 11 exclusively deals with the income derived from the property held under trust and not u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38). Hence the AO held that there is a violation u/s 13 and as a result of the same exemption u/s 11 is denied. The assessee cannot claim the alternative claim for exemption u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) because these sections do not deal with income derived from the property held under the trust. On appeal, the CIT(A) concurred with AO’s view. On further appeal, however, ITAT ruled in favour of the assessee-trust and held that "the income which is exempt u/s 10 cannot be brought to tax by virtue of sections 11 and 13 of the Act because no such pre-condition is provided either u/s 10 or 11 to 13. Therefore, sections 11 to 13 would not operate as overriding effect to the section 10 of the Act. The language of these provisions does not suggest that either section 10 is subjected to the provisions of sections 11 to 13 or sections 11 to 13 has any overriding effect over section 10. Therefore, the benefit of section 10 cannot be denied by invoking the provisions of sections 11 to 13 of the Act. Once the conditions of section 10 are satisfied then no other condition can be fastened for denying the claim under section 10 of the Act".

Amendment to section 11 now overcomes the above judicial ruling.

Calculation - For the purposes of sections 11(1)(a) and 11(1)(b), it has been held that the amount of accumulation (of 15%) is to be calculated on the total income (i.e., gross receipts) derived from such property and not on the amount remaining after application of income in India [CIT v. Programme for Community Organisation [2001] 116 Taxman 608 (SC)].

Deemed income - Deemed income (i.e., tax deducted at source) is not to be taken into account for determining the accumulation of income [CIT v. Jayashree Charity Trust [1986] 159 ITR 280 (Cal.)].

Where, due to non-investment of accumulated income in the prescribed securities in a year, such income is deemed to be the income of the trust for that year, the assessee will be entitled to accumulate prescribed percentage of the total income of that year, inclusive of such deemed income [CIT v. Investment/deposit in specified modes - The accumulated income which is exempt u/s 11(1)(a) need not be invested in Government securities. It is only in respect of any additional accumulated income beyond prescribed percentage that, if the assessee wants exemption of the additional accumulated income also, the assessee is required to invest the additional accumulated income in the manner laid down in section 11(2) after following the procedure laid down therein [S. Investment must necessarily come out of the current year's income. An investment made in the past obviously cannot satisfy this requirement [CIT v. Indian National Theatre Trust [2008] 169 Taxman 42 (Delhi)].

Generation of surplus out of gross receipts A doubt has been raised whether generation of surplus out of gross receipts would necessarily 'breach' the threshold condition that the educational institution should exist 'solely for educational purpose and not for the purpose of profit'. Perusal of prescribed provisions clearly reveal that mere generation of surplus cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) on the ground that it amounts to an activity of the nature of profit making. In fact, the third Proviso to the said clause clearly provides that accumulation of income is permissible subject to the manner prescribed therein provided such accumulation is to be applied "wholly and exclusively to the objects for which it is established". Hence, it is clarified that mere generation of surplus by educational institution from year to year cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) if it is used for educational purposes unless the accumulation is contrary to the manner prescribed under law.

4. Collection of amounts under different heads of fee from students—

It has been brought to the notice that collection of small amounts from students by way of application fee, examination fee, fee for issuing transfer certificate, subscription fee for library etc. is being treated by some Assessing Officers as profit making activity resulting in denial of exemption u/s 10(23C)(vi). Collection of small and reasonable amounts under different heads of fee, which are essentially in the nature of fee connected with imparting education and do not violate any Central or State regulation does not, in general, represent a profit making activity. Hence, there is no justification for treating the charging of small amounts under different heads of fee as profit making activity unless the amount in the nature of 'capitation fee' is charged directly or indirectly.

1.2-4d Generally - In the light of the amendments, any trust or institution claiming exemption under sections 11 to 13 will have to examine:

◆ Whether objects include any object, which could be classified as the Other Object? ◆ Whether it is pursuing any activity, which can be classified or has been classified as the Other Object?

◆ Whether the activity pursued is correctly classified as the Other Object? Can it otherwise fall under the specific objects, namely: the relief of poor, education or medical relief?

◆ Whether the activity involved in pursuit of the Other Objects is in the nature of trade?

◆ Whether the activity involved in pursuit of the Other Objects amounts to rendering of services in relation to the trade? If so, whether it is for a consideration?

◆ Whether newly inserted proviso to section 2(15) is applicable?

◆ If not, the reasons thereof.

◆ If yes, the implications, if any, in respect of the specific objects (the relief of poor or education or medical relief).

◆ Whether income derived from the property held in trust can be and is also applied towards the objects, which do not constitute charitable purpose (in particular, on account of the applicability of the proviso)?

Misappropriated fund - Where a charitable trust had itself offered misappropriated fund as its additional business income, said additional income could not be held as 'application of income' [CIT v. St. Joseph Asylum Industrial Workshop [2014] 45 taxmann.com 8/223 Taxman 149 (Kar.)].

Provision - Where an amount was set apart as provision in the accounts of the assessee and the finding of fact was that the amount was not actually applied for charitable or religious purposes, assessee would not be entitled to exemption u/s 11 in respect of that amount [Nachimuthu Industrial Association v. CIT [1999] 235 ITR 190 (SC)].

Repayment of borrowed funds - Repayment of funds borrowed for construction of building could be treated as 'application of income' for charitable purposes and, thus, entitling assessee to exemption [CIT v. Janmabhumi Press Trust [2000] 242 ITR 457 (Kar.); DIT v. Span Foundation [2009] 178 Taxman 436 (Delhi); DIT v. Govindu Naicker Estate [2009] 315 ITR 237 (Mad.)].

Salaries - Expenditure on salaries and miscellaneous expenses for purpose of carrying out objects and purposes of the trust can be considered as application of income for charitable purpose [CIT v. Birla Janahit Trust [1994] 73 Taxman 465 (Cal.)].

Scholarship - Where charitable object of assessee was advancement of higher technical education to deserving students, assessee's claim of expenditure incurred on account of scholarship paid to incumbent for pursuing engineering was allowable [CIT v. Seth Anandram Jaipuria Edu. Society Cantonment [2017] 80 taxmann.com 96 (All.)].

Statutory contributions - Statutory transfer of amount collected as mandi shulk to Mandi Parishad would constitute 'application of income' for charitable purposes [CIT v. Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti [2012] 27 taxmann.com 42/211 Taxman 32 (SC)].

Finance Act, 2020

3.3 Charitable trust, exemption of income from property held under [Section 11]

Explanation 2 to section 11(1), prior to its amendment by Finance Act, 2020, provided that any amount credited or paid out of income referred to in section 11(1)(a)/(b) read with Explanation 1, to any other trust or institution registered under section 12AA, being contributions with specific direction that they shall form part of the corpus of the trust or institution, shall not be treated as application of income. In other words, only corpus donations to other trusts or institutions registered under section 12AA are disallowed under Explanation 2.

Vide Finance Act, 2020, Explanation has been added to third proviso to section 10(23C) to clarify with effect from 1-4-2020 that corpus donations received by funds, trusts, institutions, universities, hospitals which have obtained approval under section 10(23C) are excluded from income of such funds, trust, etc. [see para 3.2].

Therefore, to cover corpus donations to such fund, trust, etc. within the ambit of Explanation 2 to section 11(1), Explanation 2 has been amended1 to also provide that any amount credited or paid out of income referred to in section 11(1)(a)/(b) read with Explanation 1, to any fund or trust or institution or any university or other educational institution or any hospital or other medical institution referred section 10(23C)(iv)/(v)/(vi)/(via), being contribution with a specific direction that they shall form part of the corpus should not be regarded as application of income for the donor-institution.

Explanation 2 has not been amended to include reference to trust or institution registered under section 12AB.

Following amendments are made in section 11(7):

Section 11(7), prior to its amendment by the Finance Act, 2020, provided that where a trust or an institution had been granted registration under section 12AA(1)(b) or had obtained registration at any time under section 12A and the said registration was in force for any previous year, then the trust would not get exemption under section 10 except in respect of agricultural income under section 10(1) or income covered by section 10(23C).

Consequent upon the insertion of section 12AB, the said sub-section has been amended with effect from 1-6-2020 to cover a trust registered under section 12AB also. In other words, a trust so registered would not be eligible to get exemption under section 10 except the aforesaid income.

Section 10(46) provides for exemption of specified income if the following conditions are fulfilled:

(a)

The income arises to a specified entity which has been established or constituted by or under a specified Act or constituted by Central/State Government.

(b)

The specified entity is established or constituted with object of regulating or administering any activity for the benefit of the general public.

(c)

The specified entity is not engaged is any commercial activity.

(d)

The specified entity is notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette for the purposes of section 10(46).

Section 11(7) has been amended with effect from 1-6-2020 to provide that an entity registered under section 12AA/12AB shall also be entitled to claim exemption under section 10(46).

Hitherto, section 11(7), on account of its language, made it evident that an entity had the option to claim exemption under section 10(23C) or section 11. Now, a proviso has been inserted in section 11(7) with effect from 1-6-2020 to provide that the registration referred to in it shall become inoperative from later of the following dates:—

(a)

the date on which the trust or institution is approved under section 10(23C), or is notified under section 10(46), as the case may be; or

(b)

the date on which the proviso comes into force, that is, 1-6-2020.

In other words, the registration shall be inoperative if an approval is obtained under section 10(23C) or the Institution is notified under section 10(46).

definition of the term 'charitable purpose' as defined in section 2(15) but in view of the fact that certification of seeds by the petitioner facilitates trade, commerce or business in the certified seeds by the client of the petitioner, the proviso to the said section would come into operation. Thus, the petitioner's activity assists the sale of certified seeds and is 'in relation to any trade, commerce or business' and therefore its activity cannot be held to be a 'charitable purpose'. Bureau of Indian Standards v. Director General of Income-tax (Exemptions) [2012] 27 taxmann.com 127/[2013] 212 Taxman 210/260 CTR 39/358 ITR 78 (Delhi)

The expressions "any activity", "rendering any service" and "in relation to any trade, commerce or business" imply that the intention of the legislature was to make the latter part of the exception broad and inclusive. It seems that the exception (the first proviso) is intended to catch with its ambit any and all commercial activity, except what falls within the second proviso (which bars application of the exception in cases where the aggregate value of the receipts from the activities mentioned therein is less than ten lakh rupees in the relevant previous year). The Bureau, it would appear at the first blush, renders service in relation to trade, commerce or business by granting certification/quality marks in return of license fee. Apparently, Parliament intended to clarify that not all activities of State agencies (some of which might be set up to carry on trading and commercial activities) can be considered charitable.

In these circumstances, "rendering any service in relation to trade, commerce or business" cannot, in the opinion of the Court, receive such a wide construction as to enfold regulatory and sovereign authorities, set up under statutory enactments, and tasked to act as agencies of the State in public duties which cannot be discharged by private bodies. Often, apart from the controlling or parent statutes, like the BIS Act, these statutory bodies (including BIS) are empowered to frame rules or regulations, exercise coercive powers, including inspection, raids; they possess search and seizure powers and are invariably subjected to Parliamentary or legislative oversight. The primary object for setting up such regulatory bodies would be to ensure general public utility. The prescribing of standards, and enforcing those standards, through accreditation and continuing supervision through inspection, etc., cannot be considered as trade, business or commercial activity, merely because the testing procedures, or accreditation involves charging of such fees. It cannot be said that the public utility activity of evolving, prescribing and enforcing standards, "involves" the carrying on of trade or commercial activity.

Ghatkopar Jolly Gymkhana v. DIT (Exemption) [2013] 40 taxmann.com 207/[2014] 147 ITD 112/160 TTJ 620 (Mum.)

First proviso to section 2(15) is a very rigorous provision which excludes the institution or trust from the definition of 'charitable trust', if such trust carries activities in the nature of trade, commerce or business, or any activity of rendering any service in relation to any trade, commerce or business, for a cess or fee or any other consideration, irrespective of the nature of use or application, or retention, of the income from such activity. So before the insertion of the second proviso from 1-4-2009, the definition of 'charitable purpose' when read with first proviso was very restrictive. However, by the insertion of the second proviso with effect from 1-4-2009 the rigour of the first proviso has been diluted and the first proviso has not been made applicable even if the trust carries on business activities and the gross receipts from such activities is Rs.10.00 lakhs or less than Rs.10.00 lakhs in the previous year. Hence, from 1-4-2009 the carrying out of the activities of trade, commerce or business even by charitable trust is not barred so as to exclude its activities from the definition of charitable purposes. However, a limitation has been imposed to the effect that the gross receipts from such activities should not exceed Rs.10.00 lakhs.

Late Shri Mohanlal Kanjibhai Pansara Education & Charitable Trust v. CIT [2013] 36 taxmann.com 338/59 SOT 169 (Rajkot)

The definition of 'Charitable Purpose' as given in section 2(15) is in the nature of inclusive definition. Charity means an act of piety and benevolence intended to benefit the society at large. Importing education would qualify to be called a charitable activity only if it is of public character directed for the benefit of the community or a section of the community and not motivated by commercial or business considerations. An activity which is motivated by commercial considerations can never qualify to be called a charitable activity. The same principle applies to education. The inherent features of 'charity' must be present in all the activities enumerated in section 2(15).

Critical Art & Media Practices v. DIT (Exemption) [2015] 56 taxmann.com 118/153 ITD 664/170 TTJ 401 (Mum.)

Where fixed deposits in name of assessee-trust worth Rs. 16 lakhs were pledged as security with bank for enabling one of members of the assessee to avail loan without adequate security and consideration, and certain transaction of purchase of lands was routed through an AOP in which all members were directors and employees of assessee, the misutilization was glaring and it could not escape the clutches of law, nor any sympathy or equities could be extended, particularly for an organization which received donations purely for the welfare of the under-privileged and needy class of the society. In view of the fact that entire transaction was within the personal knowledge of trustees, it could be said that the funds of assessee were diverted and misutilised. On facts, the assessee had violated provisions of section 13(1)(c)(ii) read with section 13(2)(b) and, thus, was not entitled for exemption [Action for Welfare & Awakening in Rural Environment (AWARE) v. DCIT [2003] 130 Taxman 82 (AP)].

When rent received by assessee-trust in respect of building constructed from borrowed funds was more than standard rent computed in accordance with Delhi Rent Control Act, question of any benefit being derived by an interested person did not arise [DIT v. Span Foundation [2009] 178 Taxman 436 (Delhi)].

Where funds of assessee-trust were utilised for purchase of car in the name of its trustee(s), there being a violation of section 13(2)(b) [CIT v. Audyogik Shikshan Mandal [2019] 101 taxmann.com 247/261 Taxman 12 (Bom.)].

Inadequate compensation for services rendered - Where the donor has given a post-dated cheque (to be honoured in next FY) and such donor have not availed any benefit in the FY in which such cheque has been given, then there being no violation of the provisions of either section 13(2)(b) or section 13(2)(d) [DIT v. Raunaq Education Foundation [2013] 29 taxmann.com 150/213 Taxman 19 (SC)].

Transaction with related party at arm's length – Where rates of purchases by assessee-trust from related party were same as with unrelated party, provisions of section 13(2)(g) held not attracted [CIT v. Shri Ramdoot Prasad Sewa Samiti, Trust [2022] 140 taxmann.com 451 (Raj.)].

'Funds', meaning of - The expression used u/s 13(2)(h) is 'funds' and not 'fund'. 'Funds' means money in hand or cash according to some dictionaries. This would be the proper meaning to be attributed to the expression 'funds' as appearing in the provisions. The fundamental requirement of section 13(2)(h) is that there must be investment of funds of a trust. If any expanded meaning is given to include assets other than money in hand or cash or credit balance in a bank account, it is evident that they are not capable of being invested as such. Other assets of the trust apart from money in hand or cash or balance in bank will have to be converted into money or cash before the same can be invested [CIT v. Birla Charity Trust [1987] 34 Taxman 504/[1988] 170 ITR 150 (Cal.)].

The term 'funds' mentioned in section 13(2)(h) includes both the corpus as well as the income derived therefrom [Teleprolu Bapanaiah Vidyadharma Nidhi Trust v. CIT [1987] 31 Taxman 399 (AP)].

Where shares in certain companies in which the specified persons had substantial interest were donated to the assessee-trust, it would not amount to 'investment' of its 'funds', since the assessee-trust did not lay out money for the shares held by it. Section 13(2)(h) will not apply, particularly when, even otherwise, the shares were not covered by the expression 'funds' [CIT v. Insaniyat Trust [1988] 40 Taxman 159 (Guj.); CWT v. Bharat Charity Trust [1993] 199 ITR 420 (Cal.); CIT v. Trustees of Kasturbai Scindia Commission Trust [1993] 69 Taxman 376 (Bom.)].

A promissory note cannot be equated to 'funds', but at best could only be an actionable claim and it is extremely difficult to conceive of an investment of an actionable claim [Auditor Dasaradha Rami Reddy Charities v. CIT [1989] 44 Taxman 453 (Mad.)].

◆ The amendment enlarges the scope of the term ‘infrastructure facility’ by including water treatment systems and solid waste management systems in its ambit alongwith roads, highways, bridges, airports, ports, rail systems, water supply projects, irrigation projects and sanitation and sewerage systems. Amendments in sections 12 and 13 relating to taxation of charitable trusts

11.4 Hitherto, section 13 provided that the income of a charitable or religious trust would not be exempt if any part of income or the property of the trust or institution was used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person such as the author of the trust or the founder of the institution, trustee of the trust or manager or relative of such person (hereinafter referred to as a ‘specified person’) or any concern in which any such person has a substantial interest.

Section 13 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2001-02 and a new sub-section (6) has been added which provides that a trust running an educational institution or a medical institution or a hospital shall not lose the benefit of exemption of any income other than the value of benefits of educational or medical facilities provided to the specified persons, solely on the ground that such benefits have been provided to specified persons. In other words, the value of any such income received from specified persons would be taxable, however, the other income would remain exempt.

The expression ‘value’ has been defined in Explanation to section 12(2) of the Act, as ‘the value of any benefit or facility granted or provided free of cost or at concessional rate’.

The new provisions would apply only to charitable or religious trust running a hospital or a medical institution or an educational institution. They would not apply to all institutions eligible for exemption under section 11 of the Act, e.g. sanitariums, religious trusts, etc., would not get the benefits of the new provisions.

It appears that the value of facility provided to the specified persons would be taxable and no deduction shall be allowed in respect of expenses incurred in providing services to the specified person.

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill reads as follows -

“The existing provisions provide that the income of a charitable or religious trust will not be available if any part of such income or any property of the trust is used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person such as the author of the trust, trustee or any relative of such persons or any concerns in which such persons have a substantial interest (referred to as a specified person). It is proposed to insert a new sub-section in section 13 to provide that a trust running an educational institution or a medical institution or a hospital shall not lose the benefit of exemption of any income other than the value of benefits of educational or medical facilities provided to the specified persons, solely on the ground that such benefits have been provided to specified persons.”

This gives an impression that the amendment is made for all categories of interested persons including concerns.

However, the residual category specified in section 13(3)(e), namely, ‘any concern in which any person referred to in clauses (a), (b), (c), (cc) and (d) has a substantial interest’ is not specifically mentioned in sections 12(2) and 13(6). Thus, it is not clear as to whether a trust will lose tax exemption if any benefit is given directly or indirectly to the residual category in section 13(3)(e).

11.4-1 Amendment of section 12 - A new sub-section (2) has been inserted in section 12 with effect from the assessment year 2001-02. It provides that the value of any medical or educational services made available by any charitable or religious trust running a hospital or medial institution or an educational institution to any specified person shall be deemed to be the income of such trust or institution derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes during the previous year in which such services are so provided and shall be chargeable to income-tax notwithstanding the provisions of section 11(1).

Amendment in forms and modes of investing or depositing the funds by charitable trusts

11.5 Exemption of income under section 11 is available to a trust only if its funds are invested or deposited in any one or more of the forms or modes specified in section 11(5).

A new clause (ixa) has been inserted in section 11(5) to provide that trusts shall now be allowed to invest its funds in public companies formed and registered in India with the main object of carrying on the business of providing long-term finance for urban infrastructure.

For this purpose,

(a) “long-term finance” means any loans or advance where the terms under which moneys are loaned or advance provide for repayment along with interest thereof during a period of not less than five years;

(b) “public company” shall have the meaning assigned to it in section 3 of the Companies Act, 1956

(c) “urban infrastructure” means a project for providing potable water supply, sanitation and sewerage, draining, solid waste management, roads, bridges and flyovers for urban transport;’.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1946-47 to 1948-49 - Assessee executed a deed of trust whereby they settled certain amount on various charities and appointed themselves as trustees - Later, in accordance with terms of trust deed, trustees assessees were appointed as managing agents of a company - Before Income-tax authorities, trustee claimed that income derived from managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Revenue authorities, however, held that income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Whether word "property" in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend "business," and if question fell to be decided solely on terms of that sub-section, managing agency formed by assessees/trustees must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether fact that trustees had option at any time to throw up managing agency was no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

FACT: 'P; 'L' and 'LS' executed a deed of trust whereby they settled a sum on various charities specified therein and appointed themselves and two others as trustees. The trust deed provided inter alia that the trustees mights with the help of the trust fund, for and on behalf of and for the benefit of the trust, carry on such business including the taking up and conducting the managing agency or selling agency of any company in such name or names as they in their absolute discretion might think fit and proper. Later the trustees were appointed as managing agents of a company. The agency was to be for a period of 20 years; but it was open to the trustees to throw it up on giving three months' notice. The managing agents were to get a remuneration of 10 per cent of the net annual profits. Before the Income-tax authorities, the assessee/trustees claimed that the income derived from the managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The Income-tax authorities held that the income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court held that no part of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which was the only property settled on trust was actually invested in the managing agency business, which could not, therefore, be regarded as trust property, and that the income received from that business was not within the exemption enacted in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: The 'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation.

'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation. It is true that a public charity is perpetual in character, and that means that it is capable of enforcement, so long as there is any property left which can be appropriated for its objects. And even if some or all of the objects become incapable of fulfilment, the trust properties will be devoted to the performance of similar or allied charitable purposes on the doctrine of cy-pres. But so far as the trust properties themselves are concerned, they will be held only on the incidents to which they are subject under the law. Thus, if the property is a leasehold interest, it must cease on the termination of the lease. Likewise, if trust property is alienated under circumstances binding on the trust, it will go out of the trust. But that does not operate as an extinction of the trust, unless there is no property at all left, with which the trust could be carried out. That is the principle enacted in section 77(c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which in terms, however, applies only to private trusts. Therefore, the fact that the trustees have the option at any time to throw up the managing agency is no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust.

In the result, it could be held that the word 'property' in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend 'business', and if the question fell to be decided solely on the terms of that sub-section, the managing agency must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

With aforesaid observation, the case was remanded to High Court for a fresh disposal on merits.

[Matter remanded to High Court]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether section 4(3)(i) relates to income from business held under trust and section 4(3)(ia) relates to income from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution where that business itself is not held on trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where business of managing agency was held in trust, it could be concluded that business carried on by trustees fell under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: Under a trust deed dated the 15-6-1945, according to the decision of the Privy Council the business of a managing agency was held in trust. Therefore, the income derived from managing agency was held by the Supreme Court as falling with section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act since the word "property" in that sub-section includes business as well. But it was contended before the Supreme Court that although the income might appear to fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act has been narrowed down by the provision in section 4(3)(ia) which deals with income from business and, therefore, the Sub-section that really applies to the determination of the question as to whether the income sought to be taxed in the hands of the trustees was exempt from tax in section 4(3)(ia) and not section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. It was common ground that if section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act was the section under which the exemption claimed was to be determined, the conditions laid down in that sub-section for the purpose of granting an exemption were not satisfied and, therefore, the assessees would not be entitled to an exemption. The question was, therefore, of vital importance to the assessees as to whether their case fell within section 4(3)(i) of section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether where assessee-trust had incurred expenses from charity fund and they were in excess 
of income earned, it was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a) - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-trust was constituted by one ‘J’ who was the manager of certain religious and charitable funds. By the deed of indenture, it was declared that the respective assets of the religious and charitable funds would be in favour of the trustees who would hold the management and operate the respective assets of those funds for the purposes stated in the trust deed. Thus, the assessee claimed exemption on that ground. The Assessing Officer held that since the expenses incurred were in excess than the income derived from various funds, the trustee was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a). The AAC, however, allowed the appeal. On further appeal, the Tribunal restored the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: The assessee had incurred expenses from the charity fund and had incurred excess expenses than the income earned. Thus, the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a). [Para 8]

The reference so made stood disposed of accordingly. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Denial of exemption) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee-trust was conducting its activities in carrying out charitable activities, i.e., education, relief to poor, etc. - During year, assessee purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing funds of assessee-trust and same was registered in name of managing trustee - Assessing Officer denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to extent of value of that vehicle on ground that objects of assessee trust were carrying out of charitable activities and fund collected for this charitable purposes was utilized for enjoyment of trustees by means of purchase of said vehicle in name of managing trustee which was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c) - Assessee submitted that car was purchased in name of managing trustee for simple reason that it gave relief by way of lower road/life tax and insurance charges - However, assessee could not prove as to what use this asset was put to by trust in work of trust and for purposes for which trust had been set up - Whether since assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased by assessee-trust with its funds and registered in name of managing trustee - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing its funds and same was registered in name of managing trustee, however, assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased

Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Denial of exemption) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee-trust was conducting its activities in carrying out charitable activities, i.e., education, relief to poor, etc. - During year, assessee purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing funds of assessee-trust and same was registered in name of managing trustee - Assessing Officer denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to extent of value of that vehicle on ground that objects of assessee trust were carrying out of charitable activities and fund collected for this charitable purposes was utilized for enjoyment of trustees by means of purchase of said vehicle in name of managing trustee which was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c) - Assessee submitted that car was purchased in name of managing trustee for simple reason that it gave relief by way of lower road/life tax and insurance charges - However, assessee could not prove as to what use this asset was put to by trust in work of trust and for purposes for which trust had been set up - Whether since assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased by assessee-trust with its funds and registered in name of managing trustee - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: ■

The assessee-trust was carrying out charitable activities like education, relief to poor, etc.

■

The Assessing Officer found that a vehicle purchased by the trust was registered in the name of the managing trustee and thus, the case of the Assessing Officer was that the assessee purchased the above said vehicle and registered in the name of the trustee was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c). Further, the case of the Assessing Officer was that the income or property of the assessee was diverted in favour of the managing trustee of the assessee and it was a clear violation as per clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 13 read with section 13(1)(c). The assessee explained that the car was purchased in the name of the managing trustee with the sole objective of saving considerable amount of road tax and insurance. However, the Assessing Officer rejected the explanation and denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to the extent of value of that car.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the view of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The submissions made by the assessee are not acceptable in registering the vehicle in managing trustee’s name by utilizing the funds of the assessee, in order to save road/life tax and insurance charges which are meant for charitable purposes. The Commissioner (Appeals) rightly confirmed the view of the Assessing Officer in denying exemption under sections 11 and 12 to the extent of value of that car. [Para 8]

On the question of goodwill, the Assistant Controller held that the managing agency firm did possess goodwill and on the death of the deceased the accountable persons were entitled to 3/16th share in the goodwill of the business of the firm and as such a sum being the value of the 3/16th share had to be included in the estate of the deceased.

On appeal, the Appellate controller upheld the order of the assistant controller and reduced the value of the building. On further appeal the Tribunal upheld the order of the Appellate Controller in respect of inclusion of value of building holding that a mere provision for the maintenance of the building by the deceased and thereafter by others could not amount to creation of a trust with reference to the building and that the exclusive use of the building from 1942 to 1958, for religious and charitable purposes did not amount to a permanent dedication of the building as a trust property. As regards the inclusion representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm, the Tribunal held that goodwill cannot be associated with the business of managing agency firm because the managing agency business is governed by the terms of the agreement between the managing agency firm and the company and the right of managing agency was more personal and could not pass on to a successor. The Tribunal also held that no share in the goodwill of the business passed to the accountable persons on the death of the deceased and that in any event no amount was actually paid to the accountable persons by way of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the business. In that view the Tribunal deleted the sum representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm.

On reference:

HELD: The Tribunal had entertained certain misconceptions as to the true nature and character of the building in question. Neither under the partition deed nor under the settlement deed the building had been taken as a partible property. It was only the devolution of the lands which had been set apart for the maintenance of the said building that had been provided for both under the partition deed and the latter settlement deed. Both the documents clearly dealt with the right to manage the building. The stone slab and the notice board in front of the building showed when it was founded and for what purpose the building was to be used.

It is well established that no express words of gift either directly or indirectly in the shape of a trust are required to create a dedication. All that is necessary is that the religious purpose or object of the donor shall be clearly specified and that the property intended for the endowment should be set apart and dedicated of those purpose.

It is also well established that the existence of a trust can be established even by the conduct of parties. Though normally a Hindu while dedicating property to a deity or any other religious or charitable object ordinarily goes through the ceremonies of sankalpa and samarpan, it could not be said that those ceremonies are essential to creation of a an endowment. The performance of these ceremonies is only relevant to show the intention of the grantor, and if there is clear and unequivocal manifestation of intention to create a trust and there is formal divestiture of the ownership in the property on part of the donor with the intention to devote it to religious and charitable purpose the dedication must be deemed to be complete. The deduction of property is not a sacrament but a secular act; but the mere renunciation of ownership by the donor with a particular object is sufficient to create an endowment. The Tribunal had not kept in mind these general and accepted principles while considering the question as to whether the building was trust property or not. There was a subsequent litigation between the daughter-in-law of the deceased, R, the adopted son of the deceased, and ‘D’ the adopted son of daughter-in-law, wherein daughter-in-law questioned, inter alia, the validity of the partition deed dated 1-3-1950, and in the course of the entire litigation the parties proceeded on the basis that the building was a trust property and the dispute between them was as to the right of management of the trust.

The conduct of the parties right from 1942, when the building was constructed, clearly showed that the building was constructed, clearly showed that the building had been specifically set apart and used for religious and charitable objects. Therefore, the view taken by the Tribunal that the building was not a trust property and as such its value had to be added on to the estate of the deceased could not be accepted.

On the question as to whether the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm could pass on his death, the observation of the Tribunal that a managing agency business could not have any goodwill could not be accepted. The Supreme Court in J. K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that the managing agency business had got goodwill.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1951-52 to 1954-55 - A partnership firm was formed by four brothers - Firm was appointed as chief agent of an insurance company - Subsequently, brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming trustees would hold said business of chief agency of said company and all benefits and profits to arise from said business upon trust for public charitable purposes - Whether principal agency conducted by assessee-trust was a business and, therefore, "property" within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which was capable of being settled upon trust - Held, yes - Whether income of assessee-trust not being one which was not governed by proviso to section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as amended by Act 25 of 1953, but was governed by operative part of section 4(3)(i), it was exempt from tax - Held, yes

FACT: A partnership firm was formed by four brothers. No deed of partnership was said to have been executed in respect of this firm. The firm was appointed the chief agent an insurance company as from 1-9-1950. On 17-2-1951, the aforesaid brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming the trustees would hold the said business of the chief agency of the said company and all the benefits and profits to arise from the said business upon trust for public charitable purposes. The said declaration of trust was registered with the Registrar of Assurances.

The assessee claimed that as from 17-2-1951, the income from agency business should be assessed in the hands of the trustees and should be allowed exemption under section 4(3)(i). The ITO, however, made the assessment in the status of an unregistered firm. The ITO held that there was no charitable trust created by the deed dated 17-2-1951. On appeal, the AAC reversed the findings of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no proper and valid contract between the insurance company and the trustees as such; that the letter of appointment was only a service agreement; that there had been no transfer of property to the trustees wholly for charitable purposes; that the alleged transfer of the agency agreement did not amount to the transfer of property. The Tribunal also held that before the income of a trust for charitable purposes was exempt from tax, it must satisfy the conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i), i.e., and in the instant case the business not being carried on the course of carrying out the primary purpose of the trust, the income was not exempt form liability to pay tax.

In the case of the assessee, not only clause 3 of the objects were in tune with the definition mentioned in section 2(15 ) but in practice the relief to the poor had been given, medical education by imparting training to the Nurses had been established and medical relief was an on going activity along with the medical research. If the property which included running business was held for charitable and religious purposes and fulfilled all the conditions envisaged under section 11 and did not come under any of the exceptional clauses under section 13, there was no authority with the Assessing Officer to deny the benefit provided to such trust under section 11. In the case of Thiagarajar Charities v. Addl. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 1010 / 92 Taxman 152 it was held that if the objects of the trust are charitable then the trust can give the direction and power to the trustees to carry on the activities which will earn income so as to meet the goal of the aims and objects which are charitable. The direction will include carrying on of business and if the business carried on by the trustee becomes part and parcel of corpus or property held under the trust and if the income produced or resulted from the trust is applied for the aims and objects of the trust, then the carrying on such business or maintaining such property by the trust will definitely be an activity which is essential ingredients of the activities of the trust and trust will be entitled for exemption under section 11.

In view of the above, the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) was confirmed, dismissing the appeal of revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Property held under trust) - Assessment years 1987-88, 1991-92, 1997-98, 1998-99, 2006-07 and 2008-09 to 2014-2015 - Whether once income of a trust is used by it to acquire a property, property so acquired will be property held under trust and income from such property will be income from property under trust - Held, yes - Assessee society was having income from two Kalyanamandapams - According to Assessing Officer these properties were not settled by settlor as trust property and hence could not be considered as properties held under trust and thus he held that income earned by assessee from its Kalyanamandapams could not be treated as income from house property but only as income from business - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld order of Assessing Officer holding that Kalyanamandapams having being built by assessee subsequent to its formation could not be considered as property under trust - However, assessee submitted that land on which Kalyanamandapams were built was part of original settlement and buildings were built therein by assessee from its income - Whether thus, rental income received by assessee from Kalyanamandapams though it was in nature of income from business, such income was nothing but income from property held under trust - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT: Property (i.e. Kalyanamandapams) built by assessee society from its income, subsequent to its formation, on land, which was part of original settlement, was to be considered as property under trust and income therefrom was income from property under trust  IT: Where predominant activity of assessee society was charity, it would be eligible for exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)

Section 2(15), read with sections 11 and 12A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable purpose (Objects of general public utility) - Assessment years 1987-88, 1991-92, 1997-98, 1998-99, 2006-07 and 2008-09 to 2014-2015 - Assessee a society registered under section 12A had claimed exemption under section 11(1) - From objects of assessee as they appeared in its Memorandum of Association, it was clear that assessee could purchase, build and let out properties for its other purposes - Assessee was having income from its two kalyanamandapams and it was also having properties from which a school, a health centre and a library were run - All activities of assessee were either in field of education or in field of medical care - Further, assessee had given donations to a trust having section 12A registration which was pursuing an object of medical relief, education or relief to poor - Whether this would be equivalent to using money for charitable purposes - Held, yes - Whether therefore, predominant activity of assessee being charity, it would be eligible for exemption claimed by it under section 11(1) - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12][In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee a society registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860 and having registration under section 12A had claimed exemption under section 11(1), in the returns filed for the impugned assessment years 1987-88, 1991-92, 1997-98, 1998-99, 2006-07 and 2008-09 to 2014-2015. The assessee was having income from two Kalyanamandapams.

According to the Assessing Officer, these properties were not settled by the settlor as trust property and hence could not be considered as properties held under trust. The Assessing Officer submitted that by running these Kalyanamandapams, business was being carried on since this was its predominant activity. Hence, Assessing Officer denied exemption claimed by the assessee under section 11 (1). For assessment years 2008-09 to 2014-15, the Assessing Officer also applied proviso to section 2(15) for denying such exemption.The Assessing Officer took a view that income earned by the assessee from its Kalyanamandapams could not be treated as income from house property but only as income from business.

In the instant case, the material found during the course of survey operation clearly established the collection of money over and above the fee prescribed by the Government for admission of a student. Therefore, it was a clear case of sale of education by the assessee-society. Thus, the assessee could not be considered as a charitable institution under section 2(15 ). Therefore, the assessee was not eligible for exemption under section 11. [Para 9] Any income derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose, should not be included in the total income. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee was not holding any property under trust for charitable purpose. It was also not the case of the assessee that any income was derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose. Moreover, it was also not the case of the assessee that any income in the form of voluntary contributions was received with a specific direction to form part of the corpus of the society. The assessee-society was running educational institution and deriving income from such institution. The assessee had also collected money over and above the fees prescribed for admitting students under management quota. In other words, the educational institution was used as a tool/apparatus for collecting money over and above the fees prescribed. The assessee-society had no other source of income/receipt. The society owned the educational institution. The Legislature has visualized two situations. One is religious and another is charitable. Section 11 provides for exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust for charitable and religious purpose. ‘Education’ falls within the definition of charitable purpose. Therefore, any income derived from property held under trust for charitable purpose and applied for education, is eligible for exemption under section 11. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee had not derived any income from any property held under trust. The only source of receipt was the education itself, i.e., from educational institution. [Para 11]

The next question that fell for consideration was whether the educational institution owned by the assessee-society would be regarded as a property held under trust by the society. Section 11 speaks of the property held under trust. The Legislature visualized two situations. One is income derived from the property held under trust and another is application of that income derived from the property held under trust for a charitable purpose. Therefore, there is a clear distinction between the property held under trust and the charitable activity. In the instant case, the assessee-society was carrying on charitable activity by establishing educational institution. Therefore, the charitable activity of the assessee was education. The income, if any, derived from the property held under the Trust and applied for the educational activity, would be construed as application of income for the purpose of charitable purpose. Therefore, the expenditure incurred in establishing the educational institution, namely, acquisition of land, construction of building, etc., are all application of income for charitable activity. If any income was generated in the course of educational activity, the said income would be construed as if it was generated in the course of carrying on the charitable activity. Therefore, such receipt/income received in the course of carrying on charitable activity was also eligible for exemption, provided the same was applied or set apart for educational purposes. However, such receipt/income cannot be construed as derived from property/business held under trust. Since such receipt/income is inevitable or consequential while carrying on the activity of education, such income also becomes eligible for exemption. The educational institution is an apparatus for carrying out the charitable activity. Therefore, the educational institution or charitable activity itself cannot be construed as the property held under trust. The establishment of an educational institution is an activity of charity. Therefore, by any stretch of imagination, the charitable activity, cannot be held as the property held under trust, even though the income/receipt incidental to such activity is eligible for exemption. However, the money collected over and above the prescribed fee for admitting students cannot be construed as income derived from/incidental to the activity of carrying on charitable activity. [Para 12]

It is a well-settled principle of law that a business held under a trust is also a property. Section 11(4) also makes it very clear that the property held under the trust includes a business undertaking. If the assessee-society runs a business incidental to the attainment of the object of the society and separate books of account are maintained by the assessee, the income derived from such business, shall be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust. The Apex Court in Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/ 115 Taxman 126 considered the provisions of section 11(4A) and held that if the business income is derived from business held under the trust and the same is utilized by the institution for achieving object of the institution, then it could be said that such income is applied for charitable purpose. The assessee-society in question had no property or business whatsoever under trust. Moreover, it was not the claim of the assessee that any income was derived from the property or business held under trust. [Para 13]

Similarly, if an expenditure is incurred for any public purpose of religious or charitable nature, it is excluded from the expenditure which attracts tax. There is no reason why a person should not be entitled to exemption from tax in respect of gifts made for public religious and charitable purposes.

Therefore, the Tribunal was not in error in taking the view it had taken as to the interpretation of the expression ‘charitable purpose’. The entire property had been settled on trust and the portion in which the settlor’s wife was staying was also a trust property. She had been given only a right of residence in that portion of the trust property for her lifetime. The trustees had been given a direction to take possession of that portion of the property on the death of the settlors wife for the purposes of the trust. It being a trust property, it was incumbent on the trustees to maintain this property in good repair in the interest of the trust. Lest the trustees might think that there was no obligation on them to keep in good order that part of the property in which the lady was staying, the direction appeared to have been given in the trust deed. In our opinion, therefore, the Tribunal also was right in not accepting this contention of the revenue.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision. The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 13, read with sections 11 and 12, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Related party transaction) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-trust operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital - In order to address financial difficulties faced by assessee, it entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) involved in healthcare sector, for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to SCPL - In return, assessee would receive either a fixed amount of Rs. 1 crore or 40 per cent of SCPL's profit, whichever was higher, as management fees - Assessing Officer was of view that said agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for benefit of related parties - Consequently, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied - It was noted that object of transfer agreement with SCPL was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally, and in doing so, purpose of charity was not violated as a reputed hospital of such huge size required professional handling - Further, agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable property to SCPL but to counter huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals - Whether, on facts, there was no infirmity in order of Commissioner (Appeals) in allowing exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-trust was registered under section 12A(a) and operated various charitable institutions, including a hospital and a medical college. Due to financial difficulties, the assessee entered into an agreement with a private limited company (SCPL) for the transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of the hospital to SCPL. In return, the assessee would receive either a fixed amount or a percentage of SCPL''s profit as management fees. The assessee had incurred heavy debts and faced a negative net worth. The agreement was seen as a means to ensure the assessee''s survival and continued charitable activities, as SCPL took over the hospital''s operations and liabilities.

■

The Assessing Officer scrutinized the agreement and found that it violated the basic principles of charity for which the trust had been granted registration under section 12AA. The Assessing Officer was of the view that the agreement resulted in undue benefits to SCPL and violated section 13, which prohibits trusts from using their income for the benefit of related parties. Consequently, the trust''s claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 was denied. The Assessing Officer also reclassified the Trust''s income as that of an Association of Persons (AOP), which would only be allowed to deduct its expenditures.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal by revenue to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The issue under consideration has been decided by the Tribunal in favour of the assessee in earlier year’s orders and also by the recent order passed by the ITAT Ahmedabad in the assessee’s own case for assessment year 2016-17 in ITA No. 416/Ahd/2020 vide order dated 20-07-2022 wherein the Tribunal held that the agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable to SCPL but to counter the huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals. Therefore, the Commissioner(Appeals) has correctly held that the activity of the trust was carried on in accordance with its objects and in the best interest of charity, therefore, the exemption under section 11(1)(a) has rightly been allowed by the Commissioner(Appeals). Similarly, the Commissioner(Appeals) has clearly held that section 13((1)(c)(ii) could apply only if any part of the charitable income of the trust has been used or applied for the benefits of the said persons during the previous year. But, since no portion of the income of the assessee has been applied for said person, therefore, the case of the assessee fell outside the scope of this section. Further, the trust is in receipt of income by way of management charges from SCPL and also all of its liabilities have been taken over by the same therefore there is a fact that there is no undue benefits of the use of trust property have been taken by any other persons. Similarly, there is no diversion of income of the trust as per Explanation of section13(2)(d) and 13(2)(g) as the trust has been benefitted greatly and its deficit of trust duly reduced to a great extent. Thus, the Commissioner(Appeals) has analyzed the facts correctly and given a judicious finding which does not call for any interference from outside. [Para 6]

On reference : HELD: By the Insurance Act, 1938, a "principal agent" is defined as meaning "a person, who, not being a salaried employee of an insurer, in consideration of any commission, (i) performs any administrative and organizing functions for the insurer and (ii) procures general insurance business whether wholly or in part by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents of behalf of the insurer". Evidently a principal agent by the definition does not merely render personal service but is concerned with performing certain administrative and organizing functions and the procuring of general insurance business by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents. Such an agent by the very definition will be regarded as carrying on the business of a principal agent. He is not merely an employee engaged for rendering services of a personal nature: he is invested with the right as an agent to perform the administrative organizing functions for the insurer and to procure general insurance business by employing, directly or indirectly, insurance agents. By section 42A of the Insurance Act principal agents are required to obtain a certificate from the Controller of Insurance or an officer authorized by him entitling them to conduct the business of principal agency, and the certificate remains in operation for a period of twelve months only from the date of issue but is liable to be renewed. It is also true that under Part A of the Sixth Schedule to the Insurance Act certain terms are deemed to be included in every contract between an insurer carrying on general insurance business and a principal agent. Under clause 2 of Part A of the Sixth Schedule the principal agent has to procure or cause to be procured through insurance agents such an amount of general insurance business as will yield a gross premium income of not less than Rs. 20,000 in each calendar year. Under clause 4, in the event of the principal agent failing to comply with the requirements of clause 2 in any two successive calendar years, the contract shall, without prejudice to the provisions of clause 3, terminate on the 31st day of March immediately following the second calendar year. Under clause 3 the agency is also liable to be forfeited in the events set out in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) thereof. By clause 5 certain restriction are placed upon the principal agent but an account of these provisions, which impose certain restrictive conditions upon the principal agent it could not be said that the appointment of a principal agent gave rise to a bare service agreement and that the remuneration paid was not for the conduct of a business but for performance of personal service. The circumstance that the appointment was liable to be terminated at short notice and the agency was not permanent and was liable to be forfeited in the events set out hereinbefore would not, affect the character of the agency as business. Following the observation made by the Supreme Court in J.K. Trust's case [1957] 32 ITR 535 the principal agency conducted by the assessee was a business and, therefore, "property" within the meaning of section 4(3)(i). Being property which was capable of being settled upon trust by the deed of trust, dated 17-2-1951, it was lawfully settled upon trust for charitable purposes. The taxing authorities are primarily concerned with the question whether the income sought to be taxed in income from property, which is held on trust for religious or charitable purpose. If the business of the principal agency was transferred to the trustees under a deed of settlement, and from that business income was received, the income will fall within section 4(3)(i) and be exempt from tax in the hands of the trustees. Therefore, under the terms of appointment made with the company firm became the principal agents conducting a business and that business was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i ) and that the alteration, sometime after their appointment as principal agents, in the constitution of the from did not alter the character of the income earned in the course of the business. The income which is liable to be included in the total income of the assessee, was income derived from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution, unless that income fulfils the conditions prescribed by clause (b). The expression "such income" in the proviso refers to the income derived from property (which expression includes a business) held for religious or charitable purposes. But that did not justify the submission that the business which was referred to in clause (b) of the proviso must be business which is held for charitable or religious purposes. The business referred to in clause (b) of the proviso need not be business which is held for religious or charitable purposes, provided it is business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution.

On application under section 256(2):
