connotes ownership as well as possession. The word 'held' cannot be interpreted only to mean in the sense of possession but would also mean an owner who is not in actual possession. In some cases, it has been held that word "held" connotes the existence of a right or a title in the holder. In the instant case, the land acquired by SMC was under legal ownership of the trust and was possessed by the trustees on behalf of the trust in their fiduciary capacity. The term 'held' has also been explained as to mean factual management. Thus, when an asset forms part of the property, it is held by the trustees for the benefit of the beneficiaries and it is not material as to whether it is held by the trustees in their names or in the name of another. Thus, the lands in question were held under the trust and there was no dispute that objects of the trust were religious and charitable.

Meaning of words 'held under trust'

The trust is a non-corporial body. It is run by persons called trustees for the benefit of persons or for the purposes or objects stated in trust deed. Therefore, a property owned by a non-corporial body like trust is held by trustees for the trust. Therefore, the phrase 'held under trust' would only mean property in possession of the trustees but legally owned by the trust. Since the term 'the property' has been interpreted in widest possible terms even the business or the organization itself would have been treated as property held under trust.

Meaning of 'property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes'

The term 'held wholly for charitable and religious purposes' would mean that property in question is not assigned to any other purpose or used directly or indirectly either in the objects clause of the trust or by the trustees in practice. Assigning of corpus, i.e., capital asset wholly for the purpose of charitable work and not assigning for any non-charitable purpose would be sufficient compliance of provisions of section 11(1A). The Circular No. 72 of the Board further supports this proposition. If the assigner partly assigns the property for charitable work and partly for non-charitable work or the property after assigning or acquisition is partly assigned to charitable work and partly to non-charitable work then on transfer of such asset, proportionate exemption to the extent asset is assigned for charitable work would be available and no exemption to capital gain in respect of that portion thereof which arises from that part of the property which is assigned for or held for non-charitable purposes, would be available. It is not the case that passive holding of the land or non-use of the land would mean that it is assigned or held for non-charitable purposes. Non-use of the land or passiveness of the land is not equivalent to its holding for non-charitable purposes which alone can forfeit the exemption as per sub-section (1A) of section 11 and Circular No. 72, dated 6-1-1972. [Para 14]

Thus, the argument of the department that land should be put to use for getting exemption from capital gains was not correct. As seen above, the word 'wholly' relates to and qualifies the word 'purpose'. If the trust is established for charitable or religious purpose and there is no other object for which property of the trust is utilized then property of the trust so held and thereafter so transferred can only give rise to income/capital gains which has to be considered within the provisions of section 11(1) and 11(1A) only. The income or capital gains from the property held under the trust can be denied exemption only to the extent the property is assigned or used or held for any non-charitable purpose or other than the objects of the trust. The assignment or use for non-charitable work would be required to be proved from the positive facts and mere non-use or keeping the property idle or passive cannot be interpreted to mean that it was used or assigned to non-charitable work. Since in the instant case, the department had only alleged non-use for charitable purpose and there was no material on record that the land was used for non-charitable work, it was to be held that the assessee could not be denied exemption from the capital gains in accordance with provisions of section 11(1A), read with section 11(5). Accordingly, the assessee was entitled to exemption from the capital gains as it had complied with the provisions of section 11(5). The appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Investment in specified securities) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee society was running a cancer hospital - Assessing Officer noticing that assessee made an investment in chit fund company, denied benefit of exemption under section 11(5) by holding that chit fund subscription would not amount to investment or deposit as specified under section 11(5) - Therefore, Assessing Officer rejected claim of exemption under section 11 - However, it was found that assessee's contribution to chit funds was made only as an arrangement for better management of funds of assessee - Whether there was no violation of section 11(5) and assessee was eligible to claim exemption under section 11 - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where contribution to chit funds was done only as an arrangement for better management of society's funds, exemption under section 11 could not be denied

FACT: The assessee was society running a cancer hospital. It filed NIL return of income after availing exemption under section 11.

The Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee made an investment in chit fund company, thereby it denied the benefit of exemption under section 11(5) by holding that the chit fund subscription would not amount to investment or deposit as specified under section 11(5). Therefore, the Assessing Officer rejected the claim of exemption under section 11.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was eligible for exemption under section 11, even though it had not obtained notification under section 10(23C). It was also observed that as there was violation of section 11(5), exemption could not be allowed.

On second appeal:

HELD: The assessee has spent the entire income earned in the year for the objects of the trust. As it has incurred excess amount, there is no surplus amount which needs to be invested under section 11(5). Section 11(5) comes in to operation only when trust has accumulated or set apart the amount under section 11(2). In the case of the assessee, there is a no surplus fund and hence, the question of investment or deposit as specified under section 11(5) does not arise. Contribution to chit fund in this case is not an investments or deposit as specified under section 11(5). It is, as submitted, only an arrangement for better management of funds of the assessee. The assessee has been complied with the provisions of section 11(1)(a) by applying entire amount for the objects of the trust. HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income, from property held under - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessing Officer disallowed exemption claimed by assessee-
 trust under section 11 on two grounds, namely, (a) that even though assessee’s buildings were being used by other societies of same group for charitable activities, such use could not be treated as use by assessee for carrying out its own charitable activities; and (b) that major expenditure was on account of agricultural and dairy activities carried on by it which was not in nature of application of its income for charitable purpose - Commissioner (Appeals), however, upheld assessee’s claim - Whether where buildings of assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature, such use could very well be treated as use by assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for purpose of exemption under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether since agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by assessee-society as separate business activities, same constituted ‘property held under trust’ as provided in section 11(4) and in any case income of said activities was to be determined after deducting expenditure incurred in connection with said business - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, gross income being more than sufficient to cover expenses incurred in connection with said activities, allowance of same by Commissioner  (Appeals) as application of its income hardly made any difference in ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to revenue - Held, yes
Circulars and Instructions - CBDT’s Circular No. 1132, dated 5-1-1978

FACT: The Assessing Officer was of the opinion that the buildings of the assessee-society, which were constructed by applying its income, were being used by other societies of the same group, though for their charitable activities, and, thus, it did not mean that income of the assessee was being applied for charitable purpose, because such use could not be treated as use by the assessee for carrying out its own charitable activities. He also found that the major expenditure was on account of agricultural and dairy activities carried on by it, which was not in the nature of application of its income for charitable purpose. He, therefore, disallowed the exemption claimed under section 11.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) however upheld the assessee’s claim.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: In the Circular No. 1132 issued by the CBDT, it has been clarified that the payment of a sum by one charitable trust to other for utilisation of the donee-trust towards its charitable objects is proper application of income for charitable purpose in the hands of donor-trust and donor-trust will not lose exemption under section 11 merely because the donee trustee did not spend the donation during the year of receipt itself. In the instant case, the buildings of the assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature and that being so, such use could very well be treated as use by the assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for the purpose of exemption under section 11. Moreover, exemption under section 11 was allowed to the assessee-society for the assessment years 1992-93 and 1993-94 by the department in the similar facts and circumstances. As such, the Commissioner (Appeals) was fully justified in treating the use of assessee’s property by other societies for charitable purposes as charitable activity carried on by the assessee and accordingly in allowing exemption under section 11 as claimed. The impugned order was, therefore, upheld. [Para 7]

Agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by the assessee’s society as separate business activities and the same, therefore, constituted ‘property held under trust’ of the assessee-society as provided in sub-section (4) of section 11 and income of the said activities, in any case, was to be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act, i.e., after deducting the expenditure incurred in connection with the said business. The assessee-society had derived income from the said activities and the amount being more than sufficient to cover the expenses incurred in connection with the said activities, the allowance of the same by the Commissioner (Appeals) as application of its income as claimed by the assessee hardly made any difference in the ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to the revenue. [Para 8]

Hence, the revenue’s appeal was to be dismissed.

in respect of such business. [Para 7]

Thus, if a property is held under trust, and such property is a business, the case would fall under section 11(4) and not under section 11(4A). Section 11(4A) would apply only to a case where the business is not held under trust. Thus, there is difference between property or business held under trust and business carried on by or on behalf of the trust. [Para 8] In the present case, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is that running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not held under trust, but it was business commenced/carried on by the Society, subsequent to the formation of trust. Though the business was commenced by the Society and it was carried on by the Society after its formation, it cannot be said to constitute property held under trust under section 11(4), it is only the business which is held under the trust that would enjoy exemption in respect of its income under section 11(1) and there is a distinction between the objects of a trust and the powers given to the trustees to effectuate the purpose of the trust. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the Memorandum of Association of the assessee. The running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not even in the contemplation of the Memorandum of Association on the basis of which the Society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust. Section 11(1) confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose.

Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1), was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust. In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

There is no connection between the activities relating to running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall and the attainment of the objects of the trust. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall are used for charitable purposes would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The application of income generated by the business is not relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. [Para 10]

The contention of the assessee that the surplus funds generated from the running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were spent towards charitable activities and therefore, the assessee is entitled for exemption under section 11(4) is not acceptable. Initially, the assessee carried on the business itself which is not at all property held under trust. This activity is a business activity and the provisions of section 11(4A) is applicable. [Para 11]

Further, there is no nexus between the activities carried on and the objects of the assessee that can constitute an activity incidental to the attainment of the objects, namely, to promote cause of charity, mission activities, welfare, employment, diffusion of useful knowledge, upliftment and education and to create an awareness of self-reliance among the members of the public etc. Being so, it is to be held that the assessee is not entitled for any exemption under section 11. [Para 14]

On cross appeal:

HELD: Exemption under section 11

■

The issues raised by the Assessing Officer that the activities of the assessee-Parishad carried on as per its objects laid down in section 15 of U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965 were not charitable activities do not hold any water after the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Asstt. CIT (Exemptions) v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 143 taxmann.com 278/291 Taxman 11/449 ITR 1 (SC), which categorically states that statutory bodies engaged in housing development, town planning etc., are involved in objects of, “general public utility” (GPU) and therefore are entitled to be considered as a charities in the GPU category. It is also observed that even earlier, the Allahabad High Court, in its orders in the case of Lucknow Development authority and others, dated 16-9-2013, in which the assessee was one of the parties, had held that the objects of the assessee society were admittedly charitable and that it was entitled to the benefit of registration under section 12AA. Therefore, once the objects and functions of the assessee-Parishad have been held to be charitable by the High Court and not challenged or overturned by way of appeal to the Supreme Court, it is held that it is not open for the Assessing Officer to contend that such objects are not charitable on the grounds that certain activities of the assessee-Parishad yielded surplus. Furthermore, it is found that the Commissioner (Appeals) had held in his order that once the registration had been granted under section 12AA, the income of the assessee had to be computed as per section 11 and not under any other head of income. There is no infirmity in this line of reasoning. For this reason, it is held that the Commissioner (Appeals) was perfectly justified in directing the Assessing Officer to compute the income of the assessee-Parishad in the manner provided under section 11, with reference to the information contained in Form 10B. HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01 - Assessee-society was formed, inter alia, with main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard - It was duly registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860 - It was also registered under section 12A - Assessee claimed exemption under section 11 - Assessing Officer denied exemption holding that, assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return, and, thus, it was earning profit and not doing any charity - However, it was found from records that assessee was duly recognised by HNB Garhwal University and strictly following university regulations with regard to admission charging of fees and course curriculum and had on its governing body nominee of State Government, HNB University and AICTE functioning under Human Resources Ministry and, thus, in fact Government managed and moreover, any surplus arising to society was utilized into activities of society and did not find its way to pocket of persons who were running society/institution - Whether, in view of said facts, it could be said that assessee was not a profit making institution and it was rendering services of education to general public and was eligible for exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-society was formed, inter alia, with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. It was duly registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. It was also registered under section 12A. For the relevant assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01, the assessee claimed exemption under section 11. The Assessing Officer denied the exemption holding that the assessee was not deriving any income out of the property held under trust, and that the income of the assessee was from fee charged from the students on account of tuition fee and other charges and whatever property had been acquired subsequently was as a result of application of this income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: The assessee was a registered society duly incorporated and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1862. The society was formed with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. The income which the assessee received in the form of tuition fee and other receipts could not have been received but for the organization and, therefore, the tuition fee and other receipts derived from other organizations was income derived from property held under trust. Such tuition fee and other receipts, received by the assessee were directly and substantially arising from the organization, which was the property held under the trust. The Assessing Officer's assertion that whatever property in the shape of office building, furniture, computer was simply an application of income was not sustainable. It is well-settled that property acquired by an organization from its own income is also a property held under trust. Thus, fixed assets and current assets held by the assessee as on 31-3-1999 and 31-3-2000 were properties held under trust. Further, the Delhi Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case vide order dated 15-12-2003 had held that department cannot guide a charitable institution as to how it should carry on its charity. It is sufficient compliance with the relevant provisions of law in case surplus of the institution is utilized into activities of the institution and does not find its way to the pocket of the persons who were running the society/institution. There was no allegation by the department that the funds had been siphoned off. Therefore, the Commissioner should not have withdrawn the registration granted to the assessee under section 12AA.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income form property held under - Assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60 - Assessee was an association of persons - Constitution of assessee revealed that neither standing committee nor managing committee nor even members of assessee could use property of assessee for any purpose except that covered by object clause of assessee - Neither before ITO nor before AAC any contention was raised by revenue that object for which assessee was constituted was not charitable one - Whether property of assessee was held under trust or under legal obligation and, therefore, assessee was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was an association of persons. The Constitution of the assessee provided for an elected standing committee, the constitution, functions and duties of the said standing committee. The Constitution also provided for a smaller body which was entitled managing committee and its constitution and other functions. The Constitution further provided that to carry out the objects of the parishad, the standing committee could raise funds and accept donations, presents charities, etc., and would have power to administer them. The issue that arose for decision was as to whether having regard to the terms of the constitution of the assessee-association, the properties of the assessee-association were held under trust or other legal obligation so as to qualify for exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

On reference:

HELD: It is now well-settled that a formal deed of trust is not absolutely essential in order to come to a conclusion that any particular property is held under trust or other legal obligation. The provisions contained in the Constitution of the assessee bound not only the standing committee and the managing committee but they equally bound every member of the assessee. In view of the provisions of the Constitution, it was impossible to urge that it would be open either to the standing committee or the managing committee or even the members of the assessee to use the property of the assessee for any purpose except that covered by the object clause of the assessee.

In that view of the matter, no other view was possible save and except to hold that the property of the assessee was held under trust or a legal obligation. As it was not open for the revenue to urge that the object was not for a charitable purpose in view of the fact that such a contention was not raised either before the ITO or at the stage of appeal before the AAC on behalf of the revenue, the provisions of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 were directly applicable.

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

■ The record further reveals that the revenue has not brought any material to establish that the rental income earned by the trust was diverted for any non-charitable purpose or that the dominant character of the trust had ceased to be charitable. On the contrary, the Income and Expenditure Account demonstrates that the receipts of the trust, whether derived from grants, donations, interest or rental income, were applied only towards the charitable objects of the trust. Thus, the source from which the income was generated has not altered the fundamental charitable character of the institution. [Para 8.5]

■

It is a settled proposition of law that the decisive test is the dominant object of the institution and not the source of its income. Income derived from property held under trust, including rental income, does not lose the benefit of exemption under Section 11 and Section 12 merely because such income arises from leasing of trust property, so long as it is applied towards the charitable purposes for which the trust has been established. The leasing of trust property, in the facts of the present case, is only an incidental mode of augmenting resources to fulfil the charitable objects and cannot be construed as an independent commercial object of the trust. [Para 8.6]

■

Accordingly, while the Tribunal disagrees with the reasoning assigned by the Commissioner (Appeals) in holding that earning rental income was itself one of the objects of the trust, the Tribunal nevertheless upholds the ultimate conclusion that the assessee cannot be denied exemption on this ground. The reasoning adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) is incorrect; however, the conclusion reached by him is sustainable on the basis that the rental income was merely incidental to the charitable activities and was admittedly applied towards the charitable objects of the trust. Consequently, the ground raised by the Revenue on this issue is devoid of merit and is dismissed. [Para 8.7]

■

Accordingly, the Tribunal concurs with the findings recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue. The ground raised by the Revenue challenging the allowability of exemption merely because the assessee earned rental income is devoid of merit and is, therefore, dismissed. [Para 8.8]

FACT: ■

The assessee, a charitable trust claimed exemption under sections 11 and 12.

■

The Assessing Officer denied exemption by treating the assessee as an Association of Persons (AOP) on ground that assessee had earned substantial rental income by leasing its immovable properties which amounted to a commercial activity inconsistent with its charitable character.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim on ground that the Assessing Officer had not brought cogent material to show that the assessee’s activities ceased to be charitable.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: (i) Rental income and leasing of properties

■

The principal basis adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) for allowing the assessee's claim is the observation that one of the objects of the trust was to lease out properties and earn rental income. However, on a careful examination of the original trust deed as well as the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the Tribunal finds that the observation is factually incorrect and contrary to the material available on record. The original trust deed, enumerates the charitable objects of the trust, namely: (i) genetic research and agricultural education; (ii) conservation of land, water and genetic resources; (iii) sustainable agriculture and environmental protection; (iv) family planning and population control; and (v) improvement of the status and literacy of women. Subsequently, by way of the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the additional charitable objects of Relief to the Poor and Education were incorporated. Significantly, neither the original trust deed nor the addendum includes, as an object of the trust, carrying on the activity of leasing or renting of immovable properties for earning rental income. [Para 8.2]

■

What is, however, contained in the trust deed is a separate enabling provision conferring powers upon the Board of Trustees. Clause VIII merely authorises the trustees to acquire, hold, manage or otherwise deal with land, buildings and other immovable properties with the funds of the trust for effectuating the charitable objects of the trust. Such an enabling clause cannot be elevated to the status of an independent charitable object. The power to acquire and manage trust properties is only incidental to the effective administration of the trust and to facilitate the attainment of its charitable purposes. Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that leasing of properties itself constituted one of the objects of the trust is clearly erroneous and is not borne out from the trust deed. [Para 8.3]

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

He also repelled the assessee's contention that it was entitled to exemption under section 11 (1)(a). On appeal, the AAC sustained the ITO's order. On second appeal, the Tribunal sustained the AAC's order, holding that although the activity of the assessee was covered by the definition "charitable purposes" as contemplated in section 2(75), yet the assessee's income which was covered by section 28(iii), was not income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a), so that it was not entitled to exemption from tax.

On reference:

HELD: By virtue of section 11(4) "property held under trust" includes a business undertaking so held. Therefore, it could not be accepted that the income derived by the assessee was not income from property as envisaged under section 11(1)(a). That apart, a perusal of the aims and objects of the assessee-society led to the conclusion that the income derived by it was income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a). SC).

The provisions of section 4(3)(i ) confer an exemption of income from property only where the property itself is held under a trust or other legal obligation. It does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created in respect of any property, but only the income derived from any particular property or source is itself held in trust as where it is set apart or charged for a charitable purpose. That is clear upon the terms of the section itself and upon the authorities. In the instant case, all the income which the assessee derived or received was in the shape of grants and subscriptions from members which could not possibly have been received by it except from its business. Therefore, the entire income of the assessee must be held to be income derived from its business which was its property. If this contention was correct, then it was further submitted that there could be also no doubt upon the terms of its memorandum of association and its purposes and objects that the assessee was holding the business in trust for charitable purposes.

Supreme Court in J.K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that "Business" would undoubtedly be property in the connotation in which it is used in section 4(3)(i). In the light of this pronouncement of the Supreme Court it is clear that "business" itself can be property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) and upon that principle the business of the assessee in the instant case would be "property" held by the assessee.

Under the circumstances, the view taken by the Tribunal was the correct view and the income of the assessee would be exempt under the provisions of section 4(3)(i).

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity. The educational institution being run by the assessee was for the general benefit of the public and not for the benefit of any class or section of the public, as (a ) the institution was duly recognized by HNB Garhwal University and strictly followed all procedures with regard to admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum as laid down by the university, and (b) the nominees of State Government, HNB University and AICTE (functioning under the Human Resources Ministry) were on the governing body of the society and, therefore, the assessee had no choice in matters of admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum. The institute, was, in fact, State Government managed.

It was also found that the working system of the assessee was as per the guidelines laid down by the University. In respect of fixing and charging fees from students, the society management had no powers. Fee was being charged from students strictly as specified and laid down by the University. The governing body of the society had no powers to workout the cost and thereafter to add on the element of overheads and profits. Therefore, there was no question of building huge margins of profits in the fees structure as conceived by the Assessing Officer.

From a plain reading of the main objects given in the Memorandum, it could very well be discerned that the society had been formed with the sole objective of imparting and spreading computer education. Further, the assessee-society was virtually Government managed. Therefore, the question of functioning like a commercial profit making institution was totally unfounded. Thus, the fees charged by the assessee was simply receipt in the hands of the society and not profit.

Further, the assessee was rendering services of education to the general public. Therefore, its activities clearly fell within the ambit of charitable purpose as defined under section 2(15). Charging of fees does not in anyway dilute the aspect of charitable purpose. It is the end use and spirit and objective which matters.

In the assessment order, the Assessing Officer had not been able to appreciate the difference in the words 'charitable purposes' as are used in the Act and the word 'charity' as had been used by the Assessing Officer in his order. The word 'charity' as used in English language and recognized in English law, implies as an act motivated by pity and may require benevolence to manifest it. However, exemption under section 11 has been prescribed with reference to 'charitable purposes' and not 'charity'. The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act.

Therefore, the property from which income was derived by the assessee was held under trust and such property was held for charitable purpose and the income derived from trust was property which was being applied for charitable purpose. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

The exemption Under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the trust deed of the assessee. The running of " Community Hall" was not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of "Community Hall" was not even in the contemplation of the trust deed on the basis of which the society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, was carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust.

Section 11(1) of the Act confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose. Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1) of the Act, was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust.

In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the charitable trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

It is thus necessary to consider the question whether the said activities carried on by the assessee were incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. One fails to see any connection between the activities relating to running of "Community Hall" with attainment of the objects of the trust. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from running of "Community Hall" is used for charitable purposes would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The application of income generated by the business is not relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. [Para 10]

It was contended by the assessee that the surplus funds generated from the running of "Community Hall" was spent towards charitable activities and therefore, the assessee is entitled for exemption under section 11(4) this contention cannot be accepted. Initially, the assessee carried on the business itself which is not at all property held under trust. This activity is a business activity and the provisions of section 11(4A) of the Act is applicable. [Para 11]

It was contended that if the profits of the business carried on by the trust are utilized by the trust for the purposes of achieving the objectives of the trust, then the business should be considered to be incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust as observed by the Supreme Court in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/115 Taxman 126. [Para 12]

Prima facie the said observation would appear to support the assessee's case in the sense that even if running of "Community Hall" is held not to constitute a business held under trust, but only as a business carried on by or on behalf of the trust, so long as the profits generated by it are applied for the charitable objects of the trust, the condition imposed under section 11(4A) of the Act should be held to be satisfied, entitling the trust to the tax exemption. Whether assessee could be denied exemption claimed by it under section 11(1) by virtue of sub-section (4A) thereof?

To answer the question, whether assessee can be denied the exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)(4A) it is to be seen whether renting out the Kalyanamandapams could be considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects of the assessee as they appear in its Memorandum of Association. On appeal to the High Court: HELD: The crux of the matter, is as to whether the 'investment' can also amount to 'application' or not. There is nothing in the provisions of section 11(1) to curtail or narrow down the meaning of the word 'application', which by definition is of wider import. The scheme of section 11 is to advance the cause of charity by allowing the religious or charitable trusts to employ their funds in such a manner, for the purpose of charity or for advancing the cause of charity. There is nothing contrary placed from the side of revenue to even indicate that purchase of immovable property in question even on lease basis was not going to serve the cause of charity as per the objects of the charitable trust in question in any manner. The investment in immovable property, if it serves the cause of charity immediately or even in near future, the rental income or otherwise cannot be said to be not serving the objects of the trust at all. On the contrary, investment in immovable property which is intended to be used for serving the cause and objects of the trust is more committed and firm 'application' of income of the trust. The burden, therefore, was on the revenue to establish that the 'investment' was for the purpose, other than, for subserving the objects stipulated in the trust deed. The revenue has utterly failed to bring on record any evidence to the contrary to the claim of exemption by assessee on the ground that the immovable property in question was being taken on lease to create a theatre or auditorium, which would be used for the purpose of the group of artists or their families or even serve the cause of general public in times of floods or to provide education to the children, etc. Unless there was evidence on record to show that the said investment of the immovable property was being used for the purpose altogether different from the objects of the trust deed, the denial of exemption on an assumed distinction between the 'application' and 'investment' was not only too far-fetched, but beyond the scheme of section 11 itself and the said view of the Tribunal, therefore, cannot be countenanced. [Para 15]

Therefore, the assessee in the instant case while making the advance in question for purchase of immovable property in question even on lease basis, cannot be said to have not applied its income during the year in question for the charitable purposes within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) and, therefore, the assessee was clearly entitled to exemption under the said provision in respect of the said investment in immovable property. [Para 16]

It cannot be said that such advance did not crystalise in any 'application of income' and was in suspended animation as already indicated above that nothing contrary was brought on record by revenue that this advance did not crystalise in any 'application of income' in favour of the assessee during the year or even subsequently. On the contrary, it was contended at the bar by the assessee that the leasehold rights were secured by the assessee with the said investment and building on the said leasehold land is under construction as of now. However, no findings could be given on facts in this regard, but per se also there is no hesitation in holding that the advance or investment in the said leasehold proprty by the assessee's charitable trust in the year in question could be held to be 'application of income' within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) and therefore, the assessee was entitled to the exemption. HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether for running a charitable activity, establishment has to be maintained, which requires payment of salaries and other establishment expenses and application of income for said purpose cannot be alien to charitable objects which are to be advanced - Held, yes - Whether nature of regulatory mechanism operated by market committees involves incurring of expenditure on establishment and mere fact that such an expenditure has been incurred, cannot be a ground to hold that application of income was not for charitable purpose - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a statutory entity under the provisions of the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961. Its activities were covered by section 2(15) and it had been registered under section 12AA. During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer held that the assessee was not eligible for exemption under sections 11 and 12 as major portion of its income was spent on running of administration, i.e., for paying salaries and other allowances to the employees and office expenses and, thus, major part of its income was not being spent for charitable purposes which was statutorily required for exemption. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that income was being used for charitable purposes and, therefore, the assessee was eligible for exemption under sections 11 and 12. The Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On the revenue's appeal to the High Court :

HELD: It cannot be disputed that for running a charitable activity, the establishment has to be maintained, which requires payment of salaries and other establishment expenses. Application of income for the said purpose cannot be alien to the charitable objects which are to be advanced. Without establishment, the charitable objects cannot be achieved at all. There is no provision that income cannot be spent for the said purpose. That being the position, the view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal could not be held to be debatable. It was not the case of the revenue that expenditure in running the administration was either excessive or unreasonable. The nature of regulatory mechanism operated by the market committees involves incurring of expenditure on establishment. Thus, mere fact that such an expenditure was incurred, could not be ground to hold that the application was not for charitable purpose. [Para 9]

Therefore, the appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 12]

On 23-11-1972, under section 17 of the Act in respect of the assessment years in question, the notices were issued on the ground that the trustees had been not only using and utilising the properties of the said trust for their own personal purposes, but had also been using and applying income therefrom directly or indirectly for their own personal benefit and/or had been acting contrary to the express provisions of the said trust.

On writ : HELD: Under section 11(1)(a), in order to be entitled to exemption income must not only be derived from the property held under trust only for charitable or religious purposes but the income entitled to exemption must be to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes, i.e., charitable or religious purpose in India or where such income is accumulated for application to such purpose in India, i.e., religious or charitable purpose to the extent the income so accumulated is not in excess of 25 per cent of income from the property or Rs. 10,000, whichever is higher. Therefore, two separate independent conditions are required to be fulfilled, that is to say, the income must be derived from the property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, and, secondly, the application or accumulation of such income in the manner indicated in clause (a ) of sub-section (1) of section 11 of the Act. 'Charitable purpose' or 'purpose of charitable or religious nature' have not been defined in the Wealth-tax Act, 1957. Therefore, it must bear the same meaning as in the Income-tax Act but under the provisions of the Income-tax Act not only should the income be derived from a trust or legal obligation of public purpose of a charitable or religious nature but the income so derived must to a certain extent be so applied. The position under the Wealth-tax Act seems to be a little different. Wealth-tax Act assessed the owning or having or possessing of the property and section 5(1)(i) of the Act stipulated that the condition for exemption was that the property must be held by the assessee under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a religious or charitable nature in India. Therefore, the holding of a property by the assessee either under a trust or other legal obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature is the statutory requirement entitling the assessee to exemption under the Act. In the ground for reopening as noted before it was not disputed that the assessees upon whom the impugned notices had been issued were not holding the property under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a charitable or religious nature. What was being suggested was that holding the property as trustees or under obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature the assessees were committing breaches of trust in acting contrary to the trust and misusing the funds of the trust for their personal benefit. The application of the money held under a trust or under legal obligation is not a relevant consideration for exemption under section 5(1)(i) of the Act. Therefore, the revenue had no material to believe that the income of the assessee had escaped assessment. This position manifests a lacuna in the present provision of law. The position, therefore, is that if the trustees hold the property for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature and if they misapply or commit breach of trust, they will continue to enjoy exemption under the Wealth-tax Act. This position should receive consideration by the legislature in order to bring it at par with the provisions of the Income-tax Act. But until that is done, the petitioners were entitled to succeed on the point that there were no grounds for believing that the wealth of the assessee had escaped assessment or had been under-assessed.

In the aforesaid view of the matter, the notices are hereby quashed and the respondents were restrained from giving effect to the same.

Note: The case was decided in favour of assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under [Business held in trust] - Assessment year 1977-78 - Whether even if business of insurance was carried out by assessee-society for carrying on primary purpose of charitable activities in accordance with aims and objects of trust, assessee would still be entitled to exemption - Held, yes [Para 9][In favour of assessee]IT : Where income from business was applied for charity as per aims and objects of assessee-society, its income will be exempt

FACT: The assessee, a society engaged in charity was assessed in status of 'Association of Persons'.

The Assessing Officer found that the assessee was also carrying insurance business to earn profit and therefore, held that it could not get exemption under section 11.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) supported the ITO.

HELD: The dominant purpose of the respondent-society was advancement of general public utility and not for education alone. The question of applicability of section 13(1)(bb) to the facts of the case would not arise for the reason that the Tribunal has found that the business of insurance was carried under trust for carrying on the primary purpose of charitable activities in accordance with the aims and objects of the trust. Thus, section 11 was applied and it cannot be excluded. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 13(1)(c), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessee-trust owned properties which were settled by L and H, who were joint owners thereof - Assessee had leased out aforesaid property to a company on a rent of Rs. 4,000 per month for purpose of residence of P, who was managing director of company and husband of L and father of H-ITO held that premises in question could fetch a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month and, hence, the assessee had allowed the trust property being used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of the authors of the trust and their relatives under section 13(1)(c), read with section 13(2)(b) - Whether in view of fact that property in question was governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act and standard rent of property was below Rs. 4,000 there was no direct or indirect benefit to authors of assessee and their relatives and, therefore, assessee was entitled to exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-trust owned the properties which were settled by L and H, who were joint owners thereof. At the time of the settlement, one company was a tenant in the aforesaid property. The company had taken the premises on lease for the purpose of residence of P and his family, who was the managing director of the company and the husband of L and the father of H. The company was paying Rs. 4,000 per month as rent to the assessee. While completing the assessment for the relevant assessment year, the ITO held that premises in question could fetch a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month and, hence, the assessee had allowed the trust property being used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of the authors of the trust and their relatives under section 13(1)(c), read with section 13(2)(b). He, therefore, disallowed exemption under section 11 to the assessee and made addition of certain amount to the income of the assessee, i.e., an amount of difference between the market rent and the actual rent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal:

HELD: It was no longer in dispute that the property in question was governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act and the standard rent of this property was below Rs. 4,000 per month which was the rent being paid by the company. In view of the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the cases of Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. NDMC [1980] 122 ITR 700, Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 435, and Amolak Ram Khosla v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 589 since in the instant case the rent payable by the company to the assessee was considered to be more than the standard rent assessable under the Delhi Rent Control Act it was not permissible to say that the rent charged by the assessee was inadequate and was intended to confer any benefit on the settlors or their relatives. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to exemption under section 11 and the addition made by the ITO to the rental income was not justified.

the main conditions, namely, ( a) the property from which the income is derived should be held in trust or other legal obligation, (b) the property should be held for charitable or religious purposes which enure for the benefit of the public, and (c) the exemption is confined to only such portion of the trust income as is applied to charitable or religious purposes or is accumulated for application to such purposes within the limits of accumulation provided in section 11(1) and (2) . 2. In the instant case, the Tribunal had found that the assessee had constructed shops from its own funds and that the income therefrom could be utilised only for carrying out its objects. It could not be distributed amongst its members. The shops, etc., owned by it were, thus, held by it under a legal obligation. The stocks and the organisation will also come within the ambit of property. Hence, it satisfied the first condition, viz., holding property under a trust or legal obligation. The restrictive clause "not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit" qualifies or governs the fourth category of charitable purposes mentioned in the definition given in section 2(15), viz. , "the advancement of any other object of general public utility". It is the object of general public utility and not its advancement or accomplishment which must not involve the carrying on of any activity for profit. The object of the assessee-association was admittedly object of general public utility. The Tribunal had held that this object involved the carrying on of an activity for profit.

3. The law is well settled that if there are several objects of a trust or institution, some charitable and some non-charitable and the trustees or the managers in their discretion can apply the income or property to any of those objects, the trust or institution would not be liable to be regarded as charitable and no part of its income would be exempt from tax. If, however, its primary or the dominant purpose is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but just merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purposes, would not prevent the trust or the institution from being a valid charitable trust.

In the instant case, the assessee's aforementioned objects were both charitable and non-charitable. Its objects, inter alia, of encouraging industry and improving the breeding of cattle, etc., could not be described as charitable purposes. Since all its objects appear to enjoy an equal status and stand on the same footing and since its trustee could apply the income to any of those objects, it could not be regarded as charitable and no part of its income was exempt. The Tribunal had also found that none of the objects was dominant in nature. No definite part of the business or of its income was related to charitable purposes only.

4. Hence, the holding of agricultural and industrial exhibition and cattle fair involved an activity for profit, within the meaning of section 2(15) and that the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a). Further, the assessee could not be said to have held property under trust within the meaning of section 11(1)(b) and, consequently, was not eligible for exemption thereunder in respect of amounts actually spent on charities.

were being meant for achieving primary objects of trust and could not be called a business. The natural corollary that followed was that the income derived from such transactions could not be called an income from the business. Assuming that it was a business as contemplated under section 2(13), the same was exempted under section 11. Further, the submission that the income would be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust could not also be disbelieved. [Para 12] The licence to run races and betting itself could be treated as property and the said property was obtained with the consent of the Hyderabad Race Club. The term ‘property’ itself has got widest import for income-tax purposes and inclusive of holding a licence. But, it is not every case of business which can be treated as property. If it were to be so treated, section 13(1)(bb) would lose its meaning. It may be that a business itself may be settled in trust of the trustees who may conduct a business on their own under the powers given to them in the trust deed. In the instant case, it was difficult to accept that the assessee-trust was conducting the business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter-venue betting for few occasions in a year. Thus, there could not be any doubt that the income derived by the trust for the relevant assessment years was from the property held under trust and as such it was exempted under section 11.

Assuming even if it was not treated as income from the property held under the trust, it could be treated as voluntary contribution given by the Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee-trust as contemplated under section 12. The conduct of the Hyderabad Race Club in respect of the transaction was only a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contributions could be characterized only as a capital receipt in the assessee’s hands. Thus, it could not be held that there had been business in the normal sense in such arrangement and in the facts and circumstances, it was not such a business which would be hit by section 13(1)(bb). It was only an activity which could constitute the property or an arrangement involved in transfer of funds from Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee’s institution in a form recognized by law and not shown to be colourable exercise or otherwise as contended by the revenue. Since it could not be said to be a business and the income derived could not be said to be a business income, the provisions of section 13(1)(bb) were not attracted. The assessee-trust was an institution, which satisfied the conditions under section 2(15), read with section 11 and as such, conclusion reached by the Tribunal should be upheld. [Para 13]

None of the objects of the trust could be said to be non-charitable in nature. Rather the objects of the trust were purely of a charitable nature. The main objects of the trust were advancement and propagation of education, medical aid and relief to the poor. In fact, promotion of sports and games was also one of the charitable objects. Merely because a discretion was vested in the trustees to utilize the income for any one or more of the objects would not make any difference. Since there was no payment of club’s funds to the trust, there was no scope for the retrieval of the funds of the race club from the assessee-trust. Thus, it satisfied the test that the objects of the trust were not only charitable in nature, but also of general public utility and as such, attracted the provisions of section 11 and, therefore, the income derived by the trust was exempted under section 11. [Para 14]

Thus, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the assessee was an institution which satisfied the conditions of section 2(15), read with section 11 and the derived income was from the property held under the trust and even otherwise, it could only be treated as a voluntary contribution given by the Hyderabad Race Club and it could not be said that the activities carried on by the assessee constituted a business and even if it were to be a business, it was not such a business as would be hit by section 13(1)(bb). [Para 15]

or religious purpose, if applied to the extent of 85 per cent on its objectives, then such income will not fall in the total income assessable of an assessee. In other words, if Rs.100 is being derived from the property held under the Trust and Rs.85 is being applied towards the charitable objective of the Trust, then nothing will be taxable upon such a ‘Charitable Society’ or Trust. However, section 13 has contemplated certain exceptions. [Para 12]

■ A perusal of section 13 would indicate that if the assessee society has availed the services or purchased any object from any specified person contemplated in sub-clause (3) and paid to such specified person in excess of what may be paid reasonably for such service in open market, then excess would be disallowed. In other words, for example, if assessee society has availed the services of an Engineer who happened to be a specified person under sub-clause (3) and paid him the service charges which he could not command in the open market, then such excess amount will be disallowed to the assessee and benefit of Section 11 would not be available on such an amount. It will be taxable. For example, assessee can purchase an item for Rs.100 but from a specified person, it has purchased at Rs.120, then this excess Rs.20 will be added to the taxable income of the assessee and benefit of section 11 will not be available to the assessee Society. A perusal of the complete assessment order reveals that Assessing Officer has nowhere made analysis of the remuneration/ honorarium paid to the members of the Management Committee vis-à-vis their services utilized for the benefit of the Society. All the persons are qualified persons, they have devoted their time for managing the affairs of the Society and it has paid only honorarium, not regular salary. Similarly, it has provided traveling facility to them which was only for fulfilling the objects of the Society. In other words, in assessment year 2015-16, a little higher amount is being incurred by the assessee because the member of the Management Committee has to travel outside India for inspection of a plane which was to be used in Aviation Wing of the Engineering College. The Assessing Officer has not examined this aspect as to how this type of facilities can be availed from the open market and the price of such services. He has simply narrated that these persons are gainfully implied in their other activities also and therefore, payment of honorarium to these persons is not in accordance with law. This cannot be a logic for denying the benefit to them. The intention of the section is not as such. It is the assessee who has to manage its affairs and to decide what is necessary for its functioning. The Assessing Officer can only examine whether excess is being paid or not, but he has not carried out any Investigation in that area. The Assessing Officer has not assigned any reason as to why he is departing from the principle of consistency where such honorarium has been allowed to these per sons. Similarly Traveling Expenses has been allowed to the assessee in earlier years. The Commissioner (Appeals) failed to record any finding qua this aspect in right perspective and blindly up held the assessment order. Therefore, all these grounds of appeal are allowed.[Para 12.1]

headnotes.text: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1946-47 to 1948-49 - Assessee executed a deed of trust whereby they settled certain amount on various charities and appointed themselves as trustees - Later, in accordance with terms of trust deed, trustees assessees were appointed as managing agents of a company - Before Income-tax authorities, trustee claimed that income derived from managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Revenue authorities, however, held that income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Whether word "property" in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend "business," and if question fell to be decided solely on terms of that sub-section, managing agency formed by assessees/trustees must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether fact that trustees had option at any time to throw up managing agency was no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether section 4(3)(i) relates to income from business held under trust and section 4(3)(ia) relates to income from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution where that business itself is not held on trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where business of managing agency was held in trust, it could be concluded that business carried on by trustees fell under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Denial of exemption) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee-trust was conducting its activities in carrying out charitable activities, i.e., education, relief to poor, etc. - During year, assessee purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing funds of assessee-trust and same was registered in name of managing trustee - Assessing Officer denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to extent of value of that vehicle on ground that objects of assessee trust were carrying out of charitable activities and fund collected for this charitable purposes was utilized for enjoyment of trustees by means of purchase of said vehicle in name of managing trustee which was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c) - Assessee submitted that car was purchased in name of managing trustee for simple reason that it gave relief by way of lower road/life tax and insurance charges - However, assessee could not prove as to what use this asset was put to by trust in work of trust and for purposes for which trust had been set up - Whether since assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased by assessee-trust with its funds and registered in name of managing trustee - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]

Section 11, read with section 13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Denial of exemption) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee-trust was conducting its activities in carrying out charitable activities, i.e., education, relief to poor, etc. - During year, assessee purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing funds of assessee-trust and same was registered in name of managing trustee - Assessing Officer denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to extent of value of that vehicle on ground that objects of assessee trust were carrying out of charitable activities and fund collected for this charitable purposes was utilized for enjoyment of trustees by means of purchase of said vehicle in name of managing trustee which was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c) - Assessee submitted that car was purchased in name of managing trustee for simple reason that it gave relief by way of lower road/life tax and insurance charges - However, assessee could not prove as to what use this asset was put to by trust in work of trust and for purposes for which trust had been set up - Whether since assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased by assessee-trust with its funds and registered in name of managing trustee - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust purchased a luxury vehicle by utilizing its funds and same was registered in name of managing trustee, however, assessee was not able to establish that said vehicle was utilized for purpose of charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 was to be denied on value of vehicle purchased

II - Section 11 of Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 2008-09 - Whether where for purpose of set up an educational institution assessee and trust purchased agricultural land as trust cannot purchase agricultural land, funds were routed through one of trustees, no adverse inference could be drawn - Held, yes - Whether where managing trustees were paid much higher in comparison to Principal and other staff whose activities were confined to their rank while these trustees had versatile experience, administrative and managerial skill and by their unstinted efforts and far-sightedness they were managing students, carrying on other administrative work, coordinating with government agencies, higher payment made to them could not be doubted - Held, yes - Whether since these trustees had to commute on day-to-day basis to various Government agencies, and other allied places which were scattered all over vast city of Ahmedabad, this cannot be branded at any stretch of imagination that trustees had been provided with excessive amenities - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, on these grounds exemption could not be denied to assessee-trust - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Property held under trust) - Assessment years 1987-88, 1991-92, 1997-98, 1998-99, 2006-07 and 2008-09 to 2014-2015 - Whether once income of a trust is used by it to acquire a property, property so acquired will be property held under trust and income from such property will be income from property under trust - Held, yes - Assessee society was having income from two Kalyanamandapams - According to Assessing Officer these properties were not settled by settlor as trust property and hence could not be considered as properties held under trust and thus he held that income earned by assessee from its Kalyanamandapams could not be treated as income from house property but only as income from business - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld order of Assessing Officer holding that Kalyanamandapams having being built by assessee subsequent to its formation could not be considered as property under trust - However, assessee submitted that land on which Kalyanamandapams were built was part of original settlement and buildings were built therein by assessee from its income - Whether thus, rental income received by assessee from Kalyanamandapams though it was in nature of income from business, such income was nothing but income from property held under trust - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT: Property (i.e. Kalyanamandapams) built by assessee society from its income, subsequent to its formation, on land, which was part of original settlement, was to be considered as property under trust and income therefrom was income from property under trust  IT: Where predominant activity of assessee society was charity, it would be eligible for exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income form property held under - Assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60 - Assessee was an association of persons - Constitution of assessee revealed that neither standing committee nor managing committee nor even members of assessee could use property of assessee for any purpose except that covered by object clause of assessee - Neither before ITO nor before AAC any contention was raised by revenue that object for which assessee was constituted was not charitable one - Whether property of assessee was held under trust or under legal obligation and, therefore, assessee was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

 trust under section 11 on two grounds, namely, (a) that even though assessee’s buildings were being used by other societies of same group for charitable activities, such use could not be treated as use by assessee for carrying out its own charitable activities; and (b) that major expenditure was on account of agricultural and dairy activities carried on by it which was not in nature of application of its income for charitable purpose - Commissioner (Appeals), however, upheld assessee’s claim - Whether where buildings of assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature, such use could very well be treated as use by assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for purpose of exemption under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether since agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by assessee-society as separate business activities, same constituted ‘property held under trust’ as provided in section 11(4) and in any case income of said activities was to be determined after deducting expenditure incurred in connection with said business - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, gross income being more than sufficient to cover expenses incurred in connection with said activities, allowance of same by Commissioner  (Appeals) as application of its income hardly made any difference in ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to revenue - Held, yes
