Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Trust deed of a trust provided that income of trust fund should be applied for benefit of any of past, present and future officers, members of staff and other employees of company ‘A’, or of any company within the management of company A, and their dependents of whatever race or class who in uncontrolled discretion of Administrators shall be deserving of consideration or help, more especially on account of indigence, ill-health or other necessitous circumstances on their retirement - By a supplementary deed, administrators were directed to pay more regard to indigence or ill-health or other specially necessitous circumstances of person or persons whose cases were being considered rather than to length of service - Whether use of fund to relieve a person from ‘some other special necessitous circumstances’ could not be said to be for relief of poverty - Held, yes - Whether further, since fund was for benefit of employees of only company ‘A’ and their subsidiary concerns, fund was not property held in trust wholly for charitable purposes - Held, yes

Section 13, read with sections 11 and 12 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Benefit to specified persons) - Assessment years 2003-04 to 2008-09 - Assessee a registered charitable organization carried on work of education through four members, who worked in dual capacity i.e. as whole time administrators, as also regular time teachers, and were being paid salaries from earning of these schools - Members were not being paid separately for managerial work done by them - Members were also furnishing their income tax returns regularly as individuals and were duly showing their income received as salaries from assessee and their said returns had also been continuously accepted by revenue - Assessee was availing benefit of exemption of its income under sections 11 and 12 - Tribunal partially affirmed salaries paid to two of trustee members and rejected claim of assessee with regard to two others - Assessee claimed that once it was registered as a charitable organization and its accounts were being accepted since very beginning, it was entitled to benefits of exemption - It further claimed that all four members had not only huge teaching experience to their credit but were also whole time employees of assessee and thus were closely associated with management as also in running of schools of assessee - It also claimed that completion of assessment against assessee as a normal business entity was also wrong and misfounded - Whether since assessee trust/society was pursuing an object of general public utility, conclusion drawn by Assessing Officer that petitioner-society was not a charitable society was misfounded - Held, yes - Whether all four members were engaged in whole time management activities of Trust and were also rendering administrative functions qua running of schools for which they were not being paid any extra salary - Held, yes - Whether thus, there was no violation of provisions of section 13(2)(c) and assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11 - Held, yes [Paras 32, 39  40] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where all members of assessee-trust were engaged in whole time management activities of Trust and as regular time teachers and were being paid salaries from earning of these schools and were not being paid any extra salary for management work, there was no violation of provisions of section 13(2)(c) and assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11

Section 11, read with sections 12AA and 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1990-91 to 1993-94 and 1999-2000 - Assessee society was formed for benefit of local people, upliftment of poor, education and other social and charitable activities - A land was given by District Collector to assessee, to construct a kalyana mandapam on specific condition that it should function for benefit of local people, mainly weavers and agriculturists - Accordingly, assessee constructed a kalyana mandapam and collected minimum nominal charges from users to meet maintenance, repairs and renovation expenses - Exemption claimed by it under section 11 was denied by Assessing Officer on ground that assessee had not undertaken any charitable activity since its inception except constructing and running a marriage hall, which was purely a commercial activity and did not have any charity involved in it - Whether by constructing kalyana mandapam and letting out same after collecting nominal rent to meet maintenance, repairs and renovation expenses sufficiently satisfied object, viz., benefit of local people, mainly weavers and agriculturists, which was condition under grant given by Collector - Held, yes - Whether failure or non-diversion of accumulated funds for any other charitable purpose by itself would not divest right conferred on assessee to claim exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with section 19 of Bombay Trust Act, 1950 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1964-65 to 1969-70, 1972-73 and 1973-74 - Lands of some villages were said to have been granted by one Mughal Emperor for upkeep of Roza in year 1670 under a Sanad and grants were confirmed by sanads issued during British regime - A suo motu enquiry was started under section 19 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 - As a result of that inquiry, Dy. Charity Commissioner made an order directing that assessee- Roza Trust be registered as a Public Trust - On appeal Charity Commissioner confirmed order of Dy. Charity Commissioner - He held that assessee-trust was a public trust and lands of villages were properties of said trust - Question for consideration was as to whether income from lands in question was income of assessee-Roza Trust assessable in hands of said trust and exempt under section 11 or whether it was assessable in hands of Sajjadanashin of Trust i.e., ‘SM’, as income from his private property - Tribunal on material before it, which included orders made by Dy. Charity Commissioner and Charity Commissioner, documents such as Sanad issued by Mughal Emperor and Sanads of Government, Survey Settlement register and historical account given in text-books, came to finding that these lands of four villages belonged to assessee-trust - Whether while it is true that tax authority, during assessment proceedings, can always inquire into question of ownership of property and decide issue in context of relevant provisions of said Act, in order to ascertain income of the assessee for bringing it to tax, it will not be open for tax authorities to ignore relevant evidence of statutory registration of a public trust and fact of the properties having been registered as properties of such public trust under provisions of Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 - Held, yes - Whether finding of Charity Commissioner in an inquiry 
under section 19 of Bombay Public Trust operates as findings in rem and cannot be ignored by authorities under Income-tax Act - Held, yes - Whether Sajjadanashin of Roza Trust was spiritual leader and integral part of Roza Trust and, therefore, provision for Sajjadanashin was not a provision for man but for institution and therefore, expenses incurred on 
 Sajjadanashin by assessee-trust could not be held to be expenses for private property - Held, yes - Whether Tribunal was justified in holding that income from lands in question was assessable in hands of assessee-trust and not in hands of Sajjadanashin and further that trust was entitled to exemption in respect of income spent as ‘Madad-E-Maash’ on maintenance of Sajjadanashin, his family and descendants - Held, yes - Whether amount received by Sajjadanashin was to be taxed as income in his hands - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under trust (Business held in trust) - Assessment years 1992-93 to 1994-95, 2001-02 and 2005-06 to 2007-08 - Assessee-trust was created with objects of establishing and maintaining of schools, colleges and study circles, advancing education and research study on modern and ancient Indian thought, etc. - After formation of trust, a business was commenced in name of trust for manufacture of katha - Assessee claimed exemption under section 11 in respect of its income and filed a return of income on that basis - Assessing Officer denied exemption - High Court by impugned order held that since katha business was commenced by trustees with aid and assistance of borrowings from sister concerns it could not be case of 'property being held under trust' within meaning of section 11(4) but would only be a case of business being carried on by and on behalf of trust and mere fact that whole or some part of income from katha business was earmarked for application of charitable objects would not render business itself being considered as incidental to attainment of objects of trust - Whether Special Leave Petition filed against impugned order was to be granted - Held, yes [Paras 19 to 22] [In favour of assessee]IT: SLP granted against High Court's ruling that where business was commenced by trustees with aid and assistance of borrowings from sister concerns, it could not be a case of 'property being held under trust'

III. Section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption (Sub-section (3)) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Whether provisions of section 13(3)(cc) would not extend to manager (or her spouse) of trust - Held, yes [Para 11.1] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) – Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under – Assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56 – Claim of assessee trust for exemption of its income under section 4(3)(i) was rejected by ITO on ground that business of trust carried on by managing trustee on behalf of trust fell within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and hence its business income was not exempt from taxation – Whether where trust carries on business and business itself is held in trust and income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for purpose of religious or charitable character, conditions prescribed under section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and income is exempt from taxation - Held, yes – Whether claim of exemption cannot be denied even if business were to be conducted by someone else acting on behalf of trust, and proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to such businesses as are not held under trust and, therefore, field of its operation is distinct and separate from that covered by main provision of section 4(3)(i) – Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid legal position, assessee being a religious and charitable trust, was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act for assessment years in question – Held, yes

Section 11 [corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922], read with  section 2(14), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religions trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1968-69 - Whether where business of Kuris (unit fund) was itself held by assessee under a trust for religious or charitable purpose, it could not be said that business was conducted 'on behalf of' religious or charitable institution to advance any object of general public utility and therefore, income derived by assessee from Kuris was exempt from taxation was exempt from taxation under section 11(1)(a) - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Application of income) - Assessment year 2008-09 - High Court by impugned order held that where assessee-trust incurred expenditure in excess of income in previous year relevant to assessment year for charitable purposes, out of accumulated charity fund, it could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(a) in respect of income of previous year relevant to assessment year, which had been admittedly applied for charitable purposes - Whether Special Leave Petition filed against impugned order was to be granted - Held, yes [Para 2] [In favour of revenue]IT : SLP granted against High Court's ruling that merely because assessee-trust incurred expenditure in excess of income in relevant previous year for charitable purposes out of accumulated charity fund, it could not be denied benefit of exemption under section 11(1)(a)

Section 13,  read with section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption [Sub-section (1)(b)] - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-society was formed with object to promote, sustain and carry out programmes and activities of Church, which were, among others, educational, charitable, religious, social and cultural etc. - It was registered under section 12A - Assessee filed return claiming exemption of income under section 11 - Revenue authorities opined that even if society's activities were for both charitable and religious purposes, since it was for benefit of one religious community alone section 13(1)(b) would be attracted and it could not be granted exemption under section 11 - Tribunal, on basis of documents submitted by assessee, found that priests were not managing affairs of society - It was also noted that activities of assessee-society, though both religious and charitable, were not exclusively meant for one particular religious community - Tribunal thus allowed assessee's claim for exemption of income - Whether findings recorded by Tribunal being findings of fact, no substantial question of law arose therefrom - Held, yes [Paras 15 and 16][In favour of assessee]IT: Assessee-society formed with object to promote, sustain and carry out programmes and activities of Church, was eligible to claim exemption under section 11

Section 11, read with section 13(1)(c), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessee-trust owned properties which were settled by L and H, who were joint owners thereof - Assessee had leased out aforesaid property to a company on a rent of Rs. 4,000 per month for purpose of residence of P, who was managing director of company and husband of L and father of H-ITO held that premises in question could fetch a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month and, hence, the assessee had allowed the trust property being used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of the authors of the trust and their relatives under section 13(1)(c), read with section 13(2)(b) - Whether in view of fact that property in question was governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act and standard rent of property was below Rs. 4,000 there was no direct or indirect benefit to authors of assessee and their relatives and, therefore, assessee was entitled to exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1961-62 to 1963-64 - An association of persons, chiefly engaged in horse racing, declared and made a trust - As per said trust deed, surplus funds were to be disposed of, (i) by making improvements to racing facilities, and/or (ii) by making donations at discretion of trustees to any recognised institution for social, cultural and physical benefits of people - Whether surplus funds really emanated from a property which was not a subject-matter of trust and as such in absence of any legal obligation fastened thereto, no exemption could be allowed under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether further, since trustees had indefeasible alternative right to apply funds to other purposes, without making any donation to charitable purposes no part of its income was exempt from tax - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from properties held under - Assessment year 1956-57 - By an indenture of trust, ‘D’ and his wife both doctors, settled upon trust an immovable property and two maternity hospitals which were run by them - Primary object of trust was to carry on and promote educational, health, cultural, social and economic interest of people particularly of backward and lower classes - Substance of indenture of trust itself was that all trust properties were transferred by both settlers to trustees and trustees made declaration that they would hold properties for objects of trust from date of deed - One of recitals clearly indicated that it was business of conducting two maternity homes that had been settled upon trust, because net annual income which was to accrue to trust from said hospitals to be arrived at after deducting all expenses for maintaining and running hospitals and after making payment to ‘D,’ s wife as provided in trust deed for managing said hospitals for and on behalf of trust during her lifetime - Whether as trust deed was duly registered it was sufficient in law to effect a valid transfer - Held, yes - Whether since business of running and conducting maternity homes itself was settled upon trust, conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act were fulfilled and, hence income from maternity homes was exempt from taxation - Held, yes - Whether for conducting maternity hospitals presence of a doctor was essential and therefore, amount paid to wife of ‘D’ was a part of normal expenditure of conducting and managing said hospitals which was allowable as admissible deduction in computation of income of trust in hands of trustees as association of persons - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1984-85 and 1985-86 - Whether expression ‘the business is mainly carried on by the beneficiaries of the institution’ in section 11(4A)(B), as it stood prior to 1-4-1992, would only mean that the activities of the business are mainly managed and controlled by the beneficiaries of the institution; it is not necessary that each and every beneficiary should personally condudct the business of assessee institution ; expression only means that the work in connection with the business of the trust or institution should not be carried on by outsiders or agents or managers or by strangers, who are not the trustees or the beneficiaries - Held, yes

facts.text:
'P; 'L' and 'LS' executed a deed of trust whereby they settled a sum on various charities specified therein and appointed themselves and two others as trustees. The trust deed provided inter alia that the trustees mights with the help of the trust fund, for and on behalf of and for the benefit of the trust, carry on such business including the taking up and conducting the managing agency or selling agency of any company in such name or names as they in their absolute discretion might think fit and proper. Later the trustees were appointed as managing agents of a company. The agency was to be for a period of 20 years; but it was open to the trustees to throw it up on giving three months' notice. The managing agents were to get a remuneration of 10 per cent of the net annual profits. Before the Income-tax authorities, the assessee/trustees claimed that the income derived from the managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The Income-tax authorities held that the income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court held that no part of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which was the only property settled on trust was actually invested in the managing agency business, which could not, therefore, be regarded as trust property, and that the income received from that business was not within the exemption enacted in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

Under a trust deed dated the 15-6-1945, according to the decision of the Privy Council the business of a managing agency was held in trust. Therefore, the income derived from managing agency was held by the Supreme Court as falling with section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act since the word "property" in that sub-section includes business as well. But it was contended before the Supreme Court that although the income might appear to fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act has been narrowed down by the provision in section 4(3)(ia) which deals with income from business and, therefore, the Sub-section that really applies to the determination of the question as to whether the income sought to be taxed in the hands of the trustees was exempt from tax in section 4(3)(ia) and not section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. It was common ground that if section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act was the section under which the exemption claimed was to be determined, the conditions laid down in that sub-section for the purpose of granting an exemption were not satisfied and, therefore, the assessees would not be entitled to an exemption. The question was, therefore, of vital importance to the assessees as to whether their case fell within section 4(3)(i) of section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act.

On reference:

■

The assessee-trust was carrying out charitable activities like education, relief to poor, etc.

■

The Assessing Officer found that a vehicle purchased by the trust was registered in the name of the managing trustee and thus, the case of the Assessing Officer was that the assessee purchased the above said vehicle and registered in the name of the trustee was a clear violation under section 13(1)(c). Further, the case of the Assessing Officer was that the income or property of the assessee was diverted in favour of the managing trustee of the assessee and it was a clear violation as per clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 13 read with section 13(1)(c). The assessee explained that the car was purchased in the name of the managing trustee with the sole objective of saving considerable amount of road tax and insurance. However, the Assessing Officer rejected the explanation and denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 to the extent of value of that car.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the view of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

‘N’ was the karta of a joint Hindu family. The joint family properties included a building which had been set apart for use of pilgrims visiting the town. Subsequently the family properties were partitioned under a partition deed between ‘N’ and his adopted son, ‘R’ as also minor, ‘D’ the adopted some of his pre-deceased son. Under that partition the building in question was directed to be maintained by ‘N’ with the income from certain lands over which he had been given a life-interest. Later on N died. At the time of his death he was a partner in the firm having a 3/16th share in the profits and losses of the said firm. The accountable persons filed an estate duty return admitting a net dutiable estate including the share capital and the share of profit and interest of the deceased in the managing agency firm, but did not include the value of the share of the deceased in the goodwill of the said managing agency firm. It also did not include the value of the building. The Assistant Controller of Estate Duty, however, proposed to value of building at Rs. 62,000 and 3/16th share in the goodwill of the firm and to include the same in the estate of the deceased. The accountable persons objected to this proposal and contended that the value of the building could not be included in the estate of the deceased because it had been set apart only for charitable purposes, with regard to the goodwill, it was contended that in the case of managing agency business, there was no goodwill at all, and that in fact the accountable persons had not obtained any amount from the firm towards the value of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the firm. The Assistant Controller, however, overruled these objections and held that the building was not a trust property and that it was owned by the deceased at the time of his death, and, therefore, its value was includible in the estate of the deceased. On the question of goodwill, the Assistant Controller held that the managing agency firm did possess goodwill and on the death of the deceased the accountable persons were entitled to 3/16th share in the goodwill of the business of the firm and as such a sum being the value of the 3/16th share had to be included in the estate of the deceased.

On appeal, the Appellate controller upheld the order of the assistant controller and reduced the value of the building.

On further appeal the Tribunal upheld the order of the Appellate Controller in respect of inclusion of value of building holding that a mere provision for the maintenance of the building by the deceased and thereafter by others could not amount to creation of a trust with reference to the building and that the exclusive use of the building from 1942 to 1958, for religious and charitable purposes did not amount to a permanent dedication of the building as a trust property. As regards the inclusion representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm, the Tribunal held that goodwill cannot be associated with the business of managing agency firm because the managing agency business is governed by the terms of the agreement between the managing agency firm and the company and the right of managing agency was more personal and could not pass on to a successor. The Tribunal also held that no share in the goodwill of the business passed to the accountable persons on the death of the deceased and that in any event no amount was actually paid to the accountable persons by way of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the business. In that view the Tribunal deleted the sum representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm.

On reference:

The assessee-trust was constituted by one ‘J’ who was the manager of certain religious and charitable funds. By the deed of indenture, it was declared that the respective assets of the religious and charitable funds would be in favour of the trustees who would hold the management and operate the respective assets of those funds for the purposes stated in the trust deed. Thus, the assessee claimed exemption on that ground. The Assessing Officer held that since the expenses incurred were in excess than the income derived from various funds, the trustee was not entitled to exemption under section 11(1)(a). The AAC, however, allowed the appeal. On further appeal, the Tribunal restored the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

By an indenture of trust dated 23-8-1954, one ‘D’ and his wife settled upon trust two maternity hospitals which were run by them and an immovable property for the purposes and objects contained in the said deed of trust. The assessee were the trustees under the said trust. The primary object of the trust was to carry on and promote the educational, health, cultural, literary, social and economic interests of the people, particularly of the backward and poorer classes. The important recitals in the trust deed were to the effect that the net annual income from the said hospitals, after deducting all the expenses for maintaining and running the hospitals including a sum of Rs. 750 per month which should be paid regularly to ‘D’s wife for managing the said hospitals for and on behalf of the trust during her lifetime, should accrue to the trust from year to year and that Dr. Divekar and Dr. Nalini Divekar did transfer the above said property and both the hospitals to the Trustees. And that the monies and properties of the trust were to be applied, firstly in payment of the expenses of carrying out of the trust and then in carrying out the other objects. The assessee claimed exemption under section 43(1)(i) of the 1922 Act. Even though the ITO accepted that the business in maternity homes was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act, he however took the view that its income was not exempt under the said section because it did not fulfil the requirements of proviso (b) thereto. This view was arrived at by him because he took the view that the primary purpose in conducting or running the two maternity homes or hospitals was not to give free medical facilities but charge the patients and then to apply the income for certain objects. Even the amount paid to D’s wife claimed as a deduction was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that the same was paid by the association of persons to one of its own members.

On appeal, the AAC held that the income from the trust was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and that the salary paid was an allowable deduction in computation of the assessees’ income.

On revenue’s further appeal, the Tribunal took the view that there was no actual transfer of immovable properties to the trustees if regard be had to the language employed in the document. The lands of some villages were said to have been granted by one Mughal emperor for the upkeep of the Roza in the year 1670 under a Sanad and grants were confirmed by the Sanads issued during the British regime. A suo motu enquiry was started under section 19 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. As a result of that inquiry, the Dy. Charity Commissioner made an order directing that the assessee-Roza Trust be registered as a Public Trust. On appeal the Charity Commissioner confirmed the order of the Dy. Charity Commissioner. He held that the assessee-trust was a public trust and the lands of villages were the properties of the said trust. However, the ITO assessed the income of village lands as income in the hands of ‘SM’, the Sajjadanashin of the trust. Protective assessment was, however, made in respect of that income in the name of the assessee-trust. The AAC, on appeal, upheld the finding of the ITO but cancelled the protective assessment which was made in the name of the assessee-trust and assessed the income in the hands of the Sajjadanashin. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the AAC had committed an error in setting aside the protective assessment.

The Tribunal concluded that the lands in question were Wakf properties belonging to the assessee-trust, and that the exemption under section 11 was available to the assessee-Roza Trust, provided the condition mentioned therein were fulfilled. It was held that the actual expenditure on the Sajjadanashin and his family not exceeding Rs. 30,000 would not be included in the income of the Roza Trust, but such amount spent by the Sajjadanashin on his maintenance as Madad-E-Maash was taxable in his hands as income. The Tribunal restored the matter to the ITO to assess the income of the lands as the income of the assessee-trust and grant the benefit under section 11 subject to fulfilment of the conditions mentioned therein, bearing in mind that the income actually spent by Sajjadanashin on his maintenance not exceeding Rs. 30,000 was not to be included in the income of the Roza Trust.

The issue for consideration for the High Court was as to whether the income from the lands in question was the income of the assessee-trust assessable in the hands of the said Trust and exempt under section 11 or it was assessable in the hands of ‘SM’, the Sajjadanashin of the trust, as income from his private property.

On cross appeals :

Facts

M/s. Claverhouse, an Investment Trust Company (ITC), used the management services of a third party, JP Morgan Fleming Asset Management (UK) Limited, to manage its investment portfolios.

The management services received by Claverhouse were charged to VAT and Claverhouse paid VAT thereon amounting GBP 2.7 million.

The management services received by Authorised Unit Trusts (AUTs) and Open-ended Investment Company (OEICs) were exempt from VAT.

The assessee argued that management services received by it were also exempt from VAT, while the Department argued that closed-ended investment companies such as the assessee were not eligible for such exemption.

Statutory Provisions, Sixth Council Directive 77/388/EEC of 17 May, 1977

Article 13B(d)(6) : Member States are to exempt the following from VAT under conditions which they are to lay down for the purpose of ensuring the correct and straightforward application of the exemptions and of preventing any possible evasion, avoidance or abuse: 'management of special investment funds as defined by Member States.'

Issue Involved

Were the services received by assessee eligible for exemption ?

The assessee, a charitable trust, had been created by the settlers by transfer of shares of certain companies, in which the settlors or the persons referred to in section 13(3) of the 1961 Act had substantial interest. The shares of those companies owned by the assessee were their shares originally settled or bonus shares received in respect of the shares originally settled and not a single share of either of the said companies was purchased by or on behalf of the trust as such. The assessee-trust was not allowed exemption under section 5(1)(i) on the grounds : (i) that the trust funds were ‘invested’ within the meaning of section 13(2)(h) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ; and (ii) that the trust was therefore assessable under section 21A, which prohibited allowance of deduction under section 5(1)(i).

On second appeal :

■

The assessee was established under a special statute enacted by Maharashtra State Legislature, namely, the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority Act, 1974 (The MMRDA Act). The assessee was set up for development of Mumbai Metropolitan Region.

■

The assessee claimed that the development functions carried out by the assessee for the entire Mumbai Metropolitan Region fell within the ambit of the term 'advancement of general public utility' i.e. charitable purpose as contained in section 2(15). The aforesaid projects were for the benefit of the general public or for advancement of general public utility and fell within the ambit of 'charitable purpose' as defined in section 2(15). Further, the activities conducted by assessee constituted 'general public utility' which is covered as 'charitable purpose'.

■

The Assessing Officer denied exemption under section 11 by stating that assessee was not a valid trust. The Assessing Officer by resorting to proviso to section 2(15), denied exemption under section 11 claimed by the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed exemption under section 11stating that the assessee acted on behalf of and as an agent of the State Government and by following order of the decision of Tribunal in assessee's own case.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

BJ was carrying on mining business. He executed a trust deed dated 1-9-1952 with a corpus of Rs. 50,000 and appointed the assessee, an AOP, as trustees. It was a charitable trust and the object was to utilise the property as also its income for charitable purpose enumerated in the trust deed. The trustees were authorised, inter alia, ( a) to start, open and carry on such business with the properties and funds owned by the trust (barring a speculation business); (b) to deal with the movable and immovable properties in any manner they chose including investment of funds with businessmen of repute; and (c ) to use the trust properties in business of trust or to let out to others or to take mining lease or contract for working mines, or any other work connected therewith. It was further provided that the income derived from such business would be the trust property. The trustees, accordingly, undertook to carry on the business of raising manganese and, under certain contracts, from mines belonging to the settlor. It also advanced loans to certain parties in the course of its mining business. It earned income from mining business and interest for the assessment year 1964-65 and only interest for the assessment years 1965-66 and 1966-67 and claimed it to be exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i). The ITO disallowed the same observing that the business itself was not held in trust and that necessary conditions laid down in proviso (b) to said section were not satisfied. The revenue's appeals before the AAC and the Tribunal were unsuccessful.

On reference:

One late 'T' had by his last will settled upon the assessee-trust all his immovable and movable properties for the benefit of three institutions and for any other charitable purposes and had appointed two persons as executors of his will. The assessee claimed exemption under section 5(1)(i) in respect of the value of the aforesaid properties settled upon it. The WTO as well as the Dy. Commissioner (Appeals) negatived the assessee's claim on the ground that since no trust-deed was executed, the properties were not held under any trust for charitable purposes.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the trust was created under a will itself and there was no necessity for executing a trust-deed by the executors of the will of the late testator. Accordingly, it held that the trustees were entitled to claim exemption under section 5(1)(i) because the exemption could not be denied on the ground that the executors of the will had not executed the formal deed of trust.

On reference :

One 'S' and four others were holding certain securities for the purpose of charity and had been applying the same for and towards charitable purposes, executed, on 8-6-1922, a deed of declaration of trust declaring that the said trust fund would be held by them on trusts more specifically therein mentioned. Clause 13 of trust deed provided that the trust fund would be held by the trustees upon the trusts to apply the net income thereof after providing for all necessary expenses in relation to the management of the trust funds, for all or any of the following purposes (a) the relief and benefit of the poor and indigent members of jewish (b) the institution, maintenance and support of hospitals and schools, colleges or other educational institutions or (c) the relief of any distress caused by the elements of nature such as famine, pestilence, fire, tempest, flood, earthquake or any other such calamity or (d) the care and protection of animals useful to mankind or (e) the advancement of religion or (f) other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the foregoing purposes. The trust deed further provided that the trustees would give preference to the poor and indigent relations or members of the family of the said 'S' including there in distant and collateral relations. The trust fund had been invested by the trustees in inter alia 3½ per cent Government securities. In the year 1930, a certificate was issued by the ITO, whereby the Reserve Bank of India was authorized not to deduct at source the tax on the said securities so held by the trustees. For the assessment years 1948-49 and 1949-50, the ITO took the view that the income from the trust fund was not exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act accordingly, he assessed the appellants. On appeals, the AAC and the Tribunal confirmed the assessment made by the ITO.

On reference, the High Court also held that the trust property was not held wholly for religious or charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

The assessee, a registered charitable trust, was running a Skin Institute which was providing medical facility in the field of skin and also carried out research fully recognised by the Board and offered courses of dermatology. The patients were divided into three categories, being free category, subsidised category and paying category. No consultation fees was charged from free category patients. The assessee-trust filed a return for the assessment year 1992-93 declaring nil income claiming exemption under section 10(22)/11. The Assessing Officer observed that 50 per cent of income generated by the trust was given to Dr. ‘P’, founder and managing trustee, and that the assessee denied to have received any donation, whereas in the profit and loss account it had claimed to have received donation, which in fact was sale proceeds of the medicines. The Assessing Officer denied exemption claimed by the assessee. On appeal, the assessee contended that Dr. ‘P’ had no income from trust except that he was charging 50 per cent of the income for rendering medical services to the trust, but he was not charging anything for managerial or administrative services and it was by mistake that medicine sale proceeds had been shown as donation. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejecting the assessee’s contention, upheld the Assessing Officer’s order.

On second appeal

■

The assessee, a charitable trust claimed exemption under sections 11 and 12.

■

The Assessing Officer denied exemption by treating the assessee as an Association of Persons (AOP) on ground that assessee had earned substantial rental income by leasing its immovable properties which amounted to a commercial activity inconsistent with its charitable character.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim on ground that the Assessing Officer had not brought cogent material to show that the assessee’s activities ceased to be charitable.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

The assessee, having income from properties and interest, was a trust constituted under a deed dated 14-8-1951, under which five trustees were appointed to manage and administer two properties dedicated by them in favour of the trust. The properties were to be held for the benefit of Chemists & Druggists Association and any surplus income available was directed to be utilised for the purpose of the Association. According to the trust deed, the legal title in the properties was vested in the trust and the Chemists & Druggists Association were the beneficiaries of the trust. The assessee-trust filed income-tax returns in respect of the assessment years 1971-72 to 1974-75 claiming exemption under section 11. The ITO held that the trust was not intended for the benefit of any cross-section of the public and hence, the benefit of section 11 was not available. He completed the assessment on the trust. On appeal, the AAC held that the trust was not an independent body having control over the management and affairs relating to the buildings; since the income really belonged to Chemists & Druggists Association, it should be assessed in the hands of the Association. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the orders of AAC.

On reference:

The assessee trust, a Charitable Organization Registered under section 12A filed its return of income on 1-11-2017. The assessee claimed to be engaged in activities of education of the people of India by conducting and/or providing booklets, pamphlets, newspaper, magazines, or in any other manner. The Assessing Officer noted that in the return of income along with income and expenditure account, the assessee had filed the balance-sheet and audit report in Form 10B declaring total income at Rs. 2.20 crores.

During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer examined the books of account and noted that the assessee was engaged in the publication which included publication of newspaper and magazine as well as carried out various commercial activities. According to Assessing Officer, case of assessee was hit by proviso to section 2(15) and thus it lost its charitable character within the meaning of section 2(15) and under section 13(8) for the assessment year in question. The Assessing Officer therefore held that the assessee trust was not eligible for any benefit and/or exemption under section 11 and accordingly taxed the entire income of the assessee trust denying the benefit of exemption under section 11.

Thereafter, the Commissioner (Exemption), issued notice under section 263 on ground that the assessee trust had claimed deduction under section 24(a) on 'service charges' received by it and wondered as to how the 'service charge' could be included in property income and standard deduction could be claimed and allowed by Assessing Officer, which action of Assessing Officer was erroneous and that the assessment order had been passed without basic verification about the allowability of claim under section 24(a) which was erroneous insofar as it was prejudicial to the interest of revenue.

Pursuant to the show cause notice of the Commissioner (Exemption), the assessee trust replied that it's commercial building had been given on leave & license basis under various agreements entered into with the respective parties. And the amenities included water and electricity supply, elevator, CCTV in common areas, and security services. And that the terms of the agreement for amenities were co-extensive with the terms of the leave & license agreement. Therefore, it was submitted that the income arising from the said agreement for amenities also formed part of income from house property within the meaning of section 23; and therefore the assessee trust was entitled to deduction under section 24(a) on the amount received by the trust in pursuance to the agreement for amenities and credited in the books of account as service charges.

However, according to the Commissioner (Exemption), the Assessing Officer had not carried out any such exercise (verification) before allowing the deduction under section 24(a), therefore, the Commissioner (Exemption) set aside the assessment order with direction to the Assessing Officer to undertake enquiry and frame de novo assessment.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee trust, registration under section 12AA, filed its return and claimed exemption under section 11(1)(a). During the year, the assessee had temporarily given loans and advances to one, MGA to earn interest income on the surplus fund for a short period of time. An interest income was received by the assessee in the next year which was utilized for charitable purposes of this Trust.

The Assessing Officer held that the said amount being accumulated amount had not been applied by the assessee for charitable purposes and, accordingly, made an addition of the said amount.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order passed by the Assessing Officer.

In instant appeal the assessee contended that when the assessee had applied 85 percent of its income for charitable purposes as per the provisions of section 11(1)(a), then the amount in question though might not be an investment as per the modes prescribed under section 11(5), the same could not be held as application of income for non-charitable purposes. Thus, the assessee had submitted that as per the provisions of section 13(1)(d) only the income on such investment could not be taxed and the principal amount could not be added or charged to tax. Hence, the assessee had submitted that at the most the interest income earned on such advances/loans could be charged to tax and not the principal amount when the assessee has already complied with the conditions as prescribed under section 11(1)(a) to the extent of application of 85 percent of income for charitable purposes.

The assessee society was getting subscription from persons belonging to 'K' community scattered all over India. In addition the assessee also had income from a house property. It was stated in the memorandum of association that income arising out of the said house property was to be spent amongst other activities of running dispensary, schools, etc. in the village from which place all the 'K's' came. The claim of the assessee that it was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act was negatived by the ITO. On appeal, the AAC, held that a part of the income from this house property was devoted to charitable objects only and such, a portion of the income was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. On further appeal to the Tribunal, this claim to partial exemption was overruled. According to the Tribunal whether the objects of the society were charitable or not, had to be gathered from the memorandum of association and if the association or its executive committee was entitled to spend amounts under any of the clauses of the objects clause, some of which were charitable in nature and others not, the only conclusion to come to was that the institution was not solely for the purposes of charity.

On reference:

The assessee was a public religious and charitable trust registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. A scheme for this trust was originally framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad way back in 1960 after finding in a suit that the suit properties were part of a public religious , trust and that the defendants were in possession as trustees for and on behalf of the general worshippers of the temple. The Court gave directions setting down the duties and obligations of the pujaries who, as trustees and managers of the temple, were allowed two-thirds of the income of the trust properties for purposes of their maintenance and temple expenses. Subsequently, in Second Appeal No. 565 of 1942, by a judgment-creditor of the then pujari-trustees, the Bombay High Court had occasion to observe that the original scheme framed by the District Court lent strong support to the view that the remuneration payable to the trustees or managers was for the services rendered by them and was their personal property. The present scheme of the trust was framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad in 1960. Under clauses 12, 13 and 14 of this scheme, after meeting outgoings on account of rates, taxes, assessment and expenses incidental to the administration of the trust and worship of the deity of the temple and also current repair and upkeep charges, the trustees were under obligation to distribute the surplus income by setting apart 50 per cent thereof for reserve fund and dividing the remaining 50 per cent equally between the two hereditary trustees, which was to be treated as their absolute property. The amount standing to the credit of the reserve fund was to be invested according to the provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, but out of the annual contribution to the fund, 20 per cent was to be utilised for religious, educational and/or medical purposes with the sanction of the District Court. In the assessment for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64, the previous years being Samvat Years 2017 and 2018, respectively, the trust claimed that the entire income from its property should be exempt from tax under section 11(1)(a). The ITO disallowed the claim holding that the properties of the trust were not held wholly for religious and charitable purposes, since the payment of 50 per cent of the surplus income to the two hereditary trustees was not for charitable purposes, inasmuch as it was not by way of remuneration or salary for the services rendered by them as employees and what they received was out of the income of the trust. According to the ITO, the only income which was entitled to be exempt under section 11(1)(b) would be the amount actually spent for religious purposes and 20 per cent of the amount of contribution set apart as reserve fund. On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's view that the case would fall under section 11(1)(b) as the income was only partly applied for religious purposes. He also rejected the alternative claim of the trust that the said payments must be treated as allowable expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal also rejected the claim and confirmed the view of the ITO and the AAC, holding that the true effect of the payments to the hereditary pujaris was the application of the income and it had no direct or indirect relation to the services, if any, rendered by them.

The 'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation.

It is true that a public charity is perpetual in character, and that means that it is capable of enforcement, so long as there is any property left which can be appropriated for its objects. And even if some or all of the objects become incapable of fulfilment, the trust properties will be devoted to the performance of similar or allied charitable purposes on the doctrine of cy-pres. But so far as the trust properties themselves are concerned, they will be held only on the incidents to which they are subject under the law. Thus, if the property is a leasehold interest, it must cease on the termination of the lease. Likewise, if trust property is alienated under circumstances binding on the trust, it will go out of the trust. But that does not operate as an extinction of the trust, unless there is no property at all left, with which the trust could be carried out. That is the principle enacted in section 77(c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which in terms, however, applies only to private trusts. Therefore, the fact that the trustees have the option at any time to throw up the managing agency is no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust.

In the result, it could be held that the word 'property' in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend 'business', and if the question fell to be decided solely on the terms of that sub-section, the managing agency must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

With aforesaid observation, the case was remanded to High Court for a fresh disposal on merits.

[Matter remanded to High Court]

■

The issue under consideration has been decided by the Tribunal in favour of the assessee in earlier year’s orders and also by the recent order passed by the ITAT Ahmedabad in the assessee’s own case for assessment year 2016-17 in ITA No. 416/Ahd/2020 vide order dated 20-07-2022 wherein the Tribunal held that the agreement was not entered into to derive profit from transfer of movable to SCPL but to counter the huge losses incurred in running two big hospitals. Therefore, the Commissioner(Appeals) has correctly held that the activity of the trust was carried on in accordance with its objects and in the best interest of charity, therefore, the exemption under section 11(1)(a) has rightly been allowed by the Commissioner(Appeals). Similarly, the Commissioner(Appeals) has clearly held that section 13((1)(c)(ii) could apply only if any part of the charitable income of the trust has been used or applied for the benefits of the said persons during the previous year. But, since no portion of the income of the assessee has been applied for said person, therefore, the case of the assessee fell outside the scope of this section. Further, the trust is in receipt of income by way of management charges from SCPL and also all of its liabilities have been taken over by the same therefore there is a fact that there is no undue benefits of the use of trust property have been taken by any other persons. Similarly, there is no diversion of income of the trust as per Explanation of section13(2)(d) and 13(2)(g) as the trust has been benefitted greatly and its deficit of trust duly reduced to a great extent. Thus, the Commissioner(Appeals) has analyzed the facts correctly and given a judicious finding which does not call for any interference from outside. [Para 6]

■

Accordingly, in view of the above, there is no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner(Appeals) so as to call for any interference.[Para 7]

■

In the result, the appeal of the Department is dismissed.[Para 8]

The Tribunal had entertained certain misconceptions as to the true nature and character of the building in question. Neither under the partition deed nor under the settlement deed the building had been taken as a partible property. It was only the devolution of the lands which had been set apart for the maintenance of the said building that had been provided for both under the partition deed and the latter settlement deed. Both the documents clearly dealt with the right to manage the building. The stone slab and the notice board in front of the building showed when it was founded and for what purpose the building was to be used.

It is well established that no express words of gift either directly or indirectly in the shape of a trust are required to create a dedication. All that is necessary is that the religious purpose or object of the donor shall be clearly specified and that the property intended for the endowment should be set apart and dedicated of those purpose.

It is also well established that the existence of a trust can be established even by the conduct of parties. Though normally a Hindu while dedicating property to a deity or any other religious or charitable object ordinarily goes through the ceremonies of sankalpa and samarpan, it could not be said that those ceremonies are essential to creation of a an endowment. The performance of these ceremonies is only relevant to show the intention of the grantor, and if there is clear and unequivocal manifestation of intention to create a trust and there is formal divestiture of the ownership in the property on part of the donor with the intention to devote it to religious and charitable purpose the dedication must be deemed to be complete. The deduction of property is not a sacrament but a secular act; but the mere renunciation of ownership by the donor with a particular object is sufficient to create an endowment. The Tribunal had not kept in mind these general and accepted principles while considering the question as to whether the building was trust property or not. There was a subsequent litigation between the daughter-in-law of the deceased, R, the adopted son of the deceased, and ‘D’ the adopted son of daughter-in-law, wherein daughter-in-law questioned, inter alia, the validity of the partition deed dated 1-3-1950, and in the course of the entire litigation the parties proceeded on the basis that the building was a trust property and the dispute between them was as to the right of management of the trust.

The conduct of the parties right from 1942, when the building was constructed, clearly showed that the building was constructed, clearly showed that the building had been specifically set apart and used for religious and charitable objects. Therefore, the view taken by the Tribunal that the building was not a trust property and as such its value had to be added on to the estate of the deceased could not be accepted.

On the question as to whether the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm could pass on his death, the observation of the Tribunal that a managing agency business could not have any goodwill could not be accepted. The Supreme Court in J. K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that the managing agency business had got goodwill.

The Tribunal was, therefore, in error in holding that the managing agency had no goodwill at all. The Tribunal had also taken the view that as no share in the goodwill of the business was actually paid to the accountable persons towards the deceased’s share in the goodwill, it was no possible to say that any share in the goodwill passed on the death of the deceased and that section 53 could not be invoked in the instant. That view of the Tribunal could not be accepted. The question was not whether the accountable persons had the benefit of the deceased’s 3/16th share in the goodwill but the question was whether that share legally passed to or vested in the accountable persons on the death of the deceased.

The Supreme Court in Khushal Kumar Shan v. Khorshed Banu [AIR 1970 SC 1147, 1149 held that an agreement between the partners that the name, the place of business and the reputation of the firm are to be utilized by the surviving partners will not necessarily warrant an inference that it was intended that the heirs of the deceased partner will not be entitled to a share in the goodwill.

A cursory perusal of the terms of the deed would show that the managing trustee was the heart and soul of the trust. The terms of the trust deed expressly provided for the trust funds being employed in any trade, industry or business, which meant that the trust could carry on the business just like an individual or a firm or a limited company. It was not the contention of the department that the trust was a mere fiction or that it was illusory. Thus, a valid trust had been constituted and the trust carried on the business during the relevant accounting years.

It is not an invariable canon of construction that the proviso in a statute should be read as a qualification or limitation upon the effect of the main enactment. The function of the proviso is very often to deal with an excepted class of cases, which may be within the principal enactment but for it. It would not however be correct to say that a proviso should always be assumed to be and read as an exception. A substantive provision may also appear in the form of a proviso and if the clear meaning of the proviso establishes that it is not a qualifying clause of the main provision it is bound to be given effect without straining to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision.

The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

’ is a saleable commodity. In the instant case, the material found during the course of survey operation clearly established the collection of money over and above the fee prescribed by the Government for admission of a student. Therefore, it was a clear case of sale of education by the assessee-society. Thus, the assessee could not be considered as a charitable institution under section 2(15 ). Therefore, the assessee was not eligible for exemption under section 11. [Para 9] Any income derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose, should not be included in the total income. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee was not holding any property under trust for charitable purpose. It was also not the case of the assessee that any income was derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose. Moreover, it was also not the case of the assessee that any income in the form of voluntary contributions was received with a specific direction to form part of the corpus of the society. The assessee-society was running educational institution and deriving income from such institution. The assessee had also collected money over and above the fees prescribed for admitting students under management quota. In other words, the educational institution was used as a tool/apparatus for collecting money over and above the fees prescribed. The assessee-society had no other source of income/receipt. The society owned the educational institution. The Legislature has visualized two situations. One is religious and another is charitable. Section 11 provides for exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust for charitable and religious purpose. ‘Education’ falls within the definition of charitable purpose. Therefore, any income derived from property held under trust for charitable purpose and applied for education, is eligible for exemption under section 11. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee had not derived any income from any property held under trust. The only source of receipt was the education itself, i.e., from educational institution. [Para 11]

The next question that fell for consideration was whether the educational institution owned by the assessee-society would be regarded as a property held under trust by the society. Section 11 speaks of the property held under trust. The Legislature visualized two situations. One is income derived from the property held under trust and another is application of that income derived from the property held under trust for a charitable purpose. Therefore, there is a clear distinction between the property held under trust and the charitable activity. In the instant case, the assessee-society was carrying on charitable activity by establishing educational institution. Therefore, the charitable activity of the assessee was education. The income, if any, derived from the property held under the Trust and applied for the educational activity, would be construed as application of income for the purpose of charitable purpose. Therefore, the expenditure incurred in establishing the educational institution, namely, acquisition of land, construction of building, etc., are all application of income for charitable activity. If any income was generated in the course of educational activity, the said income would be construed as if it was generated in the course of carrying on the charitable activity. Therefore, such receipt/income received in the course of carrying on charitable activity was also eligible for exemption, provided the same was applied or set apart for educational purposes. However, such receipt/income cannot be construed as derived from property/business held under trust. Since such receipt/income is inevitable or consequential while carrying on the activity of education, such income also becomes eligible for exemption. The educational institution is an apparatus for carrying out the charitable activity. Therefore, the educational institution or charitable activity itself cannot be construed as the property held under trust. The establishment of an educational institution is an activity of charity. Therefore, by any stretch of imagination, the charitable activity, cannot be held as the property held under trust, even though the income/receipt incidental to such activity is eligible for exemption. However, the money collected over and above the prescribed fee for admitting students cannot be construed as income derived from/incidental to the activity of carrying on charitable activity. [Para 12]

It is a well-settled principle of law that a business held under a trust is also a property. Section 11(4) also makes it very clear that the property held under the trust includes a business undertaking. If the assessee-society runs a business incidental to the attainment of the object of the society and separate books of account are maintained by the assessee, the income derived from such business, shall be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust. The Apex Court in Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/ 115 Taxman 126 considered the provisions of section 11(4A) and held that if the business income is derived from business held under the trust and the same is utilized by the institution for achieving object of the institution, then it could be said that such income is applied for charitable purpose. The assessee-society in question had no property or business whatsoever under trust. Moreover, it was not the claim of the assessee that any income was derived from the property or business held under trust. [Para 13]

The issue is whether, on the facts and circumstances of the case and having regard to the terms of the trust deed, it can be said that the activities carried on by the assessee in the form of running of community hall, was itself held under the trust. [Para 6]

It is to be noted that section 11(1) grants exemption to the income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India. There is no exhaustive definition of the words "property held under trust" in the Act; however, sub-section (4) says that for the purposes of section 11, the words "property held under trust" includes "a business undertaking so held". [Para 7]

If a property is held under trust, and such property is a business, the case would fall under section 11(4) and not under section 11(4A). Section 11(4A) would apply only to a case where the business is not held under trust. Thus, there is difference between property or business held under trust and business carried on by or on behalf of the trust. [Para 8]

This distinction was recognized by the Supreme Court in the case of Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1978] 121 ITR 1/[1979] 2 Taxman 501 wherein it was observed that if a business undertaking is held under trust for a charitable purpose, the income therefrom would be entitled to the exemption under section 11(1) of the Act. In the present case, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is that running of community Hall was incidental to the object of the trust, it was not business commenced/carried on by the assessee. Though the business was commenced by the trust and it was carried on by the trust after its formation, it cannot be said to constitute property held under trust.

Under section 11(4), it is only the business which is held under the trust that would enjoy exemption in respect of its income Under section 11(1) and there is a distinction between the objects of a trust and the powers given to the trustees to effectuate the purpose of the trust. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption Under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the trust deed of the assessee.

The running of " Community Hall" was not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of "Community Hall" was not even in the contemplation of the trust deed on the basis of which the society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, was carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust.

Section 11(1) of the Act confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose. Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1) of the Act, was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust.

In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the charitable trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

In the Circular No. 1132 issued by the CBDT, it has been clarified that the payment of a sum by one charitable trust to other for utilisation of the donee-trust towards its charitable objects is proper application of income for charitable purpose in the hands of donor-trust and donor-trust will not lose exemption under section 11 merely because the donee trustee did not spend the donation during the year of receipt itself. In the instant case, the buildings of the assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature and that being so, such use could very well be treated as use by the assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for the purpose of exemption under section 11. Moreover, exemption under section 11 was allowed to the assessee-society for the assessment years 1992-93 and 1993-94 by the department in the similar facts and circumstances. As such, the Commissioner (Appeals) was fully justified in treating the use of assessee’s property by other societies for charitable purposes as charitable activity carried on by the assessee and accordingly in allowing exemption under section 11 as claimed. The impugned order was, therefore, upheld. [Para 7]

Agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by the assessee’s society as separate business activities and the same, therefore, constituted ‘property held under trust’ of the assessee-society as provided in sub-section (4) of section 11 and income of the said activities, in any case, was to be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act, i.e., after deducting the expenditure incurred in connection with the said business. The assessee-society had derived income from the said activities and the amount being more than sufficient to cover the expenses incurred in connection with the said activities, the allowance of the same by the Commissioner (Appeals) as application of its income as claimed by the assessee hardly made any difference in the ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to the revenue. [Para 8]

Hence, the revenue’s appeal was to be dismissed.

By virtue of section 11(4) "property held under trust" includes a business undertaking so held. Therefore, it could not be accepted that the income derived by the assessee was not income from property as envisaged under section 11(1)(a). That apart, a perusal of the aims and objects of the assessee-society led to the conclusion that the income derived by it was income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a). Accordingly, the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the amount received by the assessee on account of allocation charges was not income from property held under trust.

Under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act, income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes to the extent to which such income is applied to such trust are liable to be exempted. In the instant case, the finding given by the AAC was that the assessee was the manager of the Gurudwara and that all monies received at the Gurudwara were used to be spent towards religious, educational and charitable purposes. The income received from the shops by way of rent was also used to be utilised for the said purpose. In this view of the matter, the inference was irresistible that the entire property was Gurudwara property and the same was being held by the assessee as a manager or shebait under a legal obligation wholly for religious and charitable purposes. As the entire income had to be applied for religious and charitable purposes the same was liable to be exempted under sections. 4(3)(i) and 4(3)(ii) of the 1922, Act.

A charitable trust may be created by words sufficient to show the intention. So long as there was a clear manifestation of intention to create a charitable or religious trust and there was a formal vesting of the ownership of the property the dedication was complete.

Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in holding that the income from Gurudwara and attached shops was entitled to exemption.
