The charging section 3 provides that there shall be charged for every assessment year the wealth-tax in respect of the net wealth on the corresponding valuation date of every individual, HUF and company at the rate or rates specified in Schedule I. The wealth-tax is, therefore, to be levied only on three categories of assessees, individuals, HUFs and companies. Section 21A provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 5(i), where any property is held under trust for any public purpose of a charitable or religious nature in India and any one of the three conditions stipulated in the said section are satisfied, wealth-tax shall be leviable upon, and recoverable from, the trustee in the like manner and to the same extent as if the property is held by an individual who is a citizen of India and resident in India for the purposes of the Act. It is, thus, clear that the trustees of a public charitable trust are liable to pay wealth-tax in the same manner and to the same extent as if the property is held by an individual. [Para 6]

When clause (xxiii) of section 5(1) is read in the aforesaid background, it is clear that only companies are not covered by the exemption and the other two categories of assessees are entitled to claim the exemption. When the trustees are subjected to the levy of wealth-tax as if the trust property is held by trustees as individuals, the revenue cannot deny exemption to the trust or the trustees on the ground that they are not individuals. [Para 7]

A Division Bench of the Rajasthan High Court in CWT v. Bhangur Charitable Trust [1987] 164 ITR 249/ 32 Taxman 160 has elaborately discussed the aforesaid aspect and has held that the exemption laid down under section 5(1)(xxiii) is available to a trust in respect of shares held by the trustees. [Para 8]

Accordingly, Tribunal was right in holding that assessee was entitled to exemption under section 5(1)(xxiii).

Section 11(1) grants exemption to the income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India. There is no exhaustive definition of the words "property held under trust" in the Act; however, section 11(4) says that for the purposes of section 11, the words "property held under trust" "includes a business undertaking so held". Sub-section (4A) provides that exemption shall not be available to any business income of a trust unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objectives of the trust and separate books of account are maintained by such trust in respect of such business. [Para 7]

Thus, if a property is held under trust, and such property is a business, the case would fall under section 11(4) and not under section 11(4A). Section 11(4A) would apply only to a case where the business is not held under trust. Thus, there is difference between property or business held under trust and business carried on by or on behalf of the trust. [Para 8]

In the present case, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is that running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not held under trust, but it was business commenced/carried on by the Society, subsequent to the formation of trust. Though the business was commenced by the Society and it was carried on by the Society after its formation, it cannot be said to constitute property held under trust under section 11(4), it is only the business which is held under the trust that would enjoy exemption in respect of its income under section 11(1) and there is a distinction between the objects of a trust and the powers given to the trustees to effectuate the purpose of the trust. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the Memorandum of Association of the assessee. The running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were not even in the contemplation of the Memorandum of Association on the basis of which the Society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall were carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust. Section 11(1) confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose.

Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1), was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust. In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

There is no connection between the activities relating to running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall and the attainment of the objects of the trust. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from running of community hall, kalyananmandapam and funeral ceremony hall are used for charitable purposes would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The application of income generated by the business is not relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. [Para 10]

TRUST-EXEMPTION OF INCOME FROM PROPERTY HELD UNDER TRUST-
WHETHER HANDING OVER OF ACCUMULATED INCOME TO ANOTHER CHARIT-
ABLE TRUST WOULD AMOUNT TO APPLICATION OF INCOME FOR CHARITABLE PURPOSES-HELD, YES

■

If scheme of Section 11 is being perused, then it would reveal that income derived from the property held under the Trust wholly for charitable or religious purpose, if applied to the extent of 85 per cent on its objectives, then such income will not fall in the total income assessable of an assessee. In other words, if Rs.100 is being derived from the property held under the Trust and Rs.85 is being applied towards the charitable objective of the Trust, then nothing will be taxable upon such a ‘Charitable Society’ or Trust. However, section 13 has contemplated certain exceptions. [Para 12]

■

A perusal of section 13 would indicate that if the assessee society has availed the services or purchased any object from any specified person contemplated in sub-clause (3) and paid to such specified person in excess of what may be paid reasonably for such service in open market, then excess would be disallowed. In other words, for example, if assessee society has availed the services of an Engineer who happened to be a specified person under sub-clause (3) and paid him the service charges which he could not command in the open market, then such excess amount will be disallowed to the assessee and benefit of Section 11 would not be available on such an amount. It will be taxable. For example, assessee can purchase an item for Rs.100 but from a specified person, it has purchased at Rs.120, then this excess Rs.20 will be added to the taxable income of the assessee and benefit of section 11 will not be available to the assessee Society. A perusal of the complete assessment order reveals that Assessing Officer has nowhere made analysis of the remuneration/ honorarium paid to the members of the Management Committee vis-à-vis their services utilized for the benefit of the Society. All the persons are qualified persons, they have devoted their time for managing the affairs of the Society and it has paid only honorarium, not regular salary. Similarly, it has provided traveling facility to them which was only for fulfilling the objects of the Society. In other words, in assessment year 2015-16, a little higher amount is being incurred by the assessee because the member of the Management Committee has to travel outside India for inspection of a plane which was to be used in Aviation Wing of the Engineering College. The Assessing Officer has not examined this aspect as to how this type of facilities can be availed from the open market and the price of such services. He has simply narrated that these persons are gainfully implied in their other activities also and therefore, payment of honorarium to these persons is not in accordance with law. This cannot be a logic for denying the benefit to them. The intention of the section is not as such. It is the assessee who has to manage its affairs and to decide what is necessary for its functioning. The Assessing Officer can only examine whether excess is being paid or not, but he has not carried out any Investigation in that area. The Assessing Officer has not assigned any reason as to why he is departing from the principle of consistency where such honorarium has been allowed to these per sons. Similarly Traveling Expenses has been allowed to the assessee in earlier years. The Commissioner (Appeals) failed to record any finding qua this aspect in right perspective and blindly up held the assessment order. Therefore, all these grounds of appeal are allowed.[Para 12.1]

It was not the case of the revenue that the income of the trust had been applied for any purpose which could not be regarded as charitable purpose. According to the trust deed, the discretion given to the trustee was not to choose any purpose, but only purposes which were charitable for which the trust properties and income therefrom could be utilised. The word 'properties' in the trust deed, having regard to the context, must be understood as including the income derived from the properties, as the deed specifically provided that the trust property shall be applied for charitable purposes. The reference to the application would indicate that the author of the trust intended that all that belonged to the trust was to be utilised for the purpose of charity. The mandate was, therefore, clear that the properties of the trust which, having regard to the context, should include the income from the properties, should be applied solely for charitable purposes.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the trust was a valid charitable trust and in directing the WTO to redo the assessment in the light of the provisions of section 21(1) , read with section 21A.

13 carves out an exception to the general exemption granted under sections 11 and 12 to income derived by trusts/charitable institutions. The onus lies on the revenue to bring on record, cogent material/evidence to establish that the trust/charitable institution is hit by provisions of section 13. As noted above, the Assessing Officer made out the case on presumption since there is a difference between the cost of construction shown in the books of account and estimated by the DVO. The Assessing Officer had neither brought on record any evidence nor able to point out modus operandi how was the managing trustee directly or indirectly benefited out of the construction cost of building of the society. There is no need to mention that the registered society running educational programmes are managed by Trustees. The day-to-day activities of the society are supposed to be administrated and controlled by the managing committee by holding various meetings and passing resolution etc. The building in which impugned investment stated to be made has been stated to be shown by the society in its books of account. Therefore, if any benefit is going that would be going to the society only and in these circumstances there is no violation of section 13. [Para 16]

In the light of above discussion, it is opined that the Assessing Officer has wrongly invoked section 13 and has wrongly withdrawn benefit of section 11 read with section 12. Consequently, the appeal filed by the assessee is allowed. [Para 21]

]

■

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

■ The record further reveals that the revenue has not brought any material to establish that the rental income earned by the trust was diverted for any non-charitable purpose or that the dominant character of the trust had ceased to be charitable. On the contrary, the Income and Expenditure Account demonstrates that the receipts of the trust, whether derived from grants, donations, interest or rental income, were applied only towards the charitable objects of the trust. Thus, the source from which the income was generated has not altered the fundamental charitable character of the institution. [Para 8.5]

■

It is a settled proposition of law that the decisive test is the dominant object of the institution and not the source of its income. Income derived from property held under trust, including rental income, does not lose the benefit of exemption under Section 11 and Section 12 merely because such income arises from leasing of trust property, so long as it is applied towards the charitable purposes for which the trust has been established. The leasing of trust property, in the facts of the present case, is only an incidental mode of augmenting resources to fulfil the charitable objects and cannot be construed as an independent commercial object of the trust. [Para 8.6]

■

Accordingly, while the Tribunal disagrees with the reasoning assigned by the Commissioner (Appeals) in holding that earning rental income was itself one of the objects of the trust, the Tribunal nevertheless upholds the ultimate conclusion that the assessee cannot be denied exemption on this ground. The reasoning adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) is incorrect; however, the conclusion reached by him is sustainable on the basis that the rental income was merely incidental to the charitable activities and was admittedly applied towards the charitable objects of the trust. Consequently, the ground raised by the Revenue on this issue is devoid of merit and is dismissed. [Para 8.7]

■

Accordingly, the Tribunal concurs with the findings recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue. The ground raised by the Revenue challenging the allowability of exemption merely because the assessee earned rental income is devoid of merit and is, therefore, dismissed. [Para 8.8]

The High Court held that the trust was not entitled to exemption under section 11 of the Income-tax Act because it did not satisfy the definition of 'charitable purpose' under section 2(15). The Court's observation about the necessity for scrutinising the objects of the trust is also not relevant, since such a criterion is absent for the purpose of the Wealth-tax Act. The High Court had given a clear finding that religious purpose was clear in this case, and this by itself would suffice for granting exemption, since under the Wealth-tax Act, property held in trust for a public purpose of a charitable or religious nature, is exempt. FACT: ■

The assessee, a charitable trust claimed exemption under sections 11 and 12.

■

The Assessing Officer denied exemption by treating the assessee as an Association of Persons (AOP) on ground that assessee had earned substantial rental income by leasing its immovable properties which amounted to a commercial activity inconsistent with its charitable character.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim on ground that the Assessing Officer had not brought cogent material to show that the assessee’s activities ceased to be charitable.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: (i) Rental income and leasing of properties

■

The principal basis adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) for allowing the assessee's claim is the observation that one of the objects of the trust was to lease out properties and earn rental income. However, on a careful examination of the original trust deed as well as the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the Tribunal finds that the observation is factually incorrect and contrary to the material available on record. The original trust deed, enumerates the charitable objects of the trust, namely: (i) genetic research and agricultural education; (ii) conservation of land, water and genetic resources; (iii) sustainable agriculture and environmental protection; (iv) family planning and population control; and (v) improvement of the status and literacy of women. Subsequently, by way of the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the additional charitable objects of Relief to the Poor and Education were incorporated. Significantly, neither the original trust deed nor the addendum includes, as an object of the trust, carrying on the activity of leasing or renting of immovable properties for earning rental income. [Para 8.2]

■

What is, however, contained in the trust deed is a separate enabling provision conferring powers upon the Board of Trustees. Clause VIII merely authorises the trustees to acquire, hold, manage or otherwise deal with land, buildings and other immovable properties with the funds of the trust for effectuating the charitable objects of the trust. Such an enabling clause cannot be elevated to the status of an independent charitable object. The power to acquire and manage trust properties is only incidental to the effective administration of the trust and to facilitate the attainment of its charitable purposes. Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that leasing of properties itself constituted one of the objects of the trust is clearly erroneous and is not borne out from the trust deed. [Para 8.3]

■

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

■

The respondent-trust was established for managing and running the activities popularly known as ‘Dharam Kanta’, a service of weighing precious metals provided for the benefit of public in general. It was clear from the trust deed that the beneficiaries of the trust were the general public. The trust deed also provided for a mechanism to run the activities of the trust and also made a provision for carrying on the business activities of the trust. A specific provision was to be found in the trust deed to the effect that the Committee of Management appointed by the board of directors consisting of the trustees was to carry on the business through the employees engaged for the purpose. The assessee-trust claimed exemption under section 11(4A). The assessee’s claim was disallowed.

The Tribunal, while allowing the appeals, held that the business activities of the trust having being conducted by the charitable trust for charitable object, without any object of earning profits and gains out of the charges collected by it from the weighment facility provided to the public, the assessee-trust was entitled to claim exemption under section 11(4A).

On appeal, the revenue, relying on the text of clause (b) of sub-section (4A), contended that though the business was being carried out by the charitable institution for charitable purpose, but the same was not being carried out by the beneficiaries of the institution and as such the trust was not entitled to claim the exemption under section 11(4A).

HEADNOTE: Section 11(1)(a), read with sections 11(4) and 28(iii), of the Income-tax act, 1961-charitable or religious trust-exemption of income from property held under trust-objects of assessee, a registered society, included promotion and development of hosiery industry and it used to procure, allocate and distribute to its members woollen hosiery yarn on no-profit-no-loss basis-assessee used to charge subscription, and allocation charges from its members-before tribunal, assessee claimed allocation charges received by it to be exempt from tax-whether tribunal correct in holding that although assessee's activity fell within the definition of "charitable purposes", yet its income was covered by section 28(iii) and was not income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) and was hence not entitled to exemption-held, on facts, no

FACT: The assessee, a registered society, was established, inter alia, (a) to promote, organise and encourage scientific research in the hosiery manufacturers, inventions, investments and design, (b ) to find out way and means of progress, development and improvement of hosiery industry and to safeguard and to protect its investments, (c) to procure, encourage and formulate means for collective buying of industrial raw materials and machinery on a no-profit-no-loss basis, (d) to encourage and formulate ways and means for collective selling of hosiery products, (e) to make arrangements for setting up of woollen hosiery yarn spinning plant on co-operative basis in order to provide the industry its basic raw materials on fair prices, and (f) to procure, allocate, distribute to hosiery manufacturers woollen hosiery yarn, their basic raw material, on a no-profit-no-loss basis. To meet its office and administrative expenses, the assessee charged annual subscription, special subscription and allocation charges (i.e., charges for allocation of raw yarn) from its members. For the assessment years 1969-70 and 1970-71, the ITO treated the allocation charges as the assessee's income under section 28(iii) and taxed the same. He also repelled the assessee's contention that it was entitled to exemption under section 11 (1)(a). On appeal, the AAC sustained the ITO's order. On second appeal, the Tribunal sustained the AAC's order, holding that although the activity of the assessee was covered by the definition "charitable purposes" as contemplated in section 2(75), yet the assessee's income which was covered by section 28(iii), was not income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a), so that it was not entitled to exemption from tax.

On reference:

HELD: By virtue of section 11(4) "property held under trust" includes a business undertaking so held. Therefore, it could not be accepted that the income derived by the assessee was not income from property as envisaged under section 11(1)(a). That apart, a perusal of the aims and objects of the assessee-society led to the conclusion that the income derived by it was income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a). Accordingly, the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the amount received by the assessee on account of allocation charges was not income from property held under trust.

Section 11(1) provides that in order to support a claim for exemption of income under this section, the principal object for consideration would be whether the property from which the income is derived should be the trust or other legal obligation. Secondly, the property should be so held for charitable or religious purposes which enures to the benefit of the public. Thirdly, the exemption is confined only to such portion of the trust income as is in fact applied to charitable and religious purposes.

The expression "legal obligation" cannot be separated from the "property" itself which in the instant case was a horse-racing concern, inasmuch as law enjoins that such property must be held under a trust or other legal obligation and not the fund derived therefrom.

In the instant case, the association of persons were not the subject-matter of a trust and only a trust had been created in respect of the surplus fund. The surplus fund really emanated from a property which was not a subject-matter of the trust and as such in the absence of any legal obligation fastened thereto, no exemption could be allowed under section 11.

In this connection it has been held by the Privy Council in Mohammed Ibrahim Raza v. CIT AIR 1930 PC 226 that if there are several objects of a trusts of which some are charitable and some are non-charitable, and the trustees in their discretion are to apply income to any of the objects, the whole trust fails and no part of the income is exempted from tax.

In the instant case, clause 3(a ) of the said deed envisaged that the surplus fund may be applied for making improvements to the racing facilities available at Jorhat by way of increased stake money, by increasing the facilities available to the members of the public or in such other manner connected with the races as the trustees shall consider desirable. Such object did not come within the exemption clause 10(23). Therefore, the trustees had the indefeasible alternative right to apply the funds to such purposes, without making any donation to charitable purposes. In such circumstances, the matter was hit by the above decision of the Privy Council.

In the result, the Tribunal was not right in holding that the assessee was a charitable institution within the meaning of section 11(1).

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

The property in question was purchased by the partners of the assessee-firm in their names as trustees of the trust known as 'Ganapatrai Sagarmull Charitable Trust'. The Court in the case of Ganpatrai Sagarmal ( Trustee) for Charity Fund v. CIT [1963] 47 ITR 625 (Cal.), examined the trust deed and came to the conclusion that the properties described as trust properties had remained as properties of the settlors and, therefore, the entire income was chargeable to tax in the hands of the settlors. However, for the assessment years 1973-74 and 1974-75 the Tribunal found that the property in question was transferred to and vested in the trustees of the charitable trust only. The infirmities that were pointed out by the Court earlier had been removed by the parties, who created a separate trust and registered it vesting the trust property in the trustees. The Tribunal also found that the municipal tax receipt showed that the property in question was registered in the name of the trust. The certificate of registration under section 12A issued by the Commissioner clearly showed that the revenue had examined the trust deed and satisfied itself before granting the aforesaid registration. The assessment order for the assessment year 1973-74 made on the trust, though said to be a protective measure, showed that the property in question belonged to the trust and that did not belong to the assessee. On facts, the Tribunal held that the property in question did not belong to the assessee, but belonged to the trust and that the income from the aforesaid property could not be included in the hands of the assessee.

On reference :

It was clear that the object of the trust was mainly charitable. It had been found by the Commissioner and the Tribunal that the properties owned by the assessee were held by it in trust. Section 5(1)(i) is applicable to 'any property held under trust or other legal obligation for any public purpose of a charitable or religious nature in India'. The assets held by the assessee were not assets forming part of any business. There was no finding that any part of the assets of the trust was used for any purpose outside India. The activities of the trust were running schools and managing the Mosque and Darga in Coimbatore. The activities of the assessee-trust were charitable, running of schools being the primary object. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of section 5(1)(i).

The assessee, a society engaged in charity was assessed in status of 'Association of Persons'.

The Assessing Officer found that the assessee was also carrying insurance business to earn profit and therefore, held that it could not get exemption under section 11.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) supported the ITO.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held insurance business was held on trust and income from said business was applied to charitable purpose. Therefore, the assessee's income would be exempted under section 11.

On appeal before High Court:

The provisions of section 4(3)(i ) confer an exemption of income from property only where the property itself is held under a trust or other legal obligation. It does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created in respect of any property, but only the income derived from any particular property or source is itself held in trust as where it is set apart or charged for a charitable purpose. That is clear upon the terms of the section itself and upon the authorities. In the instant case, all the income which the assessee derived or received was in the shape of grants and subscriptions from members which could not possibly have been received by it except from its business. Therefore, the entire income of the assessee must be held to be income derived from its business which was its property. If this contention was correct, then it was further submitted that there could be also no doubt upon the terms of its memorandum of association and its purposes and objects that the assessee was holding the business in trust for charitable purposes.

Supreme Court in J.K. Trust v. CIT [1957] 32 ITR 535 held that "Business" would undoubtedly be property in the connotation in which it is used in section 4(3)(i). In the light of this pronouncement of the Supreme Court it is clear that "business" itself can be property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) and upon that principle the business of the assessee in the instant case would be "property" held by the assessee.

Under the circumstances, the view taken by the Tribunal was the correct view and the income of the assessee would be exempt under the provisions of section 4(3)(i).

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity. The educational institution being run by the assessee was for the general benefit of the public and not for the benefit of any class or section of the public, as (a ) the institution was duly recognized by HNB Garhwal University and strictly followed all procedures with regard to admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum as laid down by the university, and (b) the nominees of State Government, HNB University and AICTE (functioning under the Human Resources Ministry) were on the governing body of the society and, therefore, the assessee had no choice in matters of admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum. The institute, was, in fact, State Government managed.

It was also found that the working system of the assessee was as per the guidelines laid down by the University. In respect of fixing and charging fees from students, the society management had no powers. Fee was being charged from students strictly as specified and laid down by the University. The governing body of the society had no powers to workout the cost and thereafter to add on the element of overheads and profits. Therefore, there was no question of building huge margins of profits in the fees structure as conceived by the Assessing Officer.

From a plain reading of the main objects given in the Memorandum, it could very well be discerned that the society had been formed with the sole objective of imparting and spreading computer education. Further, the assessee-society was virtually Government managed. Therefore, the question of functioning like a commercial profit making institution was totally unfounded. Thus, the fees charged by the assessee was simply receipt in the hands of the society and not profit.

Further, the assessee was rendering services of education to the general public. Therefore, its activities clearly fell within the ambit of charitable purpose as defined under section 2(15). Charging of fees does not in anyway dilute the aspect of charitable purpose. It is the end use and spirit and objective which matters.

In the assessment order, the Assessing Officer had not been able to appreciate the difference in the words 'charitable purposes' as are used in the Act and the word 'charity' as had been used by the Assessing Officer in his order. The word 'charity' as used in English language and recognized in English law, implies as an act motivated by pity and may require benevolence to manifest it. However, exemption under section 11 has been prescribed with reference to 'charitable purposes' and not 'charity'. The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act.

Therefore, the property from which income was derived by the assessee was held under trust and such property was held for charitable purpose and the income derived from trust was property which was being applied for charitable purpose. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

Since it was seen that the trust was a charitable trust and the property held under that trust was for any public purpose of charity, grant of exemption under section 5(1)(i ) could not be denied.

From the provisions of section 5(1)(i ), it is clear that the wealth-tax shall not be payable in respect of asset held by the trust for charitable or religious purpose. Section 5(1)(i ) grants exemption in respect of property held by the assessee under the trust or other legal obligation for any public purposes of charitable or religious nature in India up to the assessment year 1992-93. However, exemption under section 5(1)(i) has a proviso which withdraws exemption from wealth-tax in respect of public, charitable or religious trusts/institutions with effect from 1-4-1986, viz., the assessment year 1986-87 by the Finance Act, 1985. On that aspect, the Commissioner (Appeals) had already directed the Assessing Officer to recompute the net wealth of the assessee-trust with reference to market value of the property forming part of the business of the assessee-trust and the assessee-trust clearly conceded and stated that it had not taken any appeal on that issue.

It is clear from a comparison of section 5(1)(i ) with section 13(1)(d) of the Income-tax Act, that the word ‘wholly’ is not to be found under section 5(1)(i ). This omission is deliberate, intentional and the Legislature advisedly avoided or omitted the said words from section 5(1)(i ). Thus, for the purpose of claiming exemption under section 5(1)(i), it is a sine qua non that the property must be held under the trust wholly for purpose of charitable or religious nature in India; it is sufficient if the trust could be said to be primarily or dominantly for a public purpose of charitable nature in India.

The assessee-trust was a charitable trust in view of the objects mentioned in the trust deed. There was no justification to hold that the assessee-trust was not entitled to exemption under section 5(1)(i) in respect of the assets held by the trust. Hence, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that it was a charitable trust and not a private trust was upheld. Further, still the income from the property held by the trust was not exempt under section 11(5) read with section 13(1)(d ) of the Income-tax Act, grant of exemption under section 5(1)(i ) fully applied to the assessee-trust, conditions for grant of exemption from wealth-tax under section 5(1)(i ) being wholly different and distinct from the grant of exemption under section 11(5), read with section 13(1)(d ) of the said Act. In view of that, the assessee-trust was entitled to exemption under section 5(1)(i ).

In the result, the department appeals were to be dismissed.

V.J. Vinayakumar for the Appellant. V.S. Jayakumar for the Respondent.

However, the Assessing Officer to grant said exemption.

On second appeal:

HELD: As pointed out by the Commissioner (Appeals), the fund provided by the assessee trust has been paid to the vendor through its trustees and their relatives, precisely, to outsmart the restrictions on transfer of agricultural lands to a non-agriculturist - the assessee trust.. Since the agricultural lands could be purchased only by an agriculturist as such restriction was prevailed at that relevant time, one of the trustees - R being an agriculturist - was made as a conduit to get over the restriction.

The Assessing Officer's allegation that the purchase of the said land was intended by the trustees for their own benefits/gain etc., doesn't hold water as no documentary evidence was brought on record to thwart the assessee's claim.

With regard to the payment made by the trustees to the vendor, it was explained that the funds provided by the trust has been paid through its trustees for the reasons recorded supra and that the banakhat clearly indicates that the transaction was made for and on behalf of the assessee trust only and not for the personal benefit of any of the trustees. As highlighted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in the impugned order, the payment made towards purchase of land was shown by the assessee in its books of account under the head 'advance towards land' and the Managing Trustee had not claimed anywhere in his books of account that the said payments towards purchase of land. To towering all, neither the managing trustee nor any of his relatives for that matter have claimed that the said purchase was made on behalf of them or for their own benefits. There was confirmation of accounts furnished by the seller. There were also no documentary evidences to attribute that the said transaction took place only to benefit the managing trustee or his relatives except that the funds of the trust were routed through the trustees to the vendor which merely exhibits the expediency which prevailed at that relevant time. Moreover, the utilization of the trust fund was not for purchase of agricultural land as investment, but was a stepping stone to set up an educational institution in that land. Therefore, there was no infirmity in the conclusion of the Commissioner (Appeals) on this point.

With regard to the observation of the Assessing Officer that the funds of the trust cannot be said to be properly utilized for objects of the trust as no sale-deed had been executed or any construction work was carried out, we find that both the contractors - whom the money was advanced towards the construction work to be carried on at the proposed site -in their letters dt. 20.11.2010 confirmed before the Assessing Officer that they were in receipt of advances for the proposed construction work. This goes to prove the genuineness and dedication of the assessee trust to set up an educational institution for which, it had executed a banakhat for purchase of land; and for accomplishing the construction of the building by advancing monies to the contractors cannot be castigated as improper utilization of trust funds. In these circumstances, there was no infirmity in the finding of Commissioner (Appeals) that 'the advance given by the appellant trust to both these contractors cannot be said to be improper utilization of trust funds.'

This H was donated a sum of Rs. 85,000 by the assessee during the year under consideration relevant to the assessment year 1980-81. On appeal, the AAC also confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

When the trustees are subjected to the levy of wealth-tax as if the trust property is held by the trustees as individuals, the revenue cannot deny exemption to the trust or the trustees on the ground that they are not individuals. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption Under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the trust deed of the assessee. The running of " Community Hall" was not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of "Community Hall" was not even in the contemplation of the trust deed on the basis of which the society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, was carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust.

Section 11(1) of the Act confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose. Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1) of the Act, was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust.

In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the charitable trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

It is thus necessary to consider the question whether the said activities carried on by the assessee were incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. One fails to see any connection between the activities relating to running of "Community Hall" with attainment of the objects of the trust. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from running of "Community Hall" is used for charitable purposes would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The application of income generated by the business is not relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. [Para 10]

It was contended by the assessee that the surplus funds generated from the running of "Community Hall" was spent towards charitable activities and therefore, the assessee is entitled for exemption under section 11(4) this contention cannot be accepted. Initially, the assessee carried on the business itself which is not at all property held under trust. This activity is a business activity and the provisions of section 11(4A) of the Act is applicable. [Para 11]

It was contended that if the profits of the business carried on by the trust are utilized by the trust for the purposes of achieving the objectives of the trust, then the business should be considered to be incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust as observed by the Supreme Court in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/115 Taxman 126. [Para 12]

Prima facie the said observation would appear to support the assessee's case in the sense that even if running of "Community Hall" is held not to constitute a business held under trust, but only as a business carried on by or on behalf of the trust, so long as the profits generated by it are applied for the charitable objects of the trust, the condition imposed under section 11(4A) of the Act should be held to be satisfied, entitling the trust to the tax exemption. [Para 13]

Under section 11(1)(a), in order to be entitled to exemption income must not only be derived from the property held under trust only for charitable or religious purposes but the income entitled to exemption must be to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes, i.e., charitable or religious purpose in India or where such income is accumulated for application to such purpose in India, i.e., religious or charitable purpose to the extent the income so accumulated is not in excess of 25 per cent of income from the property or Rs. 10,000, whichever is higher. Therefore, two separate independent conditions are required to be fulfilled, that is to say, the income must be derived from the property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, and, secondly, the application or accumulation of such income in the manner indicated in clause (a ) of sub-section (1) of section 11 of the Act. 'Charitable purpose' or 'purpose of charitable or religious nature' have not been defined in the Wealth-tax Act, 1957. Therefore, it must bear the same meaning as in the Income-tax Act but under the provisions of the Income-tax Act not only should the income be derived from a trust or legal obligation of public purpose of a charitable or religious nature but the income so derived must to a certain extent be so applied. The position under the Wealth-tax Act seems to be a little different. Wealth-tax Act assessed the owning or having or possessing of the property and section 5(1)(i) of the Act stipulated that the condition for exemption was that the property must be held by the assessee under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a religious or charitable nature in India. Therefore, the holding of a property by the assessee either under a trust or other legal obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature is the statutory requirement entitling the assessee to exemption under the Act. In the ground for reopening as noted before it was not disputed that the assessees upon whom the impugned notices had been issued were not holding the property under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a charitable or religious nature. What was being suggested was that holding the property as trustees or under obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature the assessees were committing breaches of trust in acting contrary to the trust and misusing the funds of the trust for their personal benefit. The application of the money held under a trust or under legal obligation is not a relevant consideration for exemption under section 5(1)(i) of the Act. Therefore, the revenue had no material to believe that the income of the assessee had escaped assessment. This position manifests a lacuna in the present provision of law. The position, therefore, is that if the trustees hold the property for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature and if they misapply or commit breach of trust, they will continue to enjoy exemption under the Wealth-tax Act. This position should receive consideration by the legislature in order to bring it at par with the provisions of the Income-tax Act. But until that is done, the petitioners were entitled to succeed on the point that there were no grounds for believing that the wealth of the assessee had escaped assessment or had been under-assessed.

In the aforesaid view of the matter, the notices are hereby quashed and the respondents were restrained from giving effect to the same.

Assessee has not disputed the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) that rentals received from its Kalyanamandapams had to be considered under the head income from business. In fact the High Court while remitting the question back to the Commissioner (Appeals) for assessment years 1997-98, 1998-99 etc., had indicated that income of the assessee from the Kalyanamandapams was more in the nature of business income. Obviously, assessee cannot now raise a plea against the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that income of the assessee from renting out Kalyanamandapams were business income, and it has wisely done so. However, it is peeved on the view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) that such business income could not be considered as income earned from a property held under the Trust, thereby disentitling the assessee from taking advantage of section 11(4). The Commissioner (Appeals) was of the opinion that Kalyanamandapams having being built by the assessee subsequent to its formation in the year 1959, could not be considered as property under trust. The assessee during the course of his arguments has stated that the land on which Kalyanamandapams were built was part of the original settlement and the building were built therein by the assessee from its income. Be that as it may, there is no dispute that the land and building was owned by the assessee society, whether it was part of original settlement or not. It is opined that, once income of a trust is used by it to acquire a property, the property so acquired will be property held under trust. Income from such property will be income from property under the trust. Thus, rental income received by the assessee from Kalyanamandapams though it was in the nature of income from business, such income was nothing but income from property held under trust.[Para 9]

Whether assessee could be denied exemption claimed by it under section 11(1) by virtue of sub-section (4A) thereof?

To answer the question, whether assessee can be denied the exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)(4A) it is to be seen whether renting out the Kalyanamandapams could be considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects of the assessee as they appear in its Memorandum of Association. By virtue of clause (d) of the objects clause, assessee can purchase, build and let out properties for its other purposes. The purpose mentioned in clause (a) clearly indicate promotion of any object which was wholly and solely charitable in nature. No doubt Commissioner (Appeals) had mentioned this to be a very wide expressions, disentitling it from claiming exemption under section 11. It is true that clause (a) is of a wide amplitude. However what needed to be remembered is that the assessee was having registration under section 12A since 11-4-1975, and such registration still continued. If the main object of the assessee was too wide, as mentioned by the Commissioner (Appeals), it would not have been given such registration. Having given such registration, which was alive since 1975, revenue cannot now turn back and say that the main object was very wide and assessee could not be given benefit of section 11(1). Activity of renting out Kalyanamandapams could be construed as only incidental to the attainment of its main object. Assessee therefore could take advantage of section 11(4). There is no dispute that assessee had maintained separate books for its Kalyanamandapams. The audited accounts filed along with its return clearly show separate income and expenditure for each of the activities, including Kalyanamandapams. Sub-section 4A would not apply to the assessee once its business is considered as incidental to the attainment of its main objects.[Para 10]

The business of ‘Taxation’ was handed over to the assessee-trust as a running business along with its liabilities, as property to be held under trust. Also, the assessee-trust was running the said business as a necessity in terms of provisions of the trust deed so as to ensure the survival of the trust and also the carrying on of the aims and objects of the trust. The trust deed had to be executed by the surviving trustees in view of the fact that the original trust deed was not available. In the instant case, the assessee had applied under section 11 for accumulation of income and, therefore, the tax authorities were not right in holding that the assessee had not applied its income towards the primary object of the trust, i.e., charity.

Various objects mentioned in the trust deed were of general public utility which constituted the fourth limb of the definition of ‘charitable purposes’ given in section 2(15). The provisions of section 13(1)(bb) only covers the first 3 limbs of the definition, i.e., relief of the poor, education and medical relief, and therefore, would not be attracted in the case of the assessee whose claim for exemption under section 11 was clearly allowable in view of the provisions of section 11 (1)(a) read with section 11(4) whereunder ‘property held under trust’ in the form of a business undertaking was also covered for the purposes of claiming benefit under section 11. Hence, the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 11 and the provisions of section 13(1)(bb) were not attracted in the case of the assessee, as the business held under trust was being carried on to achieve the primary purposes of the trust.

Mehta Charitable Prajnalay Trust [2012] 28 taxmann.com 73/[2013] 214 Taxman 88 (Delhi), SLP granted inMehta Charitable Prajnalaya Trust v. CIT [2017] 82 taxmann.com 149/248 Taxman 145 (SC)]. Exploitation rights - The right to exploit space on either side of an overbridge for advertisements is a "property" [A. J. Patel v. CIT [1974] 97 ITR 683 (Bom.)].

Religious offerings - Offerings received by a religious teacher from his disciples would not constitute "property held under trust" [Swami Narsingh Giri v. CIT [1971] 79 ITR 544 (All.)].

INCOME

Commercial sense - It is not the 'total income' as would be assessed by the ITO that is relevant for the purpose of investing the funds of the trust or assessing the income of the trust. Taking into account the purpose for which the conditions of section 11(1)(a) are imposed, it would be clear that 'income' to be considered will be that which is arrived at in the context of what is available in the hands of the assessee subject to an adjustment of any expenses extraneous to the trust [CIT v. P. S. G. & Sons Charities [1997] 223 ITR 831 (Mad.)].

Grants - Where assessee-society was acting as a nodal agency receiving grant from Government of India and State Governments and distributed to district authorities for implementation of various schemes of Government of India and supervising execution of schemes, grants received by assessee should not be considered either as income or for ascertaining amount expanded or amount to be accumulated [CIT v. State Urban Development Society [2011] 11 taxmann.com 458 (P&H)]. Also see, DIT v. Gujarat State Council for Blood Transfusion [2014] 41 taxmann.com 449/221 Taxman 126 (Guj.).

Legal expenses - Legal expenses incurred by a charitable institution for defending its president from criminal charges are allowable as a permissible deduction while computing its income [Ananda Marga Pracharaka Sangha v. CIT [1994] 76 Taxman 88 (Cal.)].

Refund of income-tax - Refund of income-tax can by no stretch of imagination be held as income derived from property held under the trust and, hence, will not be covered u/s 11(2) [CIT v. Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) [2002] 120 Taxman 186 (Delhi)].

Returned amounts - Only the income spent on charitable or religious purposes is excluded from the total income of the trust and when that amount is returned by the beneficiaries of the trust, the receipt in the hands of the trust can only be its income of the years in which it is received; it cannot have any different character [CIT v. Cutchi Memon Union [1985] 20 Taxman 386/155 ITR 51 (Kar.)].

Taxes - Payment of taxes under VDIS is to be deducted before arriving at commercial income of assessee-trust that is available for application to charitable purposes [DIT v. National Association of Software & Services Companies [2012] 21 taxmann.com 213/208 Taxman 178 (Delhi)].

APPLICATION OF INCOME

General - If section 11(1)(a) has been fully exploited and there is still accumulated income left to be dealt with, section 11(2) can be pressed in service and if it is complied with, such additional accumulated income beyond the prescribed percentage can also earn exemption u/s 11(2) [Addl. CIT v. A. L. N. Rao Charitable Trust [1995] 83 Taxman 252 (SC)].

'Applied' need not be equated with 'spent' - The word 'applied' does not necessarily mean 'spent'. Even if the amount has been earmarked for the purposes of the institution and allocated, it may be deemed to have been applied [CIT v. Radhaswami Satsang Sabha [1954] 25 ITR 472 (All.)].

Both revenue and capital expenditure are covered - As far as the objects of the trust are concerned, the application of the amount can be for revenue or capital purposes [CIT v. Kannika Parameswari Devasthanam & Charities [1982] 133 ITR 779 (Mad.)].

Deemed income - Deemed income (i.e., tax deducted at source) is not to be taken into account for determining the application of income [CIT v. Jayashree Charity Trust [1986] 159 ITR 280 (Cal.)].

Donation - Donation of sale proceeds of capital asset made by charitable trust to another trust was to be allowed as 'application of income' for charitable purpose [PCIT v. St. Joseph's Monastery [2022] 137 taxmann.com 133 (Kar.)].

HELD: Assessee has not disputed the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) that rentals received from its Kalyanamandapams had to be considered under the head income from business. In fact the High Court while remitting the question back to the Commissioner (Appeals) for assessment years 1997-98, 1998-99 etc., had indicated that income of the assessee from the Kalyanamandapams was more in the nature of business income. Obviously, assessee cannot now raise a plea against the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that income of the assessee from renting out Kalyanamandapams were business income, and it has wisely done so. However, it is peeved on the view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) that such business income could not be considered as income earned from a property held under the Trust, thereby disentitling the assessee from taking advantage of section 11(4). The Commissioner (Appeals) was of the opinion that Kalyanamandapams having being built by the assessee subsequent to its formation in the year 1959, could not be considered as property under trust. The assessee during the course of his arguments has stated that the land on which Kalyanamandapams were built was part of the original settlement and the building were built therein by the assessee from its income. Be that as it may, there is no dispute that the land and building was owned by the assessee society, whether it was part of original settlement or not. It is opined that, once income of a trust is used by it to acquire a property, the property so acquired will be property held under trust. Income from such property will be income from property under the trust. Thus, rental income received by the assessee from Kalyanamandapams though it was in the nature of income from business, such income was nothing but income from property held under trust.[Para 9]

Whether assessee could be denied exemption claimed by it under section 11(1) by virtue of sub-section (4A) thereof?

To answer the question, whether assessee can be denied the exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)(4A) it is to be seen whether renting out the Kalyanamandapams could be considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects of the assessee as they appear in its Memorandum of Association. By virtue of clause (d) of the objects clause, assessee can purchase, build and let out properties for its other purposes. The purpose mentioned in clause (a) clearly indicate promotion of any object which was wholly and solely charitable in nature. No doubt Commissioner (Appeals) had mentioned this to be a very wide expressions, disentitling it from claiming exemption under section 11. It is true that clause (a) is of a wide amplitude. However what needed to be remembered is that the assessee was having registration under section 12A since 11-4-1975, and such registration still continued. If the main object of the assessee was too wide, as mentioned by the Commissioner (Appeals), it would not have been given such registration. Having given such registration, which was alive since 1975, revenue cannot now turn back and say that the main object was very wide and assessee could not be given benefit of section 11(1). Activity of renting out Kalyanamandapams could be construed as only incidental to the attainment of its main object. Assessee therefore could take advantage of section 11(4). However, on appeal, the Tribunal restored the finding of the Assessing Officer and held that the assessee was not entitled to exemption in respect of the advance paid by it under section 11(1)(a).

On appeal to the High Court: HELD: The crux of the matter, is as to whether the 'investment' can also amount to 'application' or not. There is nothing in the provisions of section 11(1) to curtail or narrow down the meaning of the word 'application', which by definition is of wider import. The scheme of section 11 is to advance the cause of charity by allowing the religious or charitable trusts to employ their funds in such a manner, for the purpose of charity or for advancing the cause of charity. There is nothing contrary placed from the side of revenue to even indicate that purchase of immovable property in question even on lease basis was not going to serve the cause of charity as per the objects of the charitable trust in question in any manner. The investment in immovable property, if it serves the cause of charity immediately or even in near future, the rental income or otherwise cannot be said to be not serving the objects of the trust at all. On the contrary, investment in immovable property which is intended to be used for serving the cause and objects of the trust is more committed and firm 'application' of income of the trust. The burden, therefore, was on the revenue to establish that the 'investment' was for the purpose, other than, for subserving the objects stipulated in the trust deed. The revenue has utterly failed to bring on record any evidence to the contrary to the claim of exemption by assessee on the ground that the immovable property in question was being taken on lease to create a theatre or auditorium, which would be used for the purpose of the group of artists or their families or even serve the cause of general public in times of floods or to provide education to the children, etc. Unless there was evidence on record to show that the said investment of the immovable property was being used for the purpose altogether different from the objects of the trust deed, the denial of exemption on an assumed distinction between the 'application' and 'investment' was not only too far-fetched, but beyond the scheme of section 11 itself and the said view of the Tribunal, therefore, cannot be countenanced. [Para 15]

Therefore, the assessee in the instant case while making the advance in question for purchase of immovable property in question even on lease basis, cannot be said to have not applied its income during the year in question for the charitable purposes within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) and, therefore, the assessee was clearly entitled to exemption under the said provision in respect of the said investment in immovable property. [Para 16]

It cannot be said that such advance did not crystalise in any 'application of income' and was in suspended animation as already indicated above that nothing contrary was brought on record by revenue that this advance did not crystalise in any 'application of income' in favour of the assessee during the year or even subsequently. On the contrary, it was contended at the bar by the assessee that the leasehold rights were secured by the assessee with the said investment and building on the said leasehold land is under construction as of now. However, no findings could be given on facts in this regard, but per se also there is no hesitation in holding that the advance or investment in the said leasehold proprty by the assessee's charitable trust in the year in question could be held to be 'application of income' within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) and therefore, the assessee was entitled to the exemption. [Para 17]

If, however, the department wanted to impugn the trust on the ground that it was not a bona fide trust at all, it should have taken that point in a straightforward manner. The attack through the construction of the trust deed itself might fail.

HEADNOTE: Section 5(i)  of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957 - Exemptions - Property held by charitable and religious trust - Assessee trust was constituted with object to provide educational facilities in catering - One 'K' transferred movable and immovable properties of hotel 'V' to assessee-trust for providing catering education therein - Said transfer was treated as gift in hands of 'K' but on appeal levy of gift tax was set aside by Tribunal holding that there was no gift and it was only a permission granted for a college to manage same free of rent - However, in case of assessee, Assessing Officer treated assets of hotel 'V' as assessee's wealth and computed wealth tax liability payable by assessee - Whether when assessee was not liable to pay any income-tax on income derived by it from activity carried on by it and 'K' was held not liable to pay gift-tax for transfer of property in assessee's favour, levy of wealth tax on very same property on ground that activity conducted by assessee in respect of property did not constitute a charitable or religious purpose was unjustified - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]WT : Where movable and immovable properties of a hotel were transferred to assessee-trust for providing catering education therein and in hands of doner said transfer was not treated as gift on ground that it was only a permission granted for a college, said property could not be treated as assessee's wealth in its wealth tax assessment

FACT: The assessee-trust was constituted with object to sponsor and provide educational facilities for catering courses, etc. 'K' executed a deed in favour of the assessee transferring movable and immovable property of a hotel 'V'. The said transfer was treated as a gift in the hands of 'K' and brought to tax under the provisions of the Gift tax Act, but on appeal, levy of gift tax was set aside by the Tribunal holding that there was no gift and it was only a permission granted for a college to manage the same free of rent. The assessee entered into an agreement with 'T' for the purpose of administration and operating of 'V' and claimed that it was providing training facilities from 'V'. HELD: It cannot be disputed that for running a charitable activity, the establishment has to be maintained, which requires payment of salaries and other establishment expenses. On writ : HELD: Under section 11(1)(a), in order to be entitled to exemption income must not only be derived from the property held under trust only for charitable or religious purposes but the income entitled to exemption must be to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes, i.e., charitable or religious purpose in India or where such income is accumulated for application to such purpose in India, i.e., religious or charitable purpose to the extent the income so accumulated is not in excess of 25 per cent of income from the property or Rs. 10,000, whichever is higher. Therefore, two separate independent conditions are required to be fulfilled, that is to say, the income must be derived from the property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, and, secondly, the application or accumulation of such income in the manner indicated in clause (a ) of sub-section (1) of section 11 of the Act. 'Charitable purpose' or 'purpose of charitable or religious nature' have not been defined in the Wealth-tax Act, 1957. Therefore, it must bear the same meaning as in the Income-tax Act but under the provisions of the Income-tax Act not only should the income be derived from a trust or legal obligation of public purpose of a charitable or religious nature but the income so derived must to a certain extent be so applied. The position under the Wealth-tax Act seems to be a little different. Wealth-tax Act assessed the owning or having or possessing of the property and section 5(1)(i) of the Act stipulated that the condition for exemption was that the property must be held by the assessee under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a religious or charitable nature in India. Therefore, the holding of a property by the assessee either under a trust or other legal obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature is the statutory requirement entitling the assessee to exemption under the Act. In the ground for reopening as noted before it was not disputed that the assessees upon whom the impugned notices had been issued were not holding the property under a trust or other legal obligation for a public purpose of a charitable or religious nature. What was being suggested was that holding the property as trustees or under obligation for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature the assessees were committing breaches of trust in acting contrary to the trust and misusing the funds of the trust for their personal benefit. The application of the money held under a trust or under legal obligation is not a relevant consideration for exemption under section 5(1)(i) of the Act. Therefore, the revenue had no material to believe that the income of the assessee had escaped assessment. This position manifests a lacuna in the present provision of law. The position, therefore, is that if the trustees hold the property for public purpose of a charitable or religious nature and if they misapply or commit breach of trust, they will continue to enjoy exemption under the Wealth-tax Act. This position should receive consideration by the legislature in order to bring it at par with the provisions of the Income-tax Act. But until that is done, the petitioners were entitled to succeed on the point that there were no grounds for believing that the wealth of the assessee had escaped assessment or had been under-assessed.

In the aforesaid view of the matter, the notices are hereby quashed and the respondents were restrained from giving effect to the same.

Having regard to the terms of the Trust Deed, it can be said that the activities carried on by the assessee in the form of running of community hall, was itself held under the Trust. [Para 6]

It is to be noted that section 11(1) grants exemption to the income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India. There is no exhaustive definition of the words 'property held under trust' in the Act; however, sub-section (4) says that for the purposes of section 11, the words 'Property held under trust' 'includes a business undertaking so held'. [Para 7]

Thus, if a property is held under trust, and such property is a business, the case would fall under section 11(4) and not under section 11(4A). Section 11(4A) would apply only to a case where the business is not held under trust. Thus, there is difference between property or business held under trust and business carried on by or on behalf of the trust. [Para 8]

This distinction was recognized by the Supreme Court in the case of Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1980] 121 ITR 1/[1979] 2 Taxman 501 wherein it was observed that if a business undertaking is held under trust for a charitable purpose, the income therefrom would be entitled to the exemption under section 11(1). In the present case, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is that running of the auditorium hall was not held under trust, but it was business commenced/carried on by the Society, subsequent to the formation of trust. Though the business was commenced by the Society and it was carried on by the trust after its formation, it cannot be said to constitute property held under trust under section 11(4), it is only the business which is held under the trust that would enjoy exemption in respect of its income under section 11(1) and there is a distinction between the objects of a trust and the powers given to the trustees to effectuate the purpose of the trust. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the Memorandum of Association of the assessee. The running of auditorium hall was not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of auditorium hall was not even in the contemplation of the Memorandum of Association on the basis of which the society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, was carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust. Section 11(1) confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose. Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1), was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust. In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

There is no connection between the activities relating to running of the auditorium hall and the attainment of the objects of the trust. The mere fact that whole or some part of the income from running of auditorium hall is used for charitable purposes would not render the business itself being considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects. The application of income generated by the business is not relevant consideration and what is relevant is whether the activity is so inextricably connected or linked with the objects of the trust that it could be considered as incidental to those objectives. [Para 10]

The essential conditions which enable an assessee to earn exemption are (i) the property from which the income is derived should be held under trust or other legal obligation; (ii) the property should be held for religious or charitable purposes; (iii) then where the property is held wholly for religious or charitable purposes the exemption will be available if the income, is, in fact, applied or accumulated for application to such purposes; and (iv) where property is held in part only for religious or charitable purposes the exemption is confined to income in fact applied or finally set apart for application for such purposes.

It will be clear from section 4 of Act 1922 that for a purpose to be charitable purpose, it must have a public character. In other words, it must be directed to the benefit of the community or a section of the community and not to the benefit of particular private individuals.

To summarise the effect of the provisions of the present trust deed it was held that (i) a trust had been created; (ii) its objects were as set out in clause 2 thereof; (iii) the trustees had full discretion to spend the trust fund and in doing so they might spend their entire funds on one object to the exclusion of the other and thus within the framework of the trust deed they might be able to spend the entire funds for the aid of the members of the settlor’s family. If they decide to spend for the particular object mentioned in clause 2(vi) of the trust deed then the trustees were under no obligation to spend it over persons other than the family of the settlor.

For all the relevant assessment years the trustee had not spent anything for the purposes of their family members and the entire amount had been expended on charitable objects only, but, in spite of anxious consideration, that could not induce to take any different view from that warranted by the language of the section. It was for an assessee to show that this case was covered by the exemption and in view of the nature of the objects specified in the trust deed the exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the Act, 1922 was not available to the assessee. The amendments made in the trust deed could not be held to be retrospective in operation.

Therefore the finding of the Tribunal that the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) was justified.
