On application under section 256(2) :

'Gift' as defined in section 2(xii ) means the transfer by one person to another of any existing movable or immovable property made voluntarily and without consideration in money or money's worth. 'Property' under section 2(xxii) includes any interest in property, movable or immovable, and under section 2(xxiv) 'transfer of property' means any disposition, conveyance, assignment, settlement, delivery, payment or other alienation of property, and includes amongst other things, the creation of a trust in property. The settling in trust of a fund as a charitable fund would be the creation of a trust in property and would, therefore, amount to transfer of property. There would, therefore, be a gift within the meaning of the Act if there is a creation of trust in property for a charitable purpose. There can, therefore, be no doubt whatsoever that there had been a gift under the respective trust deeds within the meaning of the Act.

If the creation of a trust in property for a charitable purpose is a gift for a charitable purpose and if the gift is so made under the trust deed as to belong to charitable fund, which was created under the trust deed for a charitable purpose, the gift could be said to be made to a fund for charitable purpose within the meaning of section 5(1)( v).

The language of section 5(1)(v ) need not be restricted so as to cover gifts made to an institution or fund subsequent to its being established and not include those that are given at the very inception or commencement of the institution or fund. It may be pointed out that a gift when it is made to a charitable fund adds to it and becomes part of it. The very initial gift by which the fund starts/constitutes the part, to which the further gifts are added. All gifts, together form the fund, which is augmented by them. If the subsequently gift, which are parts of the fund itself, are gifts to the fund, the initial gift, which starts the fund itself, could as well be a gift to the fund. Even if one was to take the view that a gift to be exempted under section 5(1)(v) must be made to a fund after it has come into existence, the trust deeds in the instant case could be regard as consisting the fund in the sense of a receptacle in which the donations go and donating the gifts to them.

Having regard to the definitions of the words "gift", "property" and "transfer of property" under the Act and the provision of section 5(1)(v ), which allows exemption in respect of gifts to charitable institutions or funds, under section 5(1)(v), the initial gifts, which were made for the purpose of starting or constituting a fund for charitable purposes of the kinds specified in section 5(1)(v) would be entitled to exemption under the said provision in the same manner in which the subsequent gifts to the fund would be.

Therefore, the initial gifts made under the respective trust deeds by the assessees in the instant case were rightly held by the AAC and the Tribunal as entitled to exemption.

Note – The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

The term 'held wholly for charitable and religious purposes' as occurring in section 11 would mean that property in question is not assigned to any other purpose or used directly or indirectly either in the objects clause of the trust or by the trustees in practice. Assigning of corpus, i.e., capital asset wholly for the purpose of charitable work and not assigning for any non-charitable purpose would be sufficient compliance of provisions of section 11(1A). The Circular No. 72 of the Board further supports this proposition. If the assigner partly assigns the property for charitable work and partly for non-charitable work or the property after assigning or acquisition is partly assigned to charitable work and partly to non-charitable work then on transfer of such an asset, proportionate exemption to the extent asset is assigned for charitable work would be available and no exemption to capital gain in respect of that portion thereof which arises from that part of the property which is assigned for or held for non-charitable purposes, would be available. It is not the case that passive holding of the land or non-use of the land would mean that it is assigned or held for non-charitable purposes. Non-use of the land or passiveness of the land is not equivalent to its holding for non-charitable purposes which alone can forfeit the exemption as per sub-section (1A) of section 11 and Circular No. 72, dated 6-1-1972.

[Para 58]

■

On giving a thoughtful consideration to the factual position emerging from the above, it is found that the sole premise of drawing adverse finding qua investment in residential flat being located in a posh society of Delhi, to have been utilized only for the personal purposes of the trustee and his family is short sighted and lacks merit. [Para 59]

■

It is held that the assessee society as a matter of practice invests its surplus towards acquisition of fixed assets which is as per the prescribed modes of investment. Further to carry out the objects of the assessee society in a smooth and efficient manner, the assessee society has also invested in residential properties out of the above. [Para 60]

■

The word 'immovable property' by natural reading, will include any type of land, residential or commercial property or any other form of property, which can be termed as immovable property as defined in the Transfer of Property Act. Thus, the society/management is allowed to invest its surplus in immovable property, including residential property. Thus, there cannot be a bar on management of Society to invest its surplus funds in acquisition of a residential property as the law does not mandate any extra bar. [Para 61]

■

(i) Rental income and leasing of properties

■

The principal basis adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) for allowing the assessee's claim is the observation that one of the objects of the trust was to lease out properties and earn rental income. However, on a careful examination of the original trust deed as well as the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the Tribunal finds that the observation is factually incorrect and contrary to the material available on record. The original trust deed, enumerates the charitable objects of the trust, namely: (i) genetic research and agricultural education; (ii) conservation of land, water and genetic resources; (iii) sustainable agriculture and environmental protection; (iv) family planning and population control; and (v) improvement of the status and literacy of women. Subsequently, by way of the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the additional charitable objects of Relief to the Poor and Education were incorporated. Significantly, neither the original trust deed nor the addendum includes, as an object of the trust, carrying on the activity of leasing or renting of immovable properties for earning rental income. [Para 8.2]

■

What is, however, contained in the trust deed is a separate enabling provision conferring powers upon the Board of Trustees. Clause VIII merely authorises the trustees to acquire, hold, manage or otherwise deal with land, buildings and other immovable properties with the funds of the trust for effectuating the charitable objects of the trust. Such an enabling clause cannot be elevated to the status of an independent charitable object. The power to acquire and manage trust properties is only incidental to the effective administration of the trust and to facilitate the attainment of its charitable purposes. Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that leasing of properties itself constituted one of the objects of the trust is clearly erroneous and is not borne out from the trust deed. [Para 8.3]

■

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

■

The record further reveals that the revenue has not brought any material to establish that the rental income earned by the trust was diverted for any non-charitable purpose or that the dominant character of the trust had ceased to be charitable. On the contrary, the Income and Expenditure Account demonstrates that the receipts of the trust, whether derived from grants, donations, interest or rental income, were applied only towards the charitable objects of the trust. Thus, the source from which the income was generated has not altered the fundamental charitable character of the institution. [Para 8.5]

■

It is a settled proposition of law that the decisive test is the dominant object of the institution and not the source of its income. Income derived from property held under trust, including rental income, does not lose the benefit of exemption under Section 11 and Section 12 merely because such income arises from leasing of trust property, so long as it is applied towards the charitable purposes for which the trust has been established. The leasing of trust property, in the facts of the present case, is only an incidental mode of augmenting resources to fulfil the charitable objects and cannot be construed as an independent commercial object of the trust. [Para 8.6]

■

Accordingly, while the Tribunal disagrees with the reasoning assigned by the Commissioner (Appeals) in holding that earning rental income was itself one of the objects of the trust, the Tribunal nevertheless upholds the ultimate conclusion that the assessee cannot be denied exemption on this ground. The reasoning adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) is incorrect; however, the conclusion reached by him is sustainable on the basis that the rental income was merely incidental to the charitable activities and was admittedly applied towards the charitable objects of the trust. Consequently, the ground raised by the Revenue on this issue is devoid of merit and is dismissed. [Para 8.7]

■

Accordingly, the Tribunal concurs with the findings recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue. The ground raised by the Revenue challenging the allowability of exemption merely because the assessee earned rental income is devoid of merit and is, therefore, dismissed. [Para 8.8]

1.2-4c Position in case of trusts or institutions having mixed objects - Section 11(1)(a) confers exemption to income applied wholly for charitable purposes.

Section 11(1)(b) of the Act confers exemption to income applied even partly for charitable purposes, in case of trusts or institutions established before 1st April, 1962.

There may be certain trusts or institutions, which may have its objects education and the Other Objects. They pursue both the objects and apply the income derived from the property on both the objects.

If the Other Objects do not constitute charitable purpose, on account of the applicability of the proviso, in terms of section 11(1)(a), it cannot be said that the income derived from the property held in trust is wholly applied towards charitable purposes.

Accordingly, such a trust or institution would lose the exemption under section 11.

Although, not intended, this is the result.

For continuation of the exemption, the trust or the institution will have to ensure that none of the objects is such that it cannot be considered as charitable purpose.

Courts have considered when it can be regarded that the income is applied wholly for charitable purposes or otherwise and have laid down the following principles or guidance.

In the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT[1976] 103 ITR 777 the Supreme Court held as follows:

“If one of the objects of the trust deed is not of a religious or charitable nature and the trust deed confers full discretion on the trustees to spend the trust funds for an object other than of a religious or charitable nature, the exemption from tax under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, is not available to the assessee.

If the primary or dominant purpose of a trust is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but which is merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purpose would not prevent the trust from being a valid charity.” (pg. 777)

It must also be noted that the existence of a non-charitable object may not render the trust invalid if the trust deed itself provides that the trustees shall not carry out any object, which is held to be non-charitable. This concept was delivered by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case of CIT v. Mahendra Mohta Sewa Nidi[1985] 152 ITR 516 where it was held that:

“There was not only a positive command in the trust deed that the objects mentioned in it which were not found charitable should not be carried out by the trustees but also in fact no amount was actually spent on such an object. Therefore, the assessee was a charitable trust entitled to exemption under section 11.” (pg. 516)

It was also very well explained in The Law and Practice of Income-tax Volume 1 by Kanga, Palkhiwala & Vyas, page no. 516

“(iv) The property may be held upon trust to apply a specified part of the income to charitable purposes and the balance of the income to non-charitable purposes. 1 For instance, where a wakf is created with a direction to apply half of the income to charity and the other half for the benefit of the wakf’s descendants, the property is held in part only upon charitable trusts. 2 However, this type of cases where a specified part of the income is directed to be applied to charity should be distinguished from cases where a specified part of the corpus is held upon charitable trusts. Where a specified part of the income is set apart by the author of the trust for charitable purposes, the case falls within sub-section (1)(b),—property held in part only for charitable purposes. But where a definite specified part of the corpus itself is held upon charitable trust, the remainder of the corpus being settled upon non-charitable trusts, qua the portion of the corpus which is settled upon charitable trusts, the case falls within sub-seciton (1)(a), since that portion of the property is held under trust wholly for charitable purposes. In Chaturbhuj Vallabhdas v. CIT 3 a testator directed that three-fourths of his estate should be utilized for charity, while the remaining one-fourth was to be given in the discretion of the trustee to the testator’s descendants. Held, the three-fourths of the estate was property held in trust wholly for charitable purposes.”

TRUST

Other legal obligation - The words 'or other legal obligation' cover a case in which the trustees of the original settlement are bound to pay income to other trustees who in their turn are bound to apply it for purposes which are religious or charitable [Vallabhdas Karsondas Natha v. CIT [1947] 15 ITR 32 (Bom.); Sree Sree Iswar Gopal Jew v. CIT [1950] 18 ITR 743 (Cal.)].

Section 11 does not apply to a case where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property, but only the income derived from any particular property or source is set apart and charged for a charitable or religious purpose. The expression 'legal obligation' cannot be separated from "property" itself, inasmuch as law enjoins that such property must be held under a trust or other legal obligation, and not the fund derived therefrom [CIT v. P. K. Barooah [1970] 77 ITR 967 (Gauhati)].

Wakfs and endowments are included - A trust under the Indian law would include Moslem wakfs and Hindu Endowments [Trustees of the 'Tribune', In re [1939] 7 ITR 415 (PC)].

Registration is not required - For purposes of section 11, there is no requirement under the law that a trust should be registered under the Societies Registration Act [CIT v. Arya Vysya Kalyana Nilaya Sangam [1986] 159 ITR 324 (AP)]. Also see, CIT v. Dr. (Miss) Chandrakanta Rohatgi [2006] 150 Taxman 19 (All.).

Determining nature of trust - Determination of nature of trust as wholly religious or wholly charitable or both charitable and religious is not a question of fact. It is but a question which requires examination of legal effects of the proven facts and documents, i.e., the legal implication of the objects of the trust as contained in the trust deed. It is only the objects of a trust as declared in the trust deed which would govern its right of exemption u/s 11 or 12 [CIT v. Dawoodi Bohara Jamat [2014] 43 taxmann.com 243/222 Taxman 228 (SC)].

'Property held under trust in part', meaning of - The expression 'in part' does not refer to an aliquot part; if half a house is held in trust wholly for religious and charitable purposes, the subject-matter of the trust is only the said half of the house, and that half is held wholly for religious and charitable purposes. The expression 'in part' therefore must apply to a case other than a property, a part of which is held wholly for religious or charitable purposes. The dichotomy between the two expressions 'wholly' and 'in part' is not based upon the dedication of the said property wholly for religious or charitable purposes or in part for such purposes [CIT v. P. Krishna Warrier [1964] 53 ITR 176 (SC)].

PROPERTY HELD UNDER TRUST [SECTION 11(4)]

Applicability - Section 11(4) would have no application in case of a charitable trust or institution falling within any of the heads of the definition 'charitable purpose' except under the head 'advancement of any other object of general public utility' [Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1979] 2 Taxman 501 (SC)].

'Income', meaning of - The income spoken of in section 11(4) appears to be the gross income and not the net income of the business undertaking [CIT v. Birla Education Trust [1985] 21 Taxman 134 (Cal.)].

Business commenced by trustees - Since katha business was commenced by trustees with the aid and assistance of borrowings from sister concerns, it could not be case of 'property being held under trust' within the meaning of section 11(4) but would only be a case of business being carried on by and on behalf of trust and mere fact that whole or some part of income from katha business was earmarked for application of charitable objects would not render business itself being considered as incidental to attainment of objects of trust [CIT v. Mehta Charitable Prajnalay Trust [2012] 28 taxmann.com 73/[2013] 214 Taxman 88 (Delhi), SLP granted inMehta Charitable Prajnalaya Trust v. CIT [2017] 82 taxmann.com 149/248 Taxman 145 (SC)].

Courts have considered when it can be regarded that the income is applied wholly for charitable purposes or otherwise and have laid down the following principles or guidance.

In the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 777 the Supreme Court held as follows: "If one of the objects of the trust deed is not of a religious or charitable nature and the trust deed confers full discretion on the trustees to spend the trust funds for an object other than of a religious or charitable nature, the exemption from tax under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, is not available to the assessee.

If the primary or dominant purpose of a trust is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but which is merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purpose would not prevent the trust from being a valid charity." (pg. 777)

It must also be noted that the existence of a non-charitable object may not render the trust invalid if the trust deed itself provides that the trustees shall not carry out any object, which is held to be non-charitable. This concept was delivered by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case of CIT v. Mahendra Mohta Sewa Nidi [1985] 152 ITR 516 where it was held that:

"There was not only a positive command in the trust deed that the objects mentioned in it which were not found charitable should not be carried out by the trustees but also in fact no amount was actually spent on such an object. Therefore, the assessee was a charitable trust entitled to exemption under section 11." (pg. 516)

It was also very well explained in The Law and Practice of Income-tax Volume 1 by Kanga, Palkhiwala & Vyas, page no. 516

"(iv) The property may be held upon trust to apply a specified part of the income to charitable purposes and the balance of the income to non-charitable purposes.1 For instance, where a wakf is created with a direction to apply half of the income to charity and the other half for the benefit of the wakf's descendants, the property is held in part only upon charitable trusts.2 However, this type of cases where a specified part of the income is directed to be applied to charity should be distinguished from cases where a specified part of the corpus is held upon charitable trusts. Amendments relating to Charitable Trusts 9.4 Section 21A of the WT Act provides that in case of a charitable trust, if any part of its property is used or applied, directly or indirectly, for the benefit of, or, any part of the income of the trust enures directly or indirectly for the benefit of, persons referred to in section 13(3) of the Income-tax Act, or its funds are invested in contravention of the provisions of the Act, such a trust will have to pay wealth-tax on its property. In other words, it would not be entitled to exemption conferred on it under section 5(i) of the WT Act.

Section 5(i) of the WT Act exempts such a trust from the levy of wealth-tax.

Section 21A, prior to its amendment before 1-4-1993, contained a non obstante clause so as to exclude exemption under section 5(i) of the WT Act. However, while making the amendment through the Finance Act, 1992 in the provision of section 21A, such non obstante clause was deleted.

The effect of such deletion was that, although, section 21A sought to tax a charitable trust in case of violation or application of the provisions of the Act, yet, it was saved by exemption contained in section 5(i).

To cure this defect, in section 21A, the non obstante clause has been inserted at the beginning, reading as follows:

"Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (i) of section 5, where any property is held".

The effect of the above clause is that a charitable trust which does not comply with the said relevant provisions of the Act, would be liable to wealth-tax irrespective of the exemption. For obvious reasons, the amendment is retrospective and applies from the assessment year 1993-94.

ANNEX 9.1

CIRCULAR NO. 495, DATED 22-9-1987 (PARA 23)

Enlarging the meaning of ownership of house property

23.1 The Amending Act has extended the meaning of the expression "ownership" for the purpose of computing income under the head "Income from house property". The expression "ownership" meaning legal ownership had the effect of excluding cases where an assessee possessed all rights to an immovable property except the husk of the title.

23.2 The practice of limited companies constructing multi-storeycd buildings and allotting or leasing flats to the shareholders is quite prevalent these days. In such a situation, though the limited company is the legal owner, the member subscribers to the shares of the company to whom the flats are allotted are the real owners who enjoy the income therefrom. In several States where the Apartment Act has not been introduced there is a legal hurdle in transferring the ownership of these flats to individual shareholders. Since the legal ownership remains with the company, the income therefrom is taxed in their hands under the head "Income from house property". At the same time, since the shareholder actually enjoys the income he is assessed under the head "Income from other sources". This has led to taxing the same income twice. There is another practice whereby property is transferred to the purchaser after receiving the consideration but without getting the sale registered under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act. This is done by executing power of attorney in favour of a person who by virtue of that power of attorney enjoys the property. In such cases, legally, the property remains with the registered owner but for all practical purposes, the holder of the power of attorney is the owner. A similar situation arises where possession of any immovable property is allowed to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. All these types of transactions have the effect of transferring the house property in fact, though not in law. With the extended definition of the expression "ownership", transactions covered by section 269UA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (including transfer of property by power of attorney), shall be considered as having the effect of transfer of title. The Amending Act by insertion of sub- clauses (iii), (iiia) and (iiib) in section 27, covers all the transactions referred to above for the purpose of determining the ownership of the property for assessing income under the head "Income from house property'.

23.3 For the sake of uniformity and consistency, consequential amendments in the Wealth-tax Act and Gift-tax Act have also been made as a similar situation exists in the allied statutes.

At the same time, since the shareholder actually enjoys the income he is assessed under the head "Income from other sources". This has led to taxing the same income twice. There is another practice whereby property is transferred to the purchaser after receiving the consideration but without getting the sale registered under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act. This is done by executing power of attorney in favour of a person who by virtue of that power of attorney enjoys the property. In such cases, legally, the property remains with the registered owner but for all practical purposes, the holder of the power of attorney is the owner. A similar situation arises where possession of any immovable property is allowed to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. All these types of transactions have the effect of transferring the house property in fact, though not in law. With the extended definition of the expression "ownership", transactions covered by section 269UA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (including transfer of property by power of attorney), shall be considered as having the effect of transfer of title. The Amending Act by insertion of sub- clauses (iii), (iiia) and (iiib) in section 27, covers all the transactions referred to above for the purpose of determining the ownership of the property for assessing income under the head "Income from house property'.

'Property', meaning of - The word 'property' in section 13(2) will have to be understood as having been used in its own generic sense to include 'movable and immovable property' [Agappa Child Centre v. CIT [1997] 92 Taxman 327 (Ker.)].

'Lending' and 'investment' - In the process of investment, the element or risk is involved and the expectation of return or profit is not assured and the depletion of capital itself is not an abnormal feature. In the case of lending, the return by way of interest is generally assured and the element of risk is minimal. When an amount is advanced on an agreed rate of interest, the transaction is within the fold of 'lending' and it cannot be considered as 'investment' [CIT v. Polisetty Somasundaram Charities [1990] 188 ITR 377 (AP)].

In the case of lending by trusts, clause (a) of section 13(2) will apply and not clause (h) [CIT v. Sarladevi Sarabhai Trust (No. 2) [1988] 40 Taxman 388 (Guj.)].

Relationship of borrower and lender must exist - For an amount to fall within the mischief of section 13(2)(a), there must be a loan. To constitute a loan, there must be a positive act of lending, coupled with an acceptance by the other side of the money as a loan. The relationship of borrower and lender must come into existence by the act of parties [CIT v. Nachimuthu Industrial Association [1983] 14 Taxman 224 (Mad.)].

Lending of income/property - The mere circumstance that a partnership concern was not in a position to pay the amounts due to the assessee-partner on the date of his retirement from the partnership firm and the fact that the amounts were shown in the books of account as due to the assessee, could not convert the amounts due as moneys of the assessee lent to the firm [CIT v. Nachimuthu Industrial Association [1983] 14 Taxman 224 (Mad.)].

Personal surety given by director of a company to which assessee-trust had advanced loan could be considered to be adequate security for allowance of exemption u/s 11 [CIT v. Shri Ram Smarak Nidhi [2004] 141 Taxman 297 (Delhi)].

Where assessee-society had advanced certain sum to its treasurer without any surety and no interest had been charged on a loan outstanding against treasurer nor any provision for accrued interest was made, assessee was not entitled to exemption u/s 11 in view of provisions contained in section 13(1)(c) and 13(2)(a) [CIT v. Audh Educational Society [2011] 15 taxmann.com 235/203 Taxman 166 (All.)].

Making available any property without adequate compensation - Where the assessee, a public charitable trust, purchased a refrigerator even before the trust buildings were completed and kept it at the disposal of the managing trustee, and it was found that the assessee never even thought of charging adequate rent or other compensation from the trustee, the case would be hit by the prohibition contained in section 13(2)(b), and the assessee-trust would not be entitled to exemption u/s 11 [Agappa Child Centre v. The assessee was a public religious and charitable trust registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. A scheme for this trust was originally framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad way back in 1960 after finding in a suit that the suit properties were part of a public religious , trust and that the defendants were in possession as trustees for and on behalf of the general worshippers of the temple. The Court gave directions setting down the duties and obligations of the pujaries who, as trustees and managers of the temple, were allowed two-thirds of the income of the trust properties for purposes of their maintenance and temple expenses. Subsequently, in Second Appeal No. 565 of 1942, by a judgment-creditor of the then pujari-trustees, the Bombay High Court had occasion to observe that the original scheme framed by the District Court lent strong support to the view that the remuneration payable to the trustees or managers was for the services rendered by them and was their personal property. The present scheme of the trust was framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad in 1960. Under clauses 12, 13 and 14 of this scheme, after meeting outgoings on account of rates, taxes, assessment and expenses incidental to the administration of the trust and worship of the deity of the temple and also current repair and upkeep charges, the trustees were under obligation to distribute the surplus income by setting apart 50 per cent thereof for reserve fund and dividing the remaining 50 per cent equally between the two hereditary trustees, which was to be treated as their absolute property. The amount standing to the credit of the reserve fund was to be invested according to the provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, but out of the annual contribution to the fund, 20 per cent was to be utilised for religious, educational and/or medical purposes with the sanction of the District Court. In the assessment for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64, the previous years being Samvat Years 2017 and 2018, respectively, the trust claimed that the entire income from its property should be exempt from tax under section 11(1)(a). The ITO disallowed the claim holding that the properties of the trust were not held wholly for religious and charitable purposes, since the payment of 50 per cent of the surplus income to the two hereditary trustees was not for charitable purposes, inasmuch as it was not by way of remuneration or salary for the services rendered by them as employees and what they received was out of the income of the trust. According to the ITO, the only income which was entitled to be exempt under section 11(1)(b) would be the amount actually spent for religious purposes and 20 per cent of the amount of contribution set apart as reserve fund. On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's view that the case would fall under section 11(1)(b) as the income was only partly applied for religious purposes. He also rejected the alternative claim of the trust that the said payments must be treated as allowable expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal also rejected the claim and confirmed the view of the ITO and the AAC, holding that the true effect of the payments to the hereditary pujaris was the application of the income and it had no direct or indirect relation to the services, if any, rendered by them.

3. There may be two meanings of this circular and one is apparently mentioned in the circular and the second one is implied. The purpose of this circular is to instruct the concerned officers not to give benefit of this exclusion to all the entities which are registered under the Income-tax Act as charitable trusts on the ground that they are registered as such under the Income-tax Act as the Income-tax Act and the law governing the service tax are different laws. The officers should give the benefit of this exclusion to these entities after going through the facts of the case. As it is already mentioned that an entity registered as a charitable trust under the Income-tax Act is fulfilling all the formalities and criteria as mentioned in the circular then even after examining the case it will not be possible for the concerned officer to take the other view.

The second meaning is that the entities which are not registered under the Income-tax Act as charitable trusts can be given the benefit of this exclusion and this second meaning is more important and now through this circular it is explained that to be eligible for this exemption it is not necessary that the person or body of individuals should be registered under the Income-tax Act as a charitable trust.

Will it resolve the controversy?

4. Normally under the Income-tax Act the trust registered as charitable trust has its objective to help poor or sufferings or the society for religious, educational, economic, public safety or medical purpose. The definition of the ‘charity’ and ‘charitable’ in the Black’s Law Dictionary is wide enough because it has words like usually, general community, religious purpose, etc., to make it more open-ended. But it will certainly give benefit to persons or body of persons which are not registered as charitable trust under the Income-tax Act.

"(15)Section 2( 15) of the Income-tax Act reads as under :

‘charitable purpose’ includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, and the advancement of any other object of general public utility."

The definition of section 2(15) is based on the definition of ‘charity’ given in the Black’s Law Dictionary as mentioned in the circular. Further to be registered under the Income-tax Act to get the exemption the trust created on or after April 1, 1962 should also comply with the following conditions :—

(a)The trust should not be created for the purpose of particular religious community or caste;

(b)No part of the income of the trust should ensure directly or indirectly, for the benefit of settlor or any other specified person;

(c)The property should be held wholly for the charitable purpose.

With all these specifications a trust is getting the exemption from income-tax then how it cannot get the exemption from the service tax also when the service tax law, i.e. , the Finance Act, 1994 does not define the word precisely in itself. How the trust registered under the Income-tax Act as such will lose this exemption under the service tax law even after purpose of the issuance of this circular has not been made clear. The entities which are really engaged in the cause of charity will now get the exemption from service tax after consideration of other material facts including the meaning of the words ‘charity’, and ‘charitable’ given in the Black’s Law Dictionary.

Conclusion

5. The above circular is just an explanation. This is issued to show the fact that the law governing the Income-tax Act and the law governing the service tax are separate and the governance of service tax does not depend on the Income-tax Act and for the purpose of word not defined in the Finance Act, 1994, it is not necessary to follow the Income-tax Act. This is the first time that it is mentioned that a specific dictionary has to be consulted for this purpose.

This is very casual approach to deal with a controversy. It will itself generate some other controversies. Our law makers have been following this method since the inception of service tax. There has been a need to clarify the meaning of the term ‘commercial concern’ since long time and how it is so far dealt with is not a very pending issue. The same process is adopted again by our law makers while defining the word ‘charitable’. They had given a very confusing clarification instead of defining the word in very clear terms.

The existing provisions of section 11 contain a primary condition that for grant of exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust, such income should be applied for the charitable purposes in India, and where such income cannot be so applied during the previous year, it has to be accumulated in the prescribed modes.

2.4-1 New sub-section (6) - No depreciation if purchase of asset claimed as application of income

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted new sub-section (6) in section 11, with effect from 1-4-2015. The said sub-section (6) provides that where any income is required to be applied or accumulated or set apart for application, then, for such purposes the income shall be determined without any deduction or allowance by way of depreciation orotherwise in respect of any asset, acquisition of which has been claimed as an application of income under this section in any previous year (See also Para 2.3).

2.4-2 New sub-section (7) - No exemption under any clause of sec. 10 except clauses (1) and (23C) if registration u/s 12A or 12AA in force

New sub-section (7), inserted with effect from 1-4-2015, applies to a trust or an institution which has been granted registration (under section 12AA or under section 12A) for purposes of availing exemption under section 11. In terms of new sub-section (7), where such registration is in force for a previous year, then such trust or institution shall not be entitled to any exemption under any provision of section 10 [other than that relating to exemption of agricultural income and income exempt under section 10(23C)].

The amendment overcomes the decision of the Tribunal in Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mum. - Trib.). In Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt. DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mumbai - Trib.) the assessee claimed that dividend income on shares and unit and long term capital gain on sale of shares are exempt u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) respectively. The AO denied the exemption on the ground that section 11 exclusively deals with the income derived from the property held under trust and not u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38). Hence the AO held that there is a violation u/s 13 and as a result of the same exemption u/s 11 is denied. The assessee cannot claim the alternative claim for exemption u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) because these sections do not deal with income derived from the property held under the trust. On appeal, the CIT(A) concurred with AO's view. On further appeal, however, ITAT ruled in favour of the assessee-trust and held that "the income which is exempt u/s 10 cannot be brought to tax by virtue of sections 11 and 13 of the Act because no such pre-condition is provided either u/s 10 or 11 to 13. Therefore, sections 11 to 13 would not operate as overriding effect to the section 10 of the Act. The language of these provisions does not suggest that either section 10 is subjected to the provisions of sections 11 to 13 or sections 11 to 13 has any overriding effect over section 10. Therefore, the benefit of section 10 cannot be denied by invoking the provisions of sections 11 to 13 of the Act. Once the conditions of section 10 are satisfied then no other condition can be fastened for denying the claim under section 10 of the Act".

1.2-4a Taxability - Any trust or institution, which in the pursuit of its Other Objects, carries on any 'specified activity' and the proviso applies to it, from assessment year 2009-10, the object would not be considered as charitable purpose and, hence, it would not be eligible for the exemption of income applied towards the objects.

Accordingly, all the provisions of the Act relating to taxability, computation, payment of taxes, filing of returns, etc., would apply.

Depending on the nature of income, it will have to be classified under the applicable heads.

While computing its income, the relevant provisions of the Act will have to be applied for determining the income as well as allowability of expenses.

Such trusts or institutions will have to note the difference between deduction of expenses and application of income. To illustrate, while they were eligible for exemption, even capital expenditure could have been claimed as application of income. However, such a claim would not be allowable in computation of its income. Similarly, voluntary contributions were not considered as income earlier on account of the specific provisions. However, once it loses the exemption, such contributions may also be considered as income liable to tax.

3.2-6c Basic exemption

Section 11(1)(a) reads as follows:

"Income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India; and, where any such income is accumulated or set apart for application to such purposes in India, to the extent to which the income so accumulated or set apart is not in excess of fifteen per cent of the income from such property". The expression "such" means the purposes referred to in the earlier part of the section, that is, charitable or religious purposes. Hence, even the income accumulated or set apart has to be applied towards charitable or religious purposes in India. Now, the amendment states that any corpus donation shall not be treated as "application of income for charitable or religious purposes". Hence, if the accumulated income up to 15% is utilized by a charitable institution for giving corpus donation, then on a literal interpretation, the income could be regarded as applied towards non-charitable/religious purpose, thus, violating the condition that even accumulated income has to be applied towards charitable or religious purposes. A consequence would be that the income of the year to which the basic exemption pertains may become taxable in the said year. To illustrate, if the 15% basic accumulation of assessment year 2014-15 is utilised for grant of corpus donation in assessment year 2018-19, the exemption given in assessment year 2014-15 may be withdrawn on the basis of literal interpretation. This does not appear to be intended and a clarification from the CBDT or a statutory amendment will help in eliminating the exposure.

Hence, even under the pre-amendment law, such corpus donations were not permitted out of income accumulated under section 11(2).

Whether the purpose is a charitable purpose will depend on the totality of the facts of the case. 1.2-3 Irrespective of its application - The proviso stipulates that even if the income derived from disqualifying activities (carrying on any activity in the nature of trade or rendering any services in relation to the trade) are used for charitable purpose, the disqualifying activities would render Other Object as non-charitable purpose.

In other words, it would not be possible for such an institution to contend that since the income derived is used for charitable purpose, it is incidental to the attainment of the objectives, it should constitute charitable purpose (as was held by Supreme Court in Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust[2001] 115 Taxman 126/247 ITR 785).

1.2-4 Effects of the amendment - Note the following:

1.2-4a Taxability - Any trust or institution, which in the pursuit of its Other Objects, carries on any ‘specified activity’ and the proviso applies to it, from assessment year 2009-10, the object would not be considered as charitable purpose and, hence, it would not be eligible for the exemption of income applied towards the objects.

Accordingly, all the provisions of the Act relating to taxability, computation, payment of taxes, filing of returns, etc., would apply.

Depending on the nature of income, it will have to be classified under the applicable heads.

While computing its income, the relevant provisions of the Act will have to be applied for determining the income as well as allowability of expenses.

Such trusts or institutions will have to note the difference between deduction of expenses and application of income. To illustrate, while they were eligible for exemption, even capital expenditure could have been claimed as application of income. However, such a claim would not be allowable in computation of its income. Similarly, voluntary contributions were not considered as income earlier on account of the specific provisions. However, once it loses the exemption, such contributions may also be considered as income liable to tax.

1.2-4b Liability to FBT - An employer is liable to fringe benefits tax, in terms of the provisions of Chapter XII-H of the Act.

Section 115W(a) defining ‘employer’ excludes any person registered under section 12AA of the Act.

In terms of the amendment, any trust or institution, to which new proviso to section 2(15) applies, may no longer continue to have registration under section 12AA of the Act and, therefore, the trust or institution would be considered as employer.

If so, the trust or institution may be liable to FBT, subject to the provisions of Chapter XII-H of the Act.

1.2-4c Position in case of trusts or institutions having mixed objects - Section 11(1)(a) confers exemption to income applied wholly for charitable purposes.

Section 11(1)(b) of the Act confers exemption to income applied even partly for charitable purposes, in case of trusts or institutions established before 1st April, 1962.

There may be certain trusts or institutions, which may have its objects education and the Other Objects. They pursue both the objects and apply the income derived from the property on both the objects.

If the Other Objects do not constitute charitable purpose, on account of the applicability of the proviso, in terms of section 11(1)(a), it cannot be said that the income derived from the property held in trust is wholly applied towards charitable purposes.

Accordingly, such a trust or institution would lose the exemption under section 11.

Although, not intended, this is the result.

For continuation of the exemption, the trust or the institution will have to ensure that none of the objects is such that it cannot be considered as charitable purpose.

Section 11

Finance Act, 2014

2.4 Rationalisation of taxation regime for charitable trusts and institutions under sections 11 to 13

The existing provisions of section 11 contain a primary condition that for grant of exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust, such income should be applied for the charitable purposes in India, and where such income cannot be so applied during the previous year, it has to be accumulated in the prescribed modes.

2.4-1 New sub-section (6) - No depreciation if purchase of asset claimed as application of income

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted new sub-section (6) in section 11, with effect from 1-4-2015. The said sub-section (6) provides that where any income is required to be applied or accumulated or set apart for application, then, for such purposes the income shall be determined without any deduction or allowance by way of depreciation or otherwise in respect of any asset, acquisition of which has been claimed as an application of income under this section in any previous year (See also Para 2.3).

2.4-2 New sub-section (7) - No exemption under any clause of sec. 10 except clauses (1) and (23C) if registration u/s 12A or 12AA in force

New sub-section (7), inserted with effect from 1-4-2015, applies to a trust or an institution which has been granted registration (under section 12AA or under section 12A) for purposes of availing exemption under section 11. In terms of new sub-section (7), where such registration is in force for a previous year, then such trust or institution shall not be entitled to any exemption under any provision of section 10 [other than that relating to exemption of agricultural income and income exempt under section 10(23C)].

The amendment overcomes the decision of the Tribunal in Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mum. - Trib.). In Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt. DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mumbai - Trib.) the assessee claimed that dividend income on shares and unit and long term capital gain on sale of shares are exempt u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) respectively. The AO denied the exemption on the ground that section 11 exclusively deals with the income derived from the property held under trust and not u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38). Hence the AO held that there is a violation u/s 13 and as a result of the same exemption u/s 11 is denied. The assessee cannot claim the alternative claim for exemption u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) because these sections do not deal with income derived from the property held under the trust. On appeal, the CIT(A) concurred with AO's view. On further appeal, however, ITAT ruled in favour of the assessee-trust and held that "the income which is exempt u/s 10 cannot be brought to tax by virtue of sections 11 and 13 of the Act because no such pre-condition is provided either u/s 10 or 11 to 13. Therefore, sections 11 to 13 would not operate as overriding effect to the section 10 of the Act. The language of these provisions does not suggest that either section 10 is subjected to the provisions of sections 11 to 13 or sections 11 to 13 has any overriding effect over section 10. Therefore, the benefit of section 10 cannot be denied by invoking the provisions of sections 11 to 13 of the Act. Once the conditions of section 10 are satisfied then no other condition can be fastened for denying the claim under section 10 of the Act".

Amendment to section 11 now overcomes the above judicial ruling.

New sub-section (7) also incorporates into the statute book the principle laid down in Bharati Vidyapeeth Medical Foundation v. Asstt. CIT [2013] 37 taxmann.com 242/144 ITD 510 that "When the law permits the assessee to claim exemption under section 10(23C) or section 11, the choice should be left to the assessee and the department cannot force the assessee to adopt only a particular provision".

The Explanatory Memorandum explains the rationale for this amendment as under :

Introduction

1. The recent decision of the CBEC to omit clause (v), which provided exemption from service tax for activities related to advancement of any other object of general public utility upto the prescribed monetary limits from the definition of 'charitable activity' from 1-4-2013 is an instance, which indicates CBEC's unfair treatment of charities, which enures to the welfare of the people of the country in terms of Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution of India ["the Constitution" for short].

The primary objective of any tax law and its administration is to raise revenue for funding Governmental expenditure, which, inter alia, is to be spent for the peoples' welfare. An important source of revenue to the Govt. is service tax. Article 38 in Chapter IV of the Constitution, titled Directive Principles of State Policy provides that the State shall, amongst others, provide that the State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice shall ensue to all institutions of social life. This directive of the Constitution is being fulfilled by direct expenditure as also by tax foregone in the form of exemptions and deductions in tax legislations, which cost to the Govt. some financial burden as cash expenditure.

This position is well recognized in most of the countries of the world. In this context, it may be appropriate to refer to the philosophy concerning concessions permissible for charitable contributions under the U.S. Internal Revenue Code. The House Ways and Means Committee, in one of its reports, has observed as under:—

"……The exemption from taxation of money or property devoted to charitable and other purposes is based upon the theory that the Government is compensated for the loss of revenue by its relief from financial burden, which would otherwise have to be met by appropriation from public funds and by the benefit resulting from the promotion of the general welfare".

2. Exemption of income of charitable bodies

2.1 Under the I.T. Act - The principle of giving tax benefits to charities and various objects of general public utility are well enshrined in the law relating to taxation of income. Section 2(15) of the I.T. Act, 1961 (Act) defines the term 'charitable purpose' (as amended) as under:—

"Charitable purpose includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, preservation of environment [including watersheds, forests and wildlife] and preservation of monuments or places or objects of artistic or historic interest and the advancement of any other object of general public utility".

To prevent the misuse of tax concessions for charities for business purposes, two provisos were added to this definition, which read as under:—

"Provided that the advancement of any other object of general public utility shall not be a charitable purpose, if it involves the carrying on of any activity in the nature of trade, commerce or business, or any activity of rendering any service in relation to any trade, commerce or business, for a cess or fee or any other consideration, irrespective of the nature of use or application or retention of the income from such activity:

Provided further that the first proviso shall not apply, if the aggregate value of the receipts from the activities referred to therein is twenty-five lakh rupees or less in the previous year."

Sections 11 and 10(23C) of the Act provide for exemption from tax of the incomes derived by charitable institutions on the fulfilment of the prescribed conditions.

For ensuring that undeserved institutions do not avail of tax benefits, the Act vide section 12A provides for registration of such institutions with the Chief Commissioners/Commissioners of Income-tax of the respective regions by making applications in the prescribed forms with relevant accounts and documents duly audited. Section 12AA prescribes the procedure for registration and lays down the time-limit within which the registration is to be granted. Sub-section (3) of section 12AA prescribes for cancellation of registration, if the activities of the Trust/Institution, which has been allowed registration, are found to be non-genuine or it is noticed that the activities of the institution are not being carried on in accordance with the objects of the trust/institution, as the case may be. Thus, I.T. Act has well-known law and procedure for giving tax benefits to charitable organizations, which are for the welfare and benefit of the people.

2.2 Under the Service Tax law - Regretfully, it is noticed that such important issue was being treated under the service tax legislation by the CBEC in a routine and arbitrary manner – not appreciating the spirit and purpose behind giving tax benefits to charitable institutions. In the pre 1-7-2013 period, the CBEC took a very narrow view regarding charitable activities, as could be seen from later discussion.

It is not necessary that the public at large must get the benefit. Hence, a matter is to be decided considering the objects of general public utility. The High Court held that what matters is some common quality of a public or impersonal nature.

Decision binding if the point is the same

2.38 Thus the principle of res judicata or estoppel though cannot strictly apply to the decisions rendered in proceedings under the Income-tax Act, they have a binding effect both on the assessee as well as the revenue, if the point on which the decision has been given is the same. On the basis of this principle the Madras High Court1 held that the decision on the question whether a certain trust is charitable or not, has nothing to do with the fluctuations in the income, and that such questions, if decided by a Court on a reference made to it, would be res judicata and the same question cannot be subsequently reagitated. It may be stated that in that case, the question was already considered by the Supreme Court2 as to whether the assessee would be entitled to exemption, wherein the claim for deduction of the donation made to the assessee-trust was rejected by the Supreme Court on the ground that the assessee-trust could not be held to be entitled to the benefit of exemption because some of the objects of the trust were not charitable and the trustees had discretion to spend the income of the trust on charitable and non-charitable objects. The matter turned on the finding already arrived at by the Supreme Court as to whether the trust in question was a charitable one or not and so the question of exemption was based on the previous finding regarding the nature of the trust.

The Supreme Court in CIT v. Durga Prasad More3, held that though neither the principle of res judicata nor the rule of estoppel was applicable to the assessment proceedings, the fact that the assessee included the income of the premises in his returns for several years after objecting to its inclusion in the year 1942-43, was a circumstance which the taxing authorities were entitled to take into consideration in the absence of any specific explanation and that the Tribunal was right in holding that the house property was not the trust property. The Supreme Court proceeded to consider the question as to whether the finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal was in any way vitiated and it was held that it was not in any way vitiated.

No grounds have been given for such omission. No change has been made in Item No.4 of the Notification, where exemption under service tax continues to be available to entities registered u/s 12AA of the I.T. Act, where the advancement of any other object of general public utility continues to enjoy exemption under the I.T. Act. Prima facie, there seems to be no ground to confine the exemption benefits to only : (i) to (iv) situations in the definition of charitable activity and close the door for other activities covered by the general clause under S.No.(v) (supra). It cannot be an arbitrary decision and there must be some reasons behind it, but unfortunately nothing has been stated for the snap decision taken to withdraw clause (v) only after less than one year of the Notification, dated 20-6-2012.

The omnibus clause in the definition of charitable purpose under the I.T. Act namely any other object of general public utility has been held to be a solid object for grant of tax exemptions under the I.T. Act. This is clear from the following discussion. :

(a)

Aspects of general public utility have been considered as charitable since long under the English law. The Statute of Elizabeth as per its preamble enumerated the following purposes as charitable:—

"The relief of aged, impotent and poor people; the maintenance of sick and mined soldiers and mariners; the maintenance of schools of learning, free schools and scholars in universities; the repair of bridges, ports, havens, causeways, churches, sea-banks and highways; the education and preferment of orphans; the relief, stock or maintenance of houses of corrections; the marriage of poor maids; the supportation, aid and help of young tradesman, handicraftsmen, and person decayed; the relief or redemption of prisoners or captives; the aid or ease of any poor inhabitants concerning payment of taxes; the setting out of soldiers."

(b)

Though the statute was repeated by the Mortmain and Charitable Uses Act, 1888 the preamble to the statute (supra) was retained in section 13(2) of the repealing Act!

(c)

The concept of charity developed in the Mortmain and Charitable Uses Act, 1888 (C.42) S. 13(2) under the four principle heads as defined or classified has been explained by Lord Macnaghten in the classic case of Commissioners for Special Purposes of Income-tax v. Pemsel [1891] AC 531, for the majority.

The dictum of Lord Macnaghten was as follows:

"Charity" in its legal sense comprises four principal divisions: trusts for the relief of poverty, trusts for the advancement of education, trusts for the advancement of religion, and trusts for other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the preceding heads. The trusts last referred to are not the less charitable in the eye of the law because incidentally they benefit the rich as well as the poor, as indeed every charity that deserves the name must do, either directly or indirectly.

Apparently, denying the exemption to the bodies that are engaged in advancing the objects of general public utility, other than those mentioned in clauses (i) to (iv) in the definition of 'charitable activity', which are no less charitable, because the same fall under the residuary head.

Concluding remarks

7. Apparently, the dropping of clause (v) from the definition of 'charitable activity' in the Notification, dated 20-6-2012 (supra) is unfair and misconceived – more so when no justification has been given for omitting it from the definition. It would be a handicap for many charitable institutions, who are doing commendable work for public welfare. The CBEC, administering the Service Tax legislation, needs to be rational in dealing with this law. It cannot be impulsive in its decisions. Taking decisions on whims and fancies, without any solid grounds, besides affecting the functioning of the concerned Department, erodes the credibility of the Government.

Act law relating to registration, audit, etc., can be introduced for the trusts/institutions, who wish to avail of the exemptionary benefit under Service-tax legislation. Income applied - Charitable purpose

Income derived from the property held under trust for charitable or religious purposes to the extent such income is applied to such purposes in India, is to be excluded for the purposes of computing the income of the trust under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961. The word ‘applied’ means ‘to put to use’ or ‘to turn to use’ or ‘to make use’ or ‘to put to practical use’. When the income of a trust is used or put to use to meet the expenses incurred for religious or charitable purposes, it is applied for charitable or religious purposes. The said application of the income takes place in the year in which income is adjusted to meet the expenses incurred for religious or charitable purposes. In other words, even if expenses for religious or charitable purposes have been incurred for the earlier year and the said expenses are adjusted to meet the expenses. In other words, even if expenses for charitable or religious purposes have been incurred for the earlier years and the said expenses are adjusted against the income of a subsequent year, the income of that year can be said to have been applied for charitable and religious purposes in the year in which the expenses incurred and adjusted [CIT v. Shri Plot Swetamber Murti Pujak Jain Mandal [1995] 211 ITR 293 (Guj.)]

However, the word has acquired a technical meaning in law, which is wide. Hence, the wide meaning will apply and not narrow dictionary meaning. Preamble to Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920 also indicates that trust created for public purpose comes under purview of that Act.

Management, Maintenance and Repair Services

As per section 65(64) of the Finance Act, 1994 (as amended w.e.f. 16-6-2005 and by the Finance Act, 2006 w.e.f. 1-5-2006), "management, maintenance or repair" means any service provided by—(i) any person under a contract or an agreement; or (ii) a manufacturer or any person authorised by him, in relation to, (a) management of properties, whether immovable or not (b) maintenance or repair of properties whether immovable or not; or (c) maintenance or repair including reconditioning or restoration, or servicing of any goods or equipment, excluding motor vehicle.

In many cases, housing societies collect the charges from members which are termed as ‘maintenance’ charges. Hence, it is alleged that the housing society provides management, maintenance or repair.

As discussed above, the activities undertaken by housing society are a bundle of various activities, some of which might fall under ‘management, maintenance or repair’ services. However, a service can be taxed if it is predominantly a taxable service. In Daelim Industrial Co. v. CCE 2003 STT 438 = 155 ELT 457 = 57 RLT 636 = 3 STR 124 (CEGAT), it was held that a works contract on turnkey basis is not a consultancy contract. A works contract cannot be vivisected and part of it subjected to tax (SLP filed by department dismissed by SC - [2004] 170 ELT A181). This was followed in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE [2005] 1 STT 183 = 2004 (174) ELT 322 = 60 RLT 505 = 3 STR 223 (CESTAT), in respect of design element of works contract.

The principle that a contract cannot be vivisected is applicable to all services.

D.O. letter No. 334/4/2006-TRU, dated 28-2-2006 states as follows, ‘Often services provided consist of more than one service. In such cases, it is important to decide, for the purpose of classification of services, whether each element of the transaction should be treated separately or as a single composite transaction, albeit, made up of two or more separate services. A composite service, even if it consists of more than one service, should be treated as a single service based on the main or principal service and accordingly classified. The decision is to be made on question of facts and law. It will not make a difference if the tax rates of the components are the same as that of the principal service. The problem may arise when some elements are taxable and others are exempt. While taking a view, both the form and substance of the transaction are to be taken into account. The guiding principle is to identify the essential features of the transaction. The method of charging does not in itself determine whether the service provided is a single service or multiple services’.

Thus, a service can be taxed only if it is predominantly a taxable service.

The so called ‘service’ provided by housing society is not predominantly a ‘management, maintenance or repair’ service.

Hence, in my view, the service of housing society cannot be classified under that head.

The words 'applied or finally set apart for application' in the second part of clause (i) of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act [corresponding to section 11 of the 1961 Act] indicated that unless the income from the property was applied or finally set apart for religious or charitable purposes within the taxable territories, it did not earn the exemption. A different meaning should not be given to the expression 'applied or accumulated for application' in the first part of the clause; for, on principle, there could not be any possible distinction between income from property wholly held in trust or that which forms a part of the property held in trust. The words 'applied' and 'accumulated', therefore, meant 'applied or finally set apart'. 'Applied' meant that the income was actually applied for charitable or religious purposes in the taxable territories; and 'accumulated' meant that the income was set apart during the year for future spending on such purposes. The expression 'accumulated' for a purpose involved a conscious act in praesenti and posited a clear indication on the part of the trustee to set apart the income for that purpose.

2.4 Rationalisation of taxation regime for charitable trusts and institutions under sections 11 to 13

The existing provisions of section 11 contain a primary condition that for grant of exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust, such income should be applied for the charitable purposes in India, and where such income cannot be so applied during the previous year, it has to be accumulated in the prescribed modes.

2.4-1 New sub-section (6) - No depreciation if purchase of asset claimed as application of income

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted new sub-section (6) in section 11, with effect from 1-4-2015. The said sub-section (6) provides that where any income is required to be applied or accumulated or set apart for application, then, for such purposes the income shall be determined without any deduction or allowance by way of depreciation or otherwise in respect of any asset, acquisition of which has been claimed as an application of income under this section in any previous year (See also Para 2.3).

2.4-2 New sub-section (7) - No exemption under any clause of sec. 10 except clauses (1) and (23C) if registration u/s 12A or 12AA in force

New sub-section (7), inserted with effect from 1-4-2015, applies to a trust or an institution which has been granted registration (under section 12AA or under section 12A) for purposes of availing exemption under section 11. In terms of new sub-section (7), where such registration is in force for a previous year, then such trust or institution shall not be entitled to any exemption under any provision of section 10 [other than that relating to exemption of agricultural income and income exempt under section 10(23C)].

The amendment overcomes the decision of the Tribunal in Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mum. - Trib.). In Jamsetji Tata Trust v. Jt. DIT (Exemption) [2014] 44 taxmann.com 447 (Mumbai - Trib.) the assessee claimed that dividend income on shares and unit and long term capital gain on sale of shares are exempt u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) respectively. The AO denied the exemption on the ground that section 11 exclusively deals with the income derived from the property held under trust and not u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38). Hence the AO held that there is a violation u/s 13 and as a result of the same exemption u/s 11 is denied. The assessee cannot claim the alternative claim for exemption u/s 10(34), 10(35) and 10(38) because these sections do not deal with income derived from the property held under the trust. On appeal, the CIT(A) concurred with AO’s view. On further appeal, however, ITAT ruled in favour of the assessee-trust and held that "the income which is exempt u/s 10 cannot be brought to tax by virtue of sections 11 and 13 of the Act because no such pre-condition is provided either u/s 10 or 11 to 13. Therefore, sections 11 to 13 would not operate as overriding effect to the section 10 of the Act. The language of these provisions does not suggest that either section 10 is subjected to the provisions of sections 11 to 13 or sections 11 to 13 has any overriding effect over section 10. Therefore, the benefit of section 10 cannot be denied by invoking the provisions of sections 11 to 13 of the Act. Once the conditions of section 10 are satisfied then no other condition can be fastened for denying the claim under section 10 of the Act".

Amendment to section 11 now overcomes the above judicial ruling.

ACCUMULATION OF INCOME

Calculation - For the purposes of sections 11(1)(a) and 11(1)(b), it has been held that the amount of accumulation (of 15%) is to be calculated on the total income (i.e., gross receipts) derived from such property and not on the amount remaining after application of income in India [CIT v. Programme for Community Organisation [2001] 116 Taxman 608 (SC)].

Deemed income - Deemed income (i.e., tax deducted at source) is not to be taken into account for determining the accumulation of income [CIT v. Jayashree Charity Trust [1986] 159 ITR 280 (Cal.)].

Where, due to non-investment of accumulated income in the prescribed securities in a year, such income is deemed to be the income of the trust for that year, the assessee will be entitled to accumulate prescribed percentage of the total income of that year, inclusive of such deemed income [CIT v. Natwarlal Chowdhury Charity Trust [1990] 52 Taxman 330 (Cal.)].

Investment/deposit in specified modes - The accumulated income which is exempt u/s 11(1)(a) need not be invested in Government securities. It is only in respect of any additional accumulated income beyond prescribed percentage that, if the assessee wants exemption of the additional accumulated income also, the assessee is required to invest the additional accumulated income in the manner laid down in section 11(2) after following the procedure laid down therein [S. RM. M. C. T. M. Tiruppani Trust v. CIT [1998] 96 Taxman 635 (SC)].

Investment must necessarily come out of the current year's income. An investment made in the past obviously cannot satisfy this requirement [CIT v. Indian National Theatre Trust [2008] 169 Taxman 42 (Delhi)].

Additional condition to apply to accumulations in excess of 15% - Additional condition by way of Explanation to section 11(2) inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2003 is intended to apply only to accumulations in excess of 15% u/s 11(2) and not to accumulations up to 15% u/s 11(1)(a) [DIT v. Bagri Foundation [2010] 192 Taxman 309 (Delhi)].

3.2 Restriction on exemption in case of corpus donation to other institutions [Section 11]

Income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes is exempt to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India and where any such income is accumulated or set apart for application to such purposes in India, the income so accumulated or set apart is also exempt to the extent it is not in excess of 15% of the income from such property [Section 11(1)(a)].

For the above purposes, it has been consistently held that donations by a charitable institution to another trust are application of income.

Generation of surplus out of gross receipts A doubt has been raised whether generation of surplus out of gross receipts would necessarily 'breach' the threshold condition that the educational institution should exist 'solely for educational purpose and not for the purpose of profit'. Perusal of prescribed provisions clearly reveal that mere generation of surplus cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) on the ground that it amounts to an activity of the nature of profit making. In fact, the third Proviso to the said clause clearly provides that accumulation of income is permissible subject to the manner prescribed therein provided such accumulation is to be applied "wholly and exclusively to the objects for which it is established". Hence, it is clarified that mere generation of surplus by educational institution from year to year cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) if it is used for educational purposes unless the accumulation is contrary to the manner prescribed under law.

4. Collection of amounts under different heads of fee from students—

It has been brought to the notice that collection of small amounts from students by way of application fee, examination fee, fee for issuing transfer certificate, subscription fee for library etc. is being treated by some Assessing Officers as profit making activity resulting in denial of exemption u/s 10(23C)(vi). Collection of small and reasonable amounts under different heads of fee, which are essentially in the nature of fee connected with imparting education and do not violate any Central or State regulation does not, in general, represent a profit making activity. Hence, there is no justification for treating the charging of small amounts under different heads of fee as profit making activity unless the amount in the nature of 'capitation fee' is charged directly or indirectly.

5. Impact of extraordinary powers of the Managing Trustees to appoint remove or nominate other trustees.

5.1 Doubt has been expressed whether extraordinary powers to the Managing Trustees to appoint or remove other trustees and also to nominate their successor affect the nature of charitable activity of the trust and whether in such an eventuality, exemption can be denied.

5.2 There is no provision under the Act which calls for denial of exemption merely on account of appointment or removal of trustees. Although answer to such a situation would normally depend on the factual implication of such arrangement, the same should generally not be a ground for denying exemption unless the nature of activities of the trust or institution get changed or modified or no longer remain to exist 'solely for educational purpose and not for purposes of profit'. Hence denial of exemption would not be justifiable only on the ground of induction of new trustees or removal of existing ones. - Circular No. 14/2015, dated 17-8-2015.
