Introduction

1. The recent decision of the CBEC to omit clause (v), which provided exemption from service tax for activities related to advancement of any other object of general public utility upto the prescribed monetary limits from the definition of 'charitable activity' from 1-4-2013 is an instance, which indicates CBEC's unfair treatment of charities, which enures to the welfare of the people of the country in terms of Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution of India ["the Constitution" for short].

The primary objective of any tax law and its administration is to raise revenue for funding Governmental expenditure, which, inter alia, is to be spent for the peoples' welfare. An important source of revenue to the Govt. is service tax. Article 38 in Chapter IV of the Constitution, titled Directive Principles of State Policy provides that the State shall, amongst others, provide that the State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice shall ensue to all institutions of social life. This directive of the Constitution is being fulfilled by direct expenditure as also by tax foregone in the form of exemptions and deductions in tax legislations, which cost to the Govt. some financial burden as cash expenditure.

This position is well recognized in most of the countries of the world. In this context, it may be appropriate to refer to the philosophy concerning concessions permissible for charitable contributions under the U.S. Internal Revenue Code. The House Ways and Means Committee, in one of its reports, has observed as under:—

"……The exemption from taxation of money or property devoted to charitable and other purposes is based upon the theory that the Government is compensated for the loss of revenue by its relief from financial burden, which would otherwise have to be met by appropriation from public funds and by the benefit resulting from the promotion of the general welfare".

2. Exemption of income of charitable bodies

2.1 Under the I.T. Act - The principle of giving tax benefits to charities and various objects of general public utility are well enshrined in the law relating to taxation of income. Section 2(15) of the I.T. Act, 1961 (Act) defines the term 'charitable purpose' (as amended) as under:—

"Charitable purpose includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, preservation of environment [including watersheds, forests and wildlife] and preservation of monuments or places or objects of artistic or historic interest and the advancement of any other object of general public utility".

To prevent the misuse of tax concessions for charities for business purposes, two provisos were added to this definition, which read as under:—

"Provided that the advancement of any other object of general public utility shall not be a charitable purpose, if it involves the carrying on of any activity in the nature of trade, commerce or business, or any activity of rendering any service in relation to any trade, commerce or business, for a cess or fee or any other consideration, irrespective of the nature of use or application or retention of the income from such activity:

Provided further that the first proviso shall not apply, if the aggregate value of the receipts from the activities referred to therein is twenty-five lakh rupees or less in the previous year."

Sections 11 and 10(23C) of the Act provide for exemption from tax of the incomes derived by charitable institutions on the fulfilment of the prescribed conditions.

For ensuring that undeserved institutions do not avail of tax benefits, the Act vide section 12A provides for registration of such institutions with the Chief Commissioners/Commissioners of Income-tax of the respective regions by making applications in the prescribed forms with relevant accounts and documents duly audited. Section 12AA prescribes the procedure for registration and lays down the time-limit within which the registration is to be granted. Sub-section (3) of section 12AA prescribes for cancellation of registration, if the activities of the Trust/Institution, which has been allowed registration, are found to be non-genuine or it is noticed that the activities of the institution are not being carried on in accordance with the objects of the trust/institution, as the case may be. Thus, I.T. Act has well-known law and procedure for giving tax benefits to charitable organizations, which are for the welfare and benefit of the people.

2.2 Under the Service Tax law - Regretfully, it is noticed that such important issue was being treated under the service tax legislation by the CBEC in a routine and arbitrary manner – not appreciating the spirit and purpose behind giving tax benefits to charitable institutions. In the pre 1-7-2013 period, the CBEC took a very narrow view regarding charitable activities, as could be seen from later discussion.

6. The service tax legislation does not contain any definition of what could be considered as charitable. However, the Income-tax law has a definition of this phrase. There is a judicial definition also. Its coverage has been comprehensively extended by the Courts (including the Apex Court) in a number of cases coming up before them, as can be seen from the discussion to follow.

In CIT v. Bar Council of Maharashtra [1981] 6 Taxman 1 (SC), it was held that purpose of State Bar Council is to ensure quality services of competent lawyers, to spread legal literacy, promote law reforms and provide legal assistance to poor. Such purpose is the advancement of the object of general public utility and it will be a charitable purpose. It was also held that a trust can carry on business for purpose of earning profit, to be utilised exclusively for charitable purposes. In Management of Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Chief Inspecting Officer AIR 2005 SC 1433, it was held that dominant purpose should be found out. If the dominant purpose is appearing as charity, then it will be admissible to benefit of a charity, even if other object ancillary or incidental to dominant purpose, is no charitable If charity is incidental purpose, it will not be ‘charitable purpose’ - relying on Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers’ Association [1979] 2 Taxman 501 (SC) - quoted with approval in CIT v. Gujarat Maritime Board [2008] 166 Taxman 58 (SC), American Hotel & Lodging Association Educational Institute v. CBDT [2008] 170 Taxman 306 (SC).

In Gujarat Maritime Board’s case (supra), it was held that Gujarat Maritime Board established for purpose of development of minor ports is ‘charitable purpose’ - relying on CIT v. Andhra Pradesh State Road Corporation [1986] 25 Taxman 63A (SC), where it was held that corporation established for providing efficient transport system having no profit motive, is not liable to Income-tax even if it earns income.

Earning surplus does not mean it is not charitable purpose - Mere earning surplus does not mean the activity is not for charitable purpose. In American Hotel & Lodging Association Educational Institute’s case (supra ) in respect of an educational institute, it was observed as follows, ‘In deciding the character of the recipient (charitable trust), it is not necessary to look at the profits of each year, but to consider the nature of activities undertaken. . . . If after meeting expenditure, surplus remains incidentally from the activity carried on by educational institution, it will not cease to be one existing solely for educational purpose. In other words, existence of surplus from the activity will not mean absence of educational purpose - relying on Aditanar Educational Institution v. Addl. CIT [1997] 90 Taxman 528 (SC).

RENT-A-CAB SERVICE

Should Parking Charges, Toll Charges and Driver Batta be included in the Gross amount for arriving at the service tax component in the case of Rent-a-Cab and Tourist Operator Services ?

Really no, but to be on safe side, in your agreement or terms and conditions, you should indicate ‘scope of service’ and say that other expenses are not part of the service. However, for administrative convenience, you will first pay and then recover on actual basis. This will make things a little more safe and you will fall within the definition of ‘pure agent’ in respect of those charges.

If a Rent-a-Cab operator takes a vehicle from some other Rent-a-Cab operator for few days/trips, is the latter liable to collect service tax from the former ?

Legally, he is also liable since as per section 65(105)(o ), any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a rent-a-cab scheme operator in relation to the renting of a cab is ‘taxable service’.

There is no law that if you make a mistake, you should continue with the mistake for rest of life and it can never be corrected.

If a Rent-a-Cab operator takes a vehicle from person, say X who is not Rent-a-Cab operator (X has purchased a vehicle out of his savings and loan and given the vehicle to a rent-a-cab operator for some revenues which are not related to the actual amounts earned by the vehicle). X is not engaged in travel business at all.

If control of vehicle is handed over, VAT is payable and not service tax. If control over vehicle is retained by X (e.g., his own driver), then it can come under ‘supply of tangible goods for use’ and service tax will be payable.

6. The service tax legislation does not contain any definition of what could be considered as charitable. However, the Income-tax law has a definition of this phrase. There is a judicial definition also. Its coverage has been comprehensively extended by the Courts (including the Apex Court) in a number of cases coming up before them, as can be seen from the discussion to follow.

Section 2(15) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 defines ‘charitable purpose’ as relief of the poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general ‘public utility’. Besides this statutory definition, the concept of charity has been widely accepted in judicial decisions in the context of conferring benefit of exemption from tax. Thus, relief of a public character to the poor is a charitable activity.

In India as well as in England, the object of ‘relief of the poor’ has always been recognized as a charitable purpose. Dealing with the scope of these words, the Supreme Court in Dharmadeepti v. CIT [1978] 114 ITR 454 observed that they include the expression ‘to give charity’ also. Thus, the object of giving charity falls within the ambit of the expression ‘relief of the poor’ used in section 2(15).

However, relief to the poor is only one facet of charitable purpose - not the primary one or the main one, as has been said in the CBEC’s circulars.

Providing education is another aspect of charitable activity for the public. In CIT v. Bar Council, Madras [1943] 11 ITR 1 (Mad.), the activity of giving facilities for legal education and training of the advocates has been held to be an educational purpose.

In Ecumenical Christian Centre v. CIT [1983] 139 ITR 226/[1982] 8 Taxman 175 (Kar.), the main objects of the assessee were diffusion of useful knowledge, publication of journal and books and promotion of search for truth. After referring to the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Lok Shikshana Trust, the Court held that the objects of diffusion of useful knowledge, publication of journals and promotion of search for truth are directly related to education. The High Court adopted a broader approach by accepting the principle that over and above normal schooling, other means of rendering scholastic instruction are also included in the definition of ‘education’ under section 2(15).

Similarly, providing medical relief has been considered to be covered under the definition of ‘charitable purpose’ under section 2(15) (supra) and accepted by the courts.

The residuary part of the definition has been held to be of very wide amplitude. One of the conditions precedent for a trust/institution to be for charitable purpose under section 2(15) is that the beneficiary thereof should be general public and that the object should not be such as resulting in private gains. The scope of the term ‘general public’ is by itself extremely wide but it is almost impossible for a particular charitable trust/institution to cover more than a section of the public. The application of the expression ‘Object of general public utility’ is not, therefore, restricted to such objects as are beneficial to the whole mankind. It is sufficient if the intention is to benefit a section of the public, provided it is well-defined and identifiable by some common quality of impersonal nature, as distinguished from specified individuals.

The classic elucidation of this phrase has been given by Lord, Macnaghten in Commr. for Special Purposes of Income-tax v. Remsel, 1891 AC 531 at 583 thus:—

"Where four principal divisions were said to be comprised-trusts for the relief of poverty, trusts for the advancement of education, trusts for the advancement of religion and trusts for other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the preceding heads. The definition in this Act makes the significant change when it speaks of ‘public utility’ and this gives a guidance to the whole meaning and purpose of the exemption [see Fazlul Rabbi Pradhan v. State of West Bengal AIR 1965 SC 1722]."

General public utility has been regarded as an important consideration in determining whether an activity is charitable or not. [This aspect has been included in describing activity of a charitable nature in the service tax law also section 65(25a)( supra). The courts’ interpretation of ‘charitable’ in the context of advancement of any other object of general public utility could be seen from some of the decisions mentioned hereinafter.

(a) Provision of employment [ see All India Spinners’ Association v. CIT [1944] 12 ITR 482 (PC), where the dominant object of providing employment is to provide means of earning adequate wages for the unemployed and the needy, the object of the activity would be charitable].

Sheth Jivandas Godidas Shankheshwar Parshwanathji Jain [2014] 41 taxmann.com 492/221 Taxman 44 (Mag.) (Guj.)]. (3) Assessee-society engaged in preparing and supplying mid-day meals to students at primary schools in various villages, as per child per month basis, the said activity being in nature of 'general public utility' [CIT v. Shri Balaji Samaj Vikas Samiti [2018] 91 taxmann.com 26/254 Taxman 93 (All.), affirmed inAsstt. CIT v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 143 taxmann.com 278 (SC)]. The law declared in the above Apex Court judgment had to be understood in context that they were applicable for assessment years in question, however, future applications had to be understood in context for assessment years which were not called upon and accordingly law declared in said judgment would be applicable, as per facts of each such assessment year [Asstt. CIT v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 144 taxmann.com 78/[2023] 290 Taxman 137 (SC)]. However, where assessee was implementing welfare schemes of various State Governments, i.e., supplying food to poor school children on funds earmarked and disbursed by State Government, implementation of such schemes would not lead to any charitable activity entitling registration [CIT v. Annadan Trust [2018] 96 taxmann.com 207/258 Taxman 54 (Ker.)].

(4) Where assessee was engaged in primary aim and objective to organise and arrange all licensed Third Party Administrators (TPAs) to be members of trust for mutual betterment of TPA business, merely because certain benefits accrued to TPA members and certain objects of trust were for advancement of business of TPA, it would not ipso facto render trust to be non-charitable [CIT v. Association of Third Party Administrators [2020] 114 taxmann.com 534/269 Taxman 579 (Delhi)].

(5) Statutory Corporations, Boards, Authorities, Commissions, etc. (by whatsoever names called) in housing development, town planning, industrial development sectors are involved in advancement of objects of general public utility, therefore, are entitled to be considered as charities in GPU categories [Asstt. CIT v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 143 taxmann.com 278 (SC)]. The law declared in the above Apex Court judgment had to be understood in context that they were applicable for assessment years in question, however, future applications had to be understood in context for assessment years which were not called upon and accordingly law declared in said judgment would be applicable, as per facts of each such assessment year [Asstt. CIT v. Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority [2022] 144 taxmann.com 78/[2023] 290 Taxman 137 (SC)].

No change has been made in Item No.4 of the Notification, where exemption under service tax continues to be available to entities registered u/s 12AA of the I.T. Prima facie, there seems to be no ground to confine the exemption benefits to only : (i) to (iv) situations in the definition of charitable activity and close the door for other activities covered by the general clause under S.No.(v) (supra). It cannot be an arbitrary decision and there must be some reasons behind it, but unfortunately nothing has been stated for the snap decision taken to withdraw clause (v) only after less than one year of the Notification, dated 20-6-2012.

The omnibus clause in the definition of charitable purpose under the I.T. Act namely any other object of general public utility has been held to be a solid object for grant of tax exemptions under the I.T. Act. This is clear from the following discussion. :

(a)

Aspects of general public utility have been considered as charitable since long under the English law. The Statute of Elizabeth as per its preamble enumerated the following purposes as charitable:—

"The relief of aged, impotent and poor people; the maintenance of sick and mined soldiers and mariners; the maintenance of schools of learning, free schools and scholars in universities; the repair of bridges, ports, havens, causeways, churches, sea-banks and highways; the education and preferment of orphans; the relief, stock or maintenance of houses of corrections; the marriage of poor maids; the supportation, aid and help of young tradesman, handicraftsmen, and person decayed; the relief or redemption of prisoners or captives; the aid or ease of any poor inhabitants concerning payment of taxes; the setting out of soldiers."

(b)

Though the statute was repeated by the Mortmain and Charitable Uses Act, 1888 the preamble to the statute (supra) was retained in section 13(2) of the repealing Act!

(c)

The concept of charity developed in the Mortmain and Charitable Uses Act, 1888 (C.42) S. 13(2) under the four principle heads as defined or classified has been explained by Lord Macnaghten in the classic case of Commissioners for Special Purposes of Income-tax v. Pemsel [1891] AC 531, for the majority.

The dictum of Lord Macnaghten was as follows:

"Charity" in its legal sense comprises four principal divisions: trusts for the relief of poverty, trusts for the advancement of education, trusts for the advancement of religion, and trusts for other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the preceding heads. The trusts last referred to are not the less charitable in the eye of the law because incidentally they benefit the rich as well as the poor, as indeed every charity that deserves the name must do, either directly or indirectly.

Apparently, denying the exemption to the bodies that are engaged in advancing the objects of general public utility, other than those mentioned in clauses (i) to (iv) in the definition of 'charitable activity', which are no less charitable, because the same fall under the residuary head.

As per section 65(64) of the Finance Act, 1994 (as amended w.e.f. 16-6-2005 and by the Finance Act, 2006 w.e.f. 1-5-2006), "management, maintenance or repair" means any service provided by—(i) any person under a contract or an agreement; or (ii) a manufacturer or any person authorised by him, in relation to, (a) management of properties, whether immovable or not (b) maintenance or repair of properties whether immovable or not; or (c) maintenance or repair including reconditioning or restoration, or servicing of any goods or equipment, excluding motor vehicle.

In many cases, housing societies collect the charges from members which are termed as ‘maintenance’ charges. Hence, it is alleged that the housing society provides management, maintenance or repair.

As discussed above, the activities undertaken by housing society are a bundle of various activities, some of which might fall under ‘management, maintenance or repair’ services. However, a service can be taxed if it is predominantly a taxable service. In Daelim Industrial Co. v. CCE 2003 STT 438 = 155 ELT 457 = 57 RLT 636 = 3 STR 124 (CEGAT), it was held that a works contract on turnkey basis is not a consultancy contract. A works contract cannot be vivisected and part of it subjected to tax (SLP filed by department dismissed by SC - [2004] 170 ELT A181). This was followed in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE [2005] 1 STT 183 = 2004 (174) ELT 322 = 60 RLT 505 = 3 STR 223 (CESTAT), in respect of design element of works contract.

The principle that a contract cannot be vivisected is applicable to all services.

D.O. letter No. 334/4/2006-TRU, dated 28-2-2006 states as follows, ‘Often services provided consist of more than one service. In such cases, it is important to decide, for the purpose of classification of services, whether each element of the transaction should be treated separately or as a single composite transaction, albeit, made up of two or more separate services. A composite service, even if it consists of more than one service, should be treated as a single service based on the main or principal service and accordingly classified. The decision is to be made on question of facts and law. It will not make a difference if the tax rates of the components are the same as that of the principal service. The problem may arise when some elements are taxable and others are exempt. While taking a view, both the form and substance of the transaction are to be taken into account. The guiding principle is to identify the essential features of the transaction. The method of charging does not in itself determine whether the service provided is a single service or multiple services’.

Thus, a service can be taxed only if it is predominantly a taxable service.

The so called ‘service’ provided by housing society is not predominantly a ‘management, maintenance or repair’ service.

Hence, in my view, the service of housing society cannot be classified under that head.

1. By the Finance Act, 2005 with effect from June 16, 2005, the services provided or to be provided by any club or association to its members were made taxable. The definition of ‘club and association’ is provided in section 65(25a) of the Finance Act, 1994 which is as under :—

"(25a) ‘Club or association’ means any person or body of persons providing services, facilities or advantages, for a subscription or any other amount, to its members, but does not include—

(i)any body established or constituted by or under any law for the time being in force; or

(ii)any person or body of persons engaged in the activities of trade unions, promotion of agriculture, horticulture or animal husbandry; or

(iii)any person or body of persons engaged in any activity having objectives which are in the nature of public service and are of a charitable, religious or political nature; or

(iv)any person or body of persons associated with press or media."

Thus, any person or body of persons engaged in any activity having objectives, which are in the nature of public service and are of charitable, religious or political nature are excluded from the definition of the club or association. It is the general conception that all the clubs or associations, which are registered under the Income-tax Act, 1961 are exempt from the service tax also.

They collect membership fees and other charges from their members and they work for the interest of trade and industries. Therefore, they do not have objectives, which could be categorized as public service. Accordingly, they do not fall within the scope of the excluded categories."

In one part of the circular, it has been said that such bodies ".....work for the interest of trade and industries" and in the same continuation, it is said that "they do not have objectives, which could be categorized as public service. ..."

It is contradiction to say that, though such bodies work for the interest of trade and industries, yet their activities cannot be categorized as public service.

It is unfortunate that CBEC wants to stick to the view, which it itself is not able to support and insistence with the same would lead to considerable proliferation of litigation.

11.3 The CBEC, in its enthusiasm to continue with untenable legal view, has arbitrarily rejected the concept of ‘charitable’ as adopted in the Income-tax legislation saying that it is not in accordance with the rules of interpretation formulated by the Courts. When there is no definition in the service tax legislation concerning charitable institution, interpretation of a provision with reference to provisions of another enactment is permissible when the two Acts are in pari materia - (Board of Muslim Waqfs v. Radha Krishna AIR 1979 SC 289, and Sanjiv V. Kudva v. CIT [1981] 127 ITR 354 (Kar.) and also Balchandra Anantrao Rakvi v. Ramchandra Tukaram [2001] 8 SCC 616). Thus, in the absence of a statutory definition, it would be open to look for the meaning of the word ‘charitable’ by reference to definitions in the sister legislation and failing that, to adopt the meaning in common parlance. Statutes are considered to be in pari materia to pertain to the same subject-matter, when they relate to the same person or thing, or to the same class of persons or things, or have the same purpose or object. Obviously, law relating to levy of Income-tax and service tax are in pari materia and, hence, definition of ‘charitable purpose’ given in the Income-tax Act will be relevant for the purposes of service tax also. Further, scheme of the two enactments also shows that the provisions of the two enactments are almost on similar lines.

Observing that "exemption under the Income-tax Act on the ground of being a public charitable institution is of no consequence or relevance for service tax purposes" only indicates an adamant view in interpretation of statutes, discarding the well laid down principles formulated by the Courts.

11.4 CII is engaged, inter alia, in the advancement of objects of general public utilities and it cannot be denied the status of a public charitable institution. The view of the CBEC is against the assurance given by the Hon’ble F.M. in regard to advancement of any other object of general public utility in the context of amendment to the Income-tax Act, as could be seen from the later discussion.

Introduction

Under the Indian trust law, a trust is an obligation of the Trustee to take care of the assets for the benefit of the Beneficiaries. As the name suggests, it is an agreement of faith/ trust which the Settlor rests in the Trustee for the benefit of the Beneficiary.

In general parlance and also under some laws in India, a trust is referred to as a person. It is accepted that each law has its own purpose and treatment under one law may not apply for another law. Therefore, a trust may be considered as an agreement under trust law and a person under another law.

For Indian tax purposes, a trust is not considered as an entity. Under the tax laws, a trustee is taxed as a representative assessee.

Trust under Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA)

Under FEMA, trust is not specifically defined anywhere. A trust is seen as merely a conduit pipe or a vehicle by means of which a donor passes on the interest, which the Donor had in the trust property, in favor of the Beneficiary.

Definition of Person under FEMA

Section 2(u) of FEMA, 1999 defines a "person" as below,

"person" includes—

(i)

an individual,

(ii)

a Hindu undivided family,

(iii)

a company,

(iv)

a firm,

(v)

an association of persons or a body of individuals, whether incorporated or not,

(vi)

every artificial juridical person, not falling within any of the preceding sub-clauses, and

(vii)

any agency, office or branch owned or controlled by such person;

The above definition is on the lines of Income Tax law. It includes several persons including agency, office and branch of a person. However, a trust is not considered as a person.

Association of Persons and Body of Individuals under FEMA

Association of Persons (AOP) or Body of Individuals (BOI) has not been defined under FEMA or Income Tax. These terms take their meaning from the law in which these are referred to. Under the Income Tax, person includes an AOP and BOI. AOP requires a voluntary coming together of people to carry out some activities jointly. A BOI is a body of individuals, and it is similar but not the same as AOP.

If individuals happen to be together with a common purpose such as to trade in investments or manage assets jointly, it will be considered as BOI.

Simply holding investments and receiving income for the joint benefit of the Beneficiaries is not enough to classify the group as a BOI, even if the Trustee manages the business for their collective benefit. Therefore, a trust may not be recognized as a BOI.

In practice, for some purposes, trust is considered as a person. If there is no definition, one will have to consider the facts and situation and then determine the residential status of a trust.

Provisions under Trust Act

Under the trust law, a Trustee is regarded as the legal owner. The Trustee functions in two roles: personally and as a Trustee. In their personal capacity, their transactions and status are separate from their role as a Trustee. In their Trustee role, they act in a fiduciary capacity toward the Beneficiaries, serving as a custodian and manager of the trust's funds. Since the Beneficiaries hold the beneficial interests, the Trustee's status is not relevant when determining the residential status of the trust.

Also, the location of Settlor is not relevant as once he settles the trust, his role is over. As far as Beneficiaries are concerned, they could be located in different countries, and they do not play a role in management of the trust. Hence prima facie, their status cannot be considered to determine the residential status of the trust.

If a trust is formed in India with an Indian address, quite likely it is an Indian trust. However, if the management of the trust is in a different country compared to the country of governing law, it will be unfair to consider only the governing law.

The place of effective management can be considered to determine residential status. The place where Trustees manage the trust may be considered to determine the residential status of the trust.

When the assets are parked in a Trust by the Settlor, for ultimate transfer/distribution of such assets to the Beneficiaries, such transfer/distribution is considered as gift of assets from Settlor to the Beneficiaries.

Hence, it can be understood that if an Indian resident wants to set up an Indian trust with Indian trustees and non-resident beneficiaries, it should be considered as Indian resident giving a gift to a non-resident and the FEMA rules will apply accordingly.

4. Taxable Service

4.1 Sub-clause (zzg) of clause (105) defines the taxable service as :

"‘Taxable service’ means any service provided or to be provided, to a customer, by any person in relation to management, maintenance or repair".

4.2 In order for the service to be a taxable service it has to be provided/to be provided to a customer. The term ‘customer’ in the present context means a person who seeks the services of the specified service provider. There need not be regular/frequent service transactions with the service provider.

4.3 Secondly, the service can be provided by any person. 4.4 Thirdly, the service has to be ‘in relation to’ to management, maintenance or repair. The use of the term ‘in relation to’ widens the scope of the term ‘taxable service’ and any service having either direct or indirect connection with specified services, i.e., maintenance, repair, reconditioning, etc., will be a taxable service.

CBEC’s interpretation of the word ‘charitable’ used in the context of service tax concerning Clubs and Associations ( supra) [Para 2]

7. The meaning of the term ‘charitable’ has been explained by the CBEC in its Master Circular No. 96/7/2007 ST, dated 23-8-2007 vide reference No. 076.01 thus : CBEC’s circular, it needs to be said with respect that, when it adheres to the dictionary meaning of the word ‘charitable’ and discards the interpretation of this term given under the Income-tax Act, 1961, which is in pari materia with the service tax legislation, it has deviated from the accepted rule of interpretation as stated earlier and has made the interpretation of the term narrow and of self-serving nature contrary to judicial thinking on this subject. The non-application of the rule of interpretation on pari materia principle in interpreting the word ‘charitable’ in the service tax legislation in a narrow and different manner from the definition given in the Income-tax Act and interpretation given to this word by the Courts, is likely to create friction in the administration of law concerning two legislations which are in pari materia.

Viewed from the angle of administration of fiscal laws, different limbs of the same Ministry (here even the same department, Department of Revenue) in the Government working under the same Minister cannot pull in different directions. If done, that would apparently appear to be contrary to collective functioning of the Department of Revenue. Hence, from this angle also the discard of income definition seems inappropriate.

Income-tax definition

8. Section 2(15 ) of the Income-tax Act defines ‘charitable purpose’ in an inclusive manner to include relief of the poor, education, medical relief, preservation of environment (including watersheds, forest and wildlife) and preservation of monuments or places or objects of artistic or historical interest and the advancement of any other object of general public utility. This is a comprehensive definition and if a club or association is engaged in rendering services for such laudable activities, there seems to be no ground for denying exemption and sticking to the narrow dictionary definition encompassing narrow fields given in the circular extracted earlier. The CBEC has to move with the advancing time and not get bogged down and limit the benefit of exemption to few areas only saying that exemption under the Income-tax Act on the ground of being a public charitable institution is of no consequence or relevance for service tax purposes. The issue is that when the Income-tax Department can be progressive in the matter of interpretation of charitable purpose, there seems to be no reason why a sister department should lag behind.

Summing up

9. The definitions of ‘charity’ and ‘charitable’ given in the CBEC Circular dated August 23, 2007 extracted earlier show an archaic approach not in tune with the ongoing advancement and need to be reviewed and amended.

Rotary Club/Lions Club are international organisa-tions spread out throughout the world, inter alia, in India.

Traditionally the above clubs are engaged in rendering social service which is in the interest and welfare of public. The following are the normal services undertaken by Rotary Club/Lions Club.

uMedical camps in connection with the normal human disorders.

uBlood donation camps

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Franchise service - Courier agency

5.10 Assessee was a courier agency with a wide network of above 45 hubs located at various stations in South India. Its agents were centered around these hubs and they collected and delivered time-sensitive letters/articles to consignees. With aid of this network, assessee acted as a courier agent and transported articles between hubs. Revenue demanded service tax from assessee in category of ‘Franchise service’ and also imposed penalty. It was found that under a standard agreement entered into with each appointed agent, the assessee and each courier agent attached to the hubs had a relation as between principal and agent. Assessee controlled and administered their activities. Those agents were not conferred with any representational right by assessee. They were entitled to use name of assessee only as an ‘authorised agent’. Registration certificates issued to those agents carried endorsement that they were agents of assessee; that they returned courier charges received from clients to assessee, while retaining their expenses and remuneration and there was no payment of fee to assessee as required by section 65(47 ).

The Tribunal held that from 16-6-2005, the franchise service involves provision of a service associated with a particular person by trade mark, service mark, trade name or logo. The registration certificates issued to the agents carried the endorsement that they were agents of the assessee. The so-called franchisees being agents who undertook the work of courier agency on behalf of the assessee, it could not be held that any other service was involved in the transactions or that there was a different person receiving the service. It was further submitted that the agents were not doing business on their own account; that they were required to use consignment notes and stationery of the assessee, with the consignment notes bearing the name of the assessee; that no fee was paid by the agents and they only made a deposit with the assessee called trade deposits; that the agents paid service tax on the charges they collected from their clients, and returned the balance after retaining their expenses and remuneration; that the assessee did not impart any skill, technical know-how or managerial expertise to the agents; and, thus, there was no service rendered by the assessee to its agents to be taxed under the category ‘Franchise service’. "Franchise means an agreement by which the franchisee is granted representational right to sell or manufacture goods or to provide service or undertake any process identified with franchisor, whether or not a trade mark, service mark, trade name or logo or any such symbol as the case may be, is involved." On the basis of facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal held that it could be said that assessee undertook only courier agency’s service, engaging several agents who did not operate as ‘principals’ and, therefore, neither those agents were franchisees nor assessee, a franchisor. Accordingly, the Tribunal set aside the impugned order and allowed the appeal filed by the assessee.

[Franch Express Network (P.) Ltd. v. CST [2008] 16 STT 10 (Chennai - CESTAT)]

23. Agricultural land can't be taken out of the purview of Section 56(2)(x) as the term 'immovable property' isn't defined: ITAT

Clayking Minerals LLP v. Income-tax Officer [2025] 174 taxmann.com 1111 (Ahmedabad - Trib.)

The assessee filed the income tax return, declaring a loss for the relevant assessment year. The case was selected for 'Limited Scrutiny' to examine whether the purchase value of a property was less than the value determined by the stamp valuation authority under section 56(2)(x).

During the proceedings, the assessee contended that the property was agricultural land at the time of purchase, and it did not qualify as a "capital asset" as per section 2(14). Therefore, section 56(2)(x) was not applicable.

However, the Assessing Officer (AO) held that the provisions of section 56(2)(x) were attracted, and the difference between the purchase consideration and the stamp duty value was liable to be taxed as "income from other sources".

On appeal, the CIT(A) upheld the order of the AO. Aggrieved-assessee filed the instant appeal before the Tribunal.

The Tribunal held that section 56(2)(x) mentions the term "any immovable property". Now the issue for consideration is whether "Agricultural land" falls within the ambit of an "immovable property" as stated in section 56(2)(x). The term "immovable property" has not been defined in section 56(2)(x) or in any other section in the Income Tax Act. This renders the word to be interpreted in general parlance.

In general, the term "Immovable Property" means an asset that cannot be moved without destroying or altering it. Therefore, going by the general definition, "immovable property" would, in the view of the Tribunal, include any rural agricultural land, in the absence of any specific exclusion in section 56(2)(x).

Notably, section 56(2)(x) does not use the word "capital asset". The sale of rural agricultural land is exempt from the seller's hands since the word "capital asset" has been specifically defined to exclude agricultural land in rural areas under section 2, clause 14. Thus, the sale of rural agricultural land shall not give rise to any capital gains in the hands of the seller, as it is not considered a capital asset itself.

However, from the point of view of the "purchaser" of immovable property, section 56(2)(x) mentions "any immovable property" which, going by the plain words of the Statute, does not specifically exclude "agricultural land". Therefore, going by the plain words of section 56(2)(x), which uses the term "immovable property", agricultural land cannot be taken out of the purview of section 56(2)(x).

11. As per section 65(25a ),definition of "club or association" does not include— (iii) any person or body of persons engaged in any activity having objectives which are in the nature of public service and are of a charitable, religious or political nature.

‘Charitable’ means ‘generous in giving to those in need’ or ‘of, or relating to, or connected with a charity or charities’. ‘Charity’ means giving voluntarily to those in need, alms-giving’ – Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Thus, the word ‘charity’ has narrow meaning in dictionary. However, the word has acquired a technical meaning in law, which is wide.

As per section 2 of Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief to poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general public utility, but does not include a purpose which relates exclusively to religious teaching or worship. As per section 2(15) of Income-tax Act, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, and the advancement of any other object of general public utility.

Thus, any object of ‘general public utility’ will be a ‘charitable purpose’. Hence, the wide meaning should apply and not narrow dictionary meaning. However, department is of the view that narrow meaning should apply – CBE&C, vide Circular No. 84/2/2006-ST dated 19-9-2006.

12. Non-statutory services provided by practising CA/CWA/CS were exempt upto 28-2-2006, unless they were falling in some other head of taxable service. This exemption was completely withdrawn w.e.f. 1-3-2006, but partially restored w.e.f. 13-7-2006, as discussed below.

Position of taxability of service since 13-7-2006 – After 13-7-2006, services provided by practising CA/CWA/CS in his professional capacity to a client, relating to representing before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice, are exempt from service tax. All other services provided by practising CA/CWA/CS in his professional capacity are taxable (Notification No. 25/2006-ST dated 13-7-2006).

Thus, following services will not be taxable – (a) Appearing before revenue authorities (income tax, customs, sales tax, excise, service tax etc.) where notice has been issued to client (b) Appearing before Tribunal (like CESTAT, ITAT) where demand of duty/tax was issued to client and/or penalty was imposed (c) Appearance before authorities like SEBI, ROC, RBI, DGFT etc. where notice has been issued to client.

Following services are not exempt even after 12-7-2006, and service tax will be payable – (a) Advice/consultation on legal and taxation matters and giving legal opinions (b) Services like preparing and submitting of returns to tax authorities, ROC, RBI etc., (c ) Services of drafting of documents like agreement, partnership deeds, memorandum, articles of association, (d) Appearance before revenue authorities in respect of issues relating to refund claims (since proceedings are not initiated by issue of notice) (e ) Representations before authorities where no notice has been issued (f) Appearing before SEBI, ROC, CLB, RBI, revenue authorities etc. where any application for permission/ authorisation/approval has been made by client (since proceedings are not initiated by issue of notice) (g) Non-statutory and statutory certification (h) Audit work (i) Inspection of documents, search of titles (j) Accounts writing.

Position during 1-3-2006 to 12-7-2006 - Service tax was payable on all services provided by practising CA/CWA/CS in his professional capacity.

Religious place (temple) as a mandap

10. We are a religious trust having a big temple and this temple has a big open ground, which we are giving regularly for organizing marriages and marriage receptions and also for other functions. We have received a notice from the Central Excise office of our city to get register under the ‘Mandap keeper service’ and pay service tax. Please advice us.

Service tax is not leviable if service provided to any person for the use of precincts of a religious place as Mandap. This has been provided in Notification No. 14/2003 - ST, dated June 20, 2003. As per this Notification the religious place means a place, which is meant for conduct of prayers or worship pertaining to a religion.

Since the service in the form of Mandap is being provided for the use of precincts of a temple or other religious place, no service tax is payable.

Club as mandap keeper

11. Our club has a big hall and certain other facilities, which we give our members to organize functions, which include marriages of their family members, and certain other functions related to them. The facilities are not hired to persons other than our own members. Till now the club was not charging from our members but now due to financial crises it has been decided that by our Managing Committee that the club will charge Rs. 25,000 for each of such function from the members using the above facility. One of the members of the committee has expressed that we will be covered under mandap keeper service. Please explain.

No, your club is not liable to pay service tax. Though it is right that it comes within the meaning of mandap keeper but the services provided or to be provided to the client are only liable to service tax and in case of your club there is no client and your club is providing the services only to its members and the club is not a distinct entity from its members and in absence of any service provider - client relationship, no service tax is payable. In this respect please refer the Calcutta High Court decision in the case of Dalhousie Institute v. Assistant Commissioner 2005 (180) ELT 18 (Cal.).

1. Tax on Management Consultant’s Services was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998. The Finance Act, 2006, w.e.f. 1-5-2006 had specified the area of consultancy. For the words "relating to conceptualising, devising, development, modification, rectification or upgradation of any working system of any organisation", the words "in relation to financial management, human resources management, marketing management, production management, logistics management, procurement and management of information technology resources or other similar areas of management" had been substituted. So, the scope of this service is made more specific in relation to certain services, which were previously undefined. The Finance Act, 2007 renamed this service as management or business consultant’s service and to explicitly include business consultancy in the definition itself.

In the clarification contained in the CBEC Circular, dated 27-6-2001, it was stated that term ‘management’ is generally understood to mean running the affairs of an organization in an organized and systematic manner. To be able to do this efficiently and effectively, management typically involves carrying out a host of activities, functions and tasks at different levels. Thus, the term ‘management’ encompasses both strategic and operational level functioning and would include tasks such as planning, organizing, staffing, directing, controlling and co-ordinating. Management also invariably involves designing organizational structure around functions such as marketing, manufacturing, research and development and finance and/or business area, such as product groups or geographical markets. Thus, management of any organization involves carrying out a wide variety of clearly defined activities across a number of organizational sub-units in a coherent and co-ordinated manner. Since the expression ‘management’ is an inclusive term, ‘management consultant’ would also be equally encompassing expression and would include any adviser, who renders services on any aspect of management.
